After the injection experiment, hypothalamus tissue was collected from fish in each group, and the mRNA expression levels of *npy* and *pomc* were detected by qRT-PCR. The primer sequences are shown in Table 1 (omitted).

 2.6 Statistical Analysis

Experimental data are expressed as mean ± standard error (Mean±SEM). One-way ANOVA was performed using SPSS 22.0 software, and Duncan's multiple comparison test was used to examine differences between groups, with *P*<0.05 considered a significant difference.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Cloning and Sequence Analysis of the Spotted Scat *pnx* Gene

The cDNA sequence of spotted scat *pnx* was successfully cloned, with an open reading frame of 240 bp encoding a 79-amino-acid precursor protein. Sequence alignment analysis showed that the spotted scat PNX precursor protein had similarities of 89.2%, 82.3%, and 78.5% with large yellow croaker, zebrafish, and tilapia, respectively, indicating that this gene is highly conserved in evolution. The precursor protein contains a typical signal peptide sequence (amino acids 1–24) and a conserved PNX mature peptide core sequence.

 3.2 Tissue Expression Characteristics of the *pnx* Gene

qRT-PCR results showed that *pnx* mRNA was expressed in all tissues of the spotted scat, but the expression levels differed significantly. Among them, the hypothalamus had the highest expression, followed by the pituitary and telencephalon; among peripheral tissues, the intestine and liver had relatively higher expression, while muscle and heart had the lowest expression (Figure 1, omitted). This expression pattern suggests that PNX may mainly function as a neuropeptide in the central nervous system, while also having potential functions in peripheral tissues.

 3.3 Effects of PNX on Feeding Behavior

Acute injection experiment results showed that within 0–2 h after PNX injection, the food intake of all dose groups was significantly lower than that of the control group (*P*<0.05), and the inhibitory effect was dose-dependent. The food intake of the high-dose group (100 ng/g) was only 52.3% of the control group, while those of the medium-dose and low-dose groups were 68.7% and 81.5%, respectively. At 2–6 h after injection, the differences in food intake among groups gradually narrowed, and by 24 h, there was no significant difference in cumulative food intake among groups (*P*>0.05), indicating that the inhibitory effect of PNX on feeding is mainly manifested in the short-term acute regulation phase.

 3.4 Effects of PNX on Growth Performance

After 14 d of continuous injection, the final body weight, weight gain rate (WGR), and specific growth rate (SGR) of spotted scat in the high-dose group were all significantly lower than those of the control group (*P*<0.05). The WGR of the high-dose group was (18.6±2.1)%, significantly lower than the (32.4±2.8)% of the control group; SGR decreased from (1.98±0.12)%/d in the control group to (1.23±0.15)%/d. The feed conversion ratio (FCR) in the high-dose group was 1.86±0.11, significantly higher than the 1.42±0.09 of the control group (*P*<0.05), indicating that PNX reduced feed utilization efficiency. There were no significant differences in growth indicators between the low-dose group and the control group (*P*>0.05).

 3.5 Changes in Hypothalamic Feeding-Related Gene Expression

The hypothalamic *npy* mRNA expression level in the high-dose PNX injection group was significantly downregulated compared with the control group (*P*<0.05), with a decrease of approximately 42%; while the *pomc* mRNA expression level was significantly upregulated (*P*<0.05), approximately 1.8 times that of the control group. The medium-dose group showed a similar trend but with a smaller magnitude of change, and the low-dose group showed no significant difference from the control group. This indicates that PNX may exert its feeding-suppressing effect by inhibiting the expression of the orexigenic factor NPY and promoting the expression of the anorexigenic factor POMC.

 4 Discussion

This study is the first to clone and identify the *pnx* gene in the spotted scat and systematically investigate its regulatory effects on feeding and growth. Tissue expression analysis showed that *pnx* mRNA is highly expressed in the hypothalamus, consistent with research results in mammals. Yosten et al. reported that PNX is mainly distributed in the arcuate nucleus and paraventricular nucleus regions of the rat hypothalamus, which are key centers for feeding regulation. The high expression of spotted scat *pnx* in the hypothalamus and pituitary suggests that it may have neuroendocrine regulatory functions.

Feeding experiment results showed that exogenous PNX can significantly inhibit short-term food intake in the spotted scat in a dose-dependent manner. This result is highly consistent with findings in mammals. At the mechanistic level, the anorexigenic effect of PNX may be mediated through the hypothalamic feeding regulation network. This study observed that after PNX injection, hypothalamic *npy* expression was downregulated and *pomc* expression was upregulated, suggesting that PNX may inhibit feeding by suppressing NPY/AgRP neuronal activity and activating the POMC/CART neuronal pathway. NPY is one of the strongest known orexigenic neuropeptides, while POMC is processed to produce α-MSH, which exerts an anorexigenic effect by activating the melanocortin 4 receptor (MC4R). PNX may influence feeding behavior by regulating the balance between these two pathways.

Long-term injection experiments further confirmed that sustained high levels of PNX not only inhibit feeding but also significantly reduce growth performance and feed conversion efficiency. This effect may result from insufficient energy intake due to reduced food intake, and may also involve direct or indirect regulation of the growth axis (GH/IGF-I) by PNX. Notably, PNX has been confirmed to promote GnRH secretion in mammals, suggesting that it may affect the secretion of growth-related hormones through the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. However, no significant growth inhibition was observed in the low-dose group in this study, indicating that the effects of PNX are dose-dependent, and PNX at physiological concentrations may mainly exert short-term feeding regulation functions rather than long-term growth inhibition.

This study also has certain limitations: first, peripheral blood PNX levels and changes in PNX expression in the gastrointestinal tract were not measured, so its peripheral regulatory role could not be comprehensively evaluated; second, the PNX receptor has not yet been identified in fish, and its signal transduction mechanism awaits further elucidation; in addition, the experimental period was relatively short, and the potential effects of PNX on gonadal development and long-term growth require further study.

 5 Conclusion

This study cloned the *pnx* gene of the spotted scat and revealed its tissue-specific expression pattern with high expression in the hypothalamus and pituitary. In vivo injection experiments confirmed that PNX can significantly inhibit short-term food intake in the spotted scat and exert an anorexigenic effect by downregulating hypothalamic *npy* and upregulating *pomc* gene expression. Long-term high-dose PNX treatment can reduce the weight gain rate, specific growth rate, and feed conversion efficiency. This study is the first to confirm that PNX participates in feeding and growth regulation in teleost fish, enriching the molecular theory of appetite regulation in fish and providing a potential target for precision nutritional management in spotted scat aquaculture.

title: Inactivation of Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus by power ultrasound during the curing processing in brining liquid and beef
text:
Inactivation Effect of Ultrasound Technology on Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus During Beef Curing

Abstract: To investigate the inactivation effect of power ultrasound on foodborne pathogens during beef curing, this study used Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus as target strains and applied ultrasound treatment at different power levels and durations in curing solution and beef matrix, respectively. The results showed that ultrasound treatment had a significant inactivation effect on both pathogens, and the inactivation rate increased with increasing ultrasound power and treatment time. In the curing solution, the inactivation effect of ultrasound treatment on Escherichia coli O157:H7 was superior to that on Bacillus cereus; in the beef matrix, the inactivation rates of both bacteria decreased, but a satisfactory bactericidal effect could still be achieved by extending the treatment time. Ultrasound treatment had no significant adverse effects on the color, texture, or water-holding capacity of beef. This study demonstrates that power ultrasound can be applied as an effective auxiliary means for microbial control during beef curing.

Keywords: power ultrasound; beef curing; Escherichia coli O157:H7; Bacillus cereus; inactivation

1 Introduction

Beef curing is an important step in meat product processing, as it can improve flavor and texture while also inhibiting microbial growth to a certain extent. However, traditional curing processes mainly rely on the antimicrobial effects of salt and nitrite, which have limited killing efficacy against certain salt-tolerant or psychrophilic pathogens. Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus are common foodborne pathogens in beef and beef products. The former can cause severe hemorrhagic diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome, while the latter may lead to food poisoning symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea. Therefore, how to effectively control these pathogens during the curing process has become an urgent problem to be solved in the field of meat processing.

Power ultrasound, as a non-thermal sterilization technology, has received widespread attention in food processing in recent years. The cavitation effect, mechanical effect, and thermal effect generated when ultrasound propagates in liquids can disrupt microbial cell walls and cell membranes, leading to leakage of cellular contents and cell death. Compared with thermal treatment, ultrasound treatment has advantages such as lower temperature, lower energy consumption, and less impact on food quality. At present, ultrasound technology has been studied in fruit and vegetable washing, dairy sterilization, and meat tenderization, but research on its application for sterilization during beef curing is still insufficient. This study aims to investigate the inactivation effect of power ultrasound on Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus in curing solution and beef matrix, providing a theoretical basis for the practical application of ultrasound technology in meat curing.

2 Key Technology Analysis

2.1 Setting of Ultrasound Treatment Parameters

The inactivation effect of ultrasound is influenced by multiple factors such as frequency, power, treatment time, and temperature. In this study, the ultrasound frequency was fixed at 20 kHz, with power levels set at 200 W, 400 W, and 600 W, and treatment times of 5 min, 10 min, and 15 min, respectively. The curing solution temperature was controlled at two levels, 4°C and 20°C, through a circulating water bath to simulate refrigerated curing and room-temperature curing conditions in actual production. The results showed that higher power and longer time resulted in more significant inactivation effects. Under the condition of 600 W and 15 min, the inactivation rate of Escherichia coli O157:H7 in the curing solution reached 5.2 log CFU/mL, and that of Bacillus cereus was 4.1 log CFU/mL. Temperature also had a certain effect on the inactivation effect, with the inactivation rate at 20°C slightly higher than at 4°C, but the difference was not significant (P>0.05).

2.2 Inactivation Effect in Curing Solution

In the curing solution, there was a significant difference in the inactivation effect of ultrasound treatment on the two pathogens. Escherichia coli O157:H7 was more sensitive to ultrasound treatment, possibly because its cell wall structure is relatively thin and its tolerance to external pressure is poor. Bacillus cereus is a Gram-positive bacterium with a thicker cell wall and the ability to form spores, giving it strong resistance to physical and chemical treatments. In this study, ultrasound treatment had a good inactivation effect on the vegetative cells of Bacillus cereus, but limited killing effect on spores. Scanning electron microscopy observation showed that after ultrasound treatment, the cell surface of Escherichia coli O157:H7 exhibited obvious depressions and ruptures, while the cell morphology of Bacillus cereus showed less change, with only some cells exhibiting surface roughness and slight deformation.

2.3 Inactivation Effect in Beef Matrix

In the beef matrix, the inactivation effect of ultrasound treatment was significantly lower than in the curing solution. This is mainly because beef tissue impedes the propagation of ultrasound waves, and components such as proteins and fats in meat can protect microbial cells. Under the condition of 600 W and 15 min, the inactivation rate of Escherichia coli O157:H7 on the beef surface was 2.8 log CFU/g, and that of Bacillus cereus was 2.1 log CFU/g. Although the inactivation rate decreased, when the treatment time was extended to 20 min, the inactivation rates of the two bacteria reached 3.5 log CFU/g and 2.9 log CFU/g, respectively. In addition, cutting beef into thin slices or increasing the contact area between the curing solution and meat could significantly improve the inactivation effect.

2.4 Effect of Ultrasound Treatment on Beef Quality

To evaluate the effect of ultrasound treatment on beef quality, this study measured the color, texture, and water-holding capacity of beef after treatment. The results showed that compared with the untreated group, the L* value (lightness), a* value (redness), and b* value (yellowness) of beef in the ultrasound-treated group showed no significant changes (P>0.05). Texture analysis showed that the hardness and elasticity of ultrasound-treated beef were not significantly different from the control group, indicating that ultrasound treatment did not cause adverse effects on beef texture. In terms of water-holding capacity, the drip loss of the ultrasound-treated group was slightly lower than that of the control group, which may be related to ultrasound treatment promoting the penetration of curing solution into the meat. Overall, power ultrasound can effectively inactivate pathogens while maintaining the sensory and physicochemical quality of beef.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

The results of this study indicate that power ultrasound has a significant inactivation effect on Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus during beef curing. In the curing solution, ultrasound treatment can significantly reduce the counts of both pathogens, and the inactivation effect on Escherichia coli O157:H7 is superior to that on Bacillus cereus. In the beef matrix, although the inactivation rate decreased, a satisfactory bactericidal effect could still be achieved by extending the treatment time or optimizing the treatment method. Ultrasound treatment had no significant adverse effects on the color, texture, or water-holding capacity of beef, indicating that this technology is feasible for practical application.

From an economic benefit perspective, the investment in ultrasound equipment is relatively low, and the operating cost is mainly electricity consumption. Taking 600 W ultrasound treatment for 15 min as an example, the additional electricity consumption per ton of beef is approximately 2.5 kWh. Calculated at industrial electricity rates, the added cost is less than 5 yuan. Compared with traditional thermal treatment, ultrasound treatment can be carried out at lower temperatures, avoiding the damage to meat quality caused by high temperatures while reducing the energy consumption required for cooling. In addition, ultrasound treatment can promote the penetration of curing solution, shorten curing time, and improve production efficiency. Therefore, applying power ultrasound to the beef curing process can not only improve product safety but also bring certain economic benefits.

From the perspective of technology promotion, ultrasound treatment equipment is easy to integrate with existing curing production lines, with simple operation and convenient maintenance. For small and medium-sized meat processing enterprises, batch-type ultrasound treatment equipment can be selected, with low investment and quick results. For large enterprises, continuous ultrasound treatment systems can be considered to achieve automated production. It should be noted that the ultrasound treatment effect is influenced by multiple factors. In practical applications, parameters such as ultrasound power, treatment time, and temperature should be optimized according to product type, curing solution formula, and microbial contamination level to achieve the best bactericidal effect.

4 Conclusion

This study systematically investigated the inactivation effect of power ultrasound on Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus during beef curing. The results showed that ultrasound treatment can effectively inactivate both pathogens in curing solution and beef matrix, and the inactivation rate increases with increasing ultrasound power and treatment time. Ultrasound treatment had no significant adverse effects on the color, texture, or water-holding capacity of beef, and can promote the penetration of curing solution and shorten curing time. As a non-thermal sterilization technology, power ultrasound has advantages such as low equipment investment, low operating cost, and minimal impact on product quality, making it suitable for promotion and application in the meat curing process. Future research can further explore the synergistic effects of ultrasound with other sterilization technologies (such as organic acids, essential oils, etc.) to further improve the bactericidal effect and broaden the scope of application.

title: Do 3D Printing Models Improve Anatomical Teaching About Hepatic Segments to Medical Students? A Randomized Controlled Study
text:
Do 3D Printing Models Improve Anatomical Teaching About Hepatic Segments to Medical Students? A Randomized Controlled Study

Abstract: Objective: To explore the application effect of 3D printed hepatic segment models in hepatobiliary anatomy teaching for medical undergraduates. Methods: A total of 120 undergraduates majoring in clinical medicine from the 2021 cohort of a medical college were selected and randomly divided into an experimental group (n=60) and a control group (n=60). The experimental group received traditional teaching combined with 3D printed hepatic segment models, while the control group received traditional teaching only. After teaching, theoretical assessment, model identification assessment, and teaching satisfaction survey were conducted. Results: The theoretical score of the experimental group was (84.6±7.2) points, and the model identification score was (88.3±6.9) points, both significantly higher than those of the control group, which were (72.4±8.5) points and (70.1±9.3) points (P<0.05). The teaching satisfaction of the experimental group was 93.3%, significantly higher than 76.7% in the control group (P<0.05). Conclusion: The 3D printed hepatic segment model can effectively improve medical undergraduates' mastery of hepatic segment anatomy and learning satisfaction, and is worthy of promotion and application in anatomy teaching.

Keywords: 3D printing; hepatic segments; anatomy teaching; medical undergraduates; randomized controlled trial

1 Introduction

The liver is the largest solid organ in the human body, and its internal ductal structures are complex. Hepatic segmentation is a key and difficult point in hepatobiliary surgery, imaging diagnosis, and anatomy teaching. Traditional teaching mainly relies on two-dimensional atlases, cadaver specimens, and multimedia courseware, which have problems such as insufficient spatial three-dimensional perception and difficulty in intuitively presenting the adjacent relationships of intrahepatic ducts, leading to students' difficulty in understanding and poor retention. In recent years, 3D printing technology, with its advantages of precision, individualization, and visualization, has gradually been applied in the field of medical education. This technology can transform CT or MRI data into physical models, intuitively displaying the branches of the intrahepatic portal vein, hepatic vein, and bile ducts, helping students establish three-dimensional spatial cognition. However, there are still relatively few randomized controlled studies on 3D printed models in hepatic segment anatomy teaching, especially insufficient empirical evidence among medical undergraduates. Through a randomized controlled trial, this study evaluated the effect of 3D printed hepatic segment models on medical undergraduates' learning of hepatic segment anatomy, in order to provide a basis for anatomy teaching reform.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Subjects

A total of 120 undergraduates majoring in clinical medicine from the 2021 cohort of a medical college were selected, all of whom had completed the systematic anatomy course. Inclusion criteria: voluntary participation in this study and signing informed consent; no prior systematic learning experience related to liver anatomy. Exclusion criteria: previous participation in 3D printing-related courses or research; absence from assessment. They were divided into an experimental group and a control group using the random number table method, with 60 students in each group. There were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in sex, age, or previous anatomy scores (P>0.05), indicating comparability.

2.2 Teaching Methods

The control group used the traditional teaching method, including classroom lectures, PPT presentations, two-dimensional anatomy atlases, and observation of cadaver specimens. On the basis of traditional teaching, the experimental group introduced 3D printed hepatic segment models. The models were based on contrast-enhanced abdominal CT data of healthy adults, and Mimics software was used to reconstruct the liver and intrahepatic ducts. Photosensitive resin material was used for printing, and the Couinaud segmentation method was used to color-code and distinguish each hepatic segment, with labeling of the portal vein, hepatic vein, and bile duct courses. During teaching, students could freely touch and disassemble the models, and teachers explained hepatic segment boundaries, duct adjacency, and clinical significance in combination with the models. The teaching duration for both groups was 4 class hours, and the same teacher taught both groups.

2.3 Evaluation Indicators

One week after the end of teaching, assessments were conducted, including: ① Theoretical assessment: closed-book written examination, full score 100 points, covering hepatic segmentation, duct courses, and clinical significance; ② Model identification assessment: unlabeled 3D printed models were provided, and students were required to point out each hepatic segment and major ducts, full score 100 points; ③ Teaching satisfaction: a self-designed questionnaire was used, divided into very satisfied, satisfied, neutral, and dissatisfied, with satisfaction = (very satisfied + satisfied)/total number × 100%.

2.4 Statistical Methods

SPSS 26.0 software was used for data analysis. Measurement data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, and independent samples t-test was used for comparison between groups; count data were expressed as rates, and χ² test was used. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Comparison of Theoretical Assessment Scores Between the Two Groups

The theoretical assessment score of the experimental group was (84.6±7.2) points, while that of the control group was (72.4±8.5) points. The experimental group was significantly higher than the control group (t=8.426, P<0.001). Among them, in questions related to hepatic segmentation and duct adjacency, the correct rate of the experimental group was significantly higher.

3.2 Comparison of Model Identification Assessment Scores Between the Two Groups

The model identification score of the experimental group was (88.3±6.9) points, while that of the control group was (70.1±9.3) points. The experimental group was significantly better than the control group (t=12.137, P<0.001). Students in the experimental group had a lower error rate when identifying the boundaries of the right lobe, left lobe, and caudate lobe of the liver, and their accuracy in identifying portal vein branches was significantly improved.

3.3 Comparison of Teaching Satisfaction Between the Two Groups

In the experimental group, 38 were very satisfied, 18 were satisfied, 3 were neutral, and 1 was dissatisfied, with a satisfaction rate of 93.3%; in the control group, 22 were very satisfied, 24 were satisfied, 10 were neutral, and 4 were dissatisfied, with a satisfaction rate of 76.7%. The satisfaction of the experimental group was significantly higher than that of the control group (χ²=6.536, P=0.011).

4 Discussion

The results of this study show that the 3D printed hepatic segment model can significantly improve medical undergraduates' theoretical scores and model identification ability in hepatic segment anatomy. The reasons are analyzed as follows: First, the 3D printed model transforms abstract two-dimensional images into touchable three-dimensional entities, helping students establish spatial three-dimensional perception, especially making the understanding of hepatic segment boundaries and intrahepatic duct courses more intuitive. Second, the model can be disassembled and colored according to hepatic segments, making it convenient for students to observe intrahepatic structures from different angles and enhancing memory depth. In addition, the model is highly interactive, which can stimulate learning interest and improve classroom participation.

Compared with traditional teaching, 3D printed models have advantages such as individualization, reusability, and no ethical restrictions. However, this study also has limitations: the sample size was small and came from only a single center; the assessment time was short, and long-term memory effects could not be evaluated; the cost of model production is relatively high, and economic feasibility needs to be considered for promotion. In the future, virtual reality technology can be combined to construct a multimodal teaching system, and the sample can be expanded for multicenter research.

5 Conclusion

The 3D printed hepatic segment model can effectively improve medical undergraduates' mastery of hepatic segment anatomy and learning satisfaction, with obvious advantages especially in spatial structure identification. This teaching method is worthy of promotion and application in anatomy and hepatobiliary surgery teaching, and provides a reference for the digital transformation of medical education.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of effect evaluation of traditional Chinese medicine in treating acute respiratory distress syndrome
text:
Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Efficacy of Traditional Chinese Medicine in the Treatment of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome

Abstract: Objective: To systematically evaluate the clinical efficacy of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) as an adjunctive therapy for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Methods: Computerized searches were conducted in databases including CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, PubMed, and the Cochrane Library to collect randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of TCM combined with conventional Western medicine for the treatment of ARDS, with the search period extending from database inception to December 2024. Two researchers independently screened the literature, extracted data, and assessed quality. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4 software. Results: A total of 12 RCTs involving 896 patients were included. Meta-analysis showed that compared with conventional Western medicine alone, TCM combined with conventional treatment significantly reduced the mortality of ARDS patients (RR=0.68, 95%CI: 0.54–0.86, P<0.01), improved the oxygenation index (MD=28.64, 95%CI: 18.32–38.96, P<0.01), shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation (MD=-2.14, 95%CI: -3.06–-1.22, P<0.01), and reduced ICU length of stay (MD=-3.27, 95%CI: -4.51–-2.03, P<0.01). Conclusion: TCM as an adjunctive therapy for ARDS has certain clinical benefits, including improving oxygenation and reducing mortality; however, due to the quality limitations of the included studies, the conclusions still require validation by high-quality, large-sample trials.

1 Introduction

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is an acute diffuse lung injury caused by various intrapulmonary and extrapulmonary pathogenic factors, which subsequently develops into acute respiratory failure. It is clinically characterized by refractory hypoxemia, respiratory distress, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary exudation. Despite continuous advances in supportive techniques such as lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning ventilation, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, the mortality rate of ARDS remains as high as 35%–45%, making it a therapeutic challenge in the field of critical care medicine.

In Traditional Chinese Medicine, ARDS is classified under categories such as "sudden asthma," "asthma collapse," and "chest bind." Its pathogenesis is considered to involve the interconnection of heat toxin, blood stasis, and water-dampness, leading to obstruction of lung qi and impaired diffusion and descent. In clinical practice, TCM preparations such as Xuebijing Injection, Xuanbai Chengqi Decoction, and Dachengqi Decoction have been widely used as adjunctive treatments for ARDS. Multiple previous small-sample studies have suggested that they can improve oxygenation and inhibit inflammatory responses. However, individual studies have small sample sizes and inconsistent conclusions, and a systematic review is still lacking. This study comprehensively evaluates the efficacy of TCM in treating ARDS through a systematic review and Meta-analysis, aiming to provide evidence-based support for clinical promotion.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Literature Search and Screening Strategy

Search strategies were formulated. Chinese search terms included "acute respiratory distress syndrome," "ARDS," "Traditional Chinese Medicine," "Chinese medicine," and "integrated Chinese and Western medicine" as subject headings. English search terms included "acute respiratory distress syndrome," "traditional Chinese medicine," and "integrated Chinese and Western medicine" as subject headings. A combination of subject headings and free-text terms was used for searching. Inclusion criteria: ① Study subjects met the diagnostic criteria for ARDS (Berlin definition or AECC criteria); ② The intervention group received TCM combined with conventional Western medicine treatment, while the control group received conventional Western medicine treatment alone; ③ Outcome measures included mortality, oxygenation index, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, etc.; ④ Study type was RCT. Duplicate publications, studies with incomplete data, and non-Chinese/English literature were excluded.

2.2 Data Extraction and Quality Assessment

Two researchers independently extracted the first author, year of publication, sample size, intervention measures, treatment course, and outcome measures, and cross-checked the data. The Cochrane risk of bias assessment tool was used to evaluate the quality of included studies, including 6 domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, completeness of outcome data, and selective reporting, classified as low risk, high risk, and unclear.

2.3 Statistical Analysis Methods

RevMan 5.4 software was used. Dichotomous variables were expressed as relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI), and continuous variables were expressed as mean difference (MD) with 95%CI. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² test. If I²<50% and P>0.1, a fixed-effects model was used; otherwise, a random-effects model was used. Subgroup analysis or sensitivity analysis was performed for apparent sources of heterogeneity. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots.

2.4 Analysis of TCM Intervention Protocol Characteristics

The TCM interventions in the included studies were mainly intravenous preparations and oral/nasogastric decoctions. Intravenous preparations included Xuebijing Injection (main components: Carthamus tinctorius, Radix Paeoniae Rubra, Ligusticum chuanxiong, etc.) and Tanreqing Injection, etc., which function to clear heat, detoxify, activate blood circulation, and resolve stasis. Decoctions were mainly modified Xuanbai Chengqi Decoction, Dachengqi Decoction, and Maxing Shigan Decoction, which treat by unblocking the bowels and purging the lungs, clearing heat, and resolving phlegm. The treatment course was mostly 7–14 days. Most studies added TCM on the basis of conventional treatment, which included lung-protective ventilation, anti-infection therapy, fluid management, and nutritional support.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

3.1 Literature Inclusion and Quality Assessment

A total of 486 relevant articles were initially retrieved. After layer-by-layer screening, 12 RCTs involving 896 patients were ultimately included, with 452 patients in the TCM group and 444 patients in the control group. All included studies mentioned randomization, but only 3 described the randomization method, 2 mentioned allocation concealment, and 1 used blinding. The overall quality of the literature was low, with a certain risk of bias.

3.2 Primary Outcome Measures

Mortality: Nine studies reported mortality. The mortality rate was 22.3% (78/350) in the TCM group and 32.9% (113/344) in the control group. Heterogeneity test showed I²=0%, and a fixed-effects model was used: RR=0.68 (95%CI: 0.54–0.86, P<0.01), suggesting that TCM adjunctive therapy can significantly reduce the mortality of ARDS.

Oxygenation index: Ten studies reported the oxygenation index, with moderate heterogeneity among studies (I²=46%), and a random-effects model was used. Meta-analysis showed that the improvement in oxygenation index in the TCM group was superior to that in the control group, MD=28.64 (95%CI: 18.32–38.96, P<0.01).

3.3 Secondary Outcome Measures

Duration of mechanical ventilation: Eight studies reported the duration of mechanical ventilation, I²=52%, and a random-effects model was used: MD=-2.14 (95%CI: -3.06–-1.22, P<0.01). The duration of mechanical ventilation in the TCM group was shortened by an average of 2.14 days.

ICU length of stay: Seven studies reported ICU length of stay, I²=48%, MD=-3.27 (95%CI: -4.51–-2.03, P<0.01). The ICU length of stay in the TCM group was shortened by an average of 3.27 days.

3.4 Benefit Analysis

From a health economics perspective, although TCM adjunctive therapy increases medication costs, it can significantly reduce overall hospitalization costs by shortening the duration of mechanical ventilation and ICU length of stay. Estimating the average daily cost of mechanical ventilation at approximately 3,000 yuan and the average daily ICU cost at approximately 5,000 yuan, approximately 23,000 yuan can be saved per patient. Meanwhile, the improvement in quality of life and social benefits brought about by reduced mortality are even more significant. TCM preparations are relatively inexpensive and convenient to administer, making them suitable for promotion in primary hospitals.

4 Conclusion

This study systematically evaluated the clinical efficacy of TCM as an adjunctive therapy for ARDS. The results showed that adding TCM on the basis of conventional Western medicine treatment can significantly reduce mortality, improve the oxygenation index, shorten the duration of mechanical ventilation and ICU length of stay, without increasing obvious adverse reactions. However, due to the methodological quality limitations of the included studies, such as unclear description of randomization methods, lack of blinding, and relatively small sample sizes, the conclusions should be interpreted with caution. It is recommended that future multi-center, large-sample, double-blind randomized controlled trials be conducted, with unified TCM intervention protocols and outcome measures, to further verify the efficacy and safety of TCM in treating ARDS and provide higher-quality evidence-based medical evidence for clinical promotion.

title: Phylogeography and evolution of infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus in China
text:
Phylogeography and Evolution of Infectious Hematopoietic Necrosis Virus in China

 Abstract

Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus (IHNV) is a highly destructive pathogen in salmonid aquaculture, causing significant economic losses to China's cold-water fish industry. In this study, based on 78 IHNV isolates collected from major salmonid farming regions in China between 2015 and 2023, combined with reference sequences published in GenBank, a systematic analysis was conducted on the geographic distribution patterns and molecular evolutionary characteristics of IHNV in China. Through genetic diversity analysis of the glycoprotein (G) gene and nucleoprotein (N) gene sequences, phylogenetic reconstruction, Bayesian phylogeographic inference, and selection pressure detection, the results showed that: Chinese IHNV isolates predominantly belong to the U genotype and can be further divided into three geographic subpopulations (Northwest subpopulation, Northeast subpopulation, and Southwest subpopulation), with significant genetic differentiation among subpopulations (Fst = 0.32–0.58, P < 0.01). Bayesian skyline plot analysis revealed that the Chinese IHNV population experienced a marked expansion between 2016 and 2019, followed by stabilization. Molecular clock estimation indicated that the most recent common ancestor of Chinese IHNV dates to approximately 1998 (95% HPD: 1995–2002), with transmission routes showing a trend of dispersal from the Northwest to the Northeast and Southwest. Selection pressure analysis detected 3 positively selected sites in the G gene, suggesting that immune escape may play an important role in the adaptive evolution of the virus. This study reveals the transmission dynamics and evolutionary patterns of IHNV in China, providing a scientific basis for vaccine development and regionalized prevention and control strategies.

Keywords: Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus; phylogeography; molecular evolution; salmonids; glycoprotein gene; selection pressure

 1 Introduction

Infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus (IHNV) is a negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the family *Rhabdoviridae*, genus *Novirhabdovirus*, with a genome of approximately 11 kb encoding six structural or non-structural proteins: nucleoprotein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), glycoprotein (G), non-virion protein (NV), and polymerase protein (L). IHNV primarily infects salmonid fish, causing infectious hematopoietic necrosis (IHN), with clinical manifestations including lethargy, darkened body coloration, exophthalmia, and trailing fecal casts from the vent. Mortality can reach 80%–100%, and the disease is listed as notifiable by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH).

Since China introduced large-scale farming of rainbow trout (*Oncorhynchus mykiss*) in the 1990s, IHNV outbreaks have occurred successively in multiple provinces. In recent years, with the rapid expansion of the cold-water fish farming industry, the epidemic range of IHNV has shown an expanding trend, becoming an important bottleneck restricting the healthy development of China's salmonid industry. However, compared with the relatively systematic molecular epidemiological studies of IHNV in North America and Europe, a comprehensive understanding of the genetic diversity, geographic transmission patterns, and evolutionary drivers of Chinese IHNV isolates is still lacking.

Phylogeography, which combines phylogenetic analysis with geographic information, can reveal the transmission routes, dispersal timing, and population dynamic history of pathogens, and has been widely applied in viral epidemiological research. This study aims to elucidate the genetic structure, transmission routes, and evolutionary timescale of IHNV in China through large-scale sequence data, and to explore the impact of selection pressure on the adaptive evolution of the virus, in order to provide a theoretical basis for precise prevention and control of the disease.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Virus Samples and Sequence Data

In this study, suspected IHN-infected fish samples were collected from rainbow trout and golden trout farms in 12 provinces of China (Qinghai, Gansu, Xinjiang, Heilongjiang, Jilin, Liaoning, Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou, Hebei, Beijing, Shandong) between 2015 and 2023. Through cell culture isolation and RT-PCR identification, a total of 78 IHNV isolates were obtained. Additionally, 45 reference sequences from China and abroad were downloaded from GenBank, covering the U, M, and L genotypes.

 2.2 Viral RNA Extraction and Gene Amplification

Approximately 50 mg of spleen and kidney tissues from diseased fish were collected, and total RNA was extracted using the Trizol method. cDNA was synthesized by reverse transcription with random primers, followed by amplification of the full-length G gene (approximately 1,600 bp) and a partial fragment of the N gene (approximately 800 bp) using specific primers. PCR products were purified and sent to a biotechnology company for bidirectional sequencing.

 2.3 Sequence Analysis and Phylogenetic Reconstruction

MEGA 11 software was used for sequence alignment and genetic distance calculation. ModelFinder was used to select the best nucleotide substitution model, and phylogenetic trees were constructed using maximum likelihood (ML) and Bayesian inference (BI) methods. ML analysis was performed using IQ-TREE software with 1,000 bootstrap replicates; BI analysis was performed using MrBayes 3.2, running 10⁷ generations with sampling every 1,000 generations.

 2.4 Phylogeographic Analysis

BEAST 2.7 software was used for Bayesian phylogeographic analysis, employing a strict molecular clock model and Bayesian Skyline Plot to reconstruct population dynamic history. Geographic location was treated as a discrete trait, and a symmetric migration model was used to infer ancestral geographic regions. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) was run for 2×10⁸ generations with sampling every 10⁴ generations, and convergence was assessed using Tracer 1.7.

 2.5 Selection Pressure Analysis

The CODEML program in PAML 4.9 was used to detect positively selected sites in the G gene and N gene through site models (M1a vs M2a, M7 vs M8) and branch-site models. Likelihood ratio tests (LRT) were used to evaluate model fit.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Genetic Diversity and Phylogenetic Relationships

The G gene sequences of the 78 Chinese IHNV isolates ranged from 1,524 to 1,596 nt in length, with a total of 142 variable sites detected, of which 87 were parsimony-informative sites. Haplotype diversity (Hd) was 0.936, and nucleotide diversity (π) was 0.018 2, indicating that the Chinese IHNV population possesses high genetic diversity.

Phylogenetic analysis showed that all Chinese IHNV isolates belonged to the U genotype, clustering with North American reference strains into the same major clade, but forming independent geographic clusters. Within the U genotype, Chinese isolates could be further divided into three geographic subpopulations: the Northwest subpopulation (Qinghai, Gansu, Xinjiang), the Northeast subpopulation (Heilongjiang, Jilin, Liaoning), and the Southwest subpopulation (Sichuan, Yunnan, Guizhou). Intra-subpopulation sequence similarity was 97.2%–99.8%, and inter-subpopulation genetic distance was 0.021–0.038. Analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA) showed that genetic variation among geographic populations accounted for 42.6% of total variation (Fst = 0.32–0.58, P < 0.01), suggesting that geographic isolation has a significant impact on viral genetic differentiation.

 3.2 Population Dynamic History

Bayesian skyline plot analysis showed that the effective population size of Chinese IHNV grew slowly between 1998 and 2015, experienced a significant expansion between 2016 and 2019 (approximately 4.7-fold increase in population size), and stabilized after 2020. This expansion period coincided with the rapid increase in China's cold-water fish farming scale and the frequent cross-regional transportation of fry and fingerlings.

 3.3 Evolutionary Timescale and Transmission Routes

Molecular clock estimation indicated that the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) of the Chinese IHNV population can be traced back to 1998 (95% HPD: 1995–2002), with an evolutionary rate of the G gene of approximately 3.2×10⁻⁴ substitutions/site/year (95% HPD: 2.1×10⁻⁴–4.5×10⁻⁴). Bayesian phylogeographic inference revealed that the transmission of IHNV in China exhibited a pattern with the Northwest region as the source, dispersing bidirectionally to the Northeast and Southwest. The dispersal event from the Northwest subpopulation to the Northeast subpopulation occurred approximately in 2005 (95% HPD: 2003–2008), and the dispersal to the Southwest subpopulation occurred approximately in 2008 (95% HPD: 2005–2011). Additionally, a small amount of recent gene flow was detected between the Northeast and Southwest subpopulations, possibly related to live fish transportation.

 3.4 Selection Pressure Analysis

Selection pressure analysis detected 3 positively selected sites in the G gene (sites 82, 256, and 378), all with posterior probabilities greater than 0.95. These sites are located in the antigenic determinant regions of the G protein, suggesting that humoral immune pressure may have driven antigenic variation of the virus. No significant positively selected sites were detected in the N gene, and its evolution was mainly constrained by purifying selection (ω = 0.087).

 4 Discussion

This study systematically revealed the genetic diversity, geographic differentiation patterns, and evolutionary history of IHNV in China. All Chinese IHNV isolates belong to the U genotype and are homologous to North American strains, corroborating the hypothesis that the virus was introduced into China through fish introduction activities. The formation of three geographic subpopulations is closely related to the geographic isolation of farming regions and the patterns of fry and fingerling transportation. The Northwest region, as the birthplace and main production area of rainbow trout farming in China, may be the source of IHNV transmission in China, subsequently spreading to the Northeast and Southwest through fry and fingerling transportation.

The population expansion during 2016–2019 coincided with the rapid increase in China's cold-water fish farming capacity during this period. Notably, the population size stabilized after 2020, which may be related to the reduction in live fish transportation during the pandemic and the improvement of biosecurity levels at farms.

The positively selected sites detected in the G gene are located in antigenic epitope regions, consistent with existing reports of antigenic drift in IHNV under vaccine immune pressure. This suggests that attention should be paid to these variable sites in vaccine design to avoid immune failure caused by antigenic variation. In contrast, the N gene is highly conserved and can serve as a stable target for molecular detection.

The limitation of this study is that sample collection was not fully balanced in time and space, with some provinces having small sample sizes, which may affect the precision of transmission route inference. Future efforts should strengthen nationwide active surveillance and incorporate whole-genome sequencing to obtain higher-resolution evolutionary information.

 5 Conclusions

(1) All Chinese IHNV isolates belong to the U genotype and can be divided into three geographic subpopulations: Northwest, Northeast, and Southwest, with geographic isolation being the primary factor driving genetic differentiation.

(2) The most recent common ancestor of Chinese IHNV dates to approximately 1998, with transmission routes showing a pattern of dispersal from the Northwest as the source to the Northeast and Southwest.

(3) The population experienced significant expansion during 2016–2019, closely related to the expansion of farming scale and fry and fingerling transportation.

(4) Three positively selected sites exist in the G gene, suggesting that immune escape plays an important role in the adaptive evolution of the virus.

(5) It is recommended to strengthen regionalized regulation of fry and fingerling transportation, promote vaccine development based on prevalent strains, and establish a nationwide IHNV molecular epidemiological surveillance network.

title: Exosome loaded genipin crosslinked hydrogel facilitates full thickness cutaneous wound healing in rat animal model
text:
Exosome-Loaded Genipin-Crosslinked Hydrogel Promotes Full-Thickness Skin Wound Healing in Rats

Abstract: Objective: To address the issues of slow healing and scar formation in full-thickness skin defect wounds, an exosome-loaded genipin-crosslinked hydrogel was prepared, and its effect on promoting wound healing was evaluated. Methods: Exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells were extracted, and a gelatin/chitosan hydrogel was prepared using genipin as a crosslinking agent, in which the exosomes were loaded. The material properties were characterized by scanning electron microscopy, swelling experiments, and in vitro release experiments. A rat full-thickness skin defect model was established, and healing was compared among groups. Results: The hydrogel had a porous structure with pore sizes of approximately 50–150 μm, and the exosomes achieved sustained release. Animal experiments showed that the wound healing rate in the exosome hydrogel group was significantly higher than that in the control group, with more orderly collagen deposition and reduced expression of inflammatory factors. Conclusion: This composite hydrogel can effectively promote full-thickness skin wound healing and has potential for clinical translation.

Keywords: exosomes; genipin; hydrogel; full-thickness skin defect; wound healing

1 Introduction

Full-thickness skin defects are commonly seen in burns, trauma, and chronic ulcers. Due to the complete loss of the epidermis and dermis, wound healing depends on granulation tissue formation and re-epithelialization, a process that is slow and prone to scar formation. Although commonly used clinical dressings such as gauze and foam dressings can provide physical protection, they lack the ability to actively promote healing. In recent years, tissue engineering strategies have provided new approaches for wound repair, among which hydrogels have become a research hotspot due to their high water content, good biocompatibility, and ability to mimic the extracellular matrix.

Exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells contain various growth factors, mRNA, and miRNA, and can regulate inflammation, promote angiogenesis and cell proliferation, while also having low immunogenicity and good stability. However, directly injected exosomes are easily cleared rapidly and require carriers for sustained release. Genipin is a natural crosslinking agent with toxicity far lower than that of glutaraldehyde, and it can form stable networks with gelatin, chitosan, and other materials. This study aimed to construct an exosome-loaded genipin-crosslinked hydrogel, characterize its properties, and evaluate its healing-promoting effects, thereby providing a feasible approach for skin repair.

2 Analysis of Key Technologies

2.1 Extraction and Identification of Exosomes

Exosomes were extracted from the culture supernatant of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells by differential centrifugation. The specific steps were as follows: cell culture supernatant was collected and centrifuged at 300×g for 10 min to remove cells, at 2000×g for 20 min to remove dead cells, at 10000×g for 30 min to remove cell debris, and finally at 100000×g for 70 min to collect the pellet. After resuspension in phosphate-buffered saline, morphology was observed by transmission electron microscopy, particle size was measured by nanoparticle tracking analysis, and the expression of CD9, CD63, and TSG101 was detected by Western blot. The results showed that the extract exhibited a typical cup-shaped morphology, with a particle size distribution of 50–150 nm, and highly expressed exosome marker proteins, consistent with exosome characteristics.

2.2 Preparation and Characterization of Genipin-Crosslinked Hydrogel

Gelatin and chitosan were dissolved in acetic acid solution at a certain ratio, genipin solution was added, and after uniform mixing, the solution was injected into a mold and crosslinked at 37°C for a certain period of time. By adjusting the genipin concentration and crosslinking time, the gelation time and mechanical properties were optimized. Scanning electron microscopy of the cross-section of the freeze-dried hydrogel revealed a uniform porous structure with pore sizes of approximately 50–150 μm, which is favorable for cell migration and nutrient exchange. Swelling experiments showed that the hydrogel reached swelling equilibrium within 4 h in phosphate-buffered saline, with a swelling ratio of approximately 800%, indicating good water absorption and retention capacity. Degradation experiments showed that the hydrogel gradually degraded in collagenase solution, with a degradation rate of approximately 60% at 14 days, which can match the wound healing cycle.

2.3 Exosome Loading and Release Behavior

The exosome solution was mixed with the genipin hydrogel precursor, and loading was achieved through physical adsorption and electrostatic interaction. Fluorescently labeled exosomes were used, and their distribution in the gel was observed by confocal microscopy, showing that the exosomes were uniformly dispersed in the pores. In vitro release experiments showed that the exosomes exhibited sustained-release characteristics in phosphate-buffered saline: approximately 25% was released on day 1, approximately 50% on day 3, and approximately 75% on day 7, with sustained release for more than 14 days. The release curve conformed to the Higuchi model, indicating that diffusion was the main release mechanism. This sustained-release behavior can avoid burst release of exosomes and prolong their duration of action.

2.4 In Vitro Cell Experiments

The extract of the exosome hydrogel was co-cultured with fibroblasts and endothelial cells. CCK-8 assay showed that cell proliferative activity was significantly higher than that of the control group. Scratch assay showed that the extract could promote fibroblast migration, with the migration rate increased by approximately 40% at 24 h. Tube formation assay showed that endothelial cells formed more tubular structures under the action of the extract, indicating that the exosome hydrogel has pro-angiogenic potential. In addition, after macrophages were co-cultured with the extract, the expression of inflammatory factors TNF-α and IL-6 decreased, while the anti-inflammatory factor IL-10 increased, suggesting that it can regulate the inflammatory microenvironment.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

3.1 Animal Experiment Design

Eight-week-old male SD rats were selected, and full-thickness skin defect models with a diameter of 1.5 cm were prepared on the back. The rats were randomly divided into four groups: blank control group, hydrogel-only group, exosome group, and exosome hydrogel group, with 10 rats in each group. After surgery, wounds were photographed and recorded on days 3, 7, and 14, and the healing rate was calculated. On day 14, wound tissues were collected for HE staining, Masson staining, and immunohistochemical analysis.

3.2 Wound Healing Effect

On day 3 after surgery, the exosome hydrogel group had less wound exudation, and granulation tissue began to form. At 7 days, the healing rate in this group was approximately 65%, significantly higher than that of the blank control group (approximately 35%) and the hydrogel-only group (approximately 45%). At 14 days, the wounds in the exosome hydrogel group were basically closed, with a healing rate of approximately 95%, while that of the blank control group was only 70%. HE staining showed that in the exosome hydrogel group, the epidermal layer was intact, and the dermal collagen fibers were dense and neatly arranged. Masson staining showed that collagen deposition was significantly increased, and the proportion of type I collagen was elevated, suggesting reduced scar formation.

3.3 Mechanism Analysis

Immunohistochemical results showed that in the wound tissue of the exosome hydrogel group, the number of CD31-positive vessels increased and VEGF expression was upregulated, indicating enhanced angiogenesis. At the same time, the expression of IL-6 and TNF-α decreased, while IL-10 increased, suggesting that the inflammatory response was inhibited. In addition, Ki67-positive cells increased, indicating active cell proliferation. These effects may be attributed to the sustained release of miRNA and growth factors in exosomes acting continuously on the wound, regulating inflammation and promoting angiogenesis and cell proliferation.

3.4 Benefit Analysis

From a clinical perspective, the raw materials for this hydrogel are readily available, the preparation process is simple, genipin has low toxicity, and complex equipment is not required, making it suitable for large-scale production. Exosomes can be derived from autologous or allogeneic mesenchymal stem cells, with low immunogenicity and good safety. Compared with existing biological dressings, this material combines a physical barrier with active repair functions, which can shorten healing time, reduce scarring, and lower the risk of infection. From an economic perspective, although the cost of exosome extraction is relatively high, the dosage required is small, and the hydrogel can be freeze-dried for storage and is convenient for transportation, making the overall cost controllable. If large-scale preparation is achieved in the future, it is expected to become a new option for the treatment of chronic wounds.

4 Conclusion

This study successfully prepared an exosome-loaded genipin-crosslinked hydrogel. The material has a porous structure, good swelling properties, and sustained-release performance. In vitro experiments showed that it can promote cell proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis, and regulate inflammation. Experiments on full-thickness skin defects in rats confirmed that the hydrogel can significantly accelerate wound healing, improve healing quality, and reduce scar formation. Its mechanism may be related to the sustained release of exosomes regulating the inflammatory microenvironment and promoting angiogenesis and collagen deposition. This composite hydrogel is simple to prepare and has good biocompatibility, with potential for clinical translation, providing an effective strategy for the repair of full-thickness skin defects. Subsequent studies will further optimize the exosome loading amount, explore its application in complex models such as diabetic chronic wounds, and conduct large animal experiments to promote clinical translation.

title: Assessment of toxicity of heavy metal-contaminated soils toward Collembola in the paddy fields supported by laboratory tests
text:
Toxicity Assessment of Heavy Metal-Contaminated Paddy Soil on Springtails: Verification Based on Laboratory Tests

 Abstract

[Objective] This study aimed to evaluate the toxic effects of combined heavy metal (Cd, Pb, Cu, Zn) contamination in typical paddy soils of southern China on springtails (Collembola), and to explore the indicative significance of laboratory test results for field ecological risk assessment. [Methods] Topsoil (0–20 cm) was collected from paddy fields surrounding a mining area. Five contamination gradients (CK, T1, T2, T3, T4) were established based on heavy metal concentrations. The model species *Folsomia candida* was used as the test organism for a 28-d chronic toxicity test, measuring survival rate, reproduction rate, and body length changes. Heavy metal bioavailability was analyzed in conjunction with soil physicochemical properties. [Results] With increasing heavy metal contamination, springtail survival rate decreased from 92.3% in the control to 31.7% in T4, reproduction rate decreased from 68.4 individuals per dish to 9.2, and body length decreased from 1.42 mm to 0.87 mm, all showing significant dose-effect relationships (*P*<0.05). Exchangeable Cd and Zn contents were significantly positively correlated with springtail reproduction inhibition rate (*r*=0.891, 0.834, *P*<0.01). [Conclusion] Combined heavy metal contamination in paddy soil exhibits significant toxicity to springtails. Laboratory tests can effectively reflect the ecological risk of contaminated soil, and springtail reproduction rate can serve as a sensitive indicator for early warning of heavy metal contamination in paddy soils.

Keywords: heavy metal contamination; paddy soil; springtail; ecotoxicity; laboratory test; bioindication

 1 Introduction

Paddy field ecosystems are an important foundation for food security in China. However, with the development of industry and mining and the extensive use of agricultural inputs, heavy metals continuously enter paddy soils through atmospheric deposition, wastewater irrigation, and fertilizer application, leading to the accumulation of Cd, Pb, Cu, Zn and other elements in the topsoil [1]. Heavy metal contamination not only affects rice yield and quality but also poses threats to human health through food chain transfer. In recent years, the problem of excessive heavy metals in paddy fields surrounding mining areas in southern China has been particularly prominent. Conducting soil ecotoxicity assessments is of great significance for ensuring agricultural product safety and ecosystem health [2].

Springtails (Collembola) are one of the most abundant microarthropods in soil, widely distributed in paddy field, upland, and forest soils. They participate in organic matter decomposition and nutrient cycling and are extremely sensitive to soil environmental changes [3]. Among them, *Folsomia candida*, due to its short life cycle, high fecundity, and ease of laboratory rearing, has been listed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) as a standard model organism for soil toxicity testing [4]. However, research on springtail toxicity in heavy metal-contaminated paddy soils in China remains relatively limited, especially lacking systematic assessments combining laboratory tests with field contamination gradients.

This study took heavy metal-contaminated paddy soil surrounding a mining area as the research object. Through laboratory chronic toxicity tests, the responses of springtail survival, reproduction, and growth indicators to combined heavy metal contamination were measured. Combined with soil heavy metal speciation analysis, the toxic effects and sensitive indicator metrics were explored, aiming to provide a scientific basis for ecological risk assessment of heavy metals in paddy soils.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Test Soil

Test soil was collected from paddy fields (0–20 cm topsoil) surrounding a lead-zinc mining area in southern China. The distances from sampling points to the mining center were 1 km (S1), 3 km (S2), 5 km (S3), 8 km (S4), and 15 km (S5, control area). After natural air-drying, the soil was passed through a 2 mm sieve, and basic physicochemical properties were determined: pH 5.62–6.38, organic matter content 21.4–28.7 g·kg⁻¹, cation exchange capacity 12.3–16.8 cmol·kg⁻¹, clay content 18.6%–24.3%. Total heavy metal concentrations in soil were determined by HCl-HNO₃-HF digestion and ICP-MS measurement; speciation was fractionated using the Tessier sequential extraction procedure, divided into exchangeable, carbonate-bound, Fe-Mn oxide-bound, organic-bound, and residual fractions [5].

 2.2 Test Organism

*Folsomia candida* was provided by a research institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. They were long-term reared in an artificial climate chamber with yeast powder as food, at 20°C, 75% relative humidity, and 16 h light/8 h dark conditions. Synchronized healthy individuals aged 10–12 d were selected for testing.

 2.3 Experimental Design

Based on heavy metal concentrations in soils from the five sampling points, five treatment groups were established: CK (S5 control soil), T1 (S4), T2 (S3), T3 (S2), T4 (S1), with four replicates per treatment. The test containers were 100 mL glass culture dishes, with 30 g of dry soil added to each dish, and water content adjusted to 50% of maximum water-holding capacity. Ten springtails were introduced into each dish and cultured at 20°C, 75% humidity, and 16 h light conditions for 28 d, with weekly water supplementation and yeast powder feeding.

 2.4 Measurement Indicators and Methods

After the test, springtails were separated by flotation, and the number of surviving individuals was recorded. Juvenile individuals were counted under a stereomicroscope for reproduction. Ten adults were randomly selected for body length measurement. The reproduction inhibition rate was calculated as: inhibition rate (%) = (control reproduction number − treatment reproduction number) / control reproduction number × 100%. Soil heavy metal bioavailability was expressed as exchangeable fraction content.

 2.5 Data Processing

SPSS 22.0 was used for one-way ANOVA and Duncan's multiple comparison, and Pearson correlation analysis was used to examine the relationship between heavy metal speciation and toxicity indicators, with significance level set at *P*<0.05. Figures were drawn using Origin 9.0.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Heavy Metal Concentrations and Speciation Distribution in Test Soils

Total heavy metal concentrations in soils from the five sampling points are shown in Table 1. Total Cd, Pb, Cu, and Zn in S1–S4 soils were all significantly higher than in S5 control (*P*<0.05). Among them, Cd content at S1 reached 3.86 mg·kg⁻¹, exceeding the risk screening value of the national soil environmental quality standard (GB 15618—2018) (0.3 mg·kg⁻¹) by 12.9 times; Pb, Cu, and Zn contents were 286.4, 98.7, and 312.5 mg·kg⁻¹, respectively, all exceeding standards to varying degrees. Speciation analysis showed that Cd had the highest exchangeable fraction proportion (18.6%–34.2%), followed by Zn (8.4%–21.7%), while Pb and Cu were mainly in residual and Fe-Mn oxide-bound fractions, with exchangeable fractions both below 10%.

 3.2 Effect of Heavy Metals on Springtail Survival Rate

With increasing contamination levels, the 28-d survival rate of springtails decreased significantly (Figure 1). The survival rate in the CK group was 92.3%, while T1, T2, and T3 groups decreased to 78.5%, 62.1%, and 48.6%, respectively, and the T4 group was only 31.7%, with significant differences among treatments (*P*<0.05). Regression analysis of survival rate against the comprehensive heavy metal pollution index showed a significant negative correlation (*R²*=0.946, *P*<0.01), indicating that combined heavy metal contamination has a clear inhibitory effect on springtail survival.

 3.3 Effect of Heavy Metals on Springtail Reproduction Rate

Reproduction rate is a key indicator reflecting the sustainability of springtail populations. The reproduction number per dish in the CK group was 68.4 individuals, while T1–T4 groups decreased to 51.2, 34.7, 19.5, and 9.2 individuals, respectively, with the reproduction inhibition rate increasing from 25.1% in T1 to 86.5% in T4 (Figure 2). ANOVA showed that T2 and above treatments differed significantly from CK (*P*<0.05), and reproduction in the T4 group was almost completely inhibited. Reproduction rate was significantly positively correlated with exchangeable Cd and Zn contents in soil (*r*=0.891, 0.834, *P*<0.01), while correlations with exchangeable Pb and Cu were weaker (*r*=0.612, 0.573, *P*<0.05), indicating that Cd and Zn are the main toxic factors inhibiting springtail reproduction.

 3.4 Effect of Heavy Metals on Springtail Body Length

Adult springtail body length shortened with increasing contamination (Figure 3). The body length in the CK group was 1.42 mm, while T1–T4 groups were 1.31, 1.18, 1.02, and 0.87 mm, respectively. T3 and T4 groups were shortened by 28.2% and 38.7% compared to CK (*P*<0.05). Body length was significantly positively correlated with both survival rate and reproduction rate (*r*=0.923, 0.897, *P*<0.01), indicating a synergistic effect between growth inhibition and population reproduction inhibition.

 3.5 Sensitivity Comparison of Toxicity Indicators

The effective concentration (EC₅₀) was used to evaluate the sensitivity of each indicator. The EC₅₀ values (based on exchangeable Cd) for survival rate, reproduction rate, and body length were 2.14, 1.06, and 1.58 mg·kg⁻¹, respectively. The reproduction rate had the lowest EC₅₀, indicating that reproduction indicators are most sensitive to heavy metal contamination.

 4 Discussion

The results of this study indicate that combined heavy metal contamination in paddy soils surrounding mining areas produces significant toxic effects on springtail survival, reproduction, and growth, with clear dose-effect relationships. This is basically consistent with domestic and international research results on heavy metal toxicity to springtails [6-7]. Springtails absorb heavy metals through body surface penetration and ingestion pathways. Cd and Zn, as non-essential and essential elements respectively, have relatively high exchangeable fractions, are easily absorbed by organisms, and interfere with their enzyme systems and reproductive physiological processes, leading to decreased survival rates and reproduction inhibition [8].

Reproduction rate was the most sensitive toxicity endpoint in this study, with its EC₅₀ significantly lower than those of survival rate and body length. This indicates that the reproductive process of *Folsomia candida* is more sensitive to heavy metal stress, possibly related to heavy metals interfering with oocyte development and embryonic hatching [9]. Therefore, in ecological risk assessment of heavy metals in paddy soils, reproduction inhibition rate can serve as a sensitive biomarker for early warning.

Heavy metal speciation analysis showed that Cd had the highest exchangeable fraction proportion and the strongest correlation with springtail reproduction inhibition rate, indicating that heavy metal bioavailability is the key factor determining toxicity, rather than total content. This finding supports the necessity of incorporating speciation analysis into ecological risk assessment systems [10]. In addition, the relatively low pH (5.62–6.38) of paddy soils can increase the solubility of Cd and Zn, further exacerbating their biological toxicity.

It is worth noting that this study was a laboratory controlled experiment. Although it can accurately reflect the toxic effects of heavy metals, the field paddy ecosystem also contains complex factors such as temperature fluctuations, water management, microbial interactions, and pesticide application, which may affect the actual responses of springtails. Therefore, future research should strengthen the integration of laboratory tests with field in-situ monitoring and establish a multi-indicator, multi-scale comprehensive assessment system.

From the perspective of agricultural safety and human health, as an important component of the paddy soil food web, the population decline of springtails may affect soil organic matter decomposition and nutrient cycling, thereby indirectly affecting rice growth. After heavy metals are enriched through soil animals such as springtails, they may also be transferred along the food chain, increasing agricultural product safety risks. Therefore, controlling heavy metal inputs into paddy fields and remediating contaminated soils have dual significance for maintaining paddy ecological health and ensuring food security.

 5 Conclusions

(1) Combined contamination of Cd, Pb, Cu, and Zn in paddy soils surrounding mining areas has significant toxicity to *Folsomia candida*. Survival rate, reproduction rate, and body length all significantly decreased with increasing contamination levels, showing clear dose-effect relationships.

(2) Springtail reproduction rate is most sensitive to heavy metal contamination, with its EC₅₀ lower than those of survival rate and body length, and can serve as a sensitive indicator for early warning of heavy metal contamination in paddy soils.

(3) Exchangeable Cd and Zn contents were significantly positively correlated with springtail reproduction inhibition rate, and heavy metal bioavailability is the key factor determining toxicity.

(4) Laboratory toxicity tests can effectively assess the ecological risk of heavy metal-contaminated paddy soils. It is recommended to combine field monitoring to construct a comprehensive assessment system, providing a scientific basis for paddy soil environmental quality management and agricultural product safety assurance.

[9] Crouau Y, Moïa C. The relative sensitivity of growth and reproduction in the springtail, *Folsomia candida*, exposed to xenobiotics in the laboratory[J]. Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety, 2006, 63(3): 399-404.

[10] Chen Tongbin, Zheng Yuanming, Chen Huang, et al. Systematic study on background values of heavy metals in Beijing soils [J]. Environmental Science, 2004, 25(1): 117-122.

title: Sheep and Goat Genome Engineering: From Random Transgenesis to the CRISPR Era
text:
Genome Engineering in Sheep and Goats: From Random Transgenesis to the CRISPR Era

 Abstract

Sheep and goats are globally important agricultural economic animals, providing humans with diverse products such as meat, milk, wool, and skin. With advances in molecular biology technologies, genome engineering has become an important tool for improving production traits, enhancing disease resistance, and expanding the use of sheep and goats as bioreactors. This paper systematically reviews the development history of genome engineering in sheep and goats, from early random transgenesis technology to somatic cell nuclear transfer-mediated gene targeting, and further to current precise editing technologies represented by CRISPR/Cas9, with a focus on analyzing the key technical characteristics and representative achievements at each stage. The paper also discusses the application benefits of genome engineering in wool quality improvement, milk protein regulation, disease-resistant breeding, and pharmaceutical protein production, and provides an outlook on future development directions. This paper aims to provide a reference for researchers and technicians engaged in animal genetic breeding and biotechnology extension.

 1 Introduction

Sheep and goats are among the earliest livestock domesticated by humans and occupy an important position in global animal husbandry. According to statistics, the global sheep population exceeds 1.2 billion, and the goat population exceeds 1 billion, widely distributed across Asia, Africa, Europe, and Oceania. Sheep and goats not only provide humans with high-quality products such as meat, milk, wool, and skin, but also play important roles in the cultural and social life of many regions.

However, traditional breeding methods face bottlenecks in improving the economic traits of sheep and goats, such as long cycles, low efficiency, and difficulties in trait integration. With the rapid development of molecular biology and genetic engineering technologies, genome engineering has opened new avenues for the genetic improvement of sheep and goats. Through targeted genome modification, researchers can more precisely improve target traits, significantly shorten breeding cycles, and even achieve trait combinations that are difficult to attain through traditional breeding.

This paper aims to systematically review the technological evolution of genome engineering in sheep and goats, from early random transgenesis technology to the current era of precise CRISPR editing, analyze the key technological breakthroughs and application outcomes at each stage, and discuss future development trends, with the hope of providing a reference for researchers and technology extension personnel in related fields.

 2 Key Technology Analysis

 2.1 Stage of Random Transgenesis Technology

From the 1980s to the 1990s, genome engineering in sheep and goats mainly relied on random transgenesis technology. The core method of this technology was to introduce exogenous DNA fragments into the pronucleus of fertilized eggs by microinjection, or to co-incubate exogenous genes with sperm followed by fertilization, with the exogenous genes randomly integrating into the host genome.

In 1985, Hammer et al. first successfully introduced exogenous genes into sheep and goat fertilized eggs and obtained transgenic offspring, marking the beginning of genome engineering in sheep and goats. Thereafter, researchers successively used this method to introduce growth hormone genes and disease resistance genes into sheep and goat genomes in attempts to improve growth rate and disease resistance. However, random transgenesis technology has obvious limitations: the integration sites of exogenous genes are random, which may cause insertional mutations in endogenous genes; the number of integrated copies is uncontrollable, and gene expression levels are unstable; in addition, transgenic efficiency is extremely low, usually less than 1%, and chimerism often occurs. These problems severely restricted the practical application of this technology in sheep and goat breeding.

 2.2 Stage of Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer and Gene Targeting

In the mid-to-late 1990s, breakthroughs in somatic cell nuclear transfer technology brought revolutionary changes to genome engineering in sheep and goats. In 1996, Wilmut et al. successfully cloned "Dolly" the sheep using adult sheep mammary epithelial cells, demonstrating that highly differentiated somatic cells can be reprogrammed in oocyte cytoplasm and develop into complete individuals. This technological breakthrough made it possible to perform precise genetic modification in somatic cells cultured in vitro.

On this basis, researchers combined gene targeting technology with somatic cell nuclear transfer to achieve targeted modification of sheep and goat genomes. Gene targeting uses the principle of homologous recombination to integrate exogenous DNA fragments at specific genomic locations, thereby achieving gene knockout or knock-in. In 2000, McCreath et al. first achieved targeted integration of the α1-antitrypsin gene in sheep, marking the success of gene targeting technology in sheep. Thereafter, researchers successively achieved myostatin gene knockout and PrP gene knockout in sheep and goats.
