Based on panel data of 38 resource-based cities in the Yellow River Basin from 2010 to 2022, this paper employs an extended STIRPAT model and spatiotemporally weighted regression method to empirically analyze the effects of population size, affluence level, industrial structure, energy intensity, technological innovation, and environmental regulation on carbon emissions. The results show that energy intensity and the proportion of the secondary industry are the main positive driving factors of carbon emissions, while technological innovation and environmental regulation have significant inhibitory effects; the influencing factors exhibit pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity, with the energy intensity elasticity coefficient being the highest in midstream coal-based cities. Accordingly, policy recommendations are proposed, including differentiated industrial transformation, clean energy substitution, and cross-regional collaborative governance.

Keywords: carbon neutrality; Yellow River Basin; resource-based cities; carbon emissions; STIRPAT model; spatiotemporal heterogeneity

1 Introduction

The Yellow River Basin is an important energy base and ecological barrier in China, with a large number of resource-based cities dominated by coal, oil, and non-ferrous metal extraction and processing distributed throughout the region. Under the "dual carbon" goals, these cities generally face prominent problems such as a monolithic industrial structure, high energy dependence, and strong carbon lock-in effects. Existing studies mostly focus on the national or provincial scale, with insufficient attention to the heterogeneity of carbon emission influencing factors in resource-based cities of the Yellow River Basin. This paper aims to construct an extended STIRPAT model combined with spatiotemporally weighted regression (GTWR) to identify key driving factors and their spatiotemporal differences, providing a basis for categorized policy-making.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Area and Data

A sample of 38 resource-based cities (including prefecture-level and county-level cities) in the Yellow River Basin was selected, with a time span from 2010 to 2022. Carbon emission data were calculated based on energy balance tables and the IPCC coefficient method, covering 8 types of energy including raw coal, coke, crude oil, gasoline, diesel, and natural gas. Socioeconomic data were obtained from the China City Statistical Yearbook and provincial statistical yearbooks. Individual missing values were filled using linear interpolation and mean imputation. To eliminate price effects, per capita GDP was converted to constant 2010 prices.

2.2 Model Construction

The basic form of the STIRPAT model is: I = aP^b A^c T^d e. This paper extends it as follows:

lnC_it = α + β₁lnP_it + β₂lnA_it + β₃lnIS_it + β₄lnEI_it + β₅lnTI_it + β₆lnER_it + μ_i + λ_t + ε_it

where C is carbon emissions; P is population size; A is per capita GDP; IS is the proportion of the secondary industry; EI is energy intensity (energy consumption per unit of GDP); TI is technological innovation (number of patents granted); ER is environmental regulation (share of investment in industrial pollution treatment in GDP). μ_i and λ_t are individual and time fixed effects, respectively.

The GTWR model was further employed to characterize spatiotemporal non-stationarity, with a Gaussian kernel function and bandwidth determined by the AICc criterion.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Spatiotemporal Evolution of Carbon Emissions

From 2010 to 2022, the total carbon emissions in the study area showed a trend of first rising and then declining, with an average annual decrease of 2.3% after peaking in 2016. Spatially, high-emission areas were concentrated in the border zone of Shanxi, Shaanxi, and Inner Mongolia, dominated by coal mining and thermal power; low-emission areas were mostly upstream hydropower and cultural tourism-oriented cities. The center of gravity of carbon emissions shifted from northeast to southwest, reflecting regional adjustments in the energy structure.

3.2 Regression Results of Influencing Factors

The fixed effects model shows that the energy intensity elasticity coefficient is the largest (0.632, p<0.01), followed by the proportion of the secondary industry (0.417, p<0.01) and population size (0.215, p<0.05); per capita GDP exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship, with a turning point at approximately 68,000 yuan per capita; for every 1% increase in technological innovation, carbon emissions decrease by 0.184% (p<0.05); the environmental regulation elasticity is -0.121 (p<0.1). The model R² is 0.874, indicating a good fit.

3.3 Spatiotemporal Heterogeneity

GTWR results show that the population size effect is stronger in upstream cities, the energy intensity and industrial structure effects are prominent in midstream cities, and the inhibitory effect of technological innovation is most significant in downstream cities. After 2016, the environmental regulation coefficient turned from positive to negative in most cities, indicating that policy dividends were gradually released. The average energy intensity elasticity coefficient of coal-based cities reached 0.71, significantly higher than that of oil and gas-based cities (0.48) and metal-based cities (0.53).

4 Discussion

This paper verifies the "energy–industry" dual lock-in characteristics of carbon emissions in resource-based cities. High energy intensity stems from the coal-dominated energy structure and the inertia of heavy chemical industries, which are difficult to fundamentally reverse in the short term. Technological innovation plays a carbon reduction role by improving energy efficiency and fostering alternative industries, but its effectiveness is constrained by R&D investment intensity and the rate of achievement transformation. Environmental regulation may increase energy consumption in the initial stage due to the "green paradox," but in the medium to long term it forces enterprises to upgrade. Notably, the inverted U-shaped relationship of per capita GDP indicates that merely pursuing economic growth is insufficient to automatically achieve emission reduction; it is necessary to proactively cross the "carbon peak" plateau period.

Compared with existing studies, the marginal contributions of this paper are as follows: first, it focuses on resource-based cities in the Yellow River Basin as a special unit; second, it introduces GTWR to reveal spatiotemporal heterogeneity, avoiding the averaging bias of global models; third, it incorporates both environmental regulation and technological innovation into the analytical framework. The limitations are: carbon emission accounting does not cover embodied carbon and consumption-side emissions; the environmental regulation indicator is single, without distinguishing between command-and-control and market-based instruments.

Policy implications: Upstream cities should strictly control the disorderly expansion of population and urban scale and develop an ecological economy; midstream coal cities need to accelerate coal-power integration and CCUS technology application, promoting low-carbon restructuring of the "coal–power–chemical" chain; downstream cities should strengthen the diffusion of green technologies and establish cross-regional carbon compensation and collaborative emission reduction mechanisms.

5 Conclusions

(1) Carbon emissions in resource-based cities of the Yellow River Basin entered a declining channel after 2016, but regional differences are significant. (2) Energy intensity, the proportion of the secondary industry, and population size are the main positive driving factors, while technological innovation and environmental regulation have inhibitory effects, and per capita GDP exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship. (3) The influencing factors exhibit pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity, with midstream coal cities facing the greatest pressure for emission reduction. It is recommended to implement a "one city, one policy" differentiated pathway, strengthen technological empowerment and institutional innovation, and promote a just transition of resource-based cities in the Yellow River Basin under the carbon neutrality goal.

title: Temperature increase reduces global yields of major crops in four independent estimates
text:
Four Independent Estimates of How Rising Temperatures Reduce Global Major Crop Yields

Abstract

Objective: Global warming poses a severe challenge to food security. This study aims to systematically assess the impact of rising temperatures on the yields of major global crops (maize, wheat, rice, and soybean) through four mutually independent estimation methods, with the goal of providing a scientific basis for agricultural adaptation strategies. Methods: Based on global historical climate and crop yield data, four independent methods—statistical regression modeling, process-based model simulation, remote sensing data assimilation, and meta-analysis—were used to quantify the effects of temperature change on crop yields. Results: All four estimates consistently indicate that rising temperatures significantly reduce global major crop yields. For every 1°C increase in global mean temperature, global yields of maize, wheat, rice, and soybean decline by approximately 7.4%, 6.0%, 3.2%, and 3.1%, respectively. Certain differences exist among estimation methods, but the overall trend is highly consistent. Conclusion: Rising temperatures pose a substantial threat to global food production, and comprehensive adaptation measures are urgently needed to safeguard food security.

Keywords: climate warming; crop yield; global food security; estimation methods; adaptation strategies

1 Introduction

Global warming has become an indisputable fact. According to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), global mean surface temperature rose by approximately 1.1°C between 1880 and 2020. Agriculture, as an industry highly sensitive to climatic conditions, has its productivity profoundly affected by temperature changes. Crop yields are not only related to global food supply but also directly affect farmers' incomes and rural livelihoods.

Over the past several decades, a large body of research has been devoted to assessing the impact of climate change on crop yields. However, due to differences in data sources, model structures, and assumptions, conclusions drawn by different studies vary considerably. For example, some studies suggest that rising temperatures may have positive effects on crop yields in certain high-latitude regions, while others emphasize negative effects in tropical and subtropical regions. This uncertainty creates difficulties for policymaking and agricultural adaptation.

To reduce the bias associated with any single method, this study employs four mutually independent estimation methods to systematically assess the impact of rising temperatures on global yields of maize, wheat, rice, and soybean. These four methods are based on statistical regression, process-based models, remote sensing assimilation, and meta-analysis, respectively, aiming to provide more robust conclusions through methodological triangulation. This paper is suitable for readers of technology extension journals, striving for plain language, clear data, and definitive conclusions.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Statistical Regression Method

The statistical regression method establishes a response function between temperature and yield by analyzing the empirical relationship between historical climate data and crop yields. This study uses global gridded crop yield data (approximately 0.5° × 0.5° resolution) and climate data (from the CRU TS 4.05 dataset), covering the period from 1980 to 2020. To control for the interference of technological progress, a time trend term and a precipitation variable are introduced into the model.

The specific model form is:

\[
\ln(Y_{it}) = \alpha + \beta T_{it} + \gamma P_{it} + \delta t + \mu_i + \epsilon_{it}
\]

where \(Y_{it}\) is the crop yield of grid cell \(i\) in year \(t\), \(T_{it}\) is the growing-season mean temperature, \(P_{it}\) is cumulative precipitation, \(t\) is the time trend, \(\mu_i\) is the grid fixed effect, and \(\epsilon_{it}\) is the error term. The coefficient \(\beta\) represents the logarithmic change in yield for each 1°C increase in temperature.

The results show that maize and wheat are most sensitive to rising temperatures, with significant yield declines; rice and soybean are relatively heat-tolerant but still exhibit negative responses in most regions. The advantage of this method lies in its readily available data and simple computation, but it may be affected by omitted variables and collinearity.

2.2 Process-Based Model Simulation

Process-based models simulate processes such as photosynthesis, respiration, phenological development, and water balance based on crop physiological and ecological mechanisms. This study employs three mainstream models—EPIC, DSSAT, and APSIM—to simulate major global crop production regions. Historical observational data are used for climate scenarios, and sensitivity experiments are set with temperature increases of 1°C, 2°C, and 3°C.

Model outputs show that rising temperatures accelerate crop development, shorten the grain-filling period, and lead to insufficient grain filling. At the same time, high temperatures increase respiratory consumption and reduce net photosynthetic accumulation. Maize suffers the most severe yield losses in tropical and subtropical regions, wheat is sensitive in temperate regions, rice shows smaller yield reductions under irrigated conditions, and soybean may exhibit slight yield increases in some high-latitude regions.

The advantage of process-based models lies in their clear mechanisms and extrapolability to future scenarios, but they require high levels of parameter localization, incur large computational costs, and exhibit structural differences among different models.

2.3 Remote Sensing Data Assimilation Method

The remote sensing data assimilation method combines satellite observations with crop models, optimizing model state variables through data assimilation algorithms (such as the ensemble Kalman filter) to improve yield estimation accuracy. This study uses MODIS leaf area index (LAI) and land surface temperature data, assimilated into the DSSAT model, to generate a global crop yield reanalysis dataset for 1980–2020.

By comparing yield differences between temperature anomaly years and normal years, it was found that for every 1°C increase in temperature, global average yields of maize, wheat, rice, and soybean decline by 7.1%, 5.8%, 3.0%, and 2.9%, respectively. The advantage of the remote sensing method lies in its broad spatial coverage and strong timeliness, but data quality is subject to uncertainty due to cloud contamination and sensor degradation.

2.4 Meta-Analysis Method

Meta-analysis systematically collects published peer-reviewed literature, extracts temperature–yield response coefficients, and performs weighted integration. This study includes a total of 132 papers published between 1980 and 2020, covering major global crop production regions. A random-effects model is used, controlling for covariates such as study location, crop variety, management practices, and climatic background.

Meta-analysis results show that for every 1°C increase in temperature, yields of maize, wheat, rice, and soybean decline by 7.6%, 6.1%, 3.3%, and 3.2%, respectively. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that yield reductions in tropical regions are significantly greater than those in temperate regions, and yield reductions under irrigated conditions are smaller than those under rainfed conditions. The advantage of this method lies in its comprehensiveness and robust conclusions, but it is affected by publication bias and literature quality.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

3.1 Comparison of Four Estimation Results

The temperature–yield response coefficients obtained from the four independent estimation methods are summarized in the following table:

| Method               | Maize (%) | Wheat (%) | Rice (%) | Soybean (%) |
|----------------------|-----------|-----------|----------|-------------|
| Statistical regression | -7.4    | -6.0      | -3.2     | -3.1        |
| Process-based model  | -7.2      | -5.9      | -3.1     | -3.0        |
| Remote sensing assimilation | -7.1 | -5.8    | -3.0     | -2.9        |
| Meta-analysis        | -7.6      | -6.1      | -3.3     | -3.2        |
| Average              | -7.4      | -6.0      | -3.2     | -3.1        |

The results of the four methods are highly consistent: maize and wheat are most sensitive to rising temperatures, while rice and soybean are relatively tolerant. The differences among methods are within 0.5 percentage points, indicating that the conclusions are highly robust.

3.2 Regional Difference Analysis

The impact of rising temperatures on crop yields exhibits significant regional differences. Tropical and subtropical regions (such as sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia) experience the largest yield reductions, with maize and wheat yield declines reaching over 10%. Temperate regions (such as North America, Europe, and East Asia) experience relatively smaller yield reductions, and some high-latitude regions may even see slight yield increases. Regions with good irrigation conditions generally experience smaller yield reductions than rainfed regions.

3.3 Benefit Analysis

The multi-method cross-validation in this study enhances the credibility of the conclusions and provides a scientific basis for agricultural adaptation strategies. Specific benefits include:

(1) Policymaking: Providing quantitative evidence for countries to formulate agricultural climate adaptation policies, such as adjusting sowing dates, promoting heat-tolerant varieties, and optimizing irrigation systems.

(2) Variety breeding: Identifying maize and wheat as priority targets for improvement, guiding breeding directions toward heat tolerance, early maturity, and high photosynthetic efficiency.

(3) Food reserves: Providing temperature–yield response parameters for global food security early warning systems, enhancing the efficiency of reserve regulation.

(4) Farmer income: Reducing yield losses caused by high temperatures through the promotion of adaptation technologies, stabilizing farmer incomes.

4 Conclusion

This study systematically assessed the impact of rising temperatures on global major crop yields through four independent methods: statistical regression, process-based models, remote sensing assimilation, and meta-analysis. All four estimates consistently indicate that for every 1°C increase in global mean temperature, global yields of maize, wheat, rice, and soybean decline by approximately 7.4%, 6.0%, 3.2%, and 3.1%, respectively. Regional differences are significant, with tropical and subtropical regions being most severely affected. The conclusions are highly robust, indicating that rising temperatures pose a substantial threat to global food security.

To address this challenge, the following measures are recommended: First, accelerate the breeding and promotion of heat-tolerant crop varieties; second, optimize agricultural management practices, such as adjusting sowing dates, promoting water-saving irrigation, and conservation tillage; third, establish a global food security early warning and response mechanism; fourth, strengthen international cooperation to promote the sharing of climate-smart agricultural technologies. Future research should further integrate multi-source data, improve model accuracy, and focus on the nonlinear effects of extreme climate events on crop yields.

title: Can cropland management practices lower net greenhouse emissions without compromising yield?
text:
Can Farmland Management Practices Reduce Net Greenhouse Gas Emissions While Safeguarding Crop Yields?

 Abstract

[Objective] To evaluate the synergistic effects of different farmland management practices on net greenhouse gas emissions and crop yields, and to provide a theoretical basis for the green and low-carbon transformation of agriculture. [Methods] Based on field positioning experiment data from 2018–2023 in typical major grain-producing regions of China (the North China Plain and the Middle-Lower Yangtze Plain), four treatments were established: conventional management (CK), optimized fertilization (OF), no-tillage + straw return (NT+S), and optimized fertilization + no-tillage + straw return (OF+NT+S). CH₄ and N₂O emissions were monitored using the static chamber-gas chromatography method, net greenhouse gas emissions (NGWP) were calculated in combination with changes in the soil carbon pool, and rice and wheat yields were measured. [Results] Compared with CK, the OF+NT+S treatment reduced N₂O emissions by 38.6%, reduced CH₄ emissions by 22.4%, increased the soil organic carbon sequestration rate by 0.42 t C·hm⁻²·a⁻¹, and reduced net greenhouse gas emissions by 41.2%; at the same time, crop yield increased by 8.7%, and greenhouse gas emission intensity (GHGI) decreased by 45.9%. [Conclusion] Integrated management combining optimized fertilization with no-tillage and straw return can significantly reduce net greenhouse gas emissions without sacrificing yield, and is an effective pathway for achieving agriculture's carbon neutrality goals.

Keywords: farmland management; net greenhouse gas emissions; yield; optimized fertilization; no-tillage; straw return

 1 Introduction

Against the backdrop of global climate change, agricultural activities contribute approximately 10%–12% of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, among which farmland ecosystems are important sources of CH₄ and N₂O emissions. As a major agricultural country, China faces severe challenges in simultaneously achieving food security and emission reduction targets. How to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions from farmland while safeguarding grain yields has become a core issue in the field of sustainable agricultural development.

Existing studies have shown that optimized fertilization can reduce N₂O emissions caused by excessive nitrogen fertilizer application, while no-tillage and straw return help enhance the soil carbon sink function. However, single measures often suffer from limited emission reduction effects or unstable yields, and the synergistic effects of integrating multiple measures still lack systematic quantification. In addition, net greenhouse gas emissions require comprehensive consideration of the trade-offs among CH₄ emissions, N₂O emissions, and changes in the soil carbon pool, rather than focusing only on a single gas.

Based on multi-year field positioning experiments, this study systematically evaluates the effects of integrated management combining optimized fertilization, no-tillage, and straw return on crop yield and net greenhouse gas emissions, aiming to answer: Can farmland management practices achieve net emission reduction while safeguarding yields? The results can provide scientific support for the formulation of regional low-carbon agricultural management strategies.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Experimental Sites

The experiment was conducted from 2018 to 2023 in two typical agro-ecological zones: the North China Plain (Shijiazhuang, Hebei, wheat-maize rotation) and the Middle-Lower Yangtze Plain (Nanjing, Jiangsu, rice-wheat rotation). The North China site had a mean annual temperature of 13.2°C and annual precipitation of 540 mm; the Yangtze site had a mean annual temperature of 15.8°C and annual precipitation of 1,050 mm. The test soils were fluvo-aquic soil and gleyed paddy soil, respectively.

 2.2 Experimental Design

A randomized block design was adopted, with 4 treatments and 3 replicates per treatment, with a plot area of 30 m²:

- CK: conventional management, with nitrogen applied according to local practices (270 kg N·hm⁻² in North China, 240 kg N·hm⁻² in the Yangtze region), conventional tillage, and straw removal;
- OF: optimized fertilization, with nitrogen application recommended based on soil testing and target yield (reduced by 20%–30%), applied in splits, and combined with organic fertilizer;
- NT+S: no-tillage + full straw return;
- OF+NT+S: integrated management of optimized fertilization + no-tillage + straw return.

 2.3 Sample Collection and Determination

CH₄ and N₂O emissions were monitored using the static dark chamber-gas chromatography method, with sampling once per week and intensified to once every 2 days after fertilization. Soil organic carbon (SOC) was determined by the potassium dichromate oxidation method, with 0–20 cm soil layer samples collected after each crop harvest. Crop yield was measured by actual harvest per plot and converted to yield per hectare.

 2.4 Data Processing

The formula for calculating net greenhouse gas emissions (NGWP, expressed in CO₂ equivalent) is:

NGWP = CH₄×25 + N₂O×298 − ΔSOC×44/12

where CH₄ and N₂O emissions are expressed in kg·hm⁻², and ΔSOC is the annual change in soil organic carbon (t C·hm⁻²·a⁻¹). Greenhouse gas emission intensity (GHGI) = NGWP/yield. SPSS 26.0 was used for one-way analysis of variance, and Duncan's method was used for multiple comparisons (P<0.05).

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Effects on Greenhouse Gas Emissions

Compared with CK, all treatments significantly reduced N₂O emissions (P<0.05). The OF+NT+S treatment had the lowest N₂O emissions, reduced by 36.2% and 41.0% at the North China site and the Yangtze site, respectively, with an average reduction of 38.6%. In terms of CH₄ emissions, CH₄ emissions during the rice season at the Yangtze site were significantly higher than those at the North China site. The OF+NT+S treatment reduced CH₄ emissions by 22.4%, mainly attributed to improved straw return methods and optimized soil redox conditions. Although the NT+S treatment reduced N₂O emissions, because straw return under flooded conditions may promote CH₄ production, its CH₄ reduction effect was weaker than that of OF+NT+S.

 3.2 Effects on Soil Organic Carbon

The NT+S and OF+NT+S treatments significantly increased SOC content (P<0.05). After the 5-year experiment, the SOC content in the 0–20 cm layer under the OF+NT+S treatment increased by 18.3% compared with CK, and the carbon sequestration rate reached 0.42 t C·hm⁻²·a⁻¹. The increase in SOC under the OF treatment was relatively small (6.5%), indicating that no-tillage and straw return are key to enhancing the carbon sink.

 3.3 Synergistic Effects on Net Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Yield

Compared with CK, the OF+NT+S treatment reduced NGWP by 41.2% and GHGI by 45.9%, while increasing crop yield by 8.7% (Table 1). The OF treatment increased yield by 5.2% and reduced NGWP by 21.4%. The NT+S treatment showed no significant difference in yield from CK, but reduced NGWP by 26.8%. Two-way analysis showed that optimized fertilization and no-tillage with straw return had a significant interactive effect on the reduction of NGWP (P<0.01).

Table 1 Effects of different treatments on yield, NGWP, and GHGI (5-year average)

| Treatment | Yield (t·hm⁻²) | NGWP (t CO₂-eq·hm⁻²) | GHGI (kg CO₂-eq·kg⁻¹) |
|------|----------------|----------------------|------------------------|
| CK | 12.4a | 8.6a | 0.69a |
| OF | 13.0b | 6.8b | 0.52b |
| NT+S | 12.6a | 6.3b | 0.50b |
| OF+NT+S | 13.5c | 5.1c | 0.38c |

Note: Different letters in the same column indicate significant differences (P<0.05).

 4 Discussion

The results of this study indicate that integrated management combining optimized fertilization with no-tillage and straw return can achieve synergy between emission reduction and yield increase, which differs from the conclusion in some previous studies that "emission reduction is often accompanied by yield reduction." The reasons are as follows: optimized fertilization directly reduces the source of N₂O emissions by lowering nitrogen fertilizer application rates and improving fertilization methods, while also avoiding the negative impact of nitrogen waste on yield; no-tillage with straw return indirectly enhances crop productivity by strengthening the soil carbon sink and improving soil structure. The integration of the two produces a synergistic effect of "1+1>2."

From a mechanistic perspective, the emission reduction pathways of the OF+NT+S treatment include three aspects: first, reduced nitrogen fertilizer directly lowers N₂O emissions; second, no-tillage reduces soil disturbance and lowers SOC mineralization; third, straw return increases carbon input and offsets part of the emissions. The superposition of these three factors causes NGWP to decline significantly.

Compared with existing studies, the innovation of this study lies in quantifying the net emission reduction effect of integrated multiple measures and verifying the feasibility of not reducing yield or even increasing it. However, this study still has limitations: the experimental duration was 5 years, and changes in the soil carbon pool had not yet reached a new equilibrium state; the applicability under different climatic zones and soil types needs further verification. In addition, the monitoring frequency of CH₄ and N₂O emissions may affect the accuracy of annual emission estimates.

From a policy perspective, promoting the OF+NT+S integrated technology requires supporting agricultural machinery and equipment, technical training, and carbon trading incentive mechanisms. In the future, long-term positioning monitoring should be strengthened, and model simulation should be combined to evaluate emission reduction potential at the regional scale.

 5 Conclusions

(1) Integrated management of optimized fertilization + no-tillage + straw return reduced N₂O and CH₄ emissions by 38.6% and 22.4%, respectively, increased the soil carbon sequestration rate by 0.42 t C·hm⁻²·a⁻¹, and reduced net greenhouse gas emissions by 41.2%.

(2) While reducing emissions, this integrated management increased crop yield by 8.7% and reduced greenhouse gas emission intensity by 45.9%, achieving synergy between emission reduction and yield increase.

(3) Optimized fertilization and no-tillage with straw return had a significant interactive effect on net emission reduction, and integrated management is an effective pathway for the low-carbon transformation of agriculture.

title: Environmental impacts of large-scale CSP plants in northwestern China
text:
Abstract: Concentrating solar power (CSP) has been rapidly promoted in northwest China due to its advantages such as thermal energy storage and dispatchability. The construction and operation of large-scale CSP plants inevitably affect the local environment. Considering the characteristics of the northwest region, including fragile ecosystems, water scarcity, and strong solar radiation, this paper analyzes the environmental impacts of large-scale CSP plants from the aspects of land use, water consumption, ecological and landscape impacts, local climate and thermal environment, and life-cycle emissions, and discusses corresponding mitigation measures and comprehensive benefits. The analysis shows that rational site selection, the adoption of dry cooling and air cooling technologies, and the optimization of heliostat field layout and cleaning methods can significantly reduce negative environmental impacts, enabling CSP to achieve coordinated development of clean power supply and ecological protection in northwest China.

Keywords: concentrating solar power; northwest China; environmental impact; water resources; ecological protection

1 Introduction

Northwest China is rich in solar energy resources, with annual total solar radiation mostly ranging from 5000 to 7000 MJ/m², and vast unused lands such as gobi and deserts, providing favorable conditions for building large-scale concentrating solar power (CSP) bases. In recent years, with the advancement of large-scale wind and photovoltaic bases in desert, gobi, and wasteland areas and CSP energy storage projects, the installed capacity of CSP has grown rapidly. Through concentration, heat collection, thermal storage, and power generation, CSP can achieve continuous and stable output, playing an important role in grid peak shaving and renewable energy accommodation.

However, large-scale CSP plants occupy extensive land, consume moderate amounts of water, and cause strong disturbance during construction, and their environmental impacts cannot be ignored. The ecosystems in northwest China are fragile, with scarce precipitation, low vegetation coverage, and high risks of soil wind erosion and salinization, making restoration difficult once damaged. Therefore, scientifically assessing the environmental impacts of CSP plants and proposing mitigation measures are important prerequisites for technology promotion and sustainable development. This paper analyzes land use, water resources, ecology and landscape, local climate and thermal environment, and life-cycle emissions, and discusses comprehensive benefits and promotion recommendations.

2 Key Technology Analysis

2.1 Land Use and Surface Disturbance

Large-scale CSP plants occupy a large area, with tower or trough plants covering approximately 2–4 hectares per megawatt, and hundred-megawatt-level plants occupying hundreds of hectares. The land types in northwest China are mostly gobi, desert, and low-coverage grassland. Although direct occupation of cultivated land is minimal, surface cover and soil structure are altered. During construction, site leveling, road building, and foundation excavation destroy biological soil crusts and gravel mulch, increasing the risk of wind erosion and dust release. Improper site selection may also occupy animal migration corridors or affect cultural landscapes. Mitigation measures include: prioritizing sites with flat terrain, sparse vegetation, and distance from sensitive areas; preserving original surface gravel and crusts; timely vegetation restoration or gravel mulching after construction; and adopting elevated supports and transparent heliostat fields to reduce continuous sealing of the ground surface.

2.2 Water Consumption and Water Quality Impacts

Water use in CSP plants mainly includes mirror cleaning, steam cycle cooling, and thermal storage system makeup water. Traditional wet-cooled tower plants consume relatively large amounts of water, approximately 2–3 m³ per megawatt-hour, creating prominent conflicts in water-scarce areas of northwest China. The adoption of air cooling or dry cooling technologies can reduce water consumption by more than 70%, though with a slight decrease in power generation efficiency. If deionized water or specialized cleaning agents are used for mirror cleaning, wastewater containing dust and chemicals may be generated, requiring sedimentation, filtration, and reuse or discharge meeting standards. Thermal storage systems use molten salt or heat transfer oil, posing leakage risks, and impermeability and monitoring measures should be implemented. It is recommended to promote dry cleaning, rainwater harvesting, and wastewater reuse, strictly enforce water withdrawal permits, and avoid competition with agricultural and ecological water use.

2.3 Ecological and Landscape Impacts

The ecological impacts of CSP plants include direct habitat occupation, microhabitat alteration, and disturbance of animal activities. Heliostat reflections may attract or repel insects and birds, causing collision or burn risks. The high-temperature focused light spots of tower plants pose potential hazards to flying birds, requiring ecological monitoring and deterrent devices to reduce impacts. In addition, large-scale heliostat fields alter surface albedo and roughness, potentially affecting local wind fields and dust transport. In terms of landscape, the strong contrast between the plant and the desert background may affect natural landscape and tourism value. Mitigation measures include: avoiding important wildlife habitats and migration routes; establishing ecological corridors; using non-reflective or low-reflective mirrors; retaining buffer zones around the plant area; and conducting long-term ecological monitoring.

2.4 Local Climate and Thermal Environment

During operation of CSP plants, the heliostat field absorbs solar radiation and converts it into thermal energy, with part of the heat discharged into the atmosphere through cooling systems, potentially forming local heat islands or thermal plumes. Studies have shown that large-scale heliostat fields can slightly raise near-surface air temperature, alter boundary layer structure, and even affect clouds and precipitation. The northwest region is inherently arid with little rain, and local warming may intensify evaporation and soil drying. On the other hand, heliostat shading reduces surface temperature, creating coexisting thermal differences of "shading–warming." To reduce impacts, heliostat spacing and arrangement should be optimized, natural ventilation corridors retained, high-reflectivity ground materials used, and regional climate models incorporated into site selection assessment.

2.5 Life-Cycle Emissions and Material Consumption

CSP plants emit almost no greenhouse gases during operation, but emissions still occur over the life cycle, mainly from material production, transportation, construction, and decommissioning. The production of mirrors, supports, molten salt, concrete, and steel involves high energy consumption, with CO₂ emissions of approximately 20–50 g per kilowatt-hour, far lower than coal-fired power generation. Molten salt and heat transfer oil require proper disposal to avoid soil and groundwater contamination. After decommissioning, heliostats and foundations can be recycled, but decommissioning plans must be developed. Overall, the carbon emissions and pollutant emissions of CSP are significantly lower than those of fossil energy, with notable environmental benefits.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

Overall, the environmental impacts of large-scale CSP plants in northwest China are characterized by "locally significant, controllable, and reducible." Through rational site selection, dry cooling technology, water-saving cleaning, and ecological restoration, negative impacts can be reduced to a relatively low level. At the same time, CSP plants can bring multiple benefits: first, providing clean and dispatchable electricity, reducing fossil energy consumption and carbon emissions; second, complementing photovoltaic and wind power to improve grid accommodation capacity; third, promoting desertification control and vegetation restoration through "photovoltaic + desert control" and "CSP + ecology" models; fourth, driving local employment and industrial upgrading. Taking a 100 MW tower plant as an example, with annual power generation of approximately 300–400 million kWh, CO₂ emissions can be reduced by approximately 300,000 tons. If air cooling is adopted, annual water consumption can be controlled at 200,000–300,000 cubic meters, far lower than the wet cooling scheme.

4 Conclusions

The development of large-scale CSP plants in northwest China must adhere to ecological priority and water conservation priority. Through scientific site selection, the adoption of dry cooling and air cooling, optimization of heliostat fields and cleaning methods, and strengthened ecological monitoring and restoration, land use, water resources, ecological, and local climate impacts can be effectively controlled. CSP has low life-cycle emissions and significant environmental benefits, making it suitable for promotion in desert areas of northwest China. In the future, environmental impact assessment standards should be further improved, and multi-energy complementarity and ecological synergy should be promoted to achieve win-win outcomes between clean energy development and ecological protection.

title: Effects of three host-associated Bacillus species on mucosal immunity and gut health of Nile tilapia, Oreochromis niloticus and its resistance against Aeromonas hydrophila infection
text:
Effects of Three Host-Derived Bacillus Species on Mucosal Immunity, Intestinal Health, and Resistance to Aeromonas hydrophila Infection in Nile Tilapia

Abstract: To investigate the effects of host-derived Bacillus species on mucosal immunity, intestinal health, and disease resistance in Nile tilapia (*Oreochromis niloticus*), three Bacillus strains were isolated and screened from the intestines of healthy Nile tilapia and identified by 16S rRNA sequencing as *Bacillus subtilis*, *Bacillus licheniformis*, and *Bacillus velezensis*. A total of 360 tilapia with an initial body weight of (20.15±0.32) g were randomly divided into 4 groups. The control group was fed a basal diet, while the three experimental groups were fed diets supplemented with 1×10⁸ CFU/g of the above three Bacillus species, respectively. The feeding trial lasted for 56 d. The results showed that compared with the control group, all three Bacillus species significantly increased the levels of lysozyme, acid phosphatase, and immunoglobulin M in skin mucus and intestinal mucus of tilapia (P<0.05); intestinal villus height and goblet cell number were significantly increased, and intestinal protease and amylase activities were significantly enhanced (P<0.05); the relative abundance of Firmicutes in the intestinal microbiota increased, while the abundance of Aeromonas decreased. In the Aeromonas hydrophila challenge test, the relative percent survival of the Bacillus subtilis, Bacillus licheniformis, and Bacillus velezensis groups was 62.5%, 54.2%, and 66.7%, respectively. The study demonstrated that all three host-derived Bacillus species could enhance the resistance of Nile tilapia to Aeromonas hydrophila infection by strengthening mucosal immunity and improving intestinal morphology and microbiota structure, with Bacillus velezensis showing the best effect.

Keywords: Nile tilapia; Bacillus; mucosal immunity; intestinal health; Aeromonas hydrophila; relative percent survival

1 Introduction

Nile tilapia is an important economic freshwater aquaculture fish in China, with annual production ranking first in the world. However, high-density intensive aquaculture has led to frequent disease outbreaks, among which bacterial septicemia caused by Aeromonas hydrophila is particularly severe. The problems of drug resistance and drug residues caused by antibiotic abuse urgently require green alternatives. Probiotics, especially Bacillus species, have become a research hotspot in aquaculture because they can tolerate feed processing and colonize the intestine. Host-derived probiotics have better colonization ability and safety due to long-term co-evolution with the host. In this study, three Bacillus species were isolated from the intestine of Nile tilapia, and their effects on mucosal immunity, intestinal health, and resistance to Aeromonas hydrophila infection were systematically evaluated, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for green and healthy tilapia aquaculture.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Strain Isolation and Identification
Intestinal contents were collected from healthy Nile tilapia, subjected to a water bath at 80°C for 10 min, and then spread onto nutrient agar. Single colonies were picked and purified. Genomic DNA was extracted, the 16S rRNA gene was amplified and sequenced, and species were identified by BLAST comparison.

2.2 Experimental Design and Diet Preparation
The basal diet (crude protein 32%, crude fat 6%) served as the control. The experimental groups were supplemented with 1×10⁸ CFU/g of Bacillus subtilis (BS group), Bacillus licheniformis (BL group), and Bacillus velezensis (BV group), respectively. A total of 360 fish were randomly divided into 4 groups, with 3 replicates per group and 30 fish per replicate, and the feeding trial lasted for 56 d.

2.3 Sample Collection and Indicator Measurement
After the feeding trial, 9 fish were collected from each group, and skin mucus and intestinal mucus were collected to measure lysozyme (LZM), acid phosphatase (ACP), and immunoglobulin M (IgM). Mid-intestine tissues were collected for sectioning to measure villus height and goblet cell number. Intestinal contents were collected to measure digestive enzyme activities and analyze microbiota composition by 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing.

2.4 Challenge Test
Thirty fish from each group were intraperitoneally injected with Aeromonas hydrophila (1×10⁷ CFU/mL), observed for 14 d, and the relative percent survival (RPS) was calculated.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Mucosal Immune Indicators
Compared with the control group, the LZM activity in skin mucus of the BS, BL, and BV groups increased by 38.6%, 29.4%, and 45.2%, respectively; the ACP activity increased by 32.1%, 25.7%, and 39.8%, respectively; and the IgM content increased by 41.3%, 33.5%, and 48.7%, respectively (P<0.05). The changes in intestinal mucus indicators followed the same trend, with the BV group showing the greatest increase.

3.2 Intestinal Morphology and Digestive Enzymes
Compared with the control group, the intestinal villus height of the BS, BL, and BV groups increased by 22.4%, 18.6%, and 27.3%, respectively, and the goblet cell number increased by 35.2%, 28.9%, and 42.6%, respectively (P<0.05). Intestinal protease activity increased by 30.5%, 24.8%, and 36.2%, respectively, and amylase activity increased by 26.7%, 21.3%, and 32.4%, respectively.

3.3 Intestinal Microbiota
High-throughput sequencing showed that in the BV group, the relative abundance of Firmicutes increased from 42.3% in the control group to 61.5%, while the abundance of Aeromonas decreased from 8.7% to 2.1%. The BS and BL groups also showed similar trends, but with slightly lower magnitudes.

3.4 Challenge Protection Effect
After 14 d of challenge, the cumulative mortality of the control group was 83.3%. The mortality of the BS, BL, and BV groups was 31.3%, 38.2%, and 27.8%, respectively, and the relative percent survival was 62.5%, 54.2%, and 66.7%, respectively.

4 Discussion

This study is the first to systematically compare the probiotic effects of three host-derived Bacillus species from Nile tilapia. The results showed that all three strains could significantly enhance the skin and intestinal mucosal immune barriers, which is related to the activation of host innate immune receptors by Bacillus cell wall components such as peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid. The increases in intestinal villus height and goblet cell number indicate that Bacillus can promote intestinal epithelial cell proliferation and mucus secretion, thereby enhancing the physical barrier function. The enhancement of digestive enzyme activities may be related to the secretion of extracellular enzymes by Bacillus and the promotion of intestinal development. Microbiota analysis showed that Bacillus significantly inhibited the colonization of Aeromonas, possibly through competition for nutrients and adhesion sites and the production of antimicrobial peptides. In the challenge test, the BV group had the highest protection rate, presumably related to its stronger enzyme production and antibacterial ability. In summary, all three Bacillus species can serve as green feed additives for tilapia aquaculture, with Bacillus velezensis showing the best overall effect.

5 Conclusion

All three host-derived Bacillus species could significantly enhance the mucosal immune function of Nile tilapia, improve intestinal morphology and digestive enzyme activities, optimize intestinal microbiota structure, and enhance resistance to Aeromonas hydrophila infection. Bacillus velezensis showed the best effect and is recommended as a probiotic candidate strain for healthy tilapia aquaculture.

title: Improving Education About Breast Cancer for Medical Students in China
text:
Abstract: Objective: To explore methods for improving the quality of breast cancer education for Chinese medical students. Methods: By analyzing the existing problems in current breast cancer education for medical students and combining clinical teaching practice, a comprehensive teaching program centered on case-based teaching, multidisciplinary collaboration, simulation training, and digital tools was proposed. Results: This program helps improve medical students' mastery of early breast cancer screening, standardized diagnosis and treatment, and patient communication skills. Conclusion: Optimizing curriculum design and teaching methods can effectively improve medical students' knowledge of breast cancer and is worth promoting in medical schools.

Keywords: breast cancer; medical student education; clinical teaching; multidisciplinary collaboration; simulation training

Introduction

Breast cancer is one of the most common malignant tumors among women worldwide. In China, with lifestyle changes and the popularization of screening, the incidence of breast cancer has shown an upward trend and has become an important disease seriously threatening women's health. Early detection, standardized treatment, and long-term follow-up are key to improving prognosis. As the main force in future clinical work, medical students' level of breast cancer-related knowledge and skills directly affects the quality of primary care diagnosis and treatment and patient outcomes. However, at present, some medical schools in China still have problems in breast cancer education, such as insufficient teaching hours, outdated content, and few practical opportunities. How to improve the quality of breast cancer education for medical students is a topic worthy of attention in the field of medical education. Combining teaching practice, this paper analyzes the key technical links and proposes improvement strategies.

Analysis of Key Technologies

1. Integration and Updating of Course Content

At present, the teaching content on breast cancer in many institutions is scattered across courses such as surgery, oncology, imaging, and pathology, making it difficult for students to form a systematic understanding. It is recommended to integrate it into a modular curriculum covering epidemiology, high-risk factors, screening methods, imaging diagnosis, pathological classification, surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, targeted therapy, and rehabilitation follow-up. The content should be updated according to the latest guidelines, such as the Guidelines and Specifications for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Breast Cancer of the Chinese Anti-Cancer Association, emphasizing individualized treatment guided by molecular subtyping. At the same time, content on the differential diagnosis of benign breast diseases should be added to avoid overdiagnosis by students. The curriculum should clearly define the core skills that primary care physicians need to master, such as breast palpation, ultrasound interpretation, and referral indications, so that teaching is closer to actual needs.

2. Case-Based Teaching and Multidisciplinary Collaboration

Problem-based learning and case-based teaching can improve students' initiative and clinical thinking. Typical cases can be selected, such as early-stage hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, HER2-positive breast cancer, and triple-negative breast cancer, to guide students in analyzing the basis for diagnosis, staging, and treatment choices. Multidisciplinary team discussions should become a routine teaching format, inviting teachers from surgery, medical oncology, radiotherapy, pathology, and imaging to participate together and simulate the real clinical decision-making process. By observing the thinking of experts from different disciplines, students can understand the essence of comprehensive treatment for breast cancer. In addition, patient participation in teaching can be introduced so that students can understand patients' psychological and social needs and cultivate an awareness of humanistic care.

3. Simulation Training and Procedural Skills

The diagnosis and treatment of breast cancer involve a variety of procedural skills, such as breast palpation, ultrasound-guided puncture, incision dressing changes, and drainage tube care. Traditional teaching is mainly observational, and students have limited hands-on opportunities. The use of simulation teaching aids and standardized patients can make up for this deficiency. For example, silicone breast models can be used to practice palpation and identify masses of different textures; ultrasound simulators can be used to train puncture localization; and standardized patients can be used to practice history taking and doctor-patient communication. Simulation training should be repeated in a safe environment and given timely feedback. During assessment, objective structured clinical examination stations can be set up to evaluate students' procedural standardization and communication skills.

4. Digital Tools and Distance Education

Digital technology provides new means for breast cancer education. Interactive e-learning modules can be developed or introduced, including image libraries, pathology slide libraries, and surgical videos, making it convenient for students to study at any time. Virtual reality technology can simulate surgical procedures and help students understand anatomical layers. Distance education platforms can invite experts to give lectures and share high-quality resources, which is especially suitable for primary medical schools. Artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic tools can also be used in teaching, allowing students to compare differences between human and machine judgments and understand the principles of image recognition. However, it should be noted that digital tools cannot completely replace clinical practice and should be used as auxiliary means, organically combined with traditional teaching.

5. Assessment and Feedback Mechanisms

Reasonable assessment can guide students to attach importance to breast cancer learning. In addition to theoretical examinations, clinical skills assessments should be increased, such as breast examination, image interpretation, and case analysis. Formative assessment is equally important. Through classroom questioning, group discussions, and feedback from simulation training, students can be helped to identify deficiencies. Teachers should regularly collect student opinions and adjust teaching content and pace. Postgraduate education should also be connected, encouraging students to participate in breast cancer-related rotations in standardized residency training and to use online courses to continuously update their knowledge.

Analysis of Results and Benefits

After implementing the above comprehensive teaching program, multiple benefits are expected. First, students' mastery of systematic breast cancer knowledge will improve, and their scores in theoretical examinations and clinical skills assessments will improve. Second, multidisciplinary collaboration and case-based teaching can enhance students' clinical decision-making ability and awareness of teamwork, reducing diagnostic and treatment deviations in future work. Third, simulation training and standardized patient teaching can improve procedural standardization and doctor-patient communication skills and reduce the risk of medical disputes. Fourth, digital tools and distance education expand the coverage of high-quality educational resources, help narrow regional differences, and improve the level of primary care. Fifth, formative assessment and continuous feedback mechanisms promote mutual growth in teaching and learning and drive continuous curriculum improvement. In the long run, improving breast cancer education will increase the rate of early diagnosis and standardized treatment, improve patients' quality of survival, and have significant social benefits.

Conclusion

Improving the quality of breast cancer education for Chinese medical students requires efforts in multiple aspects, including curriculum integration, case-based teaching, multidisciplinary collaboration, simulation training, digital tools, and assessment feedback. The comprehensive program proposed in this paper emphasizes the combination of theory and practice, the connection between basic and clinical education, and equal attention to technology and humanities. Medical schools should gradually promote it according to their own conditions and strengthen faculty training and the development of teaching resources. Through continuous improvement, more medical talents capable of standardized diagnosis and treatment of breast cancer can be cultivated, contributing to reducing the burden of breast cancer.

title: Enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers were not effective in reducing N2O emissions from a drip-irrigated cotton field in arid region of Northwestern China
text:
Enhanced Efficiency Nitrogen Fertilizers Fail to Effectively Reduce N₂O Emissions from Drip-Irrigated Cotton Fields in the Arid Region of Northwest China

 Abstract

【Objective】 To clarify the mitigation effect of enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers (EENFs) on N₂O emissions in drip-irrigated cotton fields in the arid region of Northwest China, and to provide a theoretical basis for regional agricultural greenhouse gas mitigation.【Methods】 A field positioning experiment was conducted from 2022 to 2023 in Shihezi, Xinjiang. Five treatments were established: no nitrogen fertilizer (CK), conventional urea (U), controlled-release urea (CU), urease inhibitor urea (UI), and nitrification inhibitor urea (NI). N₂O emission fluxes during the cotton growing season were monitored using the static dark chamber-gas chromatography method, and soil temperature, moisture, inorganic nitrogen content, and cotton yield were measured.【Results】 The N₂O emission peaks of all fertilized treatments occurred 7–15 d after fertilization. The cumulative N₂O emissions of CU, UI, and NI treatments were 1.82, 1.76, and 1.68 kg·hm⁻², respectively, which were only 15.3%–21.9% lower than that of conventional urea (2.15 kg·hm⁻²), and the mitigation effect did not reach a significant level (P>0.05). EENFs had no significant effect on cotton seed yield, with yields ranging from 5,820 to 6,150 kg·hm⁻² across treatments. N₂O emission flux was significantly positively correlated with soil WFPS and NO₃⁻-N content (P<0.05).【Conclusion】 Under drip irrigation in the arid region of Northwest China, EENFs failed to effectively reduce N₂O emissions from cotton fields. Their mitigation effect was comprehensively regulated by soil moisture conditions and nitrogen transformation processes, and the mitigation potential of a single inhibitor or controlled-release strategy is limited.

Keywords: enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers; N₂O emissions; drip-irrigated cotton field; arid region; mitigation effect

 1 Introduction

Nitrous oxide (N₂O) is an important greenhouse gas, with a 100-year global warming potential approximately 273 times that of CO₂, contributing significantly to global climate change. Agricultural activities are the primary source of global anthropogenic N₂O emissions, accounting for approximately 60% of total anthropogenic emissions, with nitrogen fertilizer application being a key factor driving N₂O emissions from farmland. As the world's largest consumer of nitrogen fertilizer, China's farmland N₂O mitigation is of great significance for achieving the "dual carbon" goals and green agricultural development.

Enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers (EENFs), including controlled-release fertilizers, urease inhibitors, and nitrification inhibitors, reduce nitrogen loss by regulating nitrogen release rates or inhibiting soil nitrogen transformation processes, and are considered an effective strategy that balances crop yield and environmental benefits. Numerous studies have shown that EENFs can significantly reduce N₂O emissions in humid and semi-humid regions, with mitigation rates typically ranging from 20% to 50%. However, their application effects in arid regions remain controversial. The arid region of Northwest China has a dry climate and strong evaporation, and under drip irrigation, soil moisture distribution is uneven with frequent wet-dry alternation, which may alter the mitigation efficacy of EENFs.

Xinjiang is China's largest cotton production base, with drip-irrigated cotton field area exceeding 2 million hm². Clarifying the N₂O mitigation effect of EENFs in cotton fields in this region is crucial for optimizing nitrogen fertilizer management strategies. This study hypothesizes that the mitigation effect of EENFs in drip-irrigated cotton fields in arid regions may be weakened by soil moisture limitations. Through field experiments, the effects of different EENFs on N₂O emissions and cotton yield were systematically evaluated to provide a scientific basis for regional agricultural greenhouse gas mitigation.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Experimental Site

The experiment was conducted from 2022 to 2023 at the Agricultural Experiment Station of Shihezi University (44°18′N, 86°03′E), Xinjiang. The region has a temperate continental arid climate, with an annual average temperature of 7.2°C, annual average precipitation of approximately 210 mm, and annual average evaporation exceeding 1,800 mm. The test soil was gray desert soil. The basic physicochemical properties of the 0–20 cm soil layer were: pH 8.2, organic matter 12.6 g·kg⁻¹, total nitrogen 0.82 g·kg⁻¹, available phosphorus 18.5 mg·kg⁻¹, available potassium 215 mg·kg⁻¹, and field capacity 24.5% (mass water content).

 2.2 Experimental Design

A randomized block design was adopted with 5 treatments: (1) CK: no nitrogen fertilizer; (2) U: conventional urea (containing N 46%); (3) CU: controlled-release urea (resin-coated, release period 90 d); (4) UI: urea + urease inhibitor (NBPT, added at 0.5% of pure N); (5) NI: urea + nitrification inhibitor (DMPP, added at 1% of pure N). The nitrogen application rate for all fertilized treatments was 300 kg·hm⁻², with 50% applied as basal fertilizer and 50% applied as topdressing at the early flowering stage. Phosphorus and potassium fertilizers were uniformly applied at P₂O₅ 120 kg·hm⁻² and K₂O 90 kg·hm⁻² for all treatments, all as basal fertilizer. Each treatment had 3 replicates, with a plot area of 60 m² (6 m×10 m).

The cotton variety was "Xinluzao 64," using drip irrigation under plastic film, with one film, three drip lines, and six rows of planting. The row spacing configuration was (30+60+30) cm, and the plant spacing was 10 cm. Sowing was on April 20, 2022, and April 18, 2023, with harvest in late September. Irrigation followed local conventional management, with 8–10 drip irrigation events throughout the growing season and a total irrigation amount of approximately 4,500 m³·hm⁻².

 2.3 Sample Collection and Measurement

N₂O Collection and Measurement: The static dark chamber-gas chromatography method was used. The sampling chamber was made of stainless steel (50 cm×50 cm×50 cm) with an internal fan to mix gases. Sampling was conducted on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 15, and 20 after fertilization, and thereafter every 7–10 days, with sampling time from 9:00–11:00 AM. For each sampling, 20 mL of gas was extracted from the chamber using a 20 mL syringe and injected into a vacuum vial, and N₂O concentration was determined using an Agilent 7890B gas chromatograph (ECD detector). The N₂O emission flux calculation formula was:

F = ρ × (V/A) × (Δc/Δt) × (273/(273+T))

Where F is N₂O emission flux (μg·m⁻²·h⁻¹); ρ is N₂O density under standard conditions; V is chamber volume; A is chamber base area; Δc/Δt is the rate of N₂O concentration change per unit time; T is chamber temperature (°C). Cumulative emissions were calculated using the linear interpolation method.

Soil and Plant Indicators: During the same sampling period, 0–20 cm soil temperature (soil thermometer) and moisture content (oven-drying method) were measured, and soil samples were collected to determine NH₄⁺-N and NO₃⁻-N content (continuous flow analyzer). Seed cotton yield of each plot was measured at harvest.

 2.4 Data Processing

SPSS 26.0 was used for one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), and the Duncan method was used for multiple comparisons (α=0.05). Pearson's method was used for correlation analysis. Origin 2021 was used for graphing.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Dynamics of Soil Environmental Factors

During the cotton growing season, the 0–20 cm soil temperature ranged from 18.5 to 32.6°C, with no significant differences among treatments. Soil WFPS fluctuated in response to drip irrigation events, ranging from 35% to 72%. Within one week after fertilization, the WFPS of the U treatment was slightly higher than that of EENF treatments, but the difference was not significant. Soil NO₃⁻-N content increased significantly after fertilization, with the U treatment peaking at 68.5 mg·kg⁻¹, while the peaks of CU, UI, and NI treatments were 58.2, 55.6, and 52.3 mg·kg⁻¹, respectively, which were 14.9%–23.6% lower than the U treatment. NH₄⁺-N content remained at a higher level in the UI treatment, indicating that the urease inhibitor effectively delayed urea hydrolysis.

 3.2 Dynamics of N₂O Emission Flux

The N₂O emission fluxes of all fertilized treatments exhibited distinct pulse emission characteristics (Figure 1). The first emission peak appeared 7–10 days after basal fertilization, with the U treatment having the highest peak of 486 μg·m⁻²·h⁻¹; the peaks of CU, UI, and NI treatments were 398, 372, and 345 μg·m⁻²·h⁻¹, respectively, which were 18.1%–29.0% lower than the U treatment. A second emission peak appeared 5–7 days after topdressing, with peaks generally lower than the first. The CK treatment maintained N₂O flux at a low level throughout the growing season (<50 μg·m⁻²·h⁻¹).

 3.3 Cumulative N₂O Emissions and Emission Factors

The two-year average results showed (Table 1) that the cumulative N₂O emission of the U treatment was 2.15 kg·hm⁻², while those of CU, UI, and NI treatments were 1.82, 1.76, and 1.68 kg·hm⁻², respectively, which were 15.3%, 18.1%, and 21.9% lower than the U treatment, but the differences among treatments did not reach a significant level (P>0.05). The cumulative emission of the CK treatment was 0.72 kg·hm⁻². The N₂O emission factors (EF) of EENF treatments ranged from 0.35% to 0.39%, lower than the 0.48% of the U treatment, but the reduction was limited.

 3.4 Cotton Yield

The seed cotton yields of all fertilized treatments ranged from 5,820 to 6,150 kg·hm⁻², with no significant difference between EENF treatments and the U treatment (P>0.05), but all were significantly higher than the CK treatment (4,230 kg·hm⁻²) (P<0.05). This indicates that EENFs did not affect cotton yield while reducing nitrogen loss.

 3.5 Correlation Analysis

N₂O emission flux was significantly positively correlated with soil WFPS (r=0.62, P<0.05) and NO₃⁻-N content (r=0.71, P<0.01), and weakly correlated with soil temperature (r=0.28, P>0.05). This indicates that under drip irrigation in arid regions, soil moisture and nitrate nitrogen availability are key factors regulating N₂O emissions.

 4 Discussion

The results of this study indicate that EENFs failed to significantly reduce N₂O emissions in drip-irrigated cotton fields in the arid region of Northwest China, with mitigation rates (15%–22%) far lower than the 30%–50% reported in humid regions. This result supports our hypothesis that the special hydrothermal conditions in arid regions may weaken the mitigation efficacy of EENFs. The reasons may include the following aspects:

First, soil moisture limitation weakens the effectiveness of inhibitors. The efficacy of nitrification inhibitors and urease inhibitors is highly dependent on soil moisture conditions. Under drip irrigation in arid regions, soil WFPS is often below 60%, and nitrification itself is limited by moisture and relatively weak, so the marginal effect of inhibitors is correspondingly reduced. In addition, the local wet-dry alternation caused by drip irrigation may accelerate inhibitor degradation and shorten their effective duration.

Second, the release of controlled-release urea has limited matching with crop demand. Under high-temperature conditions in arid regions, the release rate of controlled-release urea accelerates, which may cause some nitrogen to be released before the peak crop uptake period, increasing the risk of nitrification-denitrification losses. In this study, although the NO₃⁻-N peak of the CU treatment was lower than that of the U treatment, the emission peak was still evident.

Third, the N₂O emission pathway in arid region soils is dominated by nitrification. Correlation analysis showed that NO₃⁻-N was the main driving factor of N₂O emissions, indicating a large contribution from nitrification. However, the nitrification inhibitor DMPP degrades rapidly in alkaline soil (pH 8.2), and its inhibitory effect may be inferior to that in acidic soil.

Fourth, the issue of evaluation scale for mitigation effects. This study only monitored emissions during the cotton growing season, not covering the fallow period and freeze-thaw period. N₂O emission pulses during the freeze-thaw period in arid regions may contribute significantly to annual total emissions, and the residual effects of EENFs may affect non-growing season emissions, requiring further research.

Although EENFs did not significantly reduce emissions, they performed well in maintaining yield, and CU and NI treatments showed a trend of reducing emissions. In the future, comprehensive measures such as optimizing irrigation regimes (e.g., controlling drip irrigation frequency and water volume) and adjusting fertilization timing and ratios should be combined to explore mitigation pathways suitable for arid regions.

 5 Conclusions

(1) Under drip-irrigated cotton field conditions in the arid region of Northwest China, controlled-release urea, urease inhibitor urea, and nitrification inhibitor urea only reduced cumulative N₂O emissions by 15.3%–21.9% compared with conventional urea, and the mitigation effect did not reach a statistically significant level.

(2) EENFs had no significant effect on cotton seed yield, with yields of 5,820–6,150 kg·hm⁻² across treatments, indicating that EENFs are feasible for maintaining stable yield.

(3) Soil WFPS and NO₃⁻-N content are key environmental factors regulating N₂O emissions, and moisture limitation and alkaline soil conditions in arid regions may be important reasons limiting the mitigation efficacy of EENFs.

(4) The N₂O mitigation potential of a single EENF strategy in drip-irrigated cotton fields in arid regions is limited. It is recommended to combine water-fertilizer integration optimization management to explore a comprehensive mitigation technology system.

title: Enhancing organic and inorganic carbon sequestration in calcareous soil by the combination of wheat straw and wood ash and/or lime
text:
Abstract: To enhance the carbon sequestration capacity of calcareous soils, this study investigated the effects of combined application of wheat straw with wood ash and/or lime on soil organic carbon and inorganic carbon fixation. Through a field micro-plot experiment, five treatments were established: control, straw alone, straw + wood ash, straw + lime, and straw + wood ash + lime. Changes in soil organic carbon, inorganic carbon (carbonates), aggregate stability, and crop yield were analyzed. The results showed that the combined application of straw with wood ash and/or lime significantly increased soil organic carbon content (by 12.3%–27.6%) and simultaneously promoted the formation of secondary carbonates, with inorganic carbon storage increasing by 8.5%–19.2%. Among them, the straw + wood ash + lime treatment exhibited the best effect, with organic carbon and inorganic carbon increasing by 27.6% and 19.2%, respectively, compared to the control, and the proportion of water-stable macroaggregates increasing by 15.8%. This mode achieved joint fixation of organic-inorganic carbon in calcareous soils through the synergistic effect of organic materials and alkaline additives, providing both soil improvement and yield enhancement benefits, and is suitable for promotion in the calcareous soil regions of northern China.

Keywords: calcareous soil; carbon sequestration; wheat straw; wood ash; lime; organic carbon; inorganic carbon

 1 Introduction

Calcareous soils are widely distributed in the arid and semi-arid regions of northern China, accounting for more than 15% of the total land area. These soils are rich in calcium carbonate, have high pH values, rapid organic matter mineralization rates, and weak carbon fixation capacity. In recent years, straw return, as a conventional measure to enhance soil organic carbon, has been widely adopted. However, in calcareous soils, the carbon sequestration efficiency of straw return alone is limited by its decomposition rate and the alkaline soil environment. Meanwhile, wood ash and lime, as alkaline materials, can not only neutralize soil acidity (mainly serving as calcium sources and pH regulators in calcareous soils) but also promote the precipitation of carbonates, thereby fixing carbon in the soil in inorganic form. However, whether the combined application of wheat straw with wood ash and/or lime can achieve synergistic enhancement of organic carbon and inorganic carbon lacks systematic research. In this paper, through field experiments, the effects of different combined application schemes on organic carbon, inorganic carbon, and aggregate stability in calcareous soils were analyzed, aiming to provide technical basis for carbon sequestration, emission reduction, and soil improvement in this region.

 2 Key Technical Analysis

 2.1 Experimental Design and Materials

The experiment was conducted at a long-term positioning experimental site of calcareous fluvo-aquic soil in southern Hebei Province, with soil pH 8.3, calcium carbonate content 12.6%, and organic carbon content 8.2 g/kg. A randomized block design was adopted with five treatments: CK (no straw or amendments), S (wheat straw alone), S+WA (straw + wood ash), S+L (straw + lime), and S+WA+L (straw + wood ash + lime). Wheat straw was crushed to 2–3 cm and returned at full amount (approximately 4500 kg/hm²); wood ash and lime were applied at 1500 kg/hm² and 750 kg/hm², respectively, broadcast once before sowing and incorporated by plowing. Each treatment had 3 replicates, with a plot area of 20 m². Winter wheat-summer maize rotation was planted with conventional water and fertilizer management.

 2.2 Synergistic Fixation Mechanism of Organic Carbon and Inorganic Carbon

Wheat straw is rich in cellulose and lignin. After being applied to the soil, it is decomposed by microorganisms to form humus, directly increasing the organic carbon pool. Calcium ions provided by wood ash and lime can combine with humic acids produced from straw decomposition to form stable calcium-humus complexes, reducing the mineralization rate of organic carbon. Meanwhile, calcium ions react with bicarbonate in the soil solution to form secondary calcium carbonate precipitates, fixing atmospheric CO₂ in inorganic carbon form. In this experiment, the S+WA+L treatment increased soil organic carbon by 27.6% and inorganic carbon by 19.2% compared to CK, indicating a significant synergistic fixation effect of organic-inorganic carbon.

 2.3 Soil Aggregate Formation and Carbon Protection

The combined application of straw with alkaline materials promoted the formation of water-stable macroaggregates (>0.25 mm). Calcium ions in wood ash and lime acted as cementing agents, binding polysaccharides and humus produced from straw decomposition with clay particles to form stable aggregate structures. The pore structure inside aggregates can physically protect organic carbon from microbial decomposition while providing nucleation sites for carbonate precipitation. The results showed that the proportion of water-stable macroaggregates in the S+WA+L treatment increased by 15.8% compared to CK, and the mean weight diameter (MWD) of aggregates increased by 22.4%. Aggregate protection is an important mechanism for organic carbon accumulation.

 2.4 Regulation of Microbial Community and Enzyme Activity

After combined application of straw with wood ash and lime, soil bacterial and fungal populations increased by 34.2% and 28.7%, respectively, and urease and sucrase activities were significantly enhanced. The alkaline properties of wood ash and lime adjusted soil pH to an optimal range (7.8–8.0), favoring microbial metabolism. However, excessive lime may inhibit microbial activity; in this experiment, the application rate of 750 kg/hm² did not produce negative effects. Microbial necromass carbon is also an important source of organic carbon accumulation, accounting for approximately 18.5% of total organic carbon.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

Changes in organic carbon and inorganic carbon: Compared with CK, the organic carbon content in S, S+WA, S+L, and S+WA+L treatments increased by 12.3%, 19.8%, 16.5%, and 27.6%, respectively; inorganic carbon storage increased by 4.2%, 12.7%, 10.3%, and 19.2%, respectively. The S+WA+L treatment achieved the highest total carbon sequestration (organic carbon + inorganic carbon), which was 1.24 times that of CK. Crop yield: The yields of winter wheat and summer maize in the S+WA+L treatment increased by 18.6% and 15.3%, respectively, compared to CK, with yield increases mainly attributed to improved soil structure and enhanced nutrient supply. Economic benefits: After deducting material and labor costs, the net income of the S+WA+L treatment increased by approximately 2100 yuan/hm² compared to CK, with a benefit-cost ratio of 2.8:1. Environmental benefits: This mode can reduce environmental pollution from straw burning and wood ash disposal while enhancing soil carbon sink function. Based on carbon sequestration, approximately 3.2 tons of CO₂ can be fixed per hectare.

 4 Conclusion

Combined application of wheat straw with wood ash and/or lime can significantly enhance organic carbon and inorganic carbon storage in calcareous soils, with the straw + wood ash + lime combination showing the best effect, increasing organic carbon and inorganic carbon by 27.6% and 19.2%, respectively, while improving soil aggregate stability and crop yield. This technology achieves multiple benefits of carbon sequestration, soil improvement, and yield enhancement through the organic-inorganic carbon synergistic fixation mechanism, with simple operation and controllable costs, and is suitable for promotion and application in the calcareous soil regions of northern China. It is recommended to adjust the ratio of wood ash to lime according to soil calcium carbonate content and pH value in practical application to avoid soil alkalization caused by excessive application.

title: Combined electroacupuncture and auricular acupuncture for postoperative pain after abdominal surgery for gynecological diseases: study protocol for a randomized controlled trial
text:
Combined electroacupuncture and auricular acupuncture for postoperative pain after abdominal surgery for gynecological diseases: study protocol for a randomized controlled trial

Abstract: Objective To investigate the clinical efficacy and safety of electroacupuncture combined with auricular acupuncture in pain management after gynecological abdominal surgery.
