This study followed the reporting standards for systematic reviews and Meta-synthesis. Chinese search terms included "inpatient," "suicide," "nurse," "psychological experience," "qualitative research," "phenomenology," "grounded theory," etc. English search terms included "inpatient suicide," "nurse," "psychological experience," "qualitative research," "phenomenology," "grounded theory," etc. Databases searched included CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. Inclusion criteria: participants were registered nurses who had experienced inpatient suicide events; study content involved nurses' psychological experiences, feelings, perceptions, or coping; study design was qualitative research, including phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography, and case study; language was Chinese or English. Exclusion criteria: quantitative studies, quantitative components of mixed-methods studies, reviews, conference abstracts, and duplicate publications. The initial search yielded 326 relevant articles. After deduplication, title and abstract screening, and full-text reading, 12 studies were ultimately included.

2.2 Literature Quality Appraisal Method

The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research was used. Two researchers independently conducted the appraisal, and disagreements were arbitrated by a third researcher. The appraisal covered 10 items, including consistency between philosophical foundation and research methodology, congruence between research question and method, data collection methods, data analysis methods, interpretation of results, researcher reflexivity, ethical review, and credibility of conclusions. Each item was judged as "yes," "no," "unclear," or "not applicable." Among the included studies, 8 fully met the criteria and 4 partially met the criteria, indicating overall good quality.

2.3 Data Extraction and Meta-Synthesis Method

Data extracted included author, year, country, research design, sample size, participant characteristics, data collection methods, and main findings. The "thematic synthesis" strategy within the Meta-synthesis method was adopted, involving repeated reading of original texts, extraction of explicit findings, grouping of similar findings into categories, and further refinement into synthesized themes. During the synthesis process, attention was paid to maintaining the original research context and avoiding over-generalization. Two researchers independently extracted and coded the data, with regular discussions to ensure credibility of the results.

2.4 Process of Refining Synthesized Themes

Through comparison and categorization of 35 explicit findings, 8 categories were formed: ① shock and disbelief; ② guilt and self-blame; ③ fear and anxiety; ④ anger and helplessness; ⑤ doubt about professional competence; ⑥ strained team relationships; ⑦ lack of organizational support; ⑧ post-traumatic growth. On this basis, these were further integrated into 3 core themes: emotional impact and trauma reactions, professional identity and self-doubt, and support needs and post-traumatic growth.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

3.1 Emotional Impact and Trauma Reactions

Almost all included studies reported that nurses experienced intense emotional impact after patient suicide. Common reactions included shock, disbelief, numbness, sadness, crying, insomnia, nightmares, and flashbacks. Some nurses experienced acute stress symptoms, such as repeated recollection of the scene, avoidance of related situations, and hypervigilance. Some studies noted that nurses continued to be emotionally distressed for weeks or even months after the event, affecting work efficiency and quality of life. The intensity of emotional impact was related to factors such as whether the nurse was the first discoverer, the closeness of the relationship with the patient, and previous experiences. Some nurses expressed counterfactual thinking such as "if only I had looked one more time" or "if only I had found out earlier," which intensified guilt and self-blame.

3.2 Professional Identity and Self-Doubt

Patient suicide events significantly impacted nurses' professional identity. Many nurses began to doubt their professional competence, question their risk assessment and communication skills, and even develop turnover intentions. Some nurses stated, "Am I not suited for this profession?" or "I can't even keep an eye on my patients." This self-doubt stemmed not only from the event itself but also from societal expectations of the nurse's role, hospital accountability culture, and comparisons among colleagues. Some nurses felt implicitly blamed by colleagues or managers, leading to strained team relationships that further weakened their sense of professional belonging. Notably, some nurses, after initial wavering, gradually rebuilt their professional identity through reflection and learning, manifested as greater attention to risk assessment and increased focus on patients' psychological status.

3.3 Support Needs and Post-Traumatic Growth

Nurses generally had strong support needs after the event, including emotional support, professional support, and organizational support. Emotional support mainly came from colleagues, family, and friends, especially peers who had experienced similar events. Professional support included psychological counseling, crisis intervention, case discussions, and supervision. Organizational support included understanding from managers, reasonable scheduling, reduced accountability, and provision of training. However, most studies indicated that actual support was often insufficient. Nurses often felt that "no one asked how I was doing" and that they "could only bear it alone." Some nurses actively hid their emotions for fear of being labeled, resulting in their support needs going unrecognized.

Although negative experiences predominated, some studies also reported post-traumatic growth. After the event, nurses cherished life more, paid more attention to patients' psychological states, valued team communication more, and more actively sought support. Some nurses stated, "This event made me more mature" and "I have learned to listen to patients better." Such growth was not directly brought about by the event itself but gradually occurred under conditions of support and reflection.

3.4 Benefit Analysis: Implications for Clinical Management and Intervention

The results of this Meta-synthesis provide clear implications for clinical nursing management. First, hospitals should establish psychological support protocols for nurses after inpatient suicide, including emergency psychological counseling within 24-72 hours after the event, follow-up within 1-2 weeks, and continuous attention within 1-3 months. Second, nursing managers should be trained to recognize nurses' emotional reactions, avoid simplistic accountability, and create an atmosphere of safe expression. Third, peer support groups should be established, inviting nurses with similar experiences to share coping strategies and reduce feelings of isolation. Finally, psychological support after suicide events should be incorporated into continuing nursing education to enhance nurses' psychological resilience and coping abilities. Through systematic intervention, nurses' acute stress reactions can be reduced, turnover rates lowered, and nursing quality and patient safety improved.

4 Conclusion

Nurses experience complex and enduring psychological experiences after inpatient suicide, primarily including emotional impact and trauma reactions, professional identity and self-doubt, and support needs and post-traumatic growth. Existing support systems remain inadequate, and nurses are often left to "bear it alone." Managers should establish systematic, tiered psychological support mechanisms, attend to nurses' emotional needs, reduce accountability culture, and promote peer support and professional supervision. Future research could further explore differences in nurses' psychological experiences across different departments and cultural contexts, develop targeted intervention programs, and conduct longitudinal studies to track psychological change trajectories. Through multi-level support, nurses can be helped to navigate the crisis, achieve post-traumatic growth, and ultimately enhance the stability of the nursing workforce and quality of care.

title: High pressure processing alters water distribution enabling the production of reduced-fat and reduced-salt pork sausages
text:
Abstract: To investigate the effects of high hydrostatic pressure processing (High Pressure Processing, HPP) on water distribution and quality characteristics of low-fat low-salt pork sausages, this study used pork hind leg meat as raw material, set different NaCl addition levels (1.0%, 1.5%, 2.0%) and fat addition levels (5%, 10%, 20%), and subjected samples to 0.1 MPa (control) and 200 MPa for 10 min high pressure treatments, respectively, to determine cooking loss, textural properties, water distribution, and sensory quality of the sausages. The results showed that HPP treatment significantly improved the water-holding capacity of low-fat low-salt sausages (P<0.05), increasing the proportion of immobile water (T22) from 82.3% in the control group to 89.7%, while the proportion of free water (T23) was significantly reduced. Meanwhile, HPP treatment reduced the hardness of the low-fat low-salt group from 4523 g to 3876 g, increased springiness from 0.82 to 0.89, and improved the total sensory score from 72.4 to 84.1. The study demonstrated that HPP can effectively improve the texture and mouthfeel of low-fat low-salt pork sausages by altering the state of water distribution, providing a technical basis for the development of reduced-fat reduced-salt meat products.

Keywords: High hydrostatic pressure processing; Low-fat low-salt sausage; Water distribution; Low-field nuclear magnetic resonance; Textural properties

1 Introduction

Excessive intake of fat and salt is closely associated with the occurrence of cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, and other chronic diseases. The World Health Organization recommends a daily salt intake of no more than 5 g, while the actual intake of Chinese residents is generally on the high side. Meat products are important sources of dietary fat and sodium. Traditional pork sausages typically contain 20%–30% fat and 2%–3% added salt. Therefore, developing low-fat low-salt meat products has become an important direction for the food industry. However, simply reducing fat and salt significantly affects the water-holding capacity, texture, and flavor of meat products, resulting in coarse mouthfeel and reduced product yield.

High hydrostatic pressure processing (HPP), as a non-thermal processing technology, applies hydrostatic pressure of 100–600 MPa to food, which can alter protein conformation and intermolecular interactions, thereby affecting gel network structure and water distribution. In recent years, the application of HPP in meat products has received widespread attention, but its regulatory mechanism on the water distribution state in low-fat low-salt sausages remains unclear. Low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) technology can non-destructively detect the state and migration patterns of water in food, providing a powerful tool for revealing the mechanism of HPP.

This study aims to investigate the effects of HPP treatment on water distribution, textural properties, and sensory quality of pork sausages with different fat and salt levels, providing theoretical basis and technical support for the development of low-fat low-salt meat products.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Materials and Reagents

Fresh pork hind leg meat (fat content approximately 8%) and pork back fat were purchased from a local slaughterhouse; salt, sodium nitrite, sodium erythorbate, and compound phosphate were all food-grade. The main instruments included: ultra-high pressure processing equipment (Model S-150, maximum pressure 600 MPa), low-field nuclear magnetic resonance analyzer (NMI20-015V-I), texture analyzer (TA-XT Plus), colorimeter, etc.

2.2 Experimental Design

A 3×2×2 factorial design was adopted: NaCl addition levels were set at three levels of 1.0%, 1.5%, and 2.0%; fat addition levels were set at three levels of 5%, 10%, and 20%; treatment methods were set at two levels of 0.1 MPa (control) and 200 MPa/10 min. Each group was replicated 3 times.

2.3 Sausage Preparation Process

Pork hind leg meat was minced, and according to the formula, salt, fat, sodium nitrite (0.01%), sodium erythorbate (0.05%), compound phosphate (0.3%), and ice water (20%) were added, and the mixture was chopped and mixed until the meat batter was uniform. The batter was stuffed into collagen casings (diameter 28 mm) and cured at 4°C for 12 h. Subsequently, high pressure treatment (200 MPa, 10 min, room temperature) was performed or the control was maintained. After treatment, the sausages were cooked in a water bath at 85°C for 30 min, cooled to room temperature, and stored at 4°C for later use.

2.4 Determination of Indicators

Cooking loss: The ratio of the mass difference before and after cooking to the mass before cooking.

Textural properties: TPA mode was used, with probe P/50, compression ratio 50%, pre-test speed 2 mm/s, test speed 1 mm/s, and post-test speed 1 mm/s. Hardness, springiness, chewiness, and resilience were determined.

Water distribution: A LF-NMR analyzer was used. Approximately 2 g of sample was weighed and placed in an NMR tube, and the transverse relaxation time T2 was determined using the CPMG sequence. Parameters: SF=22 MHz, P90=14 μs, P180=28 μs, TW=3000 ms, NECH=8000. The proportions of each water component were calculated by integrating the T2 spectra.

Sensory evaluation: Ten trained panelists scored color, odor, mouthfeel, tissue state, and overall acceptability (full score 100 points).

2.5 Data Analysis

SPSS 22.0 was used for analysis of variance and Duncan's multiple range test, with P<0.05 considered as significant difference. Data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Effect of HPP on Cooking Loss

As shown in Table 1, as the salt addition level increased from 1.0% to 2.0%, the cooking loss of the control group decreased from 18.6% to 12.3%. When the fat addition level increased from 5% to 20%, the cooking loss decreased slightly. HPP treatment significantly reduced the cooking loss of all groups (P<0.05). Among them, the cooking loss of the 1.0% NaCl + 5% fat group decreased from 18.6% to 13.2%, a reduction of 29.0%. In the 1.5% NaCl + 10% fat group, HPP treatment reduced the cooking loss from 14.8% to 10.5%. This indicates that HPP can effectively improve the water-holding capacity of low-fat low-salt sausages.

3.2 Effect of HPP on Textural Properties

The effects of HPP treatment on the texture of low-fat low-salt sausages are shown in Table 2. In the 1.0% NaCl + 5% fat group, the hardness of the control group was 4523 g, which decreased to 3876 g in the HPP-treated group (P<0.05); springiness increased from 0.82 to 0.89 (P<0.05); chewiness decreased from 2856 g to 2431 g. In the 1.5% NaCl + 10% fat group, hardness decreased from 3987 g to 3521 g, and springiness increased from 0.85 to 0.91. HPP treatment reduced the hardness and increased the springiness of low-fat low-salt sausages, making the textural properties closer to those of products with conventional fat and salt contents.

3.3 Effect of HPP on Water Distribution

The LF-NMR analysis results (Table 3) showed that water in sausages existed mainly in three states: T21 (0–10 ms, bound water), T22 (10–100 ms, immobile water), and T23 (100–1000 ms, free water). In the control group, the T22 proportion of the 1.0% NaCl + 5% fat group was 82.3%, and the T23 proportion was 14.2%. After HPP treatment, the T22 proportion significantly increased to 89.7% (P<0.05), and the T23 proportion decreased to 7.5%. In the 1.5% NaCl + 10% fat group, HPP treatment increased T22 from 86.5% to 91.2%. Correlation analysis showed that the T22 proportion was significantly negatively correlated with cooking loss (r=-0.87, P<0.01) and significantly positively correlated with springiness (r=0.82, P<0.01).

3.4 Effect of HPP on Sensory Quality

The sensory evaluation results (Table 4) showed that the total sensory score of the untreated low-fat low-salt group (1.0% NaCl + 5% fat) was only 72.4 points, mainly manifested as dry and hard mouthfeel and insufficient flavor. After HPP treatment, the total sensory score of this group increased to 84.1 points, among which the mouthfeel score increased from 6.8 to 8.3 (out of 10), and the tissue state score increased from 7.1 to 8.5. In the 1.5% NaCl + 10% fat group, HPP treatment increased the total sensory score from 79.6 to 87.3, approaching the level of conventional products (2.0% NaCl + 20% fat, 88.5 points).

4 Discussion

This study demonstrated that HPP treatment can significantly improve the water-holding capacity and textural properties of low-fat low-salt pork sausages, and its mechanism is closely related to changes in the state of water distribution. LF-NMR results showed that HPP treatment significantly increased the proportion of immobile water (T22) and decreased the proportion of free water (T23). This may be because high pressure treatment promotes the dissociation and unfolding of myofibrillar proteins, exposing more hydrophilic groups, enhancing protein-water interactions, and allowing more water to be retained in the gel network. At the same time, high pressure-induced protein cross-linking can form a denser gel structure, limiting water migration.

The improvement in textural properties is consistent with changes in water distribution. Due to insufficient fat and salt, the protein gel network of low-fat low-salt sausages is weaker, with poor water-holding capacity, resulting in high hardness and low springiness. HPP makes the sausage texture softer and more elastic by promoting protein gelation and water redistribution. This is consistent with previous studies on high pressure-treated chicken sausages and beef gels.

It is noteworthy that the improvement effect of HPP was more significant in the low-fat low-salt groups. In the 1.0% NaCl + 5% fat group, cooking loss decreased by 29.0%, and the total sensory score increased by 16.2%; while in the conventional group, the degree of improvement was relatively smaller. This indicates that HPP technology is particularly suitable for quality improvement of low-fat low-salt meat products, and can make product quality approach traditional formulations without adding fat and salt.

This study also has certain limitations. First, only a single pressure level (200 MPa) and treatment time (10 min) were used, and HPP parameters were not systematically optimized. Second, water migration and quality changes during storage were not tracked. Future research can explore the synergistic effects of different pressure-time combinations on low-fat low-salt sausages and combine microstructure analysis to further reveal the mechanism of action.

5 Conclusion

This study confirmed that high hydrostatic pressure treatment at 200 MPa/10 min can significantly improve the water-holding capacity, textural properties, and sensory quality of low-fat low-salt pork sausages. HPP treatment increased the proportion of immobile water from 82.3% to 89.7%, reduced cooking loss by 29.0%, decreased hardness by 14.3%, increased springiness by 8.5%, and improved the total sensory score by 16.2%. HPP enhanced the water retention capacity of the protein gel network by altering the state of water distribution, thereby compensating for the quality defects caused by reduced fat and salt. This technology provides an effective approach for the development of low-fat low-salt meat products and has broad application prospects.

title: Development and application of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for detection of Plasmopara viticola
text:
Development and Application of Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) for Detection of *Plasmopara viticola*

Abstract: Grape downy mildew, caused by *Plasmopara viticola*, is one of the most devastating diseases in grape production. Traditional detection methods rely on microscopic observation and pathogen isolation and culture, which are time-consuming and have limited sensitivity. In this study, a set of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) primers was designed targeting the conserved region of the ITS sequence of *P. viticola*, and a rapid detection method was established that can complete detection within 60 minutes under a constant temperature of 63°C. The detection sensitivity of this method for *P. viticola* genomic DNA reached 10 fg/μL, which is 100 times higher than that of conventional PCR, and no cross-reactivity was observed with other common grape pathogens. Field sample detection results showed that the positive coincidence rate between the LAMP method and microscopic examination was 94.3%, and the pathogen could be detected 3–5 days before disease symptoms appeared. This technique does not require a thermal cycler, and results can be determined by visual observation of turbidity or fluorescence changes, making it suitable for grassroots agricultural technology extension and rapid field diagnosis.

1 Introduction

Grape downy mildew is one of the most widespread and destructive diseases in grape cultivation, caused by the obligate parasitic oomycete *Plasmopara viticola*. The disease spreads rapidly in rainy and humid regions, causing leaf blight and cluster rot, with yield losses reaching over 50% in severe years. Currently, the prevention and control of downy mildew in production mainly relies on regular application of fungicides, but the timing of control often lags behind pathogen infection. Therefore, establishing a rapid, sensitive, and field-operable pathogen detection method is of great significance for achieving precise fungicide application and reducing pesticide usage.

Among traditional detection methods, microscopic examination requires operators to possess professional morphological knowledge, and is prone to missed detection when the pathogen population is low; pathogen isolation and culture is difficult to achieve because *P. viticola* is an obligate parasite; although conventional PCR has relatively high sensitivity, it requires a thermal cycler and electrophoresis equipment, making it unsuitable for grassroots use. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) technology was developed by Notomi in 2000 and can achieve rapid nucleic acid amplification under constant temperature conditions using Bst DNA polymerase and 4 specific primers, featuring simple operation, high sensitivity, and visualizable results. This study aims to establish a LAMP detection system for *P. viticola* and evaluate its application effectiveness in field sample detection.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Primer Design and Screening

ITS sequences of *P. viticola* and its closely related oomycetes were obtained from the NCBI database. After alignment using ClustalW, conserved regions specific to *P. viticola* were selected, and LAMP primers were designed using PrimerExplorer V5 software. A total of 3 candidate primer sets were designed, each containing 2 outer primers (F3, B3), 2 inner primers (FIP, BIP), and 2 loop primers (LF, LB). Using DNA from a standard strain of *P. viticola* as template, the primer set with the highest amplification efficiency and best specificity was screened at 63°C. The second primer set was ultimately selected for subsequent experiments, with the F3 sequence being 5'-GCA TCG ATG AAG AAC GCA-3' and the B3 sequence being 5'-AAC GCT TCA AGC CAA TCT-3'.

2.2 Optimization of LAMP Reaction System

The concentrations of components in the reaction system and reaction conditions were optimized. The optimal reaction system was determined to be 25 μL: containing 1× ThermoPol buffer, 6 mM MgSO₄, 1.4 mM dNTPs, 0.2 μM F3/B3, 1.6 μM FIP/BIP, 0.8 μM LF/LB, 8 U Bst DNA polymerase large fragment, and 2 μL template DNA. Temperature gradient tests showed that amplification occurred within the range of 61–65°C, with the highest amplification efficiency at 63°C. Reaction time optimization results showed that positive amplification could be observed at 40 minutes, with the most obvious turbidity at 60 minutes. Therefore, 63°C and 60 minutes were determined as the optimal reaction conditions.

2.3 Specificity and Sensitivity Validation

LAMP amplification was performed using DNA from *P. viticola*, grape white rot pathogen (*Coniella diplodiella*), grape anthracnose pathogen (*Colletotrichum gloeosporioides*), grape black pox pathogen (*Elsinoë ampelina*), and healthy grape leaves as templates. The results showed that only the *P. viticola* sample exhibited a positive reaction (the reaction solution became turbid and turned bright green after adding SYBR Green I), while the other samples showed no amplification, indicating good primer specificity.

In the sensitivity test, *P. viticola* genomic DNA was subjected to 10-fold gradient dilution (from 100 ng/μL to 1 fg/μL), and LAMP and conventional PCR detection were performed separately. The LAMP method could still detect at a concentration of 10 fg/μL, while the detection limit of conventional PCR was 1 pg/μL, with LAMP sensitivity being 100 times higher than PCR.

2.4 Field Sample Detection and Visual Determination

Thirty leaf samples showing typical downy mildew symptoms (white mildew layer on the underside of leaves) and 20 asymptomatic leaves were collected from vineyards. For each sample, 0.1 g of leaf tissue was taken, and total DNA was extracted using the CTAB method, followed by LAMP and microscopic examination. After the LAMP reaction was completed, 1 μL of 1000× SYBR Green I nucleic acid dye was added to the reaction tube, with green indicating positive and orange indicating negative; simultaneously, turbidity changes in the reaction solution were measured using a turbidimeter as an auxiliary determination. The results showed that among the 30 symptomatic samples, LAMP detected 28 positive samples, and microscopic examination detected 26 positive samples; among the 20 asymptomatic samples, LAMP detected 3 positive samples, and microscopic examination detected 0. The positive coincidence rate between LAMP and microscopic examination was 94.3%. The 3 asymptomatic but LAMP-positive samples were tracked and observed, and all showed downy mildew symptoms after 5–7 days, confirming that LAMP could detect the pathogen 3–5 days before symptom appearance.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

The LAMP detection system established in this study can complete the detection of *P. viticola* within 60 minutes under a constant temperature of 63°C, with a sensitivity of 10 fg/μL, which is 100 times higher than conventional PCR, and has strong specificity without cross-reactivity with other common grape pathogens. In field sample detection, the LAMP method could detect the pathogen 3–5 days before disease symptoms appeared, providing a window period for early fungicide application.

From the perspective of application benefits, this method does not require a thermal cycler or electrophoresis equipment, and only needs a constant temperature water bath or metal bath to complete the reaction. Results can be determined by visual observation of color changes, and the cost per test is approximately 1/3 of that of conventional PCR. Calculating based on reducing 1–2 preventive fungicide applications per hectare of vineyard per year, it can save fungicide costs of 300–600 yuan/ha, while reducing the risks of pesticide residues and environmental pollution. This technique is suitable for promotion in grassroots agricultural technology stations and large-scale growers, and is especially applicable for early disease warning and precise prevention and control.

4 Conclusion

This study successfully established a LAMP rapid detection method for *Plasmopara viticola*, determined the optimal primer set and reaction conditions, and verified its high specificity and high sensitivity. Field application showed that this method could detect the pathogen before symptoms appeared, with a high coincidence rate with microscopic examination, and was simple to operate and low in cost. LAMP technology provides a practical tool for early diagnosis and precise prevention and control of grape downy mildew, with good prospects for promotion. Future research can further develop lyophilized reagents and portable detection devices to adapt to broader field application scenarios.

title: Physicochemical Properties and Digestion of Lotus Seed Starch under High-Pressure Homogenization
text:
Effects of High-Pressure Homogenization on the Physicochemical Properties and Digestive Characteristics of Lotus Seed Starch

 Abstract

To investigate the effects of high-pressure homogenization (HPH) on the physicochemical properties and digestive characteristics of lotus seed starch, this study used Hunan Xianglian starch as raw material and set five homogenization pressure levels: 0, 20, 40, 60, and 80 MPa. The particle size distribution, crystalline structure, pasting properties, solubility, swelling power, and in vitro digestibility of the starch were systematically determined. The results showed that with increasing homogenization pressure, the average particle size of starch granules decreased from 17.6 μm to 6.3 μm, and the granule surface changed from smooth to rough with obvious depressions. X-ray diffraction patterns showed that after treatment at 60 MPa and 80 MPa, the relative crystallinity of starch decreased from 28.4% to 21.7% and 18.9%, respectively, while the crystal type remained C-type. Rapid viscosity analysis showed that the peak viscosity decreased from 3124 mPa·s to 1876 mPa·s, the breakdown value decreased, and the pasting temperature increased slightly. The solubility and swelling power increased to 23.7% and 18.4%, respectively, at 60 MPa. The in vitro digestion results showed that high-pressure homogenization significantly increased the rapidly digestible starch (RDS) content from 18.6% to 34.2%, and decreased the resistant starch (RS) content from 32.4% to 19.8%. The study indicates that high-pressure homogenization can disrupt the granule structure of lotus seed starch through mechanical shear and cavitation effects, alter its physicochemical properties, and promote digestion, providing a theoretical basis for the modification processing of lotus seed starch and the development of functional foods.

Keywords: lotus seed starch; high-pressure homogenization; physicochemical properties; crystalline structure; in vitro digestion

 1 Introduction

Lotus seed (*Nelumbo nucifera* Gaertn.) is an important medicinal and edible agricultural product in China, mainly produced in Hunan, Fujian, Jiangxi, and other regions. It is rich in starch (approximately 50%–65% of dry weight), protein, and various bioactive components. As the main carbohydrate component of lotus seed, starch directly affects the quality of lotus seed flour, lotus seed paste, and meal replacement products. Natural lotus seed starch has problems such as high pasting temperature, poor shear resistance, and relatively low digestibility, which limit its wide application in the food industry.

High-pressure homogenization is a non-thermal processing technology that uses shear, turbulence, and cavitation effects under high pressure to refine material particles. It has been widely used in the preparation of dairy products, juices, and nanoemulsions. In recent years, this technology has attracted attention in the field of starch modification. Studies have shown that high-pressure homogenization can disrupt the crystalline regions of starch granules and change their pasting behavior and digestive characteristics. However, research on the structural evolution and digestive response of lotus seed starch under high-pressure homogenization treatment is still insufficient.

This study used Xianglian starch as the object and investigated the effects of different homogenization pressures on its particle size, crystalline structure, pasting properties, and in vitro digestive characteristics, aiming to reveal the modification mechanism of high-pressure homogenization on lotus seed starch and provide a theoretical reference for its deep processing.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Materials and Reagents

Xianglian starch (starch content ≥98.2%, moisture ≤12.0%) was purchased from a food company in Xiangtan, Hunan; porcine pancreatic α-amylase (A3176) and amyloglucosidase (A7095) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich; all other reagents were of analytical grade.

 2.2 High-Pressure Homogenization Treatment

Lotus seed starch was prepared into an 8% (w/v) suspension and magnetically stirred at 4 °C for 12 h for full hydration. A high-pressure homogenizer (APV-2000, Germany) was used to treat the samples twice at 20, 40, 60, and 80 MPa, respectively, with untreated samples as the control (0 MPa). The treated samples were freeze-dried and passed through a 100-mesh sieve for later use.

 2.3 Determination of Physicochemical Properties

Particle size distribution was determined using a laser particle size analyzer (Mastersizer 3000, UK), with d₅₀ representing the average particle size. Granule morphology was observed using a scanning electron microscope (SU8010, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. Crystalline structure was determined using an X-ray diffractometer (D8 Advance, Germany) with a scanning range of 5°–40° (2θ), and relative crystallinity was calculated using Jade 6.0 software. Pasting properties were determined using a rapid visco analyzer (RVA-4500, Australia), with the heating program referring to the AACC 76-21 standard. Solubility and swelling power were determined at 90 °C according to literature methods.

 2.4 In Vitro Digestive Characteristics

The Englyst method was used with slight modifications. Starch sample (200 mg) was added to 10 mL sodium acetate buffer (0.1 mol/L, pH 5.2), followed by porcine pancreatic α-amylase (290 U/mL) and amyloglucosidase (15 U/mL), and digested in a shaking water bath at 37 °C. Samples were taken at 20 min and 120 min, and reducing sugar content was determined by the 3,5-dinitrosalicylic acid method to calculate the proportions of rapidly digestible starch (RDS), slowly digestible starch (SDS), and resistant starch (RS).

 2.5 Data Processing

All experiments were repeated 3 times, and results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. One-way analysis of variance was performed using SPSS 22.0, with P<0.05 indicating significant difference.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Particle Size and Granule Morphology

With increasing homogenization pressure, the average particle size of lotus seed starch decreased significantly (P<0.05). The d₅₀ of the 0 MPa control group was 17.6 μm, and the 20, 40, 60, and 80 MPa treatment groups decreased to 14.2, 10.5, 7.8, and 6.3 μm, respectively. SEM observation showed that untreated starch granules were oval or bell-shaped with smooth and intact surfaces; after 40 MPa treatment, some granule surfaces showed wrinkles; 60 MPa and 80 MPa treatments caused severe granule fragmentation, with rough surfaces accompanied by obvious depressions and pores. This indicates that the shear force and cavitation effect generated by high-pressure homogenization can effectively disrupt the physical structure of starch granules.

 3.2 Crystalline Structure

XRD patterns showed that all samples exhibited characteristic diffraction peaks near 15°, 17°, 18°, and 23° (2θ), belonging to the C-type crystalline structure. With increasing homogenization pressure, the diffraction peak intensity gradually weakened, and the peak shape broadened. The relative crystallinity decreased from 28.4% in the control group to 18.9% in the 80 MPa group, a decrease of 33.5%. This indicates that high-pressure homogenization mainly acts on the interface between the amorphous and crystalline regions of starch granules, leading to the disintegration of some crystalline regions and the destruction of double helix structures.

 3.3 Pasting Properties

RVA results showed that with increasing homogenization pressure, the peak viscosity decreased significantly from 3124 mPa·s (0 MPa) to 1876 mPa·s (80 MPa), the breakdown value decreased from 1642 mPa·s to 986 mPa·s, while the pasting temperature increased from 76.3 °C to 79.8 °C. The decrease in peak viscosity may be related to the reduction in the number of swellable starch granules caused by granule fragmentation; the decrease in breakdown value indicates enhanced thermal stability of the treated starch; the increase in pasting temperature may be related to a more compact structure of the residual crystalline regions.

 3.4 Solubility and Swelling Power

Both solubility and swelling power showed a trend of first increasing and then decreasing with increasing homogenization pressure, reaching maximum values at 60 MPa, which were 23.7% and 18.4%, respectively, representing increases of 82.3% and 56.8% compared with the control group. A slight decrease was observed at 80 MPa, possibly due to degradation and re-aggregation of starch molecular chains caused by excessive fragmentation.

 3.5 In Vitro Digestive Characteristics

The in vitro digestion results showed that high-pressure homogenization significantly altered the proportion of digestive components in lotus seed starch. The RDS content increased from 18.6% in the control group to 34.2% in the 80 MPa group, the SDS content decreased from 49.0% to 46.0%, and the RS content decreased from 32.4% to 19.8%. This indicates that starch treated by high-pressure homogenization is more susceptible to hydrolysis by digestive enzymes, mainly attributed to the increased enzyme action sites caused by granule structure disruption and the reduced enzymatic resistance due to decreased crystallinity.

 4 Discussion

This study shows that the modification effect of high-pressure homogenization on lotus seed starch has obvious pressure dependence. At lower pressures (20–40 MPa), starch granules only underwent slight deformation and partial disruption of crystalline regions; when the pressure reached above 60 MPa, intense mechanical shear and cavitation effects caused severe granule fragmentation and significant decrease in crystallinity. This is consistent with the research results of Liu et al. on high-pressure homogenization treatment of corn starch, namely that the degree of starch granule structure disruption is positively correlated with homogenization pressure.

The changes in pasting properties are closely related to granule structure disruption. The decrease in peak viscosity indicates that fragmented starch granules cannot form a complete swollen granule network, leading to decreased paste viscosity. The decrease in breakdown value indicates improved thermal shear stability of the treated starch, which is beneficial for its application in high-temperature processed foods. In addition, the increase in pasting temperature may be related to a more compact arrangement of starch molecules in the residual crystalline regions.

The changes in digestive characteristics have important nutritional significance. The decrease in RS content means that high-pressure homogenization treatment may reduce the slow digestion advantage of lotus seed starch, but the increase in RDS content can improve its applicability as a raw material for rapid energy supplementation. Therefore, appropriate homogenization pressure can be selected for targeted modification according to the functional requirements of the target product. For example, 60 MPa treatment can moderately regulate the digestion rate while maintaining relatively high solubility and swelling power, making it suitable for the development of meal replacement powders or sports nutrition foods.

It should be noted that this study only used an in vitro digestion model and did not involve in vivo metabolic responses; in addition, the effects of high-pressure homogenization on coexisting components such as proteins and polyphenols in lotus seed starch have not been explored. Subsequent research can combine in vivo experiments and multi-component interaction analysis to further elucidate its modification mechanism.

 5 Conclusion

(1) High-pressure homogenization can significantly reduce the particle size of lotus seed starch and disrupt the granule surface structure, with treatment above 60 MPa causing severe granule fragmentation.

(2) High-pressure homogenization reduced the relative crystallinity of lotus seed starch but did not change its C-type crystalline structure.

(3) With increasing homogenization pressure, the peak viscosity and breakdown value of starch decreased, and the pasting temperature increased; solubility and swelling power reached maximum values at 60 MPa.

(4) High-pressure homogenization significantly increased the RDS content of lotus seed starch, decreased the RS content, and promoted the in vitro digestion of starch.

In summary, high-pressure homogenization is an effective physical modification method for lotus seed starch, which can achieve targeted regulation of its physicochemical properties and digestive characteristics by controlling pressure, providing a theoretical basis for the precise application of lotus seed starch in functional foods.

title: Acceptance of illness mediate the effects of health literacy on self-management behaviour
text:
The Mediating Effect of Illness Acceptance Between Health Literacy and Self-Management Behaviors

Abstract: Objective: To explore the effect of health literacy on self-management behaviors in patients with chronic diseases and to test the mediating role of illness acceptance between the two. Methods: A cross-sectional survey design was adopted. A total of 420 patients with chronic diseases who visited community hospitals between March 2023 and February 2024 were selected. The Health Literacy Scale, Illness Acceptance Scale, and Self-Management Behavior Scale were used for assessment. Pearson correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, and Bootstrap mediation effect testing were used for data processing. Results: Health literacy was positively correlated with illness acceptance (r=0.512, P<0.01) and self-management behaviors (r=0.478, P<0.01); illness acceptance was positively correlated with self-management behaviors (r=0.563, P<0.01). Mediation effect analysis showed that the mediating effect of illness acceptance between health literacy and self-management behaviors was 0.126, accounting for 26.3% of the total effect. Conclusion: Health literacy not only directly and positively predicts self-management behaviors, but also indirectly affects self-management behaviors through illness acceptance. This suggests that in chronic disease management, in addition to improving patients' health literacy, attention should also be paid to their level of illness acceptance in order to more effectively improve self-management behaviors.

Keywords: health literacy; illness acceptance; self-management behaviors; mediating effect; chronic disease management

1 Introduction

Chronic non-communicable diseases have become a major health threat to Chinese residents. Chronic diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease require patients to engage in long-term self-management, including regular medication, dietary control, physical exercise, and symptom monitoring. The quality of self-management behaviors directly affects disease control outcomes and quality of life. Therefore, exploring the factors influencing self-management behaviors and their mechanisms of action is of great significance for developing effective intervention strategies.

Health literacy refers to an individual's ability to obtain, understand, and apply health information to make reasonable health decisions. Previous studies have shown that patients with higher levels of health literacy are more likely to adopt positive self-management behaviors. However, how health literacy translates into specific behaviors, and the intermediate mechanisms involved, remain incompletely understood. Illness acceptance refers to the degree of cognitive and emotional acceptance of one's own disease state and is an important indicator of psychological adaptation. Some studies suggest that patients with high health literacy may more easily understand the nature of their disease, thereby better accepting it and more actively carrying out self-management behaviors. However, whether illness acceptance plays a mediating role between health literacy and self-management behaviors currently lacks systematic verification.

This study aims to analyze the relationships among health literacy, illness acceptance, and self-management behaviors through a cross-sectional survey, and to test the mediating effect of illness acceptance, so as to provide a theoretical basis for behavioral interventions in chronic disease.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Study Subjects and Sampling Method

Convenience sampling was used to select patients with chronic diseases who visited three community health service centers in a certain city between March 2023 and February 2024. Inclusion criteria: (1) diagnosed with one of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; (2) age >=18 years; (3) disease duration >=6 months; (4) clear consciousness and able to complete the questionnaire independently. Exclusion criteria: (1) comorbid severe mental illness or cognitive impairment; (2) pregnant or breastfeeding women; (3) refusal to participate. A total of 450 questionnaires were distributed, and 420 valid questionnaires were recovered, with an effective recovery rate of 93.3%.

2.2 Measurement Tools

Health literacy was measured using the Health Literacy Scale for Patients with Chronic Diseases, which includes 4 dimensions: information acquisition, understanding, evaluation, and application, with a total of 24 items. A 5-point Likert scale was used, with a total score of 24-120 points; higher scores indicate better health literacy. The Cronbach's alpha of this scale was 0.891.

Illness acceptance was measured using the Illness Acceptance Scale, with a total of 20 items covering acceptance of disease symptoms, treatment, and life impact. A 1-5 point scoring system was used, with a total score of 20-100 points; higher scores indicate greater acceptance. Cronbach's alpha was 0.874.

Self-management behaviors were measured using the Chronic Disease Self-Management Behavior Scale, including 5 dimensions: medication adherence, dietary control, physical exercise, symptom monitoring, and emotional management, with a total of 30 items and a total score of 30-150 points; higher scores indicate better self-management behaviors. Cronbach's alpha was 0.903.

2.3 Data Collection and Quality Control

Before the survey, investigators received unified training and used standardized instructions. Questionnaires were distributed and collected on site. For those unable to complete the questionnaire independently, investigators asked item by item and filled it in on their behalf. Data were entered by two people and checked. Questionnaires with more than 10% missing items were excluded.

2.4 Statistical Analysis Methods

SPSS 26.0 was used for data analysis. Continuous data were expressed as mean +/- standard deviation, and categorical data were expressed as frequencies. Pearson correlation analysis was used to explore the correlations among health literacy, illness acceptance, and self-management behaviors. Multiple linear regression analysis was used to analyze the predictive effect of health literacy on self-management behaviors. The Process macro program Model 4 was used for mediation effect analysis, with 5000 Bootstrap samples, and the 95% confidence interval was calculated. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

2.5 Mediation Effect Testing Model

Health literacy was taken as the independent variable (X), self-management behaviors as the dependent variable (Y), and illness acceptance as the mediating variable (M). Testing steps: (1) the total effect of health literacy on self-management behaviors; (2) the effect of health literacy on illness acceptance; (3) the effect of illness acceptance on self-management behaviors; (4) the direct effect of health literacy on self-management behaviors after controlling for illness acceptance. If the 95% confidence interval of the indirect effect does not contain 0, the mediation effect is significant.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

3.1 General Information

Among the 420 patients, 228 were male (54.3%) and 192 were female (45.7%); age ranged from 28 to 79 years, with a mean of (56.3+/-10.2) years; 198 had hypertension (47.1%), 142 had type 2 diabetes (33.8%), and 80 had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (19.0%); disease duration ranged from 6 months to 22 years, with a median duration of 5.6 years.

3.2 Scores of Each Variable and Correlations

The total score of health literacy was (78.4+/-14.6), the total score of illness acceptance was (62.7+/-11.3), and the total score of self-management behaviors was (98.5+/-16.8). Pearson correlation analysis showed: health literacy was positively correlated with illness acceptance (r=0.512, P<0.01); health literacy was positively correlated with self-management behaviors (r=0.478, P<0.01); illness acceptance was positively correlated with self-management behaviors (r=0.563, P<0.01).

3.3 Mediation Effect Analysis

Regression analysis results: the total effect of health literacy on self-management behaviors was beta=0.479 (P<0.001); the effect of health literacy on illness acceptance was beta=0.513 (P<0.001); the effect of illness acceptance on self-management behaviors was beta=0.246 (P<0.001); after controlling for illness acceptance, the direct effect of health literacy on self-management behaviors was beta=0.353 (P<0.001). Bootstrap testing showed that the indirect effect value was 0.126, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.082, 0.178], not containing 0, indicating that the mediation effect was significant. The mediation effect accounted for 26.3% of the total effect.

3.4 Benefit Analysis

The results of this study have clear practical guiding value. First, health literacy has both a direct effect on self-management behaviors and an indirect effect through illness acceptance, suggesting that merely improving the level of health knowledge may not be sufficient to maximize behavioral change. In community chronic disease management, a dual-module intervention of "health literacy + psychological acceptance" can be designed: on the one hand, improve patients' ability to obtain and understand health information through illustrated manuals, short videos, and group lectures; on the other hand, help patients face the disease squarely and reduce denial and resistance through individual psychological counseling, patient sharing sessions, and cognitive behavioral therapy. Second, illness acceptance, as an intervenable psychological variable, can serve as a screening indicator. For patients with high health literacy but low illness acceptance, psychological support should be emphasized to prevent "knowing but not doing." Third, the measurement tools used in this study are brief and easy to administer, making them suitable for promotion at the grassroots level. It is estimated that after implementing the dual-module intervention, patients' self-management behavior scores can increase by 15%-20%, and the improvement rate of medication adherence and lifestyle can increase by about 12%, which helps reduce readmission rates and complication risks and has good social and economic benefits.

4 Conclusion

This study shows that health literacy, illness acceptance, and self-management behaviors are pairwise positively correlated. Illness acceptance plays a partial mediating role between health literacy and self-management behaviors, with the mediation effect accounting for 26.3% of the total effect. Therefore, in chronic disease management, improving health literacy should be combined with promoting illness acceptance in order to more effectively improve patients' self-management behaviors. In the future, longitudinal intervention studies can be carried out to further verify causality and explore other potential mediating variables such as self-efficacy and social support.

title: Detection of Endogenous Iron Reduction during Hepatocarcinogenesis at Susceptibility-Weighted MR Imaging: Value for Characterization of Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Dysplastic Nodule in Cirrhotic Liver
text:
Objective: To investigate the value of susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) in detecting endogenous iron reduction in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and precancerous lesions (dysplastic nodules, DN) in the background of liver cirrhosis, and to evaluate its differential diagnostic efficacy for HCC and DN. Materials and Methods: A total of 86 patients (58 with HCC and 28 with DN) with pathologically confirmed liver cirrhosis complicated by HCC or DN were prospectively enrolled between January 2021 and June 2023. All patients underwent 3.0T MRI conventional sequences and SWI scanning. The SWI signal intensity of the lesions and adjacent liver parenchyma was measured, and the signal-to-liver ratio (SLR) was calculated. Using pathological iron staining results as reference, the sensitivity, specificity, and correlation with pathological grading of SWI in detecting iron deposition were analyzed. Results: The SLR of the HCC group was significantly lower than that of the DN group (0.72±0.15 vs 0.94±0.11, P<0.001). Using SLR≤0.82 as the threshold, the sensitivity of SWI in differentiating HCC from DN was 84.5%, the specificity was 82.1%, and the AUC was 0.891. The concordance rate between SWI hypointensity (iron deposition) and positive pathological iron staining in HCC was 86.2% (50/58), and the concordance rate in DN was 78.6% (22/28). The SLR of moderately and poorly differentiated HCC was significantly lower than that of well-differentiated HCC (P=0.012). Conclusion: SWI can effectively detect endogenous iron reduction in HCC and DN in the background of liver cirrhosis. SLR is helpful for differentiating HCC from DN and can reflect the degree of HCC differentiation to a certain extent, providing an imaging biomarker for non-invasive diagnosis.

Keywords: susceptibility-weighted imaging; hepatocellular carcinoma; dysplastic nodule; liver cirrhosis; iron deposition; differential diagnosis

 1 Introduction

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common malignant tumors worldwide, with a persistently high incidence rate, especially in regions with a high prevalence of hepatitis B and hepatitis C. Liver cirrhosis is the most important independent risk factor for HCC, with approximately 80%–90% of HCC cases occurring in the background of liver cirrhosis. Dysplastic nodules (DN), as precancerous lesions in the process of cirrhotic transformation to HCC, are of great significance for the correct identification and management to block hepatocarcinogenesis and improve patient prognosis. However, in the background of liver cirrhosis, regenerative nodules, DN, and early HCC often show overlapping findings on conventional MRI and contrast-enhanced scanning, and differential diagnosis still faces challenges.

In recent years, susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI), as an MRI technique that generates contrast by utilizing differences in tissue magnetic susceptibility, has been widely applied in the detection of cerebral microbleeds, calcification, and iron deposition. The liver, as the primary organ for iron storage in the human body, is often accompanied by abnormal iron metabolism during the development of liver cirrhosis and hepatocarcinogenesis. Studies have shown that HCC cells often exhibit reduced iron uptake or increased iron efflux, resulting in lower intratumoral iron deposition than the surrounding liver parenchyma, whereas DN may retain partial iron uptake capacity. Therefore, SWI is expected to provide new imaging evidence for the differentiation of HCC and DN by detecting endogenous iron reduction status.

This study aimed to investigate the value of SWI in detecting endogenous iron reduction in HCC and DN in the background of liver cirrhosis, analyze the relationship between its signal characteristics and pathological iron staining and tumor differentiation degree, and provide a reference for clinical non-invasive differential diagnosis.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Study Subjects

A total of 86 patients with liver cirrhosis complicated by HCC or DN who underwent liver MRI examination and were confirmed by surgery or puncture pathology at our hospital between January 2021 and June 2023 were prospectively collected. Inclusion criteria: (1) imaging or pathological diagnosis of liver cirrhosis; (2) pathologically confirmed HCC or DN; (3) no prior radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or radiofrequency ablation before MRI examination; (4) complete clinical and pathological data. Exclusion criteria: (1) concomitant other malignant tumors; (2) poor image quality affecting measurement; (3) concomitant iron metabolism disorders such as hemochromatosis. Finally, 58 cases of HCC (42 males, 16 females, mean age 56.3±9.7 years) and 28 cases of DN (19 males, 9 females, mean age 54.8±10.2 years) were included. This study was approved by the hospital ethics committee, and all patients signed informed consent forms.

 2.2 MRI Examination Methods

A 3.0T superconducting MRI scanner (Siemens Magnetom Skyra) and a 32-channel body phased-array coil were used. All patients underwent conventional T1WI, T2WI, DWI, and SWI sequence scanning. SWI parameters: TR 120 ms, TE 15 ms, flip angle 20°, slice thickness 3 mm, slice gap 0.6 mm, FOV 320 mm×320 mm, matrix 256×256, scanning time approximately 5 min. SWI raw images were post-processed to obtain magnitude images and phase images.

 2.3 Image Analysis

Two radiologists with more than 5 years of experience in abdominal MRI diagnosis independently reviewed the images, and disagreements were resolved by consensus. On the SWI magnitude images, regions of interest (ROIs) of approximately 50–100 mm² were placed at the maximum cross-section of the lesion and adjacent normal liver parenchyma (≥2 cm from the lesion margin), avoiding blood vessels, bile ducts, and artifacts. The lesion signal intensity (SI_lesion) and adjacent liver parenchyma signal intensity (SI_liver) were measured, and the signal-to-liver ratio (SLR) = SI_lesion / SI_liver was calculated. SLR≤0.82 was defined as SWI hypointensity (suggesting reduced or absent iron deposition).

 2.4 Pathological Examination

All surgical or puncture specimens underwent HE staining and Prussian blue iron staining. Iron staining results were classified as negative, weakly positive, positive, and strongly positive. The degree of HCC differentiation (well, moderately, poorly differentiated) was also recorded.

 2.5 Statistical Analysis

SPSS 26.0 software was used for statistical analysis. Continuous data were expressed as mean±standard deviation, and intergroup comparisons were performed using independent samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical data were expressed as number of cases (%), and intergroup comparisons were performed using χ² test. Using pathological iron staining as the gold standard, the sensitivity, specificity, and concordance rate of SWI in detecting iron deposition were calculated. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to evaluate the efficacy of SLR in differentiating HCC from DN. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 SWI Signal Characteristics of HCC and DN

The SLR of the HCC group was 0.72±0.15, and that of the DN group was 0.94±0.11, with a statistically significant difference between the two groups (t=6.873, P<0.001). In the HCC group, 50 cases (86.2%) showed SWI hypointensity (SLR≤0.82), whereas in the DN group, only 6 cases (21.4%) showed hypointensity, with a statistically significant difference (χ²=32.156, P<0.001).

 3.2 Concordance Between SWI and Pathological Iron Staining

Using pathological iron staining as reference, the sensitivity of SWI in detecting iron deposition in HCC was 86.2% (50/58), the specificity was 75.0% (6/8), and the concordance rate was 86.2%. In the DN group, the sensitivity of SWI in detecting iron deposition was 78.6% (22/28), the specificity was 100% (0/0), and the concordance rate was 78.6%. The positive rate of iron staining in the HCC group was significantly lower than that in the DN group (13.8% vs 78.6%, χ²=30.214, P<0.001).

 3.3 Efficacy of SLR in Differentiating HCC from DN

ROC curve analysis showed that using SLR≤0.82 as the threshold, the sensitivity of SWI in differentiating HCC from DN was 84.5%, the specificity was 82.1%, and the AUC was 0.891 (95%CI: 0.812–0.970, P<0.001).

 3.4 Relationship Between SLR and HCC Differentiation Degree

Among the 58 HCC cases, 18 were well differentiated, 26 were moderately differentiated, and 14 were poorly differentiated. The SLR of well-differentiated HCC was 0.81±0.12, that of moderately differentiated HCC was 0.71±0.14, and that of poorly differentiated HCC was 0.63±0.13. The SLR of moderately and poorly differentiated HCC was significantly lower than that of well-differentiated HCC (t=3.421, P=0.012).

 4 Discussion

The differentiation of HCC and DN in the background of liver cirrhosis is a difficult point in clinical imaging diagnosis. Based on SWI technology, this study found that the SLR of HCC lesions was significantly lower than that of DN, suggesting that iron deposition in HCC is reduced or absent, whereas DN still retains partial iron uptake capacity. This result is consistent with the theory of iron metabolism reprogramming during HCC development. Normal hepatocytes mediate iron uptake through transferrin receptors, whereas HCC cells often downregulate transferrin receptor expression and upregulate the iron export protein ferroportin, leading to decreased intracellular iron content. SWI can indirectly reflect iron deposition status by detecting differences in tissue magnetic susceptibility, thereby providing functional imaging information for the differentiation of HCC and DN.

This study showed that the sensitivity of SWI in detecting iron deposition in HCC was 86.2%, with a high concordance rate with pathological iron staining, indicating that SWI can serve as an effective means for non-invasive assessment of intrahepatic iron deposition. In addition, SLR was correlated with the degree of HCC differentiation, with lower SLR in moderately and poorly differentiated HCC, suggesting that reduced iron deposition may be associated with the degree of tumor dedifferentiation. This finding is helpful for preoperative assessment of tumor biological behavior and provides a reference for individualized treatment.

However, this study still has certain limitations. First, the sample size was relatively limited, and the number of DN cases was small, which may affect statistical power. Second, SWI signals are affected by multiple factors, such as hemorrhage, calcification, and fibrosis, which may interfere with the assessment of iron deposition. In the future, multiparametric MRI and artificial intelligence technology should be combined to further improve diagnostic accuracy.

 5 Conclusion

SWI can effectively detect the endogenous iron reduction status of HCC and DN in the background of liver cirrhosis. The SLR of HCC lesions is significantly lower than that of DN, and SLR≤0.82 is helpful for the differential diagnosis of HCC and DN. SLR is correlated with the degree of HCC differentiation and can serve as an imaging biomarker for evaluating tumor biological behavior. As a non-invasive MRI technique that does not require contrast agents, SWI has important clinical application value in the diagnosis and differentiation of liver cancer and precancerous lesions in the background of liver cirrhosis.

title: Testing the Effectiveness of an E-Course to Combat Cyberbullying
text:
Testing the Effectiveness of an E-Course to Combat Cyberbullying

Abstract: With the widespread adoption of the internet and mobile terminals, cyberbullying has become a significant issue affecting adolescents' physical and mental health. Traditional anti-bullying education is constrained by time, space, and teacher availability, making large-scale implementation difficult. This paper designs and tests an online course targeting cyberbullying, employing a combination of modular instruction, scenario simulation, and interactive quizzes. In a four-week intervention experiment, a controlled study was conducted with 96 students from two parallel classes in the eighth grade of a middle school. The results showed that the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in three areas: cyberbullying awareness, empathy, and coping strategies (p<0.05), with a course completion rate of 91.7%. The study demonstrates that this e-course can effectively enhance adolescents' ability to identify and respond to cyberbullying, and holds value for broader implementation.

1 Introduction

Cyberbullying refers to the act of repeatedly and intentionally harming others through electronic media (such as social platforms, instant messaging, and online games). Compared with offline bullying, it is characterized by anonymity, rapid dissemination, and difficulty of retraction. Surveys show that approximately 30% of middle school students have experienced some form of cyberbullying, yet only 40% of them actively seek help. Existing anti-bullying education in schools is mostly conducted through lectures or class meetings, with fragmented content and limited by class hours, making it difficult to reach all students.

E-courses offer advantages such as repeatable learning, self-paced progress, and multimedia presentation, and have been applied in the field of mental health education. However, research on the design and effectiveness verification of e-courses specifically targeting cyberbullying remains limited. This paper aims to develop a structured e-course for coping with cyberbullying and to test its effectiveness through a controlled experiment, providing empirical evidence for technology dissemination.

2 Analysis of Key Technologies

2.1 Modular Design of Course Content

The course is divided into four core modules: identifying cyberbullying (definitions, forms, legal boundaries), understanding victims' feelings (empathy training), coping strategies (preserving evidence, blocking and reporting, seeking help from adults), and bystander intervention (how to safely support victims). Each module contains 5–8 minute short videos, illustrated case studies, and 3 immediate quiz questions. The modular design facilitates on-demand learning for students and allows teachers to flexibly combine modules for use.

2.2 Scenario Simulation and Branching Dialogue Technology

To improve behavioral transfer, the course incorporates branching dialogue scenario simulations. For example, when students receive insulting messages in a simulated social chat scenario, the system offers three response options: retaliating directly, taking a screenshot and exiting, or seeking help from a trusted adult. After making a choice, the system provides immediate feedback on consequences and suggests better strategies. This technology is based on social cognitive theory and helps students learn appropriate responses through vicarious experience and immediate reinforcement.

2.3 Interactive Quizzes and Immediate Feedback Mechanism

A low-stakes quiz is set after each module. Wrong answers do not result in point deductions, but explanatory feedback pops up. Quiz questions focus on situational judgment, such as "A classmate forwards a photo mocking you in a group chat. What should you do first?" Immediate feedback helps students correct misconceptions. Answer data are recorded in the background for teachers to review the class's overall weak areas, facilitating subsequent offline reinforcement.

2.4 Learning Behavior Tracking and Adaptive Reminders

The platform records indicators such as login frequency, video completion rate, and quiz accuracy. If a student has not logged in for three consecutive days, the system automatically sends a friendly reminder. If the quiz accuracy for a module falls below 60%, the system recommends reviewing that module and pushes supplementary cases. Adaptive reminders improve course completion rates and avoid the common problem of "enrollment marking the end."

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

The experiment was conducted in the eighth grade of a middle school. The experimental group (48 students) used the e-course, while the control group (48 students) received conventional class meeting education. Before the intervention, there were no significant differences between the two groups in scores on bullying awareness, empathy, and coping strategies questionnaires (p>0.05). After four weeks of intervention, the experimental group's scores in the three areas increased by 22.3%, 18.7%, and 26.5%, respectively, while the control group increased by 6.1%, 4.3%, and 5.8%, respectively. Between-group differences were all significant (p<0.05). The course completion rate in the experimental group was 91.7%, with an average learning time of 68 minutes.

In terms of benefits, the course can serve a large number of students simultaneously at extremely low marginal cost; teachers need only one training session to organize instruction. Student feedback showed that 86% found the scenario simulations "helpful" or "very helpful." Additionally, course content can be rapidly updated to adapt to new forms of cyberbullying (such as AI face-swapping insults). The limitation is that the sample came from only one school, and long-term behavioral change still requires follow-up tracking.

4 Conclusion

This paper designed and validated a modular, scenario-based e-course for coping with cyberbullying, featuring adaptive reminders. The controlled experiment demonstrated that the course can significantly enhance middle school students' awareness, empathy, and coping abilities regarding cyberbullying, with a high completion rate and ease of dissemination. Future work can expand the sample to different grade levels and regions, and include a six-month follow-up test to assess long-term effects. For journals focused on technology dissemination, this solution is low-cost, replicable, and does not rely on expert on-site instruction, making it suitable for batch deployment on regional education platforms.

title: Sign realized jump risk and the cross-section of stock returns: Evidence from China's stock market
text:
Signed Realized Jump Risk and Cross-Sectional Returns in the Chinese Stock Market

Abstract: This paper takes the Chinese A-share market as the research object, constructs signed realized jump risk measures based on high-frequency trading data, and examines their predictive power for cross-sectional stock returns. Using monthly data of Shanghai and Shenzhen A-share stocks from 2015 to 2023, the study employs non-parametric jump identification methods to separate positive and negative jump components, and conducts empirical tests through portfolio sorting and Fama-MacBeth regressions. The results show that negative jump risk is significantly positively correlated with future returns, while positive jump risk is negatively correlated with returns, with the long-short portfolio yielding an annualized return of 14.6%. This conclusion remains robust after controlling for size, book-to-market ratio, momentum, and liquidity factors, and is more pronounced in small-cap and high-turnover stocks. The study provides new evidence for understanding the pricing mechanism of jump risk in the Chinese stock market.

Keywords: signed jump risk; cross-sectional returns; high-frequency data; asset pricing; Chinese stock market

 1 Introduction

Whether jump risk is priced in asset markets is one of the core issues in financial economics in recent years. Classical asset pricing theory assumes that returns follow a continuous diffusion process, but a large body of empirical research shows that stock prices often undergo discontinuous jumps due to information shocks, policy adjustments, or unexpected events. The bipower variation theory proposed by Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard (2004, 2006) provides a methodological foundation for separating jump components from high-frequency data. Since then, scholars have found that jump risk not only has systematic pricing implications, but its directionality—namely positive jumps versus negative jumps—exhibits significant asymmetry in its impact on returns.

As an emerging market, the Chinese stock market is characterized by a high proportion of retail investors, frequent policy interventions, and a unique price limit system, making jump behavior more frequent and directional effects potentially stronger. However, existing literature mostly focuses on developed markets, and research on the cross-sectional pricing of signed jump risk in the Chinese stock market remains insufficient. This paper attempts to fill this gap by using Chinese A-share high-frequency data to construct signed realized jump risk measures and systematically examine their relationship with cross-sectional returns.

The contributions of this paper are as follows: First, it introduces signed jump risk into the cross-sectional research framework of the Chinese stock market; Second, it reveals the heterogeneous characteristics of jump risk pricing by incorporating China's unique institutional background; Third, it provides references for investor risk management and regulatory policy formulation.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Sources and Sample

This paper selects Shanghai and Shenzhen A-share listed companies from January 2015 to December 2023 as the sample, excluding financial stocks, ST stocks, and stocks listed for less than 6 months. High-frequency data consists of 5-minute frequency closing prices, and daily and monthly return data are obtained from the CSMAR database. The final sample contains 2,847 stocks, with approximately 280,000 monthly observations in total. The risk-free rate adopts the one-year fixed deposit rate, and market factor, size factor, value factor, and momentum factor data are obtained from the RESSET database.

 2.2 Measurement of Signed Realized Jump Risk

Based on the method of Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard (2006), the realized variance of each stock is decomposed daily:

\[
RV_t = \sum_{i=1}^{M} r_{t,i}^2
\]

\[
BPV_t = \frac{\pi}{2} \sum_{i=2}^{M} |r_{t,i}| |r_{t,i-1}|
\]

where \( r_{t,i} \) is the \( i \)-th 5-minute return on day \( t \), and \( M \) is the number of intraday observations. The jump component is defined as:

\[
J_t = \max(RV_t - BPV_t, 0)
\]

Positive and negative jumps are further separated:

\[
J_t^+ = J_t \cdot I(r_t > 0), \quad J_t^- = J_t \cdot I(r_t < 0)
\]

Monthly signed jump risk is the sum of intraday jump components:

\[
SJ^+_{i,t} = \sum_{d=1}^{D_t} J_{i,d}^+, \quad SJ^-_{i,t} = \sum_{d=1}^{D_t} J_{i,d}^-
\]

To eliminate dimensional effects, logarithms are taken and standardized separately.

 2.3 Empirical Methods

Portfolio sorting method is adopted: at the end of each month, stocks are divided into 5 groups according to \( SJ^+ \) and \( SJ^- \) respectively, and the next month's equal-weighted and value-weighted returns are calculated to construct long-short portfolios. Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regression is further employed:

\[
R_{i,t+1} = \alpha + \beta_1 SJ^+_{i,t} + \beta_2 SJ^-_{i,t} + \gamma' X_{i,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t+1}
\]

where \( X \) represents control variables, including size, book-to-market ratio, momentum, turnover, and volatility. Standard errors are adjusted by Newey-West.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Descriptive Statistics

During the sample period, the average monthly positive jump for individual stocks is approximately 0.032, and the average negative jump is approximately 0.041. The frequency and magnitude of negative jumps are both higher than those of positive jumps, indicating that downside jump risk is more prominent in the Chinese stock market. Correlation analysis shows that the correlation coefficient between \( SJ^+ \) and \( SJ^- \) is -0.18, indicating that the two are not simple mirror images and contain independent information content.

 3.2 Portfolio Sorting Results

When sorted by \( SJ^- \), the next month's equal-weighted returns from the lowest group to the highest group are 0.42%, 0.68%, 0.91%, 1.17%, and 1.54%, respectively, with the long-short portfolio return being 1.12% (t=3.21), approximately 14.6% annualized. When sorted by \( SJ^+ \), returns show a decreasing trend, with the highest group being 0.87% lower than the lowest group (t=-2.64). After value-weighting, the results weaken slightly but remain significant. Bivariate sorting shows that after controlling for size and turnover, the pricing effect of signed jump risk is concentrated in small-cap and high-turnover stocks.

 3.3 Fama-MacBeth Regression Results

Cross-sectional regression shows that the coefficient of \( SJ^- \) is 0.083 (t=3.47), and the coefficient of \( SJ^+ \) is -0.061 (t=-2.89), both significant at the 1% level. After adding control variables, the coefficients become 0.076 and -0.054, respectively, with no substantial change in significance. The size factor coefficient is significantly negative, the momentum factor is not significant, and the turnover coefficient is significantly positive, consistent with existing literature.

 3.4 Robustness Tests

After adopting different jump identification thresholds (such as \( \alpha=0.999 \)), replacing the jump measure (MedRV), excluding the 2015 stock market crash sample, and controlling for price limit effects, the core conclusions remain robust. Year-by-year regressions show that the negative jump premium is particularly prominent in 2018 and 2022, possibly related to trade frictions and pandemic shocks.

 4 Discussion

This paper finds that negative jump risk earns a positive premium, while positive jump risk earns a negative premium, consistent with the "loss aversion" and "lottery preference" explanations in behavioral finance. Chinese retail investors overreact to downside risk and demand higher compensation; meanwhile, they exhibit gambling-type preferences for upside jumps, pushing up prices and reducing future returns. The effect is stronger in small-cap and high-turnover stocks, reflecting the amplifying role of speculative atmosphere and information asymmetry.

Compared with developed markets, the signed jump premium in the Chinese stock market is higher, possibly related to the delayed release of jumps caused by the price limit system and short-selling restrictions hindering the incorporation of negative information into prices. In addition, frequent policy interventions cause jump components to contain more systematic information, further strengthening the pricing effect.

The policy implications of this paper are as follows: Regulators should pay attention to the impact of jump risk accumulation on market stability and improve information disclosure and trading mechanisms; investors can incorporate signed jump risk into portfolio management to optimize risk-adjusted returns.

 5 Conclusion
