NCBI BLAST and DNAMAN software were used for sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis; ExPASy ProtParam and SMART online tools were used to predict protein physicochemical properties and conserved domains.

 2.3 Expression Analysis

Total RNA was extracted using RNAprep Pure Plant Kit, and cDNA was synthesized by reverse transcription. Using pear *Actin* as the internal reference gene, specific primers for BBX16, MYB10, DFR, UFGT, and CHS were designed for real-time quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR). The reaction system was 20 μL, and the program was 95°C for 30 s; 95°C for 5 s, 60°C for 30 s, 40 cycles. The 2^-ΔΔCt method was used to calculate relative expression levels. Anthocyanin content was determined by the pH differential method.

 2.4 Subcellular Localization

The BBX16 coding region without the stop codon was cloned into the pCAMBIA1300-GFP vector to construct the 35S::BBX16-GFP fusion expression vector. Agrobacterium-mediated transformation was used to transform tobacco leaf epidermal cells, and GFP fluorescence signals were observed under a laser confocal microscope after 24 h of dark culture.

 2.5 Protein Interaction Verification

Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) and bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assays were used to verify the interaction between BBX16 and MYB10. In the Y2H assay, BBX16 and MYB10 were cloned into pGADT7 and pGBKT7 vectors, respectively, co-transformed into Y2H Gold yeast strain, spread on SD/-Leu/-Trp/-His/-Ade deficient medium, and cultured at 30°C for 3–5 d to observe colony growth. In the BiFC assay, nYFP-BBX16 and cYFP-MYB10 vectors were constructed, co-transformed into tobacco leaves, and YFP fluorescence was observed after 48 h of dark culture.

 2.6 Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assay

The pGreenII 0800-LUC-PDFR and pGreenII 0800-LUC-PUFGT reporter vectors, as well as 35S::BBX16 and 35S::MYB10 effector vectors, were constructed. The reporter and effector vectors were co-transformed into tobacco leaves, and after 48 h of culture, firefly luciferase (LUC) and Renilla luciferase (REN) activities were measured, and the LUC/REN ratio was calculated.

 2.7 Genetic Transformation and Functional Verification

The pCAMBIA1300-BBX16 overexpression vector and pTRV2-BBX16 silencing vector were constructed and transformed into pear callus, respectively. Overexpression callus was cultured under light for 7 d, and silencing callus was subjected to light treatment to detect anthocyanin content and related gene expression.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Cloning and Sequence Characteristics of BBX16 Gene

The full-length coding sequence of BBX16 was cloned from red pear peel cDNA, with a length of 1,134 bp, encoding 377 amino acids, with a predicted molecular weight of 41.6 kDa and a theoretical isoelectric point of 5.82. Sequence analysis showed that BBX16 contains one B-box domain and one CCT domain, belonging to the fourth subfamily of the B-box family. Phylogenetic analysis showed that BBX16 is most closely related to apple MdBBX16 and peach PpBBX16, with amino acid sequence homologies of 92.3% and 85.7%, respectively.

 3.2 BBX16 Expression Is Light-Induced and Correlated with Anthocyanin Accumulation

qRT-PCR results showed that BBX16 expression in red pear peel was significantly induced by light. At 6 h after bag removal and light exposure, BBX16 expression rapidly increased, peaked at 12 h, reaching approximately 8.6 times that of the dark-treated control, and then gradually declined. Correspondingly, anthocyanin content began to accumulate significantly at 12 h after light treatment and reached a relatively high level at 24 h. In the green bud sport mutant, BBX16 expression was significantly lower than that in red pear, and anthocyanin content was extremely low. Correlation analysis showed that BBX16 expression was significantly positively correlated with anthocyanin content (r=0.91, P<0.01).

 3.3 BBX16 Is Localized in the Nucleus

Subcellular localization results showed that the green fluorescence signal of the 35S::BBX16-GFP fusion protein was concentrated only in the nucleus region of tobacco epidermal cells, overlapping with the nuclear marker dye DAPI signal, whereas the empty vector GFP control fluorescence was distributed in the cytoplasm and nucleus. This indicates that BBX16 is a nuclear-localized protein, consistent with the characteristics of a transcription factor.

 3.4 BBX16 Interacts with MYB10 Protein

In the Y2H assay, the yeast strain co-transformed with BBX16-AD and MYB10-BD grew normally on SD/-Leu/-Trp/-His/-Ade deficient medium, while the control group could not grow, indicating that BBX16 interacts with MYB10. The BiFC assay further confirmed that obvious YFP fluorescence signals were observed in the nucleus of tobacco leaf cells co-expressing nYFP-BBX16 and cYFP-MYB10, while the negative control showed no fluorescence, verifying their interaction in planta.

 3.5 BBX16 Enhances the Activation Activity of MYB10 on Downstream Genes

Dual-luciferase reporter assays showed that expression of MYB10 alone increased LUC activity driven by DFR and UFGT promoters by 3.2-fold and 2.8-fold, respectively. When BBX16 was co-expressed with MYB10, the LUC/REN ratios were significantly increased to 5.7-fold and 5.1-fold, respectively, indicating that BBX16 can enhance the activation effect of MYB10 on downstream structural gene promoters. However, expression of BBX16 alone had no significant effect on DFR and UFGT promoter activity.

 3.6 BBX16 Overexpression Promotes Anthocyanin Accumulation

Overexpression of BBX16 in pear callus resulted in approximately 2.4-fold higher anthocyanin content in overexpression lines compared with the control after 7 d of light culture, and the expression levels of DFR and UFGT were upregulated by 3.1-fold and 2.7-fold, respectively. Conversely, after silencing BBX16, light-induced anthocyanin content decreased by approximately 62% compared with the control, and the expression levels of DFR and UFGT decreased by 58% and 54%, respectively. This indicates that BBX16 is a positive regulator of light-induced anthocyanin accumulation.

 4 Discussion

Light signals are important environmental factors regulating plant anthocyanin biosynthesis, and the BBX protein family, as a key component of the light signaling pathway, plays an important role in the regulation of pigment accumulation. In this study, BBX16 was cloned from red pear, and it was confirmed to be light-induced and positively correlated with anthocyanin accumulation, similar to the light-responsive patterns of apple MdBBX20 and Arabidopsis BBX21. Subcellular localization showed that BBX16 is localized in the nucleus, suggesting that it may function as a transcriptional regulatory factor.

This study reveals for the first time the protein interaction between BBX16 and MYB10. MYB10 is the core transcription factor for anthocyanin biosynthesis in pear, but the mechanism regulating its activity remains unclear. This study found that BBX16 does not directly bind to the DFR and UFGT promoters, but instead promotes downstream gene expression by enhancing the transcriptional activation activity of MYB10. This mechanism is consistent with the BBX20-MYB10 regulatory model in apple, but this is the first report in pear. It is speculated that BBX16 may act as a co-activator of MYB10, stabilizing the MBW complex or promoting its binding to downstream promoters.

In addition, BBX16 expression was significantly reduced in the green bud sport mutant, suggesting that the difference in its expression may be an important reason for the lack of anthocyanin accumulation in the bud sport mutant. This study provides new insights into the molecular mechanism of red pear color formation, and BBX16 can serve as a candidate gene for color improvement in red pear. However, whether BBX16 directly participates in the light signal transduction pathway and its regulatory relationship with photoreceptors (such as CRY and PHY) still requires further study.

 5 Conclusion

In this study, the BBX16 gene was cloned from red pear, and it was confirmed to be a nuclear-localized protein, light-induced, and significantly positively correlated with anthocyanin accumulation. BBX16 interacts with MYB10 and can enhance the activation activity of MYB10 on downstream structural genes DFR and UFGT. Overexpression of BBX16 promotes anthocyanin accumulation, while silencing BBX16 inhibits light-induced anthocyanin biosynthesis. In summary, BBX16 acts as a positive regulator that mediates light-induced anthocyanin accumulation in red pear peel by activating MYB10.

title: Exploring the bacterial community and fermentation characteristics during silage fermentation of abandoned fresh tea leaves
text:
Exploration of Bacterial Community and Fermentation Characteristics During the Ensiling Fermentation of Discarded Fresh Tea Leaves

Abstract: In Chinese tea gardens, a large amount of discarded fresh tea leaves is generated annually during pruning and picking operations. Due to their high moisture content and high tannin levels, direct ensiling is prone to spoilage. In this study, discarded fresh tea leaves were used as raw material, and two treatments were established: direct ensiling (CK) and addition of a lactic acid bacteria preparation (LAB). After 45 days of ensiling, fermentation quality, nutritional composition, and bacterial community structure were measured. The results showed that the addition of lactic acid bacteria rapidly reduced pH to below 4.0, significantly increased lactic acid content, decreased the proportion of ammonia nitrogen, and inhibited the counts of aerobic bacteria and molds. High-throughput sequencing revealed that in the LAB treatment, Lactobacillus became the absolutely dominant genus, with a relative abundance of 78.6%, whereas the CK group was dominated by Enterobacter and Weissella. Correlation analysis indicated that pH was significantly negatively correlated with Lactobacillus and positively correlated with Enterobacter. In summary, the addition of a lactic acid bacteria preparation can effectively improve the ensiling fermentation quality of discarded fresh tea leaves, achieve resource utilization of waste, and is suitable for promotion in tea-producing areas and livestock farms.

Keywords: discarded fresh tea leaves; ensiling fermentation; bacterial community; lactic acid bacteria; fermentation quality

 1 Introduction

China is a major tea-producing country, with tea garden area and output ranking first in the world. During tea plant pruning, fresh leaf picking, and processing, a large amount of discarded fresh tea leaves, old leaves, and pruned branches and leaves is generated. It is estimated that each mu of tea garden can produce 200–400 kg of discarded fresh tea leaves annually. These wastes have high moisture content (70%–80%) and are rich in protein, carbohydrates, and tea polyphenols. Direct return to the field easily causes rotting and odor, while burning pollutes the environment. How to convert them into usable resources is a practical problem faced by tea-producing areas.

Ensiling is a mature technology for preserving green forage. Through anaerobic fermentation by lactic acid bacteria, organic acids are produced, pH is lowered, harmful microorganisms are inhibited, and feed nutrients are preserved for the long term. However, discarded fresh tea leaves differ from conventional ensiling raw materials: their moisture content is relatively high, soluble sugars are relatively insufficient, and anti-nutritional factors such as tannins and caffeine are present at relatively high levels. During direct ensiling, lactic acid bacteria start slowly, and butyric acid fermentation and protein degradation are likely to occur. Therefore, studying the microbial succession patterns during ensiling and seeking effective regulatory measures has important production significance.

In recent years, high-throughput sequencing technology has been widely applied in ensiling microbiology research, revealing changes in microbial communities that are difficult to detect with traditional culture methods. In this study, discarded fresh tea leaves were used as the subject to compare the fermentation characteristics and bacterial community differences between direct ensiling and ensiling with added lactic acid bacteria preparation, providing a technical basis for the feed utilization of waste in tea-producing areas.

 2 Key Technical Analysis

 2.1 Raw Material Characteristics and Pretreatment

Discarded fresh tea leaves were collected from young shoots and old leaves within 24 hours after pruning in a tea garden. The moisture content was approximately 76%, water-soluble carbohydrate (WSC) content was 4.2% fresh weight, crude protein content was 5.8% dry matter, and tannin content was 2.1% dry matter. After transport to the laboratory, the raw material was chopped to 2–3 cm using a forage chopper and mixed evenly. Two treatments were established: CK was direct ensiling; LAB was addition of a commercial lactic acid bacteria preparation (mainly containing Lactobacillus plantarum and Lactobacillus buchneri, viable count ≥1×10¹⁰ CFU/g) at a dosage of 5 g per ton of fresh material, dissolved in a small amount of water and sprayed evenly. Each treatment had 3 replicates, packed into 5-L plastic silage buckets, compacted and sealed, and stored at room temperature (20–25°C) for 45 days.

 2.2 Determination of Fermentation Quality and Nutritional Composition

After ensiling, representative samples were taken to determine pH, organic acids, and ammonia nitrogen. pH was measured with a pH meter; lactic acid, acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid were determined by high-performance liquid chromatography; ammonia nitrogen was determined by the phenol-sodium hypochlorite colorimetric method and expressed as a proportion of total nitrogen. Nutritional composition determination included dry matter, crude protein, neutral detergent fiber, and acid detergent fiber, referring to conventional feed analysis standards. Meanwhile, fresh samples were taken for microbial counts: lactic acid bacteria on MRS medium, aerobic bacteria on nutrient agar, and molds and yeasts on Bengal red medium, all using the plate counting method.

 2.3 High-Throughput Sequencing and Bacterial Community Analysis

About 10 g of ensiling sample was taken, washed with sterile phosphate buffer under shaking, and microbial cells were collected by centrifugation for total DNA extraction. PCR amplification was performed targeting the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene, with primers 338F and 806R. The amplification products were purified, quantified, and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform. After quality control and chimera removal, the raw sequences were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) using QIIME2 software at 97% similarity. Species annotation was performed based on the Silva database, and the Shannon index, Chao1 index, and relative abundance were calculated. Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was used to compare differences in community structure, and Spearman correlation coefficients were used to analyze the relationship between dominant bacterial genera and fermentation indicators.

 2.4 Data Processing and Statistics

Experimental data were organized using Excel, and one-way analysis of variance was performed using SPSS 22.0. Significant differences were tested using Duncan's method (P<0.05). Sequencing data were used to draw bar charts and heatmaps using R language. All results are expressed as mean ± standard deviation.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

 3.1 Changes in Fermentation Quality

After 45 days of ensiling, the pH of the CK group was 5.12, which was noticeably high, lactic acid content was only 1.8% dry matter, acetic acid and butyric acid contents were relatively high, and ammonia nitrogen accounted for 12.6% of total nitrogen, indicating poor fermentation quality and a risk of spoilage. The pH of the LAB group decreased to 3.86, lactic acid content reached 5.6% dry matter, acetic acid content was moderate, butyric acid was not detected, and the proportion of ammonia nitrogen decreased to 6.3%. This indicates that the addition of a lactic acid bacteria preparation can rapidly produce acid and inhibit undesirable fermentation. Microbial counts showed that the number of lactic acid bacteria in the LAB group was 8.9 log CFU/g, significantly higher than 6.7 log CFU/g in the CK group; the counts of aerobic bacteria and molds were reduced by 1.5 and 2.1 orders of magnitude, respectively, compared with the CK group. In terms of nutritional composition, the dry matter loss rate of the LAB group (4.2%) was lower than that of the CK group (8.7%), and the crude protein preservation rate increased by about 9 percentage points. There was no significant difference in neutral detergent fiber and acid detergent fiber contents between the two groups, indicating that the addition of lactic acid bacteria had limited effect on fiber components.

 3.2 Bacterial Community Composition

A total of approximately 480,000 valid sequences were obtained by sequencing, with an average of 42,000 sequences per sample, and coverage was greater than 99% for all samples. The Shannon index of the CK group was 2.86, while that of the LAB group decreased to 1.92, indicating that the addition of lactic acid bacteria reduced bacterial diversity. At the phylum level, the CK group was dominated by Proteobacteria (52.3%) and Firmicutes (41.5%); the LAB group was absolutely dominated by Firmicutes (91.2%), with Proteobacteria accounting for only 6.8%. At the genus level, the dominant bacteria in the CK group were Enterobacter (28.4%), Weissella (19.7%), Lactobacillus (15.2%), and Pseudomonas (8.1%); in the LAB group, the relative abundance of Lactobacillus reached 78.6%, Weissella decreased to 7.3%, and Enterobacter was only 2.5%. PCoA analysis showed that the samples of the two groups were clearly separated on the coordinate axes, indicating that the addition of lactic acid bacteria significantly changed the bacterial community structure.

 3.3 Relationship Between Dominant Bacterial Genera and Fermentation Indicators

Spearman correlation analysis showed that the relative abundance of Lactobacillus was significantly negatively correlated with pH (r=-0.89), ammonia nitrogen (r=-0.82), and butyric acid content (r=-0.76), and significantly positively correlated with lactic acid content (r=0.91). Enterobacter and Pseudomonas were positively correlated with pH, ammonia nitrogen, and butyric acid, and negatively correlated with lactic acid. Weissella was weakly negatively correlated with pH, but its abundance was relatively high in the CK group, possibly participating in early fermentation. These results indicate that the rapid colonization of Lactobacillus is the key to inhibiting harmful bacteria such as Enterobacter and improving fermentation quality.

 3.4 Benefit Analysis

From the perspective of technical benefits, the addition of a lactic acid bacteria preparation can increase the success rate of ensiling discarded fresh tea leaves from less than 50% to more than 95%. The silage has an acidic and fragrant odor, a soft texture, and significantly improved palatability. From the perspective of economic benefits, each mu of tea garden can collect about 300 kg of discarded fresh tea leaves annually, and about 270 kg of fermented feed can be obtained after ensiling. Based on the calculation that each ton of silage replaces 0.2 tons of concentrate, about 100–150 yuan in feed costs can be saved. If promoted in tea-producing areas, a thousand-mu tea garden can convert 300 tons of waste annually and produce 270 tons of silage, with direct economic benefits of about 80,000–120,000 yuan, while also reducing waste treatment costs and environmental pollution. From the perspective of ecological benefits, ensiling utilization avoids methane and leachate pollution caused by the decomposition of fresh tea leaves, realizes carbon and nitrogen recycling, and conforms to the direction of green agriculture development.

 4 Conclusion

Through comparison of direct ensiling and ensiling with added lactic acid bacteria of discarded fresh tea leaves, this study clarified the regulatory effects of a lactic acid bacteria preparation on fermentation quality and bacterial community. The main conclusions are as follows: the addition of a lactic acid bacteria preparation can rapidly reduce pH, increase lactic acid content, inhibit Enterobacter and molds, and reduce protein degradation and dry matter loss; Lactobacillus becomes the dominant genus, and its abundance is significantly negatively correlated with pH, ammonia nitrogen, and butyric acid, making it the core microbial group for improving fermentation quality. This technology is simple to operate, low in cost, and obvious in benefits, and is suitable for promotion in tea-producing areas and livestock farms. In practical application, it is recommended to pay attention to raw material moisture regulation (appropriate drying or addition of wheat bran) and to select products mainly composed of homofermentative lactic acid bacteria to further improve ensiling stability. In the future, dedicated composite microbial preparations can be developed by combining tea polyphenol-degrading bacteria and fiber-decomposing bacteria to enhance the feed value of discarded fresh tea leaves.

title: Spatiotemporal Variation and Pollution Assessment of Pb/Zn from Smelting Activities in China
text:
Abstract: To reveal the spatiotemporal differentiation characteristics and ecological health risks of Pb/Zn pollution caused by lead-zinc smelting activities in China, this study constructed geostatistical analysis and pollution assessment models based on surface soil and crop sample data from major smelting areas nationwide from 2010 to 2022. The results showed that the average contents of Pb and Zn were 168.3 mg·kg⁻¹ and 312.7 mg·kg⁻¹, respectively, significantly higher than the corresponding background values. Temporally, the pollution level was relatively high from 2010 to 2015, and showed a declining trend after 2016, but strong ecological risks still existed in some local areas. Spatially, pollution hotspots were concentrated in smelting-intensive areas such as Hunan, Yunnan, Guangxi, and Shaanxi, and exhibited a concentric-circle decreasing pattern centered on smelters. The Nemerow comprehensive pollution index showed that approximately 32.6% of sampling points were at the heavy pollution level, and the potential ecological risk of Pb was higher than that of Zn. The exceedance rate of Pb in the edible parts of crops was 18.4%, and that of Zn was 9.7%. The study indicated that smelting activities are the main source of Pb/Zn pollution in Chinese farmland, and source control and zoned remediation need to be strengthened.

Keywords: lead-zinc smelting; spatiotemporal variation; pollution assessment; ecological risk; China

 1 Introduction

Lead (Pb) and zinc (Zn) are important non-ferrous metal resources and are widely used in industries such as batteries, galvanizing, alloys, and chemicals. China is the world's largest producer and consumer of lead and zinc, with refined lead and zinc output in 2022 accounting for approximately 44% and 47% of the global total, respectively. However, the lead-zinc smelting process releases large amounts of waste gas, wastewater, and waste residue containing Pb and Zn, which enter surrounding soil and water bodies through atmospheric deposition, surface runoff, and waste stockpiling, causing persistent heavy metal pollution. Pb has neurotoxicity and is non-degradable, while excessive Zn can affect crop metabolism and the human immune system. In recent years, China has successively implemented policies such as the "Twelfth Five-Year Plan for Comprehensive Prevention and Control of Heavy Metal Pollution" and the "Action Plan for Soil Pollution Prevention and Control," and pollution control in smelting areas has achieved certain results, but regional differences are significant, and the spatiotemporal pattern of pollution remains unclear.

Existing studies mostly focus on a single smelter or a short time scale, lacking spatiotemporal comparison and systematic assessment of Pb/Zn pollution at the national scale. Therefore, this study integrated soil and crop monitoring data from major lead-zinc smelting areas in China from 2010 to 2022, analyzed the spatiotemporal variation characteristics of Pb/Zn contents, and used the Nemerow comprehensive pollution index and potential ecological risk index for pollution assessment, aiming to provide a scientific basis for zoned management and control of heavy metal pollution in smelting areas and safe agricultural production.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Overview of the Study Area

This study selected 12 typical lead-zinc smelting areas as study areas, including Zhuzhou in Hunan, Qujing in Yunnan, Hechi in Guangxi, Baoji in Shaanxi, Huludao in Liaoning, and Jiyuan in Henan. These areas have long smelting histories and concentrated production capacity, and are mostly surrounded by farmland and residential areas, making them representative. The climate types include subtropical monsoon, temperate monsoon, and semi-arid climates, and the soil types are mainly red soil, yellow-brown soil, fluvo-aquic soil, and cinnamon soil.

 2.2 Sample Collection and Analysis

Surface soil (0–20 cm) samples were collected in four periods: 2010, 2015, 2018, and 2022. Thirty to fifty sampling points were set up in each smelting area and divided into four gradients according to distance from the smelter: <1 km, 1–3 km, 3–5 km, and >5 km, yielding a total of 1,860 valid soil samples. During the same periods, 620 samples of edible parts of crops such as rice, wheat, and corn were collected. Soil samples were air-dried, ground, and digested, and Pb and Zn contents were determined by ICP-MS; crop samples were dried, crushed, and microwave-digested, and determined by the same method. Blanks and standard reference materials (GBW07401) were set for each batch of samples for quality control, and recovery rates ranged from 92% to 107%.

 2.3 Assessment Methods

The Nemerow comprehensive pollution index method was used to assess the degree of soil pollution:

\[
P_i = C_i / S_i
\]

\[
P_{comprehensive} = \sqrt{\frac{(P_{i,ave})^2 + (P_{i,max})^2}{2}}
\]

Where \(C_i\) is the measured content, and \(S_i\) is the soil background value (26.0 mg·kg⁻¹ for Pb and 74.2 mg·kg⁻¹ for Zn). Classification standards: \(P_{comprehensive} \leq 0.7\) is safe, 0.7–1.0 is warning, 1.0–2.0 is slight pollution, 2.0–3.0 is moderate pollution, and >3.0 is heavy pollution.

The Hakanson potential ecological risk index was used to assess ecological risk:

\[
RI = \sum E_i = \sum T_i \times C_i / S_i
\]

The toxicity response coefficients \(T_i\) for Pb and Zn were taken as 5 and 1, respectively. \(RI < 150\) is low risk, 150–300 is moderate risk, 300–600 is relatively high risk, and >600 is high risk.

Geostatistics and GIS spatial interpolation were used to analyze spatiotemporal distribution, and SPSS 26.0 was used for analysis of variance and correlation tests.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Temporal Changes in Pb/Zn Contents

From 2010 to 2022, the average soil Pb content in the study area decreased from 201.5 mg·kg⁻¹ in 2010 to 142.6 mg·kg⁻¹ in 2022, a decrease of 29.2%; the average Zn content decreased from 356.8 mg·kg⁻¹ to 278.4 mg·kg⁻¹, a decrease of 22.0%. The Pb contents in the four periods were 201.5, 178.3, 156.7, and 142.6 mg·kg⁻¹, and the Zn contents were 356.8, 324.1, 295.6, and 278.4 mg·kg⁻¹, all showing significant downward trends (P<0.05). The decline rate was relatively fast from 2010 to 2015, slowed from 2015 to 2018, and some areas showed a slight rebound from 2018 to 2022, possibly related to the transfer of smelting capacity and secondary pollution.

The Pb content in the edible parts of crops decreased from 0.21 mg·kg⁻¹ in 2010 to 0.13 mg·kg⁻¹ in 2022, and Zn decreased from 28.6 mg·kg⁻¹ to 22.4 mg·kg⁻¹. Using the GB 2762—2022 limit as the standard, the Pb exceedance rate decreased from 26.3% to 12.5%, and the Zn exceedance rate decreased from 14.8% to 6.9%, but exceedances remained severe in some local high-pollution areas.

 3.2 Spatial Distribution of Pb/Zn Contents

Spatially, Pb/Zn contents showed significant heterogeneity. The average soil Pb contents in Zhuzhou, Hunan, Qujing, Yunnan, and Hechi, Guangxi were 246.7, 198.4, and 187.2 mg·kg⁻¹, respectively, significantly higher than those in Huludao, Liaoning (112.5 mg·kg⁻¹) and Jiyuan, Henan (126.8 mg·kg⁻¹). Zn content was highest in Qujing, Yunnan (412.3 mg·kg⁻¹), followed by Zhuzhou, Hunan (368.5 mg·kg⁻¹) and Baoji, Shaanxi (321.7 mg·kg⁻¹). Overall, the pattern showed that southern smelting areas were higher than northern ones, and old industrial bases were higher than newly built parks.

With the smelter as the center, Pb/Zn contents decreased in concentric circles. The average Pb and Zn contents at <1 km from the plant area were 382.6 and 596.4 mg·kg⁻¹, respectively, decreasing to 186.3 and 327.8 mg·kg⁻¹ at 1–3 km, 112.4 and 198.6 mg·kg⁻¹ at 3–5 km, and 68.7 and 112.3 mg·kg⁻¹ at >5 km. The attenuation rate of Pb was faster than that of Zn, indicating that Pb is more likely to settle and accumulate in near-source areas, while Zn has relatively stronger mobility.

 3.3 Pollution Assessment

The Nemerow comprehensive pollution index showed that heavily polluted sampling points accounted for 48.2% in 2010 and decreased to 24.6% in 2022, but moderate or above pollution still accounted for 32.6%. The mean single-factor pollution index of Pb decreased from 7.75 to 5.48, and that of Zn decreased from 4.81 to 3.75, with Pb pollution being higher than Zn. The potential ecological risk index indicated that the mean RI in 2010 was 286.4, belonging to moderate risk; in 2022 it decreased to 198.7, still close to the lower limit of moderate risk. Among these, the average contribution rate of Pb to RI was 78.3%, making it the main risk factor. Spatially, RI values were highest in Zhuzhou, Hunan and Qujing, Yunnan, still reaching 312.5 and 276.8 in 2022, respectively, belonging to the relatively high risk level.

The crop health risk assessment showed that the average daily exposure of children to Pb through rice intake was higher than the safety threshold, and sampling points with non-carcinogenic risk index HQ>1 accounted for 21.7%, while that for adults was below 1. The HQ of Zn was less than 1 in all cases, but in high-zinc areas the HQ for children was close to 0.8, requiring attention.

 4 Discussion

This study shows that soil Pb/Zn pollution in China's lead-zinc smelting areas has generally shown an improving trend, which is closely related to national heavy metal emission reduction policies, upgrades in smelting technology, and remediation of contaminated sites. The decline from 2010 to 2015 was significant, benefiting from key regional remediation and the elimination of backward production capacity during the "Twelfth Five-Year Plan" period; the slowdown after 2016 indicates that the remaining pollution is mostly historically inherited and deeply accumulated, making treatment more difficult. Local rebounds may be related to the secondary utilization of smelting waste residue, continued input from atmospheric deposition, and adjustments in monitoring points.

Spatial differentiation is jointly affected by smelting scale, historical duration, topography and climate, and land use patterns. In the humid and hot southern region, leaching is strong and Zn mobility is high, but Pb easily combines with iron-manganese oxides and remains retained; in the arid northern region, atmospheric deposition contributes more, and the pollution belt is wider. Distance from the plant is the core factor controlling pollution, but wind direction, topography, and irrigation methods can alter its spatial pattern. For example, some sampling points in Zhuzhou, Hunan still showed high values at 3–5 km downwind, indicating that atmospheric transport has a significant impact.

The pollution assessment results are basically consistent with existing regional studies, but this study is the first to compare spatiotemporal changes across multiple smelting areas at the national scale. The ecological risk of Pb is higher than that of Zn, mainly because of its high toxicity coefficient, low mobility, and easy accumulation in the surface layer. Although the exceedance rate in crops has decreased, the health risk to children still cannot be ignored, especially in major rice-producing areas. Although Zn has lower risk, excessive intake can affect copper absorption and immune function, and it needs to be included in integrated management.

This study has certain limitations: the data are an integration of multi-period monitoring, and sampling density and periods are not completely consistent across regions; the differentiated effects of smelting types (lead smelting, zinc smelting, and combined smelting) were not considered; and the health risk assessment did not incorporate dietary structure and bioavailability. Future studies should combine isotope tracing, multi-media models, and long-term fixed-point observations to improve assessment accuracy.

 5 Conclusions

(1) From 2010 to 2022, the average soil Pb and Zn contents in China's major lead-zinc smelting areas decreased from 201.5 and 356.8 mg·kg⁻¹ to 142.6 and 278.4 mg·kg⁻¹, respectively, showing significant downward trends, but in 2022 they were still 5.5 times and 3.8 times higher than the background values. The exceedance rates of Pb and Zn in crops decreased to 12.5% and 6.9%, respectively.

(2) Spatially, pollution hotspots were concentrated in southern smelting areas such as Zhuzhou in Hunan, Qujing in Yunnan, and Hechi in Guangxi, showing a concentric-circle decrease centered on smelters, and the near-source accumulation characteristics of Pb were stronger than those of Zn.

(3) The Nemerow comprehensive pollution index showed that in 2022, heavily polluted sampling points accounted for 24.6%, and moderate or above pollution accounted for 32.6%; the mean potential ecological risk index was 198.7, belonging to moderate risk, with Pb contributing 78.3% and being the main risk factor.

(4) Sampling points with non-carcinogenic risk index HQ>1 for children's Pb intake through rice accounted for 21.7%, requiring key control. It is recommended to strengthen source emission reduction in smelting areas, treatment of historical waste residue, and zoned safe utilization of farmland, with particular attention to major rice-producing areas in the south and children's exposure risks.

title: Carbon neutrality, bank lending, and credit risk: Evidence from the Eurozone
text:
Carbon Neutrality, Bank Credit, and Credit Risk: Evidence from the Euro Area

Abstract: Achieving carbon neutrality requires large-scale funding, and bank credit is an important source of such funding. However, the low-carbon transition may alter borrowers' repayment capacity, thereby affecting banks' credit risk. Based on data from major euro area banks from 2010 to 2022, this paper analyzes the relationship between changes in bank credit structure and credit risk during the advancement of carbon neutrality policies. The study finds that with the implementation of carbon neutrality-related policies, banks' credit exposure to high-carbon industries has gradually declined, while credit allocation to green projects has continued to rise. In the short term, the default risk of clients in high-carbon industries has increased somewhat, but banks' overall credit risk has remained stable, and some banks that actively adjusted their credit structure even exhibited lower non-performing loan ratios. This paper argues that banks should proactively incorporate carbon neutrality goals into their credit management framework, and by optimizing asset portfolios and strengthening environmental risk assessment, control credit risk while supporting the economy's low-carbon transition.

Introduction: Climate change is one of the major challenges facing the world today. As an active promoter of global climate policy, the euro area has proposed a long-term goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. Achieving this goal requires not only government policy guidance but also the support of the financial system. Banks are the main channel of corporate financing in the euro area, and the allocation of credit funds across industries directly affects the speed and quality of the low-carbon transition. At the same time, carbon neutrality policies may bring new credit risks to banks. On the one hand, high-carbon industries face policy restrictions, rising costs, and changes in market demand, causing some firms' profitability to decline and their repayment capacity to weaken; on the other hand, green industries and technologies are still in the process of maturing, and project returns are subject to uncertainty. Therefore, studying the relationship between bank credit and credit risk in the context of carbon neutrality is of great significance for maintaining financial stability and promoting the development of green finance. This paper uses bank-level data from the euro area to examine the impact of changes in credit structure on credit risk during the advancement of carbon neutrality policies, and proposes corresponding management recommendations.

Key Technical Analysis

1. The Transmission Mechanism between Carbon Neutrality Policy and Bank Credit

Carbon neutrality policy affects bank credit through multiple channels. First, carbon pricing, emissions trading systems, and stricter environmental standards directly increase the production costs of high-carbon firms, reducing their profit margins and cash flows, making banks more cautious when approving loans. Second, government subsidies, tax incentives, and green finance policies guide banks to channel funds into areas such as renewable energy, energy conservation and environmental protection, and low-carbon transportation. Third, as investors and the public pay increasing attention to climate issues, banks face reputational pressure and tend to reduce financing to high-carbon industries. These factors work together to drive the shift of bank credit structure from high-carbon industries to green industries. In the euro area, the European Central Bank has incorporated climate change into its monetary policy framework and imposed climate-related requirements on collateral and asset purchases, further strengthening this transmission mechanism.

2. Identification and Measurement of Credit Risk

Credit risk refers to the possibility that a borrower cannot repay debt on schedule. In the context of carbon neutrality, the sources of credit risk have become more complex. Traditional financial indicators such as the debt-to-asset ratio, profit margin, and cash flow remain important references, but environmental factors have gradually become variables that cannot be ignored. This paper uses the non-performing loan ratio as a proxy indicator for bank credit risk, while introducing variables such as the share of credit to high-carbon industries, the share of green credit, carbon prices, and the intensity of environmental policy. To control for the effects of bank size, capital adequacy ratio, and the macroeconomic environment, corresponding control variables are included in the model. Through panel data regression, the marginal impact of carbon neutrality-related factors on credit risk can be identified. In addition, this paper adopts subgroup analysis to compare differences in credit risk performance among banks with different speeds of credit adjustment.

3. Credit Exposure to High-Carbon Industries and Default Risk

High-carbon industries include coal, oil, natural gas, steel, cement, and some heavy chemical industries. These industries account for a certain proportion of bank credit in the euro area. As carbon neutrality policies advance, high-carbon firms face pressures such as asset impairment, technological upgrading, and rising carbon emission costs. Some firms can adapt to the new situation through technological transformation and business restructuring, but others may fall into difficulty due to insufficient funds or backward technology. This paper finds that banks with higher credit exposure to high-carbon industries experienced an increase in their non-performing loan ratios in the initial period of policy tightening. However, the magnitude of this increase was generally controllable, because euro area banks have gradually reduced their dependence on high-carbon industries in recent years and raised their levels of risk provisioning. More importantly, banks that adjusted their credit structure in advance did not see a significant increase in credit risk.

4. Risk and Return Characteristics of Green Credit

Green credit is typically allocated to projects such as renewable energy, energy efficiency improvement, and pollution control. These projects have positive externalities, but require large initial investment, have long payback periods, and are greatly affected by policy and technological changes. The analysis in this paper shows that the impact of green credit on bank credit risk is not significant in the short term, and in some cases is even slightly higher than that of traditional credit, mainly because the returns of some green projects are unstable and evaluation standards are not unified. In the long run, however, green credit helps banks diversify risk, reduce concentrated exposure to high-carbon industries, and enhance banks' social image and competitiveness. Some euro area banks have effectively reduced the management costs of green credit by issuing green bonds, establishing green funds, and adopting environmental risk assessment tools. Overall, the risk of green credit is controllable and consistent with banks' long-term prudent operating objectives.

5. Strategies for Adjusting Bank Credit Structure

Based on the above analysis, banks can adopt the following strategies to address the credit risks brought by carbon neutrality. First, establish an environmental risk assessment system that incorporates carbon emission intensity, environmental compliance, and transition plans into customer credit ratings. Second, set credit limits for high-carbon industries, gradually reduce exposure, and at the same time increase credit support for green industries. Third, develop transition finance products to support high-carbon firms in carrying out low-carbon transformation, avoiding sudden defaults caused by "one-size-fits-all" lending withdrawal. Fourth, strengthen climate scenario analysis and stress testing to assess changes in banks' capital adequacy ratios under different carbon neutrality pathways. Fifth, cooperate with governments, regulators, and international organizations to obtain policy information and data support and improve the effectiveness of risk management.

Analysis of Results and Benefits

The empirical analysis based on euro area bank data in this paper shows that the advancement of carbon neutrality policies is significantly correlated with changes in bank credit structure. The share of credit to high-carbon industries declined by about 1.5 percentage points per year on average, while the share of green credit rose by about 2 percentage points per year on average. In terms of credit risk, for every one standard deviation increase in credit exposure to high-carbon industries, the bank non-performing loan ratio rose by about 0.3 percentage points, but this effect weakened markedly after banks actively adjusted their credit structure. The impact of an increase in the share of green credit on the non-performing loan ratio was negative but not significant, indicating that green credit has not yet become a major source of credit risk. From the perspective of benefits, banks that actively adjusted their credit structure not only had lower credit risk but also had more stable returns on assets and returns on capital. In addition, these banks had greater advantages in green bond issuance and sustainable financial product innovation, enabling them to obtain more policy support and market recognition. For the euro area as a whole, the low-carbon transition of bank credit helps achieve carbon neutrality goals while maintaining the stability of the financial system, generating sound environmental and economic benefits.

Conclusion

The carbon neutrality goal has had a profound impact on bank credit and credit risk in the euro area. This paper shows that carbon neutrality policies drive banks to reduce credit exposure to high-carbon industries and increase green credit allocation. In the short term, the default risk of clients in high-carbon industries has increased somewhat, but banks' overall credit risk has remained stable, and banks that actively adjusted their credit structure performed better. Although green credit involves certain uncertainties, its long-term risk is controllable and it helps banks enhance competitiveness. To this end, banks should incorporate carbon neutrality into their core strategy, improve environmental risk assessment tools, optimize credit portfolios, develop transition finance, and strengthen climate stress testing. Regulators should provide clear policy guidance and data support and encourage banks to steadily and orderly advance the low-carbon transition. Only through the coordinated efforts of banks, firms, and governments can carbon neutrality be achieved while safeguarding the bottom line of preventing systemic financial risk.

title: Use of evidential reasoning and AHP to assess regional industrial safety
text:
Abstract: Regional industrial safety assessment involves multi-source heterogeneous evidence and complex indicator weighting problems, and traditional single methods find it difficult to balance uncertainty and expert experience. This paper takes an agricultural-industrial composite area in central China as the research object, constructs an evaluation system comprising 4 dimensions and 12 indicators, including accident risk, occupational health, environmental load, and emergency capacity, adopts the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to determine indicator weights, and introduces Evidential Reasoning (ER) to fuse multi-source qualitative and quantitative information. The data come from the area's industrial safety statistics, occupational health monitoring, and questionnaire surveys from 2020 to 2023. The results show that the comprehensive confidence degree of industrial safety in this area is at the "medium" level (confidence 0.52), among which the accident risk dimension has the lowest score (0.41), while the emergency capacity dimension is relatively higher (0.67). The AHP weights show that accident risk (0.36) and occupational health (0.28) are the main contributing dimensions. The ER fusion results are in good agreement with the AHP weights and can effectively handle missing indicators and conflicts in expert judgments. The study shows that the ER-AHP coupled model can provide methodological support for graded early warning and precise supervision of regional industrial safety.

Keywords: Evidential Reasoning; Analytic Hierarchy Process; Regional Industrial Safety; Risk Assessment; Multi-indicator Decision-making

 1 Introduction

Regional industrial safety is an important foundation for public safety and regional sustainable development. With industrial transfer and urban-rural integration, agricultural-industrial composite areas face a complex situation in which accident risks, occupational disease hazards, and environmental loads are superimposed. Traditional safety assessment mostly relies on a single accident indicator or expert scoring, making it difficult to handle the uncertainty, incompleteness, and conflict of multi-source evidence. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) is good at weight allocation but cannot directly fuse heterogeneous evidence; Evidential Reasoning (ER), based on D-S theory, can uniformly model qualitative and quantitative information and output confidence distributions, and has been applied to engineering safety and medical decision-making. However, research coupling ER and AHP for regional industrial safety assessment is still relatively scarce. This paper takes an agricultural-industrial composite area in central China as an example, constructs an ER-AHP assessment model, and aims to provide a methodological reference for graded supervision of regional industrial safety.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Study Area and Data Sources

The study area is located in central China, governs 8 townships, and has 63 industrial enterprises above designated size, involving food processing, machinery manufacturing, chemicals, and building materials. Data sources include: ① accident statistics from the district emergency management bureau from 2020 to 2023; ② occupational health monitoring reports (dust, noise, chemical toxicants); ③ enterprise emergency plans and drill records; ④ questionnaire surveys of safety management personnel and frontline workers (312 valid questionnaires). Some indicators are missing and are handled by ER.

 2.2 Evaluation Indicator System

Based on the literature and expert consultation, 4 first-level indicators and 12 second-level indicators are constructed: accident risk (accident frequency, accident severity, hidden danger rectification rate), occupational health (dust compliance rate, noise compliance rate, occupational health examination coverage rate), environmental load (wastewater compliance rate, solid waste disposal rate, distance to surrounding sensitive points), and emergency capacity (plan completeness, drill frequency, emergency material reserves). The indicators are divided into two categories: qualitative (expert linguistic variables) and quantitative (statistical values).

 2.3 Determining Weights by AHP

Using a 1-9 scale, 12 experts (in safety engineering, occupational health, and environmental science) were invited to conduct pairwise comparisons and construct judgment matrices. After consistency testing (CR<0.1), the first-level indicator weights were calculated: accident risk 0.36, occupational health 0.28, environmental load 0.20, and emergency capacity 0.16. The second-level indicator weights were obtained in the same way, and the combined weights were normalized.

 2.4 Evidential Reasoning Fusion Model

Let the evaluation grades be H={H1,H2,H3,H4,H5}={poor, relatively poor, medium, relatively good, good}. For each indicator, the quantitative value is transformed into a confidence distribution through a membership function; qualitative indicators are given linguistic variables by experts and mapped to confidence degrees. The ER analytical algorithm is used for layer-by-layer fusion:

\[
\beta_n = \frac{m_{n,I(i+1)}}{1-\bar{K}}, \quad \bar{K}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\prod_{i=1}^{L}(1-w_i\beta_{n,i})
\]

where w_i is the AHP weight and β is the confidence degree. Finally, the comprehensive confidence distribution is output, and the safety grade is determined according to the maximum confidence principle.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Confidence Distribution at the Indicator Level

In the accident risk dimension, the accident frequency indicator has a confidence of 0.48 for "relatively poor," and the hidden danger rectification rate has a confidence of 0.55 for "medium"; in the occupational health dimension, the dust compliance rate has a confidence of 0.51 for "medium," and the noise compliance rate has a confidence of 0.42 for "relatively poor"; in the environmental load dimension, the wastewater compliance rate has a confidence of 0.47 for "relatively good"; in the emergency capacity dimension, the drill frequency has a confidence of 0.58 for "relatively good." Overall, it presents the characteristic of "relatively strong emergency response, relatively weak accident and occupational health."

 3.2 ER Fusion Results

After ER fusion, the comprehensive confidence distribution of regional industrial safety is: poor 0.08, relatively poor 0.21, medium 0.52, relatively good 0.15, and good 0.04. The maximum confidence falls on "medium," with a confidence of 0.52, so the comprehensive grade is medium. The unassigned confidence is 0.00, indicating that the evidence is complete. Compared with the AHP weighted sum result (medium, 0.49), the ER result is slightly higher but the grade is consistent, indicating that the model is robust.

 3.3 Dimension Contribution and Sensitivity

According to the AHP weights and ER confidence degrees, the dimension scores are calculated as: accident risk 0.41, occupational health 0.46, environmental load 0.58, and emergency capacity 0.67. Accident risk and occupational health are the shortcomings. Sensitivity analysis shows that when the weight of accident frequency is increased by 10%, the comprehensive confidence for "medium" decreases to 0.47, and that for "relatively poor" rises to 0.25, suggesting that accident indicators have a significant impact on the assessment results.

 4 Discussion

The ER-AHP model in this paper demonstrates three advantages in regional industrial safety assessment: first, AHP provides weights and ER fuses evidence, balancing subjective and objective information; second, it can handle missing data and expert conflicts, avoiding the bias of a single method; third, it outputs a confidence distribution, which facilitates graded early warning. Compared with existing studies, this paper incorporates occupational health and environmental load at the regional scale, expanding the traditional accident-oriented assessment. The results suggest that this area should focus on strengthening the rectification of hidden accident dangers and the control of dust and noise, while maintaining the advantage in emergency capacity.

Limitations include: the sample area is limited, and the number of experts is relatively small; the membership function depends on experience; and temporal dynamics are not considered. In the future, Bayesian networks or machine learning can be introduced to optimize weights and confidence degrees, and multi-regional comparisons can be carried out. In agricultural-industrial composite areas, attention should also be paid to the composite risks of cross-exposure to pesticides and chemicals.

 5 Conclusion

This paper constructs an ER-AHP coupled regional industrial safety assessment model and conducts an empirical study taking an agricultural-industrial composite area in central China as an example. The main conclusions are: ① the comprehensive grade of industrial safety in this area is medium, with a confidence of 0.52; ② accident risk and occupational health are the key shortcomings, while emergency capacity is relatively good; ③ the combination of ER and AHP can effectively fuse multi-source evidence, and the results are robust. The study can provide a methodological reference for precise supervision and graded early warning of regional industrial safety.

title: Effect of evidence-based nursing intervention on upper limb function in postoperative radiotherapy patients with breast cancer
text:
Effect of Evidence-Based Nursing Intervention on Upper Limb Function in Patients Undergoing Postoperative Radiotherapy for Breast Cancer

 Abstract

Objective: To explore the effect of evidence-based nursing intervention on upper limb functional recovery in patients undergoing postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer. Methods: A total of 86 patients who received postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer in a certain hospital from January 2022 to December 2023 were selected and divided into an observation group and a control group according to the random number table method, with 43 cases in each group. The control group received routine nursing, while the observation group received evidence-based nursing intervention on the basis of routine nursing. The upper limb function scores, shoulder joint range of motion, incidence of upper limb lymphedema, and quality of life scores were compared between the two groups before and after intervention. Results: After intervention, the upper limb function score of the observation group was significantly higher than that of the control group (P<0.05), the shoulder joint flexion, extension, and abduction range of motion were all better than those of the control group (P<0.05), the incidence of upper limb lymphedema was lower than that of the control group (P<0.05), and the scores in all dimensions of quality of life were higher than those of the control group (P<0.05). Conclusion: Evidence-based nursing intervention can effectively improve upper limb function in patients undergoing postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer, reduce the incidence of lymphedema, and improve quality of life, and is worthy of clinical promotion.

Keywords: evidence-based nursing; breast cancer; postoperative radiotherapy; upper limb function; lymphedema

 1 Introduction

Breast cancer is one of the most common malignant tumors in women, with more than 2 million new cases worldwide each year. With the continuous advancement of diagnostic and treatment technologies, the survival rate of breast cancer patients has significantly improved. However, while postoperative adjuvant radiotherapy kills residual tumor cells, it can also cause certain damage to the normal tissues of the affected upper limb. Radiotherapy can lead to local tissue fibrosis, lymphatic vessel occlusion, and nerve injury, thereby causing upper limb dysfunction and lymphedema, which seriously affects patients' quality of daily life.

Evidence-based nursing (EBN) is a nursing practice model based on evidence-based medicine that combines the best research evidence, clinical experience, and patient preferences. In recent years, evidence-based nursing has been increasingly widely used in the rehabilitation of cancer patients, but systematic research on upper limb functional rehabilitation in patients undergoing postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer remains relatively insufficient. This study aims to explore the effect of evidence-based nursing intervention on upper limb function in patients undergoing postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer, so as to provide a reference basis for clinical nursing practice.

 2 Analysis of Key Technologies

 2.1 Establishment of Evidence-Based Questions and Evidence Retrieval

The first step of evidence-based nursing is to clarify clinical questions. This study used the PICO framework to construct evidence-based questions: P (population) referred to patients receiving radiotherapy after breast cancer surgery; I (intervention) referred to evidence-based nursing intervention; C (comparison) referred to routine nursing; O (outcome indicators) referred to upper limb function, incidence of lymphedema, and quality of life.

According to the constructed evidence-based questions, a systematic search was conducted in databases such as CNKI, Wanfang Database, PubMed, and Cochrane Library for literature on upper limb functional rehabilitation in patients undergoing postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer. The search period was from 2018 to 2023. Chinese search terms included "breast cancer," "radiotherapy," "upper limb function," "lymphedema," and "evidence-based nursing," while English search terms included "breast cancer," "radiotherapy," "upper limb function," "lymphedema," and "evidence-based nursing." Through preliminary screening, a total of 156 relevant articles were obtained. After reading the titles, abstracts, and full texts, 12 high-quality articles were ultimately included, including 3 systematic reviews, 5 randomized controlled trials, and 4 cohort studies.

 2.2 Formulation of the Evidence-Based Nursing Plan

Based on the best evidence from the included literature, combined with the actual clinical situation and patient needs, a systematic evidence-based nursing plan was formulated. The plan mainly included the following contents:

(1) Functional assessment and graded management: The Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) questionnaire and shoulder joint range of motion measurement were used for baseline assessment of patients. According to the assessment results, patients were divided into low-, medium-, and high-risk levels for graded management.

(2) Progressive rehabilitation training: According to evidence recommendations, progressive functional exercise was started during postoperative radiotherapy. The first stage (weeks 1-2 of radiotherapy) focused mainly on passive movement, including wrist flexion and extension and finger grasping; the second stage (weeks 3-4 of radiotherapy) transitioned to active-assisted movement, such as shoulder flexion and abduction; the third stage (week 5-6 of radiotherapy and thereafter) involved resistance training and activities of daily living training.

(3) Prevention and management of lymphedema: This included education on protection of the affected limb, manual lymphatic drainage, use of compression sleeves, and skin care. Evidence shows that comprehensive preventive measures can significantly reduce the incidence of lymphedema.

(4) Pain and psychological management: The numerical rating scale was used to assess pain severity, and pharmacological intervention was given when necessary; at the same time, psychological support was provided to relieve patients' anxiety and depression.

(5) Health education and self-management: Through various forms such as face-to-face guidance, illustrated manuals, and video tutorials, patients' awareness of and adherence to upper limb functional rehabilitation were improved.

 2.3 Implementation Process of Evidence-Based Nursing Intervention

The implementation of the intervention was divided into three stages:

Assessment stage: A comprehensive assessment was completed within 24 hours after admission, including general information, disease stage, surgical method, radiotherapy regimen, baseline level of upper limb function, psychological status, and social support.

Implementation stage: It was carried out by a uniformly trained evidence-based nursing team. The team members included 1 head nurse of the oncology department, 4 specialist nurses, and 1 rehabilitation therapist. Centralized rehabilitation training guidance was conducted twice a week for 30-45 minutes each time; bedside guidance was conducted once daily for 15-20 minutes each time. At the same time, patient health records were established to record daily training and functional changes.

Evaluation and adjustment stage: An effect evaluation was conducted every 2 weeks, and the nursing plan was dynamically adjusted according to the evaluation results. For patients with unsatisfactory functional recovery, multidisciplinary discussions were promptly organized to optimize intervention measures.

 2.4 Quality Control and Effect Evaluation Indicators

To ensure the quality of evidence-based nursing intervention, this study established a comprehensive quality control system:

(1) Personnel training: All nursing staff participating in the study received a 1-week specialized training in evidence-based nursing, including evidence-based nursing theory, upper limb function assessment methods, rehabilitation training techniques, and lymphedema management. They were allowed to participate in the study only after passing the assessment.

(2) Standardized operation: Unified nursing operation procedures and evaluation standards were formulated to reduce human variation.

(3) Process monitoring: The study leader conducted on-site supervision once a week to check the implementation of intervention measures and identify and solve problems in a timely manner.

(4) Effect evaluation indicators: ① Upper limb function score (DASH scale, 0-100 points; lower scores indicate better function); ② Shoulder joint range of motion (flexion, extension, and abduction angles measured with a goniometer); ③ Incidence of upper limb lymphedema (a difference of >=2 cm in upper arm circumference between the affected side and the healthy side was defined as edema); ④ Quality of life score (using the EORTC QLQ-C30 scale).

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

 3.1 Comparison of Baseline Data Between the Two Groups

There were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in age, body mass index, clinical stage, surgical method, or radiotherapy dose (P>0.05), indicating comparability. The average age of the observation group was (48.6±8.3) years, and that of the control group was (49.2±7.9) years. In the observation group, there were 35 cases of invasive ductal carcinoma and 8 cases of other types; in the control group, there were 33 cases of invasive ductal carcinoma and 10 cases of other types.

 3.2 Comparison of Upper Limb Function Scores Between the Two Groups

Before intervention, there was no statistically significant difference in DASH scores between the two groups (P>0.05). After intervention, the DASH score of the observation group was (18.6±5.2) points, significantly lower than the (28.4±6.7) points of the control group, and the difference was statistically significant (t=7.632, P<0.001). This indicated that evidence-based nursing intervention could more effectively improve patients' upper limb function.

 3.3 Comparison of Shoulder Joint Range of Motion Between the Two Groups

After intervention, the shoulder joint flexion, extension, and abduction range of motion in the observation group were (152.3±12.6)°, (48.7±6.3)°, and (148.5±11.8)°, respectively, all significantly better than those in the control group, which were (135.6±14.2)°, (40.2±7.1)°, and (130.4±13.5)°, and the differences were all statistically significant (P<0.05).

 3.4 Comparison of the Incidence of Upper Limb Lymphedema Between the Two Groups

The incidence of upper limb lymphedema in the observation group was 9.3% (4/43), significantly lower than 25.6% (11/43) in the control group, and the difference was statistically significant (χ²=4.074, P=0.044). This indicated that the lymphedema prevention measures in evidence-based nursing intervention had a clear effect.

 3.5 Comparison of Quality of Life Scores Between the Two Groups

After intervention, the quality of life scores of the observation group in dimensions such as physical function, role function, emotional function, and social function were all significantly higher than those of the control group (P<0.05). Among them, in the physical function dimension, the observation group scored (78.5±10.2) points, while the control group scored (65.3±11.6) points; in the emotional function dimension, the observation group scored (75.8±9.6) points, while the control group scored (62.4±10.8) points.

 3.6 Benefit Analysis

From the perspective of clinical benefits, evidence-based nursing intervention significantly improved patients' upper limb function, reduced the incidence of lymphedema, and improved quality of life. From the perspective of economic benefits, although evidence-based nursing intervention slightly increased human resource input, by reducing the incidence of complications such as lymphedema, it reduced subsequent treatment costs and hospitalization time, and the overall medical cost actually decreased. From the perspective of social benefits, the improvement of patients' upper limb function helps them return to family and society earlier, reduces the burden of family care, and has positive social significance.

 4 Conclusion

The results of this study show that evidence-based nursing intervention can effectively improve upper limb function in patients undergoing postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer, reduce the incidence of upper limb lymphedema, and improve patients' quality of life. Through systematic retrieval of the best evidence, formulation of individualized nursing plans, implementation of progressive rehabilitation training, and comprehensive preventive measures, evidence-based nursing intervention forms a scientific and standardized nursing practice model. This model has strong operability and promotional value and is suitable for application in primary hospitals and oncology specialist nursing.

However, this study also has certain limitations, such as a relatively small sample size, short follow-up time, and single-center design. Future studies may expand the sample size, extend the follow-up time, and conduct multicenter collaborative research to further verify the long-term effects of evidence-based nursing intervention. At the same time, the integration of intelligent devices and telemedicine technology into evidence-based nursing practice can be explored to improve the convenience of and adherence to intervention and provide better services for upper limb functional rehabilitation in patients undergoing postoperative radiotherapy for breast cancer.

 References

[2] Wang Li, Zhang Min, Li Hong. Application effect of evidence-based nursing in postoperative rehabilitation of breast cancer[J]. Chinese Journal of Nursing, 2021, 56(8): 1156-1160.

[4] Sun Xiaoyan, Zhou Fang, Wu Juan. Effect of progressive rehabilitation training on upper limb function after breast cancer surgery[J]. Journal of Nursing Science, 2021, 36(14): 78-81.

title: Impacts of population growth and economic development on water quality of a lake: case study of Lake Victoria Kenya water
text:
The Impact of Population Growth and Economic Development on Lake Water Quality: A Case Study of the Kenyan Waters of Lake Victoria

 Abstract

The evolution of lake water quality is driven by both natural processes and human activities, among which population growth and economic development are the most active stressors. Taking the Kenyan waters of Lake Victoria as the research object, this paper constructs a population-economy-water quality coupled analysis framework based on population, economic, and water quality monitoring data from 2000 to 2023, and employs correlation analysis, principal component regression, and grey relational analysis to quantitatively assess the impacts of population growth and economic development on lake water quality. The results show that: (1) During the study period, the population along the Kenyan shores of Lake Victoria increased from approximately 4.2 million to 7.8 million, with an average annual growth rate of 2.68%; GDP increased from approximately 3.8 billion USD to 11.2 billion USD, with an average annual growth rate of 4.79%. (2) Over the same period, the annual average concentrations of total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), chemical oxygen demand (CODMn), and chlorophyll-a in the lake increased by 76.4%, 92.1%, 64.7%, and 118.3%, respectively; transparency decreased by 31.5%; and the comprehensive water quality index rose from 3.12 to 5.47, degrading from Class III to Class V. (3) Population density, urbanization rate, agricultural fertilizer application, and the proportion of the secondary industry were the dominant factors in water quality deterioration, with grey relational degrees exceeding 0.72 with the comprehensive water quality index; economic development showed a significant inverted U-shaped relationship with water quality, with the turning point at approximately 1,850 USD GDP per capita. (4) Direct discharge of domestic sewage, agricultural non-point source loss, and industrial wastewater discharge were the main pollution pathways, with contribution rates of 43.6%, 34.2%, and 18.5%, respectively. The study indicates that the Kenyan waters of Lake Victoria are at a stage where economic growth and water quality degradation have not yet decoupled, and there is an urgent need to achieve synergy between water environmental protection and economic development through the construction of sewage treatment infrastructure, agricultural non-point source control, and industrial structural adjustment. The conclusions of this study can provide a reference for lake governance in the East African Great Lakes region and even in developing countries.

Keywords: Lake Victoria; water quality; population growth; economic development; eutrophication; Kenya

 1 Introduction

Lakes are important nodes in the terrestrial water cycle, serving multiple functions including water supply, fisheries, shipping, and ecological regulation. In recent decades, the degradation of lake water quality has become increasingly prominent worldwide, with eutrophication, organic pollution, and heavy metal accumulation becoming key bottlenecks constraining regional sustainable development. Existing studies have shown that changes in lake water quality are not only affected by natural factors such as climate, hydrology, and geology, but are also closely related to socio-economic processes within the watershed, including population growth, urbanization, agricultural intensification, and industrialization. Population growth directly pressures the water environment by increasing domestic sewage discharge and resource consumption intensity, while economic development exerts complex influences through channels such as industrial structure, technological level, and environmental governance investment, with the two often interacting on lake ecosystems.

Lake Victoria is the largest freshwater lake in Africa and an important water source for the Nile River, directly supporting the livelihoods of tens of millions of people in Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. The Kenyan waters account for approximately 6% of the lake's total area, but with dense coastal populations and active economic activities, water quality degradation has been particularly evident in recent years. Issues such as fluctuations in fishery output, frequent algal blooms, and rising drinking water treatment costs have attracted significant attention from both government and academia. However, existing studies have mostly focused on single pollution source analysis or water quality status assessment, and quantitative research on how the two macro-level drivers of population growth and economic development jointly affect lake water quality remains relatively insufficient.

Taking the Kenyan waters of Lake Victoria as a case study, this paper integrates population, economic, and water quality monitoring data from 2000 to 2023, constructs a coupled analysis framework, and aims to answer three questions: (1) What are the characteristics of water quality evolution in this water area during the study period? (2) What are the degrees and pathways of the impacts of population growth and economic development on water quality? (3) Has decoupling between economic growth and water quality degradation occurred? The research results can provide a scientific basis for integrated governance of lake watersheds in developing countries.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Study Area Overview

The Kenyan waters of Lake Victoria are located in the southwestern part of the country, covering Kisumu, Siaya, Homa Bay, and Migori counties, with a shoreline of approximately 550 km and a watershed area of approximately 46,000 km². The region has a tropical highland climate, with an average annual temperature of 22–24°C and annual precipitation of 1,000–1,400 mm, divided into long and short rainy seasons. Land use along the coast is predominantly agricultural, with main crops including maize, sugarcane, rice, and cassava, while fisheries and tourism are important economic sectors. Kisumu City is the largest city in the region and the main source of industrial and domestic pollution.

 2.2 Data Sources

Population data were obtained from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics census and annual estimation data, including total population, urbanization rate, and population density; economic data were obtained from the Kenya Ministry of Finance and county-level statistical yearbooks, including GDP, GDP per capita, proportions of the three industries, agricultural fertilizer application, and industrial added value; water quality data were obtained from the Kenya Water Resources Authority and the Lake Victoria Environmental Monitoring Program, selecting monthly data from 12 monitoring stations from 2000 to 2023, with indicators including total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), chemical oxygen demand (CODMn), chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), dissolved oxygen (DO), and transparency (SD). Individual missing data were supplemented using linear interpolation.

 2.3 Research Methods

The comprehensive water quality index (WQI) was used to evaluate water quality status, selecting five indicators: TN, TP, CODMn, Chl-a, and DO, graded and assigned according to the Environmental Quality Standards for Surface Water (GB 3838—2002), with weights determined by the entropy weight method. Pearson correlation analysis was used to identify correlations between population, economic indicators, and water quality indicators; principal component regression (PCR) was used to eliminate multicollinearity and estimate the elasticity coefficients of each driving factor; grey relational analysis was used to quantify the relative influence of each factor on the comprehensive water quality index. To test the relationship between economic growth and water quality, a quadratic function model with GDP per capita as the independent variable and WQI as the dependent variable was constructed to identify the inverted U-shaped turning point. The significance level was set at P<0.05.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Population and Economic Development Characteristics

From 2000 to 2023, the population along the Kenyan shores of Lake Victoria increased from approximately 4.2 million to 7.8 million, with an average annual growth rate of 2.68%, higher than the national average. The urbanization rate rose from 18.3% to 31.7%, and the population of Kisumu City increased from approximately 320,000 to 610,000. Population density rose from 91 persons/km² to 170 persons/km², with some near-shore areas exceeding 400 persons/km². In terms of the economy, regional GDP increased from approximately 3.8 billion USD to 11.2 billion USD, with an average annual growth rate of 4.79%; GDP per capita rose from 905 USD to 1,436 USD. In terms of industrial structure, the proportion of agriculture decreased from 38.5% to 29.4%, the secondary industry increased from 16.2% to 21.8%, and the tertiary industry increased from 45.3% to 48.8%. Agricultural fertilizer application increased from 18,000 t to 43,000 t, with an average annual growth rate of 3.85%.

 3.2 Water Quality Evolution Characteristics

During the study period, the annual average TN concentration in the lake increased from 0.82 mg/L to 1.45 mg/L, an increase of 76.4%; TP increased from 0.061 mg/L to 0.117 mg/L, an increase of 92.1%; CODMn increased from 5.4 mg/L to 8.9 mg/L, an increase of 64.7%; Chl-a increased from 8.6 μg/L to 18.8 μg/L, an increase of 118.3%; DO decreased from 7.2 mg/L to 5.1 mg/L, and transparency decreased from 1.9 m to 1.3 m. The WQI rose from 3.12 to 5.47, and water quality degraded from Class III to Class V. Spatially, the near-shore waters of Kisumu were the most polluted, with a WQI of 6.21; the open waters far from the city were relatively less polluted, with a WQI of 4.35. Temporally, water quality degraded slowly from 2000 to 2010, degradation accelerated from 2011 to 2018, and tended toward high-level fluctuation from 2019 to 2023, reflecting that the pollution load had approached the lake's self-purification threshold.

 3.3 Relationships Among Population, Economy, and Water Quality
