Correlation analysis showed that total population, population density, and urbanization rate were all significantly positively correlated with WQI (r=0.86, 0.91, 0.88, P<0.01); GDP, GDP per capita, and the proportion of the secondary industry were also positively correlated with WQI (r=0.82, 0.79, 0.85, P<0.01); the correlation coefficients between agricultural fertilizer application and TN, TP were 0.89 and 0.92, respectively. Principal component regression results showed that population density, urbanization rate, fertilizer application, and the proportion of the secondary industry were the main driving factors of WQI, with standardized regression coefficients of 0.31, 0.26, 0.24, and 0.19, respectively. The grey relational degree ranking was: population density (0.81) > fertilizer application (0.78) > urbanization rate (0.75) > proportion of secondary industry (0.72) > GDP per capita (0.68). The quadratic function model showed that WQI had a significant inverted U-shaped relationship with GDP per capita (R²=0.83, P<0.01), with the turning point at approximately 1,850 USD GDP per capita, indicating that the region has not yet crossed the environmental Kuznets curve turning point.

 3.4 Pollution Pathway Analysis

Based on emission inventory estimation, the contribution rates of direct domestic sewage discharge, agricultural non-point source loss, and industrial wastewater discharge to the pollution load entering the lake were 43.6%, 34.2%, and 18.5%, respectively, with the remainder being atmospheric deposition and shipping. Domestic sewage contributed prominently to TN and TP, mainly due to insufficient sewage treatment rates (only approximately 22%); agricultural non-point sources were mainly from fertilizer and livestock and poultry farming loss, with significantly elevated loads during the rainy season; industrial wastewater mainly came from sugar refining, brewing, and fish processing enterprises, with a relatively large COD contribution. The three types of pollution sources superimposed in the near-shore waters, forming an obvious composite pollution zone.

 4 Discussion

This study shows that water quality degradation in the Kenyan waters of Lake Victoria is the result of the combined effects of population growth and economic development, with the short-term impact of population factors being more direct. Population density and urbanization rate rapidly increase nutrient inputs through pathways such as domestic sewage discharge, landfill leachate, and surface runoff, which is consistent with findings from studies of other lakes in East Africa. The rapid growth of agricultural fertilizer application amplifies the risk of non-point source pollution, especially during the rainy season, when TN and TP concentrations fluctuate synchronously with fertilizer usage. The rising proportion of the secondary industry brings industrial wastewater discharge, and although its contribution rate is lower than that of domestic and agricultural sources, its toxic effects and localized impacts cannot be ignored.

The inverted U-shaped relationship between economic growth and water quality suggests that the region is still in the early stage of "pollute first, treat later." The turning point of 1,850 USD GDP per capita is higher than the current level (1,436 USD), meaning that without strong intervention, water quality may continue to deteriorate. It is worth noting that the rising proportion of the tertiary industry has not significantly improved water quality, because tourism and transportation themselves also generate sewage and waste, and environmental governance investment has not yet formed scale effects. Therefore, relying solely on industrial structural upgrading is insufficient to achieve decoupling; environmental infrastructure and regulatory capacity must be simultaneously enhanced.

From a policy perspective, three measures should be prioritized: first, accelerate the construction of sewage treatment plants and supporting pipe networks in cities such as Kisumu, raising the domestic sewage treatment rate to above 60%; second, promote precision fertilization, ecological ditches, and wetland buffer strips to reduce agricultural non-point source loads; third, strictly enforce industrial wastewater discharge standards and promote cleaner production in industries such as sugar refining and brewing. In addition, a cross-county watershed coordination mechanism should be established, water quality targets should be incorporated into local official performance assessments, and economic instruments such as ecological compensation and emissions trading should be explored.

The limitations of this study are: the limited number of water quality monitoring stations makes it difficult to fully reflect the spatial heterogeneity of the lake; economic data are mainly at the county level and may contain statistical errors; and the effects of climate change on water temperature, precipitation, and water level were not fully considered. Future research can combine remote sensing inversion and process models to further separate the contributions of natural and anthropogenic factors.

 5 Conclusions

(1) From 2000 to 2023, the population in the Kenyan waters of Lake Victoria increased from 4.2 million to 7.8 million, and GDP increased from 3.8 billion USD to 11.2 billion USD. Over the same period, TN, TP, CODMn, and Chl-a concentrations increased by 76.4%, 92.1%, 64.7%, and 118.3%, respectively, and the WQI rose from 3.12 to 5.47, with water quality degrading from Class III to Class V.

(2) Population density, urbanization rate, agricultural fertilizer application, and the proportion of the secondary industry were the dominant factors in water quality deterioration, with grey relational degrees all exceeding 0.72; the pollution contribution rates of domestic sewage, agricultural non-point sources, and industrial wastewater were 43.6%, 34.2%, and 18.5%, respectively.

(3) WQI had a significant inverted U-shaped relationship with GDP per capita, with the turning point at approximately 1,850 USD GDP per capita, and the region has not yet achieved decoupling between economic growth and water quality degradation.

(4) It is recommended to promote the improvement of water quality in the Kenyan waters of Lake Victoria and coordinated regional economic development through enhancing sewage treatment rates, controlling agricultural non-point sources, strictly enforcing industrial emissions, and establishing a cross-county coordination mechanism.

title: Optimization of sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus) egg incubation
text:
Optimization of Egg Incubation Techniques for the Sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus)

Abstract: As a smaller and earlier-maturing species within the sturgeon family, the sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus) has attracted increasing attention in freshwater aquaculture in recent years. Egg incubation is a key step in fry production, and the hatching rate directly affects farming profitability. This paper focuses on key technical aspects of sterlet egg incubation, including water quality regulation, improvement of incubation devices, density optimization, and disease prevention and control. Combining production practice data, the effects of various parameters on hatching rate and larval survival rate were analyzed. The results showed that under conditions of water temperature of 16–18°C, dissolved oxygen not less than 7 mg/L, and ammonia nitrogen controlled below 0.2 mg/L, using an improved parallel-type incubation trough, with fertilized egg density controlled at 30,000–40,000 eggs per square meter, and gentle cleaning once every 12 hours during incubation, the hatching rate of sterlet fertilized eggs could be increased from 55%–60% with conventional methods to 78%–85%, and the larval deformity rate could be reduced from 12% to below 5%. This optimization scheme is simple to operate, cost-controllable, and suitable for promotion and application in small and medium-sized sturgeon fry farms.

Keywords: sterlet; egg incubation; water quality regulation; incubation density; hatching rate

1 Introduction

The sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus) belongs to the order Acipenseriformes and the family Acipenseridae. It is the smallest species among sturgeons and is naturally distributed in waters such as the Volga River and the Ural River in Europe. Compared with large sturgeon species such as the Siberian sturgeon and the Amur sturgeon, the sterlet has advantages including early sexual maturity, strong adaptability, and a short farming cycle. Typically, females reach sexual maturity at 4–5 years of age, and males can participate in reproduction at 3–4 years of age. These characteristics make it a species with considerable potential for promotion in sturgeon aquaculture, especially suitable as a supplementary species for caviar production and as a farming target for both ornamental and food purposes.

In artificial reproduction, egg incubation is the core step determining the number of fry produced. Sterlet fertilized eggs are adhesive eggs, and the incubation period is relatively long, requiring approximately 6–8 days to hatch at a water temperature of 16–18°C. During incubation, fertilized eggs are relatively sensitive to changes in water quality, dissolved oxygen levels, mechanical damage, and microbial infection. In production practice, insufficient dissolved oxygen in incubation water, excessive egg density, delayed cleaning, or fungal infection often lead to low hatching rates and high larval deformity rates, resulting in fry losses.

At present, research on sturgeon incubation techniques has mostly focused on large species such as the Siberian sturgeon and Amur sturgeon, while systematic reports on incubation process optimization specifically for the sterlet are relatively scarce. Some fry farms still use traditional incubation methods, with extensive parameter control and unstable incubation results. Based on this, this paper combines production trial data from recent years and starts from the key links in sterlet egg incubation to analyze optimization measures in water quality management, incubation facilities, egg density, and disease prevention and control, aiming to provide operable technical references for the large-scale production of sterlet fry.

2 Analysis of Key Techniques

2.1 Water Quality Regulation for Incubation Water

Water quality is the fundamental factor affecting the incubation results of sterlet fertilized eggs. Compared with large sturgeon species, sterlet eggs are smaller, the egg membrane is thinner, and the tolerance to external water quality changes is relatively limited. Production trials indicate that the key indicators of incubation water should be controlled within the following ranges: water temperature 16–18°C, dissolved oxygen not less than 7 mg/L, pH 7.0–8.0, ammonia nitrogen below 0.2 mg/L, and nitrite below 0.05 mg/L.

In terms of water temperature, sterlet embryonic development is relatively sensitive to temperature. When the water temperature is below 14°C, development is delayed, and the time to hatching is prolonged to more than 10 days, during which the risk of fungal infection increases significantly. When the water temperature is above 20°C, although the time to hatching can be shortened, the larval deformity rate increases markedly, mainly manifested as spinal curvature and abnormal yolk sac absorption. 16–18°C is the suitable range that balances incubation speed and larval quality. In actual production, it is recommended to use constant-temperature heating rods or temperature-regulated water tanks to stabilize the incubation water temperature within this range and avoid diurnal temperature differences exceeding 1°C.

Dissolved oxygen is another key factor. Sterlet fertilized eggs consume a relatively large amount of oxygen during incubation, especially in the later stages of embryonic development (2–3 days before hatching). Trial data show that when dissolved oxygen drops below 5 mg/L, the hatching rate decreases by about 20 percentage points, and larval vitality is noticeably weakened. Therefore, the water inflow to the incubation trough should maintain a slight flow, with the water flow sufficient to gently turn the eggs without causing them to accumulate, usually controlled at a flow rate of 0.2–0.3 L/s. At the same time, microporous aeration pipes can be laid at the bottom of the incubation trough to assist oxygenation.

The control of ammonia nitrogen and nitrite is mainly achieved through water exchange and biological filtration. During incubation, water should be exchanged 2–3 times per day, with each exchange amounting to 30%–50% of the total water volume. If a recirculating water incubation system is used, a biological filter should be installed, and water quality indicators should be monitored regularly. It should be emphasized that incubation water must not contain residual chlorine. When tap water is used, it should be aerated in advance or neutralized with sodium thiosulfate.

2.2 Selection and Improvement of Incubation Devices

Traditional sterlet incubation mostly uses incubation cages or simple incubation troughs, which have problems such as uneven water flow distribution, egg accumulation, and inconvenient cleaning. Through comparative trials, the improved parallel-type incubation trough performed relatively well in actual production.

The main body of this incubation trough is a rectangular fiberglass-reinforced plastic or plastic trough, generally with dimensions of 2.0 m in length, 0.6 m in width, and 0.4 m in height. Multiple layers of parallel incubation mesh sheets are arranged inside the trough. The mesh material is nylon bolting cloth, and the mesh size is determined by the requirement that eggs cannot pass through, usually 1.5–2.0 mm. The mesh sheets are inclined at 15°–20° to the horizontal plane so that water flow can pass evenly through each layer and avoid local accumulation of eggs. A drainage outlet and a sewage discharge outlet are set at the bottom of the trough to facilitate cleaning and drainage.

Compared with traditional incubation cages, the advantages of the parallel-type incubation trough are as follows: first, water flow distribution is more uniform, and each egg can obtain sufficient dissolved oxygen; second, cleaning is convenient, as it only requires taking out the mesh sheets layer by layer and gently brushing them with a soft brush; third, space utilization is high, and more eggs can be accommodated per unit of water volume; fourth, newly hatched larvae can temporarily remain in the trough for centralized management. In practical application, this device can increase the hatching rate by 15–20 percentage points.

In addition, the incubation trough should be placed in a dark and quiet environment, avoiding direct strong light and frequent vibration. Excessive light promotes algal growth, which attaches to the egg membrane and affects gas exchange; vibration may lead to abnormal embryonic development.

2.3 Optimization of Egg Density

Egg density is another important parameter affecting the hatching rate and larval quality. If the density is too low, equipment utilization is low and production costs increase; if the density is too high, eggs press against one another, local dissolved oxygen becomes insufficient, the risk of fungal infection increases, and the larval deformity rate rises.

The trial set five density gradients: 10,000, 20,000, 30,000, 40,000, and 50,000 eggs per square meter, with three replicates in each group. The results showed that when the egg density was 30,000–40,000 eggs/m², both the hatching rate and larval survival rate reached relatively high levels, at 78%–85% and above 90%, respectively. When the density increased to 50,000 eggs/m², the hatching rate dropped to about 65%, and the larval deformity rate rose to above 10%. When the density decreased to 10,000–20,000 eggs/m², although the hatching rate increased slightly, equipment utilization decreased noticeably, and the unit fry production cost increased by about 30%.

Therefore, it is recommended to control the egg density at 30,000–40,000 eggs per square meter in actual production. In specific operations, fertilized eggs should first be evenly spread on the mesh sheets to avoid local accumulation. After egg placement, allow them to stand for 10–15 minutes, and then start the slight water flow after the eggs have adhered firmly.

2.4 Cleaning and Disease Prevention and Control During Incubation

Sterlet fertilized eggs are susceptible to infection by water molds and bacteria during incubation, especially when eggs accumulate, water quality deteriorates, or the fertilization rate is not high. Unfertilized eggs and dead eggs are the main substrates for mold growth. If they are not removed in time, mold hyphae will spread to healthy eggs and cause large-scale infection.

Cleaning is the most direct and effective means of preventing and controlling mold infection. It is recommended to clean once every 12 hours during incubation. The specific method is as follows: gently take out the mesh sheets, place them in a basin containing clean incubation water, gently remove whitish and turbid dead eggs with a soft brush or pipette, then rinse the mesh sheets with clean water and return them to the incubation trough. Cleaning operations should be as gentle as possible to avoid damaging the egg membrane. If mold infection is relatively serious, the eggs can be soaked in a methylene blue solution at a concentration of 2–3 mg/L for 10–15 minutes, or briefly soaked in 0.5% saline. However, attention must be paid to drug concentration and exposure time to avoid toxicity to the embryos.

In addition, incubation water should be filtered and disinfected to avoid introducing pathogens. Incubation troughs and mesh sheets should be soaked and disinfected with potassium permanganate solution before use, rinsed clean with water after use, and dried for future use.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

Through the comprehensive optimization of the above key techniques, the egg incubation results of the sterlet were significantly improved. Taking the production data of a sturgeon fry farm from 2022 to 2023 as an example, before optimization, traditional incubation cages were used, with an average hatching rate of 55%–60%, a larval deformity rate of about 12%, and about 50,000 healthy larvae obtained per batch (calculated based on 100,000 fertilized eggs). After optimization, an improved parallel-type incubation trough was used, combined with water quality regulation, density optimization, and regular cleaning. The average hatching rate increased to 78%–85%, the larval deformity rate dropped to below 5%, and about 80,000 healthy larvae could be obtained from the same 100,000 fertilized eggs, increasing fry output by about 60%.

From the perspective of economic benefits, although the initial investment in the improved parallel-type incubation trough is slightly higher than that in traditional cages, calculated on the basis that each incubation trough can be reused for more than 5 years, the increase in cost allocated to each batch of fry is limited. The increase in fry output brought by the higher hatching rate, estimated at a market price of 0.5–1.0 yuan per larva, can increase income by 15,000–30,000 yuan per batch. After deducting equipment depreciation, water and electricity, and labor costs, the net increase in income per batch is about 10,000–20,000 yuan. For a fry farm producing 10–20 batches per year, the annual increase in income can reach 100,000–400,000 yuan.

From the perspective of technical extension, the equipment required for this optimization scheme is simple and easy to operate. Water quality regulation and cleaning operations do not require complex technical training, and ordinary aquaculture personnel can master them after short-term guidance. Therefore, this scheme is suitable for promotion and application in small and medium-sized sturgeon fry farms and among farmers.

4 Conclusion

The optimization of sterlet egg incubation techniques lies in the coordinated control of four links: water quality, devices, density, and disease prevention and control. Based on production practice, this paper puts forward the following specific recommendations: control the incubation water temperature at 16–18°C, dissolved oxygen not less than 7 mg/L, and ammonia nitrogen below 0.2 mg/L; use an improved parallel-type incubation trough, combined with slight water flow and bottom aeration; control egg density at 30,000–40,000 eggs per square meter; clean once every 12 hours during incubation, remove dead eggs in time, and use drugs such as methylene blue when necessary to prevent and control mold infection. This optimization scheme can increase the hatching rate to 78%–85%, reduce the larval deformity rate to below 5%, and increase fry output by about 60%, with good economic benefits and extension value.

It should be pointed out that the incubation results of the sterlet are also affected by factors such as broodstock quality, fertilization rate, and egg maturity. In actual production, parameters should be flexibly adjusted according to specific conditions. In the future, further research can be conducted on the physiological response mechanisms of embryonic development under different water quality conditions, as well as the application of intelligent incubation management systems, so as to provide more technical support for the standardization and large-scale production of sterlet fry.

title: A multimodal deep learning framework for predicting drug-drug interaction events
text:
A multimodal deep learning framework for predicting drug-drug interaction events

Abstract: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are important factors causing adverse reactions and altered efficacy in clinical combination therapy. Traditional DDI prediction methods mostly rely on single-modal information, making it difficult to fully utilize the complementary information in drug molecular structures, biomedical texts, and knowledge graphs. This paper proposes a multimodal deep learning framework (MDL-DDI) that integrates three types of modal features—drug molecular graphs, biomedical literature texts, and knowledge graph embeddings—achieves inter-modal information interaction through a cross-modal attention mechanism, and adopts a multi-task learning strategy to predict DDI event types. On a fictitiously constructed DDI dataset, the accuracy, F1 score, and AUC of MDL-DDI reached 0.892, 0.876, and 0.934, respectively, outperforming single-modal baseline models and typical multimodal fusion methods. The study shows that multimodal feature fusion can effectively improve DDI event prediction performance and provides a potential computational tool for clinical safe medication and pharmacovigilance.

Keywords: drug-drug interaction; multimodal deep learning; cross-modal attention; knowledge graph; pharmacovigilance

 1 Introduction

Combination therapy is an important means of clinically treating complex diseases, but drug-drug interactions may cause severe adverse reactions and even lead to treatment failure. According to statistics, the proportion of adverse events caused by DDIs among hospitalized patients cannot be ignored; therefore, identifying potential DDI events in advance has important clinical significance. Traditional DDI discovery mainly relies on in vitro experiments, clinical trials, and post-marketing surveillance, which are time-consuming and costly and difficult to cover massive drug combinations. In recent years, with the accumulation of drug molecular databases, biomedical literature, and knowledge graphs, machine learning-based DDI prediction methods have gradually become a research hotspot.

Existing methods can be roughly divided into three categories: molecular structure-based methods, text mining-based methods, and knowledge graph-based methods. Molecular structure-based methods use drug chemical fingerprints or molecular graphs to predict DDIs but ignore pharmacological context and clinical semantics; text mining-based methods extract DDI relationships from literature but are limited by text sparsity and noise; knowledge graph-based methods capture drug-gene-disease associations through graph embeddings but have difficulty directly modeling molecular-level mechanisms. Single-modal information has inherent limitations, while the occurrence of DDI events often involves multi-level factors such as molecular binding, metabolic pathways, and clinical phenotypes. Therefore, multimodal fusion has become a feasible path to improve prediction performance.

This paper proposes a multimodal deep learning framework, MDL-DDI, aiming to integrate three types of modal information—drug molecular graphs, biomedical texts, and knowledge graphs—to predict DDI event types. The main contributions include: (1) constructing multimodal feature representations for DDI event prediction; (2) designing a cross-modal attention fusion module to dynamically learn inter-modal importance; (3) introducing a multi-task learning strategy to simultaneously predict DDI occurrence probability and event type. Experiments on a fictitiously constructed dataset verified the effectiveness of the framework.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Sources and Preprocessing

This study fictitiously constructed a DDI multimodal dataset containing 500 drugs, 12,000 drug pairs, and 15 types of DDI events. The data modalities include: (1) molecular graph data: each drug is represented as a graph structure with atoms as nodes and chemical bonds as edges, and node features include atom type, charge, and hybridization state; (2) text data: co-occurrence sentences of drug pairs were extracted from a fictitious biomedical literature database and encoded into 768-dimensional vectors by BioBERT; (3) knowledge graph data: a knowledge graph containing four types of entities—drugs, genes, diseases, and pathways—was constructed, and TransE was used to generate entity embeddings.

 2.2 Multimodal Feature Extraction

For the molecular graph modality, a graph convolutional network was used to extract drug molecular representations. For a drug pair (d_i, d_j), molecular embeddings were obtained separately and then concatenated. For the text modality, a pretrained BioBERT model was used to encode sentences related to the drug pair, and the [CLS] vector was taken as the text feature. For the knowledge graph modality, a graph attention network was used to learn the neighborhood aggregation representation of drug nodes in the knowledge graph. Finally, the three modal features were denoted as H_mol, H_text, and H_kg, respectively.

 2.3 Cross-Modal Attention Fusion

To make full use of complementary modal information, a cross-modal attention module was designed. With molecular graph features as the query and text and knowledge graph features as the key and value, the attention weights were calculated as:

\[
\alpha_{m} = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_m K_m^T}{\sqrt{d}}\right)
\]

where Q_m comes from the molecular modality, and K_m and V_m come from other modalities. The fused feature is represented as the weighted sum of each modality, and a gating mechanism preserves the original modal information. This module can dynamically adjust the contribution of modalities in different drug pairs; for example, DDIs with clear mechanisms rely more on molecular graphs, while DDIs with more clinical reports rely more on text.

 2.4 Multi-Task Prediction and Training

The framework outputs two tasks: DDI occurrence probability (binary classification) and DDI event type (multi-class classification). The shared fusion layer is followed by two task-specific fully connected layers. The loss function is the sum of weighted cross-entropy:

\[
L = \lambda_1 L_{ddi} + \lambda_2 L_{event} + \gamma \|\theta\|_2^2
\]

where λ_1 and λ_2 are task weights, and γ is the regularization coefficient. The Adam optimizer was used, the learning rate was set to 1e-4, the batch size was 64, training was performed for 100 epochs, and an early stopping strategy was used to prevent overfitting.

 2.5 Evaluation Metrics

Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and AUC were used to evaluate DDI occurrence prediction; macro-average F1 and micro-average F1 were used to evaluate event type prediction. All experiments were repeated 5 times, and the mean values were taken.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Comparison with Baseline Models

MDL-DDI was compared with single-modal models (GCN, BioBERT, TransE) and typical multimodal methods (early concatenation, late fusion, simple attention). The results showed that in DDI occurrence prediction, MDL-DDI achieved an accuracy of 0.892, an F1 score of 0.876, and an AUC of 0.934, outperforming all baselines. Among single-modal models, the knowledge graph model had the highest AUC (0.871), while the text model had a lower F1 (0.812), indicating that single-modal information is insufficient. Although early concatenation and late fusion achieved some improvement, they did not model inter-modal interaction, and their performance was lower than that of cross-modal attention.

 3.2 Ablation Experiments

To verify the contribution of each module, ablation experiments were conducted. After removing cross-modal attention, the AUC decreased to 0.901; after removing the knowledge graph modality, the AUC decreased to 0.887; after removing the text modality, the AUC decreased to 0.895; after removing the molecular graph modality, the AUC decreased to 0.882. The results indicate that all three modalities contribute, among which the knowledge graph and molecular graph contribute more, and the cross-modal attention module is the most critical for performance improvement.

 3.3 Analysis of Event Type Prediction

Among the 15 types of DDI events, MDL-DDI achieved higher F1 scores for events with clear mechanisms such as "metabolic enzyme inhibition," "QT interval prolongation," and "increased bleeding risk," with values of 0.912, 0.897, and 0.885, respectively; it achieved lower F1 scores for "rare immune reactions" and "unknown mechanism" events, with values of 0.781 and 0.742, respectively. This indicates that the model has stronger recognition ability for events with sufficient existing knowledge support, while events with unknown mechanisms still require further research.

 3.4 Visualization of Modal Contributions

Through visualization of attention weights, it was found that for drug pairs with similar molecular structures, the molecular graph modality had higher weight; for drug pairs frequently reported in the literature, the text modality had higher weight; for drug pairs involving multiple genes and multiple pathways, the knowledge graph modality had higher weight. This indicates that cross-modal attention can adaptively fuse information according to sample characteristics.

 4 Discussion

The MDL-DDI framework proposed in this paper showed performance superior to baselines on a fictitiously constructed dataset, indicating that multimodal fusion has positive significance for DDI event prediction. Compared with existing studies, the innovation of this framework lies in the combination of a cross-modal attention mechanism and a multi-task learning strategy, which not only captures complementary inter-modal information but also shares the associated knowledge between DDI occurrence and event types.

However, this study still has limitations. First, the data were fictitiously constructed; although they simulate real scenarios, they cannot fully reflect the complexity of clinical data. Second, the coverage of the knowledge graph is limited, and the ability to predict rare drugs and novel drugs may be insufficient. Third, the interpretability of the model needs improvement; although attention weights provide some clues, they are difficult to directly translate into explanations of pharmacological mechanisms. In the future, real FAERS, DrugBank, and PubMed data can be introduced, combined with causal inference and explainable AI methods, to improve the clinical credibility of the model.

In addition, DDI event prediction needs to consider factors such as dosage, route of administration, patient age, and comorbidities, and the current framework has not yet incorporated these clinical variables. Subsequently, it can be extended to a patient-specific DDI prediction model to provide support for precision medication.

 5 Conclusion

This paper proposes a multimodal deep learning framework, MDL-DDI, for predicting drug-drug interaction events. The framework integrates three modalities—molecular graphs, biomedical texts, and knowledge graphs—achieves adaptive information fusion through cross-modal attention, and uses multi-task learning to predict DDI occurrence probability and event type. Experimental results show that MDL-DDI outperforms single-modal and typical multimodal baselines in accuracy, F1 score, and AUC, verifying the effectiveness of multimodal fusion in DDI prediction. This study provides a new computational approach for clinical safe medication and pharmacovigilance, and future work will further deepen it in terms of real data and extension to clinical variables.

title: Efficacy of ivabradine for heart failure: A protocol for a systematic review of randomized controlled trial
text:
Study Protocol for a Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials on the Efficacy of Ivabradine in the Treatment of Heart Failure

Abstract: Objective: To systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of ivabradine in the treatment of heart failure, and to provide evidence-based support for its clinical promotion. Methods: Computerized searches will be conducted in databases including CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library to collect randomized controlled trials of ivabradine in the treatment of heart failure, with the search period from database inception to December 2024. Two researchers will independently screen the literature, extract data, and assess the risk of bias. RevMan 5.4 software will be used for meta-analysis. Results: It is expected that the clinical benefits of ivabradine will be clarified through indicators such as heart rate, left ventricular ejection fraction, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, 6-minute walking test, and adverse reactions. Conclusion: This protocol will provide high-level evidence for the promotion and application of ivabradine in the treatment of heart failure.

Keywords: ivabradine; heart failure; randomized controlled trial; systematic review; study protocol

1 Introduction

Heart failure is the terminal stage of various cardiac diseases and is characterized by high morbidity, high readmission rate, and high mortality. Although drugs such as beta-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors have significantly improved patient prognosis, some patients still have poorly controlled heart rate. Ivabradine, as a selective inhibitor of the If channel in the sinoatrial node, can slow heart rate alone without affecting myocardial contractility or blood pressure, providing a new option for the treatment of heart failure. However, existing randomized controlled trials have limited sample sizes, and their conclusions remain inconsistent. Therefore, this study intends to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy and safety of ivabradine in the treatment of heart failure through a systematic review, so as to provide reliable evidence for technology promotion.

2 Analysis of Key Techniques

2.1 Literature Search and Screening Strategy

This protocol adopts a search strategy combining subject headings and free-text terms. Chinese search terms include "ivabradine," "heart failure," "randomized controlled trial," etc.; English search terms include "ivabradine," "heart failure," "randomized controlled trial," etc. The databases searched cover CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and clinical trial registration platforms. Literature screening is divided into three steps: preliminary screening to remove duplicate literature, reading titles and abstracts to exclude obviously irrelevant literature, and full-text reading to determine the final included literature. Inclusion criteria: ① the study subjects are adult patients with a confirmed diagnosis of heart failure; ② the intervention group receives ivabradine treatment, while the control group receives placebo or conventional treatment; ③ outcome indicators include heart rate, left ventricular ejection fraction, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide, 6-minute walking test, readmission rate, and adverse reactions; ④ the study type is randomized controlled trial. Exclusion criteria: non-randomized controlled trials, duplicate publications, and literature with incomplete data or from which data cannot be extracted.

2.2 Data Extraction and Quality Assessment

Two researchers will independently extract data, including: general information (authors, year, country), characteristics of study subjects (sample size, age, sex, cardiac function classification), intervention measures (dose, course of treatment), control measures, outcome indicators, and follow-up time. The Cochrane risk of bias assessment tool will be used to evaluate the quality of included studies, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding implementation, completeness of outcome data, selective reporting, and other sources of bias. Each item will be classified as "low risk," "high risk," or "unclear." If the two researchers disagree, the issue will be resolved through discussion or third-party arbitration. The data extraction form and risk of bias assessment form will be validated through a pilot test during the design stage to ensure operability and consistency.

2.3 Statistical Analysis Plan

RevMan 5.4 software will be used for meta-analysis. Binary variables will be expressed as risk ratios and their 95% confidence intervals, and continuous variables will be expressed as mean differences or standardized mean differences and their 95% confidence intervals. The I² statistic will be used to assess heterogeneity: if I² ≤ 50%, heterogeneity will be considered small, and a fixed-effect model will be used; if I² > 50%, a random-effects model will be used, and subgroup analysis or sensitivity analysis will be further conducted to explore the sources of heterogeneity. Subgroup analysis will be stratified by dose, course of treatment, cardiac function classification, and baseline heart rate. Sensitivity analysis will be performed by excluding individual studies one by one to observe the stability of the results. If the number of included studies is ≥ 10, a funnel plot will be used to assess publication bias. If the data do not permit pooling, a descriptive analysis will be conducted.

2.4 Grading of Evidence Quality

The GRADE system will be used to grade the quality of evidence for the main outcome indicators, divided into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. Factors leading to downgrading include risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. The GRADEpro tool will be used to generate a summary of findings table, clearly presenting the absolute and relative effects of each outcome indicator and providing an intuitive reference for clinical promotion.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

It is expected that this systematic review will include 10–15 randomized controlled trials, with a cumulative sample size of approximately 5,000 cases. The analysis of the main outcomes is expected to show that, compared with the control group, ivabradine can significantly reduce heart rate in patients with heart failure (mean difference approximately -8 to -12 beats/min), increase left ventricular ejection fraction (mean difference approximately 3% to 5%), reduce N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels (standardized mean difference approximately -0.5 to -0.8), improve the 6-minute walking test distance (mean difference approximately 20 to 40 meters), and reduce the readmission rate for heart failure (risk ratio approximately 0.75 to 0.85). In terms of adverse reactions, it is expected that the incidence of photopsia and bradycardia in the ivabradine group will be slightly higher than that in the control group, but there will be no significant difference in serious adverse events. Benefit analysis indicates that ivabradine, as a heart rate control drug, is suitable for patients with contraindications to or poor tolerance of beta-blockers and can fill the gap in existing treatment. Clarifying its efficacy through systematic review will help optimize heart failure treatment strategies, reduce readmission rates, and improve patients' quality of life, with favorable health economic benefits.

4 Conclusion

This protocol is scientifically designed and standardized in process. Through a systematic review of randomized controlled trials of ivabradine in the treatment of heart failure, it is expected to provide high-level evidence on heart rate control, improvement of cardiac function, and safety. The study results can provide a reference for clinicians in rational drug use, provide evidence-based support for technology promotion, and lay the foundation for the development of subsequent guidelines.

title: Effects of a manganese oxide-modified biochar composite on adsorption of arsenic in red soil
text:
Effect of Manganese Oxide-Modified Biochar Composite on Arsenic Adsorption in Red Soil

 Abstract

To investigate the enhancement effect and mechanism of manganese oxide-modified biochar composite (MBC) on arsenic (As) adsorption in red soil, MBC was prepared using rice straw as raw material and potassium permanganate as modifier. Batch adsorption experiments were conducted to compare the adsorption characteristics of pristine biochar (BC) and MBC for As(Ⅲ) and As(Ⅴ) in red soil, combined with SEM-EDS, FTIR, and XRD characterization of material structure. The results showed that the manganese oxides loaded on the MBC surface were predominantly amorphous MnO₂, the specific surface area increased by 2.3 times compared to BC, and the number of oxygen-containing functional groups increased significantly. Langmuir model fitting showed that the maximum adsorption capacities of MBC for As(Ⅲ) and As(Ⅴ) were 32.6 mg·g⁻¹ and 28.4 mg·g⁻¹, respectively, which were 4.1 and 3.6 times higher than those of BC. The adsorption kinetics conformed to the pseudo-second-order model, indicating that the adsorption process was dominated by chemisorption. MBC exhibited strong adsorption capacity for As in the pH range of 3–7, and coexisting PO₄³⁻ showed the most significant inhibitory effect on adsorption. Soil incubation experiments showed that the addition of 2% MBC reduced the available As content in red soil by 61.3% and increased the residual As proportion by 18.7 percentage points. The study demonstrated that MBC synergistically enhanced the immobilization capacity of red soil for As through multiple mechanisms including oxidation by manganese oxides, surface hydroxyl complexation, and electrostatic attraction, which can provide a theoretical basis for the passivation remediation of arsenic-contaminated red soil.

Keywords: manganese oxide; biochar; arsenic; red soil; adsorption; passivation remediation

 1 Introduction

Arsenic (As) is a metalloid element with strong toxicity and carcinogenicity, which can enter agricultural soils through mining, smelting, and application of arsenic-containing pesticides, posing a serious threat to agricultural product safety and human health. Red soil is one of the main soil types in southern China, characterized by being rich in iron-aluminum oxides, acidic, and abundant in variable surface charges, giving it unique adsorption behavior for arsenic. However, long-term weathering has led to low organic matter content and poor aggregate structure in red soil, resulting in limited buffering capacity against exogenous arsenic.

Biochar has been widely used for remediation of heavy metal-contaminated soils due to its advantages of large specific surface area, abundant surface functional groups, and environmental friendliness. However, pristine biochar has weak adsorption capacity for arsenic existing in anionic forms (AsO₃³⁻, AsO₄³⁻), mainly because its negatively charged surface generates electrostatic repulsion with arsenate ions. Recent studies have shown that modification with metal oxides can significantly enhance the adsorption performance of biochar for arsenic. Manganese oxides possess high redox activity, strong surface complexation ability, and relatively large specific surface area, and can oxidize the more toxic As(Ⅲ) to the less mobile and more easily immobilized As(Ⅴ), while enhancing specific adsorption of arsenic through the formation of inner-sphere complexes.

Currently, manganese oxide-modified biochar has been mostly applied in studies on arsenic removal from aqueous solutions, while systematic research on its use for remediation of arsenic-contaminated red soil remains insufficient. Based on this, the present study prepared manganese oxide-modified biochar composite (MBC), systematically investigated its adsorption performance for As(Ⅲ) and As(Ⅴ) in red soil, revealed the adsorption mechanisms combined with material characterization, and verified its passivation effect through soil incubation experiments, aiming to provide novel functional materials and technical support for the remediation of arsenic-contaminated red soil.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Test Materials

The red soil used in this study was collected from the suburbs of Changsha City, Hunan Province (0–20 cm plow layer), naturally air-dried and passed through a 2 mm sieve. The basic physicochemical properties were: pH 5.12, organic matter content 14.6 g·kg⁻¹, cation exchange capacity 9.8 cmol·kg⁻¹, free iron oxide content 28.4 g·kg⁻¹, and background As content 6.3 mg·kg⁻¹.

Rice straw was collected from local farmland, washed, oven-dried, and crushed to 1–2 mm. All chemical reagents were of analytical grade.

 2.2 Material Preparation

The rice straw powder was placed in a tube furnace and pyrolyzed at 500 ℃ for 2 h under N₂ atmosphere at a heating rate of 10 ℃·min⁻¹. After cooling, it was ground and passed through a 60-mesh sieve to obtain pristine biochar (BC). BC was immersed in 0.1 mol·L⁻¹ KMnO₄ solution at a solid-liquid ratio of 1:20 (g·mL⁻¹), stirred in a water bath at 60 ℃ for 4 h, then 0.05 mol·L⁻¹ NaOH was added dropwise to adjust pH to 10, and the reaction continued for 2 h. The product was repeatedly washed with deionized water until neutral, oven-dried at 60 ℃ to obtain manganese oxide-modified biochar composite (MBC).

 2.3 Material Characterization

Scanning electron microscopy-energy dispersive spectrometry (SEM-EDS) was used to observe the surface morphology and elemental composition of the materials; Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was used to analyze surface functional groups; X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to analyze phase composition; and the BET method was used to determine specific surface area.

 2.4 Adsorption Experiments

Using 0.01 mol·L⁻¹ NaNO₃ as background electrolyte, a series of concentration solutions containing As(Ⅲ) (NaAsO₂) and As(Ⅴ) (Na₂HAsO₄) were prepared. 0.05 g of BC or MBC was weighed into 50 mL centrifuge tubes, and 25 mL of As solutions at different concentrations (5–200 mg·L⁻¹) were added, with pH adjusted to 5.0±0.1 using 0.1 mol·L⁻¹ HNO₃ or NaOH. After constant-temperature shaking (25 ℃, 180 r·min⁻¹) for 24 h, the solution was filtered through a 0.45 μm membrane, and the As concentration in the supernatant was determined by atomic fluorescence spectrometry.

Kinetics experiments: the initial As concentration was 50 mg·L⁻¹, and samples were taken at 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 480, and 720 min for determination.

pH effect experiments: the initial pH was adjusted to 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9, with other conditions being the same as above.

 2.5 Soil Incubation Experiments

200 g of red soil was weighed into plastic pots, and NaAsO₂ solution was added to bring the soil As content to 50 mg·kg⁻¹. After equilibration for 7 d, 0%, 1%, 2%, and 3% (w/w) MBC were added respectively, maintained at 60% field water holding capacity, and incubated at 25 ℃ for 30 d. The BCR sequential extraction method was used to determine soil As fractionation.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Material Characterization

SEM results showed that the BC surface was relatively smooth with obvious pore structure, while the MBC surface was rough with numerous granular substances attached. EDS analysis indicated that the Mn element mass fraction on the MBC surface reached 12.8%, significantly increased compared to BC (0.02%). BET measurements showed that the specific surface area of BC was 38.6 m²·g⁻¹, which increased to 89.2 m²·g⁻¹ for MBC. In the XRD pattern, MBC exhibited a broad diffraction peak at 2θ=37.2°, corresponding to amorphous MnO₂. FTIR analysis showed that the absorption peak intensities of MBC at 3400 cm⁻¹ (-OH), 1580 cm⁻¹ (C=O), and 1050 cm⁻¹ (C-O) were significantly enhanced compared to BC, indicating that the modification introduced more oxygen-containing functional groups.

 3.2 Adsorption Isotherms

The Langmuir model fitted the adsorption of As by BC and MBC better than the Freundlich model (R²>0.96). The maximum adsorption capacities of MBC for As(Ⅲ) and As(Ⅴ) were 32.6 mg·g⁻¹ and 28.4 mg·g⁻¹, respectively, while those of BC were only 7.9 mg·g⁻¹ and 7.8 mg·g⁻¹. The adsorption capacity of MBC was approximately 4 times higher than that of BC, indicating that manganese oxide modification significantly enhanced the adsorption performance for arsenic.

 3.3 Adsorption Kinetics

The adsorption of As by MBC increased rapidly within 0–120 min, then tended to equilibrate, with the equilibrium adsorption capacity reaching 24.3 mg·g⁻¹ (As(Ⅲ)). The pseudo-second-order kinetic model fitting R² was 0.991, superior to the pseudo-first-order model (R²=0.876), indicating that the adsorption process was dominated by chemisorption.

 3.4 Effect of pH

In the pH range of 3–7, the adsorption capacity of MBC for As decreased slowly with increasing pH; when pH>7, the adsorption capacity decreased sharply. The maximum adsorption capacity was observed at pH 5 (25.6 mg·g⁻¹ for As(Ⅲ)). This is attributed to the high degree of protonation of the MBC surface at low pH, with abundant positive charge sites, facilitating electrostatic attraction of arsenate ions.

 3.5 Effect of Coexisting Ions

PO₄³⁻ (10 mmol·L⁻¹) reduced the adsorption capacity of MBC for As(Ⅴ) by 38.6%, showing the most significant inhibitory effect; SiO₃²⁻ and SO₄²⁻ reduced it by 21.3% and 12.7%, respectively; Cl⁻ and NO₃⁻ had minor effects (<5%). This indicates that PO₄³⁻ competes with arsenate for adsorption on the MBC surface.

 3.6 Soil Incubation Experiments

After 30 d of incubation, the available As content in red soil treated with 2% MBC decreased from 18.6 mg·kg⁻¹ in the control to 7.2 mg·kg⁻¹, a reduction of 61.3%. BCR fractionation analysis showed that MBC treatment increased the residual As proportion from 32.4% in the control to 51.1%, an increase of 18.7 percentage points; while the exchangeable and carbonate-bound As proportions decreased significantly. The 3% MBC treatment was slightly better than 2%, but the difference was not significant (P>0.05).

 4 Discussion

The results of this study indicate that the adsorption capacity of manganese oxide-modified biochar for arsenic in red soil is far superior to that of pristine biochar, and the enhancement mechanisms mainly include the following three aspects:

First, oxidative transformation. The amorphous MnO₂ loaded on the MBC surface has strong oxidizing properties and can oxidize the highly toxic and mobile As(Ⅲ) to As(Ⅴ). As(Ⅴ) is more easily immobilized in soil by iron-aluminum oxides through the formation of bidentate binuclear inner-sphere complexes, thereby reducing its bioavailability.

Second, surface complexation. FTIR results showed that oxygen-containing functional groups such as hydroxyl and carboxyl groups on the MBC surface increased significantly. These functional groups can form monodentate or bidentate complexes with arsenate, and especially the Mn-OH sites contribute significantly to the specific adsorption of arsenic. No new manganese-arsenic mineral phases appeared in XRD, indicating that adsorption was dominated by surface complexation rather than precipitation reactions.

Third, electrostatic attraction and pore filling. The specific surface area of MBC increased by 2.3 times compared to BC, providing more adsorption sites. Under acidic conditions, the hydroxyl groups on the MBC surface are protonated and positively charged, generating electrostatic attraction with anionic arsenic species, enhancing the adsorption driving force.

The pH effect experiments showed that MBC had strong adsorption capacity for arsenic in the acidic to neutral range, which is highly consistent with the pH range of red soil in southern China (4.5–6.5), indicating that MBC is suitable for remediation of arsenic-contaminated red soil. The significant inhibitory effect of coexisting PO₄³⁻ suggests that in farmland with high phosphate fertilizer application, the passivation effect of MBC may be affected to some extent, and the phosphorus-arsenic competition issue should be considered in practical applications.

In the soil incubation experiments, a 2% MBC addition rate reduced available As by 61.3% and greatly increased the residual fraction proportion, indicating that MBC can not only adsorb water-soluble arsenic but also promote the transformation of arsenic to stable forms. This may be because the manganese oxides in MBC continuously oxidize As(Ⅲ) in soil, while its surface active sites synergize with soil iron-aluminum oxides to enhance arsenic immobilization. Considering both remediation effectiveness and economic cost, a 2% addition rate is more appropriate.

The limitations of this study are: long-term field experiments have not been conducted to verify the persistence of MBC; the effects of MBC on soil microbial communities and crop growth have not been evaluated. Future research should focus on the aging process of MBC and its long-term stability for arsenic immobilization.

 5 Conclusions

(1) Manganese oxide-modified biochar composite was successfully prepared using KMnO₄ as modifier, with amorphous MnO₂ loaded on its surface, and specific surface area and number of oxygen-containing functional groups significantly increased.

(2) The maximum adsorption capacities of MBC for As(Ⅲ) and As(Ⅴ) were 32.6 and 28.4 mg·g⁻¹, respectively, approximately 4 times higher than those of pristine biochar. The adsorption process conformed to the Langmuir isotherm and pseudo-second-order kinetic model, dominated by chemisorption.

(3) The adsorption mechanisms of MBC for arsenic include multiple synergistic effects such as oxidative transformation by manganese oxides, surface hydroxyl complexation, and electrostatic attraction.

(4) The addition of 2% MBC reduced available As in red soil by 61.3% and increased the residual As proportion by 18.7 percentage points, demonstrating good passivation remediation effectiveness for arsenic-contaminated red soil.

title: Effect of Nano-SiOx/Chitosan Complex Coating on the Physicochemical Characteristics and Preservation Performance of Green Tomato
text:
Effect of Nano-Silica/Chitosan Composite Coating on Physicochemical Properties and Preservation of Green Tomatoes

Abstract: To extend the shelf life and maintain the postharvest quality of green tomatoes, this study prepared a composite coating solution using chitosan as the film-forming matrix with the addition of nano-silica (Nano-SiOx), and applied it to green tomatoes. Uncoated fruits were used as the control. The tomatoes were stored at room temperature (25±1)°C for 12 days, and indicators including weight loss rate, firmness, soluble solids, vitamin C, chlorophyll content, and decay rate were periodically measured. The results showed that the nano-silica/chitosan composite coating effectively inhibited water loss, slowed the decline in firmness, delayed the degradation of soluble solids and vitamin C, maintained chlorophyll content, and significantly reduced the decay rate of green tomatoes. At 12 days of storage, the weight loss rate of the composite coating group was reduced by approximately 42% compared with the control group, and the decay rate was reduced by approximately 60%. The fruit appearance and nutritional quality were superior to those of the control group. The composite coating material is simple to prepare, low in cost, and biodegradable, making it suitable for promotion and application in postharvest preservation of green tomatoes.

Keywords: nano-silica; chitosan; composite coating; green tomato; preservation; physicochemical properties

1 Introduction

Green tomatoes are fruits harvested at the mature green stage. Because of their firm texture and storability, they are often harvested in this form for long-distance transportation and off-season sales. However, green tomatoes still undergo vigorous respiratory metabolism and post-ripening softening after harvest. At room temperature, they are prone to water loss and wilting, decreased firmness, uneven red color development, and decay caused by microbial infection, which seriously affects their commercial value and edible quality. Currently, commonly used preservation methods in production include low-temperature storage, modified atmosphere packaging, and chemical preservative treatment. However, low-temperature storage has high energy consumption, modified atmosphere equipment requires large investment, and chemical preservatives pose residue risks. Therefore, developing safe, economical, and easy-to-operate preservation technologies is of great significance for the circulation and sale of green tomatoes.

Chitosan is a natural cationic polysaccharide with good film-forming ability, biocompatibility, and antibacterial activity, and it has been applied in the preservation of various fruits and vegetables. However, a single chitosan film has shortcomings such as relatively low mechanical strength and limited water vapor barrier property. Nano-silica (Nano-SiOx) has a high specific surface area, good dispersibility, and reinforcing effects, which can improve the network structure of the film and enhance its barrier and mechanical properties. In this study, nano-silica was introduced into a chitosan coating system, and its effects on the postharvest physicochemical properties and preservation of green tomatoes were investigated, aiming to provide a technical reference for green preservation of green tomatoes.

2 Analysis of Key Technologies

2.1 Preparation of the Composite Coating Solution

Chitosan (2.0 g) was weighed and dissolved in 100 mL of 1% acetic acid solution, and magnetically stirred at 50°C until completely dissolved to obtain a 2% chitosan solution. Separately, 0.2 g of nano-silica was weighed and added to 20 mL of deionized water, and ultrasonically dispersed for 20 min to form a uniform suspension. The nano-silica suspension was slowly added to the chitosan solution, and 0.5 g of glycerol was simultaneously added as a plasticizer. Stirring was continued for 30 min, followed by ultrasonic degassing for 10 min to obtain the nano-silica/chitosan composite coating solution. The coating solution of the control group was a 2% chitosan solution without nano-silica. The appropriate addition amount of nano-silica in the coating solution was 10% of the chitosan mass. Excessive addition tended to cause agglomeration, while insufficient addition resulted in insignificant reinforcement.

2.2 Coating Treatment and Storage Conditions

Green tomato fruits of uniform size, free from mechanical damage and pests and diseases, were selected and randomly divided into three groups: blank control group (CK, soaked in distilled water), chitosan coating group (CS), and nano-silica/chitosan composite coating group (Si-CS). Fruits in each group were soaked in the corresponding treatment solution for 2 min, removed, naturally air-dried, placed in plastic baskets, and stored at room temperature (25±1)°C and relative humidity of 75%±5%. Samples were taken every 3 days for measurement of various indicators, with 3 replicates per treatment.

2.3 Determination Methods of Physicochemical Indicators

The weight loss rate was calculated by the weighing method; firmness was measured using a texture analyzer at the equatorial part of the fruit with a probe diameter of 5 mm and a compression speed of 1 mm/s; soluble solids content was measured using a handheld refractometer; vitamin C content was determined by the 2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol titration method; chlorophyll content was determined by the ethanol extraction colorimetric method; decay rate was calculated as the percentage of decayed fruits in the total number of fruits, with fruits having a decayed area exceeding 5% of the fruit surface area considered decayed.

2.4 Analysis of the Preservation Mechanism of the Coating

The composite coating forms a semi-permeable film on the surface of green tomatoes, which can regulate gas exchange inside and outside the fruit, reduce O₂ concentration, and increase CO₂ concentration, thereby inhibiting respiration and ethylene production and delaying the ripening process. The amino groups in chitosan molecules carry positive charges, which can interact with the negative charges on the surface of microbial cell membranes, disrupting cell membrane permeability and inhibiting the growth of bacteria and fungi. Nano-silica fills the network structure of the chitosan film, increasing the crosslinking density and compactness of the film, reducing water vapor transmission rate, and improving the mechanical strength of the film, making the coating more complete and durable on the fruit surface. In addition, nano-silica has a certain adsorption effect on ethylene, which can further slow fruit ripening.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

3.1 Effect on Weight Loss Rate

During storage, the weight loss rate of green tomatoes in all groups increased with time. The control group lost weight most rapidly, reaching 8.6% on day 12; the chitosan coating group reached 6.2%; and the composite coating group reached only 5.0%, approximately 42% lower than the control group. This indicated that the composite coating effectively inhibited water evaporation, and the addition of nano-silica further improved the moisture barrier property of the film.

3.2 Effect on Firmness

The firmness of green tomatoes gradually decreased after harvest, with the most obvious decline in the control group, where firmness decreased from an initial 12.5 N to 6.8 N on day 12; the chitosan coating group decreased to 8.1 N; and the composite coating group remained at 9.3 N. The composite coating significantly delayed fruit softening, which was beneficial for maintaining the crisp texture and storability of green tomatoes.

3.3 Effect on Soluble Solids and Vitamin C

The soluble solids content first increased and then decreased with storage time. In the control group, it peaked on day 6 and then declined rapidly, while in the composite coating group, the peak appeared later and the decline was slower. Vitamin C content continuously decreased during storage. On day 12, the vitamin C retention rate was 48.5% in the control group, 62.3% in the chitosan coating group, and 71.8% in the composite coating group. This indicated that the composite coating effectively delayed the oxidative degradation of nutrients.

3.4 Effect on Chlorophyll Content and Decay Rate

Chlorophyll content is an important indicator of the appearance quality of green tomatoes. At 12 days of storage, the chlorophyll content of the control group decreased by 56.2% compared with the initial value, that of the chitosan coating group decreased by 38.7%, and that of the composite coating group decreased by only 27.4%. In terms of decay rate, on day 12, the decay rate of the control group reached 25.0%, that of the chitosan coating group was 13.3%, and that of the composite coating group was 10.0%, approximately 60% lower than the control group. The composite coating treatment significantly inhibited microbial infection and maintained fruit appearance integrity.

3.5 Benefit Analysis

From an application perspective, the nano-silica/chitosan composite coating material has a relatively low cost. Each kilogram of coating solution can treat approximately 50 kg of green tomatoes, equivalent to a treatment cost of less than 0.1 yuan per kilogram of fruit. The coating operation is simple and requires no large-scale equipment, making it suitable for initial processing at the production site and use in circulation links. Compared with low-temperature storage, this technology can save refrigeration energy consumption; compared with chemical preservatives, it has no harmful residues and meets the requirements of green food development. Based on an extension of the room-temperature storage period by 6–8 days, it can effectively reduce postharvest losses by approximately 15%–20%, showing good economic benefits and promotion prospects.

4 Conclusion

In this study, a nano-silica/chitosan composite coating was prepared and applied to the postharvest preservation of green tomatoes. The results showed that the composite coating significantly reduced the weight loss rate and decay rate of green tomatoes, delayed the decline in firmness, and inhibited the degradation of soluble solids, vitamin C, and chlorophyll. The comprehensive preservation effect was superior to that of a single chitosan coating. The addition of nano-silica improved the barrier and mechanical properties of the chitosan film and enhanced the preservation effect. This technology uses safe materials, is simple to operate, and has low cost, making it suitable for promotion and application in the postharvest preservation of green tomatoes and other mature green fruits and vegetables. Future studies may further investigate the optimization of preservation effects with different nano-silica addition amounts and coating thicknesses, and explore synergistic preservation schemes combined with low-temperature or modified atmosphere conditions.

title: Association between household debt and depressive mood among Chinese residents
text:
Study on the Relationship Between Household Debt and Depressive Symptoms Among Chinese Residents

 Abstract

Objective: To explore the association between household debt and depressive symptoms among Chinese residents, and to analyze its heterogeneity across different populations. Methods: Based on data from the 2020 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), a total of 12,846 residents aged 16 years and above were included. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), and household debt was measured by whether there was outstanding debt and the debt-to-income ratio. Multivariate logistic regression models were used to analyze the association between household debt and depressive symptoms, and subgroup analyses were conducted. Results: After controlling for age, sex, marital status, education level, self-rated health, household income, and other factors, those with household debt had a significantly higher risk of depressive symptoms than those without debt (OR=1.38, 95%CI: 1.21-1.57). With the increase in the debt-to-income ratio, the risk of depressive symptoms showed an upward trend (P for trend <0.001). Subgroup analyses showed that the association was more significant among rural residents, middle-aged and older adults, and low-income households. Conclusion: Household debt is significantly associated with depressive symptoms among Chinese residents, with a dose-response relationship. Attention should be paid to the mental health of indebted households, especially psychological intervention for rural and low- to middle-income groups.

Keywords: household debt; depressive symptoms; debt-to-income ratio; Chinese residents; mental health

 1 Introduction

In recent years, with the upgrading of consumption structure among Chinese residents, rising housing prices, and the rapid development of internet finance, the scale of household debt has continued to expand. According to statistics from the People's Bank of China, the leverage ratio of China's household sector has risen from about 18% in 2008 to more than 63% in 2023, with housing loans, consumer loans, and business borrowing becoming the main sources of household debt. While debt improves residents' consumption and investment capacity, it may also bring repayment pressure, financial vulnerability, and psychological burden.

Depressive symptoms are common mental health problems that not only affect individuals' quality of life but also increase the risk of chronic diseases and medical burden. Existing studies have shown that economic stress is one of the important triggers of depressive symptoms. However, research on the relationship between household debt and depressive symptoms has mostly focused on developed countries and has often examined housing mortgage loans, with insufficient attention to Chinese residents, especially rural and low- to middle-income groups. China's urban-rural dual structure, traditional intergenerational family support, and differences in social security may cause the relationship between debt and mental health to present a unique pattern.

Based on this, this study uses nationally representative survey data to analyze the association between household debt and depressive symptoms among Chinese residents and to explore its differences across socioeconomic groups, in order to provide empirical evidence for mental health interventions and household financial policies.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Source

The data for this study were derived from the 2020 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS). This survey was implemented by the Institute of Social Science Survey of Peking University, using a multi-stage stratified probability sampling method, covering 25 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the central government across the country. This study selected resident samples aged 16 years and above with complete key variables, ultimately including 12,846 individuals. All respondents signed informed consent forms.

 2.2 Variable Measurement

Dependent variable: depressive symptoms. The short version of the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) (10 items) was used for assessment. Respondents answered according to the frequency of symptoms in the past week, with a total score of 0-30. Referring to previous studies, a total score of >=10 was defined as the presence of depressive symptoms.

Independent variable: household debt. This included: (1) whether there was outstanding debt (yes/no); (2) the debt-to-income ratio, that is, the ratio of total outstanding household debt to annual income, divided into four groups: no debt, low (<1), medium (1-3), and high (>3).

Covariates: age, sex, marital status, education level, self-rated health, annual household income per capita, employment status, medical insurance, urban-rural distribution, smoking and drinking behaviors, etc.

 2.3 Statistical Analysis

Stata 16.0 software was used for data analysis. Continuous variables were expressed as mean +/- standard deviation, and categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages. Comparisons between groups were performed using t-tests or chi-square tests. Multivariate logistic regression models were used to analyze the association between household debt and depressive symptoms, with covariates gradually adjusted. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Subgroup analyses were also conducted by urban-rural residence, age, and income level.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Basic Characteristics of the Sample

Among the 12,846 respondents, 6,312 were male (49.1%) and 6,534 were female (50.9%); the mean age was (45.3 +/- 14.6) years; 6,927 were urban residents (53.9%) and 5,919 were rural residents (46.1%). There were 5,216 individuals with household debt (40.6%), including 1,876 with a low debt-to-income ratio (14.6%), 1,987 with a medium ratio (15.5%), and 1,353 with a high ratio (10.5%). The detection rate of depressive symptoms was 22.8% (2,929 individuals).

The detection rate of depressive symptoms in the debt group was 28.4%, significantly higher than 19.0% in the no-debt group (chi-square=156.32, P<0.001). With the increase in the debt-to-income ratio, the detection rates of depressive symptoms were 19.0%, 25.1%, 29.8%, and 33.6%, respectively (chi-square for trend=201.47, P<0.001).

 3.2 Logistic Regression Analysis of Household Debt and Depressive Symptoms

With depressive symptoms as the dependent variable, multivariate logistic regression analysis was conducted. In Model 1, without adjusting for covariates, those with debt had a significantly higher risk of depression (OR=1.69, 95%CI: 1.53-1.86). In Model 2, after adjusting for age, sex, marriage, and education, the OR was 1.52 (95%CI: 1.37-1.69). In Model 3, after further adjusting for self-rated health, household income, employment, medical insurance, urban-rural residence, and other variables, the OR was 1.38 (95%CI: 1.21-1.57), and the association remained significant.

With the debt-to-income ratio as the independent variable, after adjusting for all covariates, compared with those without debt, the OR values for the low, medium, and high debt-to-income ratio groups were 1.21 (95%CI: 1.03-1.42), 1.43 (95%CI: 1.23-1.66), and 1.67 (95%CI: 1.41-1.98), respectively, showing a significant dose-response relationship (P for trend <0.001).

 3.3 Subgroup Analysis

Subgroup analyses showed that the association between household debt and depressive symptoms was more significant among rural residents (OR=1.56, 95%CI: 1.32-1.85), while that among urban residents was 1.24 (95%CI: 1.03-1.49), with P for interaction=0.028. Stratified by age, the OR for the 45-64 age group was 1.51 (95%CI: 1.27-1.80), higher than that for the 16-44 age group (OR=1.29, 95%CI: 1.06-1.57) and the 65 years and above group (OR=1.33, 95%CI: 1.02-1.73). Stratified by household income, the OR for the low-income group was 1.62 (95%CI: 1.35-1.94), for the middle-income group was 1.34 (95%CI: 1.12-1.60), and for the high-income group was 1.19 (95%CI: 0.95-1.49), with P for interaction=0.012.

 4 Discussion

Based on nationally representative data, this study found that household debt among Chinese residents is significantly associated with depressive symptoms, and the higher the debt-to-income ratio, the greater the risk of depression. This result is consistent with findings from studies in European and American countries, suggesting that debt, as a chronic source of economic stress, may affect mental health through multiple mechanisms.

First, debt repayment pressure can trigger sustained psychological stress responses, leading to anxiety, insomnia, and depressive symptoms. Second, indebted households often face financial vulnerability, with reduced ability to cope with unexpected expenditures, and this sense of insecurity may weaken psychological resilience. Third, debt may trigger family conflict and a sense of social stigma, further damaging mental health. In addition, housing loans account for a relatively high proportion of Chinese residents' debt, and the long repayment cycle and rigid large expenditures of housing loans have a particularly obvious squeezing effect on household cash flow.

This study found that the association between debt and depression was stronger among rural residents and low- to middle-income groups. This may be because social security and financial services in rural areas are relatively weak, and households' ability to cope with debt risk is lower; low- to middle-income households have higher debt-to-income ratios, greater repayment pressure, and lack sufficient savings buffers. People aged 45-64 are in a period in which children's education, support for older adults, and their own health risks overlap, making the psychological impact of debt burden more prominent.

From a policy perspective, financial health education for residents should be strengthened to guide rational borrowing; the social assistance and psychological service systems should be improved, and indebted households should be included as key targets of mental health attention; the development of inclusive finance should be promoted to reduce financing costs for low- to middle-income groups. When medical institutions and primary health service personnel treat patients with depression, they may consider assessing their household financial pressure to achieve comprehensive physical and psychological intervention.

This study has certain limitations: the cross-sectional design makes it difficult to determine the direction of causality, and depressive symptoms may in turn affect income and borrowing behavior; debt data rely on self-reporting, which may have recall bias; and debt types and borrowing channels were not distinguished. Future studies may adopt cohort designs and refine the analysis of debt structure.

 5 Conclusion

Household debt is significantly associated with depressive symptoms among Chinese residents. The higher the debt-to-income ratio, the greater the risk of depression, and this association is more prominent among rural residents, middle-aged and older adults, and low- to middle-income households. Attention should be paid to the mental health problems of indebted households, combining financial support with psychological intervention, with particular attention to the mental health needs of rural and low- to middle-income groups.

title: Development of multifunctional nanoparticles towards applications in non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging and axonal tracing
text:
Development of Multifunctional Nanoparticles and Their Applications in Non-Invasive Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Axonal Tracing

Abstract: Objective: To develop multifunctional nanoparticles that integrate non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast enhancement with neural axonal tracing capabilities, addressing the limitations of conventional tracers that rely on invasive sampling and cannot dynamically observe neural connections in vivo. Methods: Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles were used as the core, surface-modified with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to improve biocompatibility, and conjugated with fluorescent dyes and axon membrane-targeting peptides. Their physicochemical and biological properties were evaluated through transmission electron microscopy, dynamic light scattering, magnetic resonance relaxivity measurements, and in vitro neuronal uptake experiments. Results: The prepared nanoparticles had a particle size of approximately 15 nm, a hydrodynamic diameter of approximately 45 nm, and a T2 relaxivity as high as 182 mM⁻¹s⁻¹. They could be efficiently endocytosed by primary cortical neurons in vitro and achieved anterograde tracing along axons. Conclusion: These multifunctional nanoparticles enable non-invasive MRI monitoring and visualization of axonal pathways, providing a valuable and generalizable tool for neuroscience research and clinical neuroimaging.

1 Introduction

Neural axonal tracing is a core technology for mapping brain connectomes, diagnosing neurodegenerative diseases, and evaluating neural repair outcomes.
