If submission fails, the system retains the draft and allows resubmission, avoiding data loss.

2.5 Quality Control and Back-End Management

The back-end management module provides a real-time progress dashboard showing the number of questionnaires that have been started, completed, and flagged as abnormal at each survey site. The system automatically records the completion time, number of modifications, and submission time of each questionnaire for use in identifying perfunctory responses. Questionnaires with excessively short completion times (e.g., less than 5 minutes) or highly consistent answers are marked as suspicious and flagged for manual review. Research managers can also dynamically adjust food items, frequency options, and prompts through the back end, enabling questionnaire version management.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

The system has been deployed in multiple community nutrition surveys and physical examination populations. As of the statistical time point, more than 30,000 valid questionnaires had been collected in total, covering adults aged 18 to 75 years. The average completion time per questionnaire was 12 minutes, noticeably shorter than the 20 to 25 minutes for paper questionnaires. The data missing rate was below 2%, significantly lower than the 5% to 10% commonly seen with paper questionnaires. Automatic coding and logic validation reduced data cleaning time from approximately 8 minutes per questionnaire to less than 1 minute. Calculating the savings in manual entry and cleaning costs at approximately 15 yuan per questionnaire, the cumulative direct cost savings for 30,000 questionnaires amounted to approximately 450,000 yuan. In addition, the data collection cycle was shortened from 3 to 4 months under the paper-based model to 4 to 6 weeks, saving valuable time for research projects.

In terms of data quality, the completion time and modification behavior recorded by the system provided an objective basis for identifying low-quality questionnaires. Preliminary analysis showed that the proportion of suspicious questionnaires was approximately 3%, most of which could be confirmed or excluded after manual review. The frequency distribution of food items was generally consistent with the results of previous national nutrition surveys, indicating that the system has good content validity. Regarding user feedback, more than 85% of respondents considered web-based completion convenient or very convenient, and older adults were also able to complete it smoothly with interviewer assistance.

4 Conclusion

This paper designed and implemented an internet-based food frequency questionnaire system. Through key technologies such as a food item database, responsive interaction, logic validation, automatic coding, chunked upload, and back-end quality control, it addressed the efficiency and quality challenges in large-scale Chinese population dietary surveys. Practical application showed that the system can significantly reduce survey costs, shorten the data collection cycle, and improve data completeness and coding accuracy, making it suitable for promotion and use in nutritional epidemiology, food safety risk assessment, and chronic disease prevention and control research. In the future, it can be further combined with mobile mini-programs, voice input, and image recognition technologies to improve the completion experience for older adults and populations with lower educational levels, and to explore data integration with wearable devices and electronic health records.

title: Education curriculum for surgical interns that improves stress management and grit levels
text:
Research on an Educational Curriculum for Stress Management and Grit Enhancement in Surgical Interns

 Abstract

Objective: To explore the effects of a specially designed educational curriculum on stress management ability and grit levels of surgical interns. Methods: A total of 80 interns who underwent surgical internship at a tertiary hospital from June 2022 to June 2023 were selected as research subjects and randomly divided into an intervention group (n=40) and a control group (n=40). The control group received routine internship teaching, while the intervention group received an 8-week stress management and grit enhancement curriculum in addition to routine teaching. The Chinese Perceived Stress Scale (CPSS), the Short Grit Scale (Grit-S), and the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) were used for assessment before and after the intervention. Results: After the intervention, the CPSS score of the intervention group (35.24±6.18) was significantly lower than that of the control group (42.87±7.32) (P<0.01); the Grit-S score of the intervention group (3.62±0.54) was significantly higher than that of the control group (3.18±0.61) (P<0.01); the SAS score of the intervention group (45.36±8.24) was significantly lower than that of the control group (51.72±9.15) (P<0.01). Conclusion: The specially designed educational curriculum can effectively improve the stress management ability and grit levels of surgical interns, reduce anxiety, and is worthy of promotion and application in clinical teaching.

Keywords: surgical interns; stress management; grit; educational curriculum; clinical teaching

 1 Introduction

Surgical internship is a crucial clinical practice stage in medical education, during which interns need to complete the role transition from medical student to clinical doctor in a short period of time. In this process, interns face high-intensity workload, complex doctor-patient relationships, frequent night shift rotations, and the high-risk nature of surgical operations. These factors together constitute enormous sources of psychological stress. Studies have shown that more than 60% of surgical interns experience varying degrees of anxiety and depression. Insufficient stress management ability not only affects their physical and mental health but may also lead to increased clinical operational errors and even affect the work efficiency of the entire medical team.

Grit, as a personality trait, is defined as sustained passion and persistent effort toward long-term goals. In recent years, grit levels have been confirmed to be significantly correlated with career achievement, stress resilience, and clinical decision-making quality among medical practitioners. However, traditional surgical internship education mainly focuses on the transmission of professional knowledge and surgical skills, with insufficient attention to the systematic cultivation of interns' psychological resilience and stress management abilities. Existing studies mostly focus on stress interventions for resident physicians or nursing staff, and research on educational curricula targeting surgical interns as a special group remains a gap.

This study aims to design an educational curriculum that integrates stress management techniques with grit cultivation and to verify its effects on stress levels, grit ability, and anxiety of surgical interns through a randomized controlled trial, providing empirical evidence for improving the surgical clinical teaching system.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Research Subjects

A total of 80 clinical medicine interns who underwent surgical internship at a tertiary hospital from June 2022 to June 2023 were selected as research subjects. Inclusion criteria: (1) full-time fifth-year clinical medicine students; (2) internship duration ≥6 months; (3) voluntary participation with signed informed consent. Exclusion criteria: (1) those with a history of mental illness or currently receiving psychological treatment; (2) those who recently experienced major life events. The research subjects were divided into an intervention group and a control group using the random number table method, with 40 people in each group. There were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in age, gender, distribution of internship departments, and baseline scale scores (P>0.05), indicating comparability.

 2.2 Intervention Methods

The control group received routine surgical internship teaching, including department rotations, surgical observation, case discussions, and skill operation training. The intervention group received an 8-week stress management and grit enhancement curriculum in addition to routine teaching, once per week, 90 minutes per session, in small-group teaching format (10 people per group). The curriculum content was designed based on cognitive behavioral theory and social learning theory, including four modules:

(1) Stress cognition and assessment (weeks 1-2): Teaching the physiological mechanisms of stress, stressor identification, and self-assessment methods, guiding interns to establish correct cognition of stress.

(2) Emotion regulation and relaxation techniques (weeks 3-4): Training in abdominal breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, mindfulness meditation, and other techniques to help interns quickly regulate emotions in high-pressure situations.

(3) Grit cultivation (weeks 5-6): Through goal-setting theory, growth mindset training, and role model learning, strengthening interns' persistence and passion for long-term career goals.

(4) Problem-solving and peer support (weeks 7-8): Training problem-solving strategies in clinical stress situations, establishing peer support groups, and promoting experience sharing and emotional support.

The curriculum was co-taught by clinical teachers with psychological counseling qualifications and surgical supervising teachers to ensure the professionalism and clinical relevance of the curriculum.

 2.3 Assessment Tools

The Chinese Perceived Stress Scale (CPSS) was used to assess stress levels, with 14 items, using a 0-4 point 5-level scoring system, with a total score of 0-56 points; higher scores indicate greater stress. The Short Grit Scale (Grit-S) was used to assess grit levels, with 8 items, using a 1-5 point 5-level scoring system, taking the average score; higher scores indicate higher grit levels. The Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) was used to assess anxiety, with 20 items; a standard score ≥50 indicates the presence of anxiety. All scales were distributed and collected uniformly by trained researchers before the intervention and 8 weeks after the intervention, filled out on-site, and checked for completeness.

 2.4 Statistical Methods

SPSS 26.0 software was used for data analysis. Measurement data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (x̄±s), with independent sample t-tests for between-group comparisons and paired sample t-tests for within-group pre-post comparisons. Count data were expressed as frequencies and percentages, using χ² tests. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Comparison of CPSS Scores Between the Two Groups Before and After Intervention

Before the intervention, the CPSS scores of the intervention group and control group were (43.15±7.86) and (42.92±8.14), respectively, with no statistically significant difference (t=0.13, P=0.897). After 8 weeks of intervention, the CPSS score of the intervention group decreased to (35.24±6.18), significantly lower than that of the control group (42.87±7.32) (t=5.02, P<0.01). The within-group comparison of the intervention group before and after intervention showed a statistically significant difference (t=5.87, P<0.01), while the within-group comparison of the control group before and after intervention showed no statistically significant difference (t=0.08, P=0.936). The results indicate that the educational curriculum can effectively reduce the stress perception level of surgical interns.

 3.2 Comparison of Grit-S Scores Between the Two Groups Before and After Intervention

Before the intervention, the Grit-S scores of the two groups were (3.12±0.58) and (3.15±0.62), respectively, with no statistically significant difference (t=0.22, P=0.824). After the intervention, the Grit-S score of the intervention group increased to (3.62±0.54), significantly higher than that of the control group (3.18±0.61) (t=3.41, P<0.01). The within-group comparison of the intervention group before and after intervention showed a statistically significant difference (t=4.56, P<0.01), while the within-group comparison of the control group before and after intervention showed no statistically significant difference (t=0.31, P=0.758). This indicates that the curriculum has a significant effect on improving interns' grit levels.

 3.3 Comparison of SAS Scores Between the Two Groups Before and After Intervention

Before the intervention, the SAS scores of the two groups were (52.14±9.36) and (51.87±9.72), respectively, with no statistically significant difference (t=0.13, P=0.899). After the intervention, the SAS score of the intervention group decreased to (45.36±8.24), significantly lower than that of the control group (51.72±9.15) (t=3.27, P<0.01). The within-group comparison of the intervention group before and after intervention showed a statistically significant difference (t=4.12, P<0.01), while the within-group comparison of the control group before and after intervention showed no statistically significant difference (t=0.11, P=0.913). The anxiety detection rate of the intervention group after intervention (17.5%) was significantly lower than that of the control group (40.0%) (χ²=4.94, P=0.026).

 3.4 Curriculum Satisfaction Evaluation

The overall satisfaction of interns in the intervention group with the curriculum was 92.5% (37/40), with the highest satisfaction for the "emotion regulation and relaxation techniques" module (95.0%), which was considered "highly practical and easy to apply in clinical practice." 85.0% of interns indicated that the curriculum helped improve their ability to cope with night shift and surgical stress.

 4 Discussion

The results of this study show that the specially designed stress management and grit enhancement curriculum can significantly reduce the stress perception level (decreased CPSS score), improve grit level (increased Grit-S score), and alleviate anxiety (decreased SAS score) of surgical interns, consistent with related domestic and international research conclusions. The reasons may include the following aspects:

First, the curriculum adopts a cognitive behavioral theoretical framework to help interns identify and reconstruct negative cognitions about stressful events, thereby reducing stress perception. Surgical interns often view surgical operational errors or criticism from superiors as evidence of "insufficient ability." Through cognitive restructuring training, the curriculum guides them to view these events as opportunities for learning and growth, which is consistent with the core viewpoint of growth mindset theory.

Second, the grit cultivation module enhances interns' commitment to long-term career goals through goal decomposition and role model learning. The training period for surgeons is long with a high elimination rate, and the internship stage is a critical period for the formation of professional identity. The curriculum invited senior surgeons to share their career growth experiences, providing imitable role models for interns and helping maintain their career passion.

Third, the establishment of peer support groups provides a platform for emotional catharsis and experience exchange for interns. Surgical interns often suppress emotional expression due to fear of being evaluated as "vulnerable," and a peer support environment can reduce their psychological defenses and promote help-seeking behavior.

The limitations of this study include: small sample size, single-center design, short follow-up time, and failure to assess the long-term maintenance of intervention effects. Future research can expand the sample size, conduct multi-center collaboration, extend the follow-up period, and explore the optimal model for integrating the curriculum into the routine surgical internship teaching system.

 5 Conclusion

The stress management and grit enhancement educational curriculum for surgical interns designed in this study can effectively reduce interns' stress perception level and anxiety, and improve grit quality. The curriculum has the characteristics of systematic content, flexible format, and strong clinical relevance. It is recommended to incorporate stress management and psychological resilience cultivation into the routine content of surgical internship teaching to promote the physical and mental health development of interns and improve clinical teaching quality.

title: A ras-related small GTP-binding protein, RabE1c, regulates stomatal movements and drought stress responses by mediating the interaction with ABA receptors
text:
A ras-related small GTP-binding protein, RabE1c, regulates stomatal movements and drought stress responses by mediating the interaction with ABA receptors

Abstract

Drought is one of the major abiotic stresses limiting crop yield. The plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA) plays a central role in regulating stomatal closure and drought resistance. In this study, using Arabidopsis thaliana as material, we found that a ras-related small GTP-binding protein, RabE1c, is involved in ABA signal transduction. RabE1c gene knockout mutants were insensitive to ABA-induced stomatal closure and exhibited significantly reduced drought resistance, whereas overexpression of RabE1c enhanced stomatal response to ABA and improved drought resistance. Mechanistically, RabE1c physically interacts with the ABA receptor RCAR1/PYL9 and promotes the dissociation of the receptor from the downstream phosphatase PP2C complex, thereby activating SnRK2 kinases. This study reveals that RabE1c is a novel component connecting receptors to downstream effectors in the ABA signaling pathway, providing a potential target for crop drought resistance breeding.

1 Introduction

Approximately one-third of global arable land is threatened by drought, and improving crop water use efficiency is key to ensuring food security. Stomata are the main channels for plant water loss, and their opening and closing are finely regulated by ABA. When plants encounter drought, ABA concentration increases, binds to PYR/PYL/RCAR family receptors, thereby inhibiting PP2C-mediated dephosphorylation of SnRK2, activating SnRK2, and ultimately promoting stomatal closure. Although this core pathway has been relatively well elucidated, how receptors are precisely transmitted to downstream effectors and whether membrane trafficking-related proteins are involved remain incompletely understood.

Small GTP-binding proteins (Rab family) are key regulators of membrane vesicle trafficking in eukaryotic cells and have recently been found to also participate in hormone signaling. RabE1c is a member of the Arabidopsis RabE subfamily, and previous transcriptome data showed that it is induced by drought and ABA. This study aims to clarify the function and molecular mechanism of RabE1c in ABA-regulated stomatal movement and drought resistance.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Construction and Phenotypic Characterization of Mutants and Overexpression Lines

T-DNA insertion mutant rabe1c (SALK_054321) and overexpression line (35S:RabE1c-GFP) were used. Seeds were germinated on 1/2 MS medium, transplanted, and subjected to water withholding treatment. Results showed that under normal conditions, there was no difference in stomatal aperture between mutants and wild type (WT); however, after treatment with 10 μM ABA, WT stomatal aperture decreased by approximately 60%, while mutants decreased by only 25% (P<0.01). The overexpression line showed a 75% decrease in stomatal aperture, significantly higher than WT. In leaf water loss rate experiments, the water loss rate of detached leaves of mutants after 6 hours was 32% higher than WT, while that of the overexpression line was 28% lower. After 14 days of drought followed by rewatering, the survival rate of WT was 65%, mutants 28%, and overexpression line 85%. These results indicate that RabE1c positively regulates ABA-induced stomatal closure and drought resistance.

2.2 Subcellular Localization and Expression Pattern Analysis

A RabE1c promoter-driven GUS reporter gene was constructed. GUS staining showed that RabE1c is highly expressed in stomatal guard cells, vascular bundles, and root tips. Confocal microscopy observation of 35S:RabE1c-GFP transiently transformed into tobacco leaves showed that GFP signals were mainly distributed in the cytoplasm, plasma membrane, and endosomal vesicles, partially co-localizing with endoplasmic reticulum markers. After 30 minutes of ABA treatment, vesicular signals were enhanced. Real-time quantitative PCR showed that both drought and ABA treatment induced RabE1c transcription, peaking at 2 hours (approximately 4-fold). This localization pattern suggests that RabE1c may participate in vesicle trafficking-dependent dynamic regulation of receptors.

2.3 Protein Interaction Verification: Y2H, BiFC, and Co-IP

To identify RabE1c-interacting proteins, RabE1c was used as bait to screen an Arabidopsis cDNA library, and the ABA receptor RCAR1/PYL9 was obtained. Yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) showed that RabE1c could interact with full-length RCAR1 and PYL8, but not with PYL1 or PYL4. Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) reproduced the interaction in tobacco epidermal cells, with fluorescence signals located at the plasma membrane and cytoplasm. Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) using leaves co-expressing 35S:RabE1c-GFP and 35S:RCAR1-Myc, anti-GFP antibody pulled down RCAR1-Myc. GST pull-down confirmed that recombinant RabE1c directly binds to RCAR1. These results demonstrate that RabE1c physically interacts with specific ABA receptors.

2.4 Functional Analysis of ABA Signaling Pathway: PP2C-SnRK2 Module

In protoplasts, ABA induces SnRK2.6 phosphorylation. In WT, ABA increased SnRK2.6 phosphorylation levels by 3.5-fold; in rabe1c mutants, only by 1.8-fold; and in overexpression lines, by 5-fold. In vitro phosphatase experiments showed that in the presence of RabE1c, the inhibitory effect of RCAR1 on PP2C (HAB1) was enhanced 2.3-fold; without RabE1c, no significant enhancement was observed. Yeast three-hybrid showed that RabE1c promotes the dissociation of RCAR1 from HAB1. It is speculated that RabE1c may act as a scaffold or transport protein, delivering RCAR1 to the vicinity of PP2C or altering receptor conformation, thereby enhancing ABA signaling efficiency.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

Main results of this study: ① RabE1c is a positive regulator of ABA-induced stomatal closure and drought resistance; ② RabE1c localizes to the plasma membrane and vesicles and is induced by ABA; ③ RabE1c directly interacts with the ABA receptor RCAR1/PYL9; ④ RabE1c enhances receptor inhibition of PP2C and activates SnRK2.

Benefit analysis: At the level of technology extension, RabE1c can serve as a molecular marker for drought-resistant germplasm screening. Overexpression of RabE1c in Arabidopsis improved survival rate by 20 percentage points, with no significant growth defects observed. If this gene is applied to crops such as wheat and maize, upregulating its expression or optimizing its interaction interface through gene editing could potentially stabilize yield under limited water conditions. Furthermore, the interaction mechanism between RabE1c and receptors provides new targets for developing small molecule agonists, potentially reducing the cycle of traditional drought resistance breeding.

4 Conclusion

RabE1c is a key small GTP-binding protein connecting ABA receptors to the downstream PP2C-SnRK2 module, enhancing ABA signaling by mediating vesicle trafficking-related processes, thereby regulating stomatal closure and drought resistance. This study expands the understanding of Rab family functions in hormone signaling and provides theoretical basis and candidate genes for genetic improvement of crop drought resistance. Future work needs to verify the function of RabE1c homologous genes in major crops and elucidate the dynamic regulation of its GTP hydrolysis activity on interactions.

title: Microbial carbon source utilization in rice rhizosphere soil with different tillage practice in a double cropping rice field
text:
Characteristics of Microbial Carbon Source Utilization in Rice Rhizosphere Soil Under Different Tillage Practices in a Double-Cropping Paddy Field

 Abstract

【Objective】To investigate the effects of different tillage practices on the metabolic activity of microbial carbon source utilization in rice rhizosphere soil of a double-cropping paddy field, and to provide microbiological evidence for paddy soil quality assessment and tillage system optimization.【Methods】Based on a long-term positioning experiment, four treatments were established: conventional tillage (CT), rotary tillage (RT), no-tillage (NT), and conventional tillage + straw return (CTS). The Biolog-ECO microplate method was used to collect rhizosphere soil at the maturity stage of early rice and late rice, and to analyze the utilization characteristics of six categories of carbon sources and diversity indices.【Results】Compared with CT, NT and CTS significantly increased the average well color development (AWCD), Shannon index, and McIntosh index of rhizosphere soil microorganisms (P<0.05), with CTS showing the best effect. Microorganisms in all treatments showed higher utilization rates of carbohydrates, amino acids, and carboxylic acids, and lower utilization rates of amines and phenolic acids. Principal component analysis indicated that microbial carbon source utilization patterns differentiated under different tillage practices, with CTS and NT being relatively similar, while CT and RT clustered together. Redundancy analysis revealed that soil organic carbon, total nitrogen, and available potassium were the key factors driving the differences in microbial carbon source utilization.【Conclusion】No-tillage and straw return can enhance the metabolic activity of rhizosphere soil microorganisms in double-cropping paddy fields, alter carbon source utilization preferences, and contribute to improving soil microbial functional diversity.

Keywords: double-cropping paddy field; tillage practice; rhizosphere soil; microbial carbon source utilization; Biolog-ECO; straw return

 1 Introduction

Soil microorganisms are the core drivers of material cycling and energy flow in paddy field ecosystems, and their community metabolic activity is directly related to soil organic matter transformation, nutrient supply, and crop productivity. The rhizosphere, as the most active interface of plant-soil-microbe interactions, harbors microbial communities that are particularly sensitive to tillage disturbance. Different tillage practices regulate the microbial habitat environment and substrate availability by altering soil physical structure, aeration, moisture conditions, and straw return amounts.

The double-cropping rice system occupies an important position in the rice-growing regions of southern China. Long-term intensive tillage has led to increasingly prominent problems such as shallowing of the plow layer, decline in organic carbon, and degradation of microbial functions. In recent years, conservation tillage measures such as no-tillage, rotary tillage, and straw return have received widespread attention, but systematic comparisons regarding their effects on rhizosphere soil microbial carbon source metabolic characteristics in double-cropping paddy fields are still lacking. The Biolog-ECO microplate technique can rapidly characterize the ability of microbial communities to utilize various carbon sources and has been widely used to evaluate soil microbial functional diversity in agricultural fields.

This study used a long-term positioning experiment in a double-cropping paddy field as a platform, employed the Biolog-ECO method, and analyzed the characteristics of microbial carbon source utilization in rice rhizosphere soil under different tillage practices and their relationships with soil physicochemical factors. The aim was to reveal the mechanisms by which tillage measures affect rhizosphere microbial metabolic functions in paddy fields, and to provide a scientific basis for optimizing tillage systems in the double-cropping rice region of southern China.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Site Description

The experiment was located in the suburbs of Changsha City, Hunan Province (113°04′E, 28°18′N), which has a subtropical monsoon climate with an annual mean temperature of 17.2 °C and annual mean precipitation of 1360 mm. The test soil was paddy soil developed from Quaternary red earth. Before the experiment, the basic physicochemical properties of the plow layer (0–20 cm) were: pH 5.82, organic carbon 18.6 g·kg⁻¹, total nitrogen 1.95 g·kg⁻¹, alkaline hydrolyzable nitrogen 142.3 mg·kg⁻¹, available phosphorus 21.5 mg·kg⁻¹, and available potassium 98.7 mg·kg⁻¹.

 2.2 Experimental Design

The long-term positioning experiment began in 2012, using a randomized complete block design with four treatments, three replicates per treatment, and a plot area of 30 m². The treatments were: (1) conventional tillage (CT): plowing to 20 cm after each rice harvest, with no straw return; (2) rotary tillage (RT): rotary tillage to 12 cm, with no straw return; (3) no-tillage (NT): no tillage throughout the year, with no straw return; (4) conventional tillage + straw return (CTS): plowing to 20 cm with full straw return after each rice season. Fertilizer application rates were consistent across all treatments. For early rice, pure N 150 kg·hm⁻², P₂O₅ 75 kg·hm⁻², and K₂O 120 kg·hm⁻² were applied; for late rice, pure N 180 kg·hm⁻², P₂O₅ 75 kg·hm⁻², and K₂O 150 kg·hm⁻² were applied. Nitrogen fertilizer was applied at a ratio of basal fertilizer∶tillering fertilizer∶panicle fertilizer = 5∶3∶2.

 2.3 Soil Sample Collection

At the maturity stage of early rice (mid-July) and late rice (early November) in 2023, rhizosphere soil was collected using the root-shaking method. Five rice plants were randomly selected from each plot. After removing surface soil, soil tightly adhering to the root surface was collected and mixed into one sample. After passing through a 2 mm sieve, each sample was divided into two parts: one part was air-dried for physicochemical property determination, and the other was stored at 4 °C for Biolog analysis.

 2.4 Determination Methods

Soil organic carbon was determined by the potassium dichromate external heating method, total nitrogen by the Kjeldahl method, available phosphorus by the Olsen method, available potassium by flame photometry, and pH by the potentiometric method with a water-to-soil ratio of 2.5∶1.

Biolog-ECO microplate analysis: Fresh soil equivalent to 10 g dry soil was weighed and added to 90 mL sterile physiological saline (0.85% NaCl), shaken for 30 min, and then allowed to stand. The supernatant was diluted to 10⁻³. A 150 μL aliquot of the dilution was added to each well and incubated at 28 °C in the dark. Absorbance was measured at 590 nm every 24 h for 168 h continuously. Net absorbance was calculated by subtracting the absorbance of the control well from that of each sample well. Average well color development (AWCD) = Σ(Ci−R)/31. Carbon sources were classified into six categories: carbohydrates, amino acids, carboxylic acids, polymers, amines, and phenolic acids. Data at 120 h of incubation were selected to calculate the Shannon index, Simpson index, and McIntosh index.

 2.5 Data Processing

Excel 2019 and SPSS 26.0 were used for data organization and analysis of variance (Duncan's method, α=0.05). Origin 2021 was used for plotting, and CANOCO 5.0 was used for principal component analysis (PCA) and redundancy analysis (RDA).

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Effects of Different Tillage Practices on Rhizosphere Soil Microbial AWCD

With prolonged incubation time, AWCD in all treatments showed an increasing trend, but the growth rates differed. At 120 h of incubation, the AWCD values of CT, RT, NT, and CTS in the early rice season were 0.68, 0.72, 0.85, and 0.93, respectively; in the late rice season, they were 0.61, 0.66, 0.79, and 0.88, respectively. Compared with CT, NT and CTS significantly increased AWCD (P<0.05). CTS increased AWCD by 36.8% (early rice) and 44.3% (late rice) compared with CT; RT showed no significant difference from CT. AWCD in all treatments was generally lower in the late rice season than in the early rice season, possibly related to the decrease in temperature during the late rice season.

 3.2 Differences in Microbial Carbon Source Utilization Types

The utilization intensity of the six carbon source categories by microorganisms in all treatments followed the order: carbohydrates > amino acids > carboxylic acids > polymers > amines > phenolic acids. Compared with CT, the CTS treatment increased the utilization rates of carbohydrates, amino acids, and carboxylic acids by 42.1%, 35.6%, and 31.8%, respectively (P<0.05); the NT treatment increased them by 28.4%, 24.7%, and 21.3%, respectively. For phenolic acids and amines, CTS and NT treatments were also significantly higher than CT. The RT treatment showed slightly higher utilization rates for each carbon source than CT, but the differences did not reach a significant level. This indicates that no-tillage and straw return enhanced the metabolic capacity of microorganisms for readily utilizable carbon sources and also improved the decomposition potential for recalcitrant carbon sources.

 3.3 Microbial Functional Diversity Indices

The Shannon index followed the order CTS>NT>RT>CT, with CTS and NT significantly higher than CT (P<0.05). The McIntosh index showed the same trend as the Shannon index. The Simpson index differed little among treatments, with only CTS significantly higher than CT. Diversity indices were generally higher in the early rice season than in the late rice season. This suggests that straw return and no-tillage are conducive to maintaining higher microbial functional diversity, while conventional tillage reduced community metabolic evenness.

 3.4 Principal Component Analysis of Carbon Source Utilization Patterns

PCA was performed on the utilization data of 31 carbon sources, and the first two principal components cumulatively explained 78.6% of the variance. PC1 (56.3%) separated CTS and NT from CT and RT, while PC2 (22.3%) further distinguished CTS from NT. CTS had the highest score on PC1 and was positively correlated with carbohydrates and amino acid carbon sources; CT had a higher score in the negative direction of PC1 and was closely associated with phenolic acid and amine carbon sources. This indicates that different tillage practices shaped distinctly different microbial carbon source utilization patterns.

 3.5 Redundancy Analysis of Soil Physicochemical Factors and Carbon Source Utilization

RDA results showed that the first two axes cumulatively explained 81.2% of the variation in microbial carbon source utilization. Soil organic carbon (explanation rate 42.6%, P=0.002), total nitrogen (18.3%, P=0.008), and available potassium (11.5%, P=0.021) were the main driving factors. Organic carbon was significantly positively correlated with the utilization of carbohydrates and amino acids, and available potassium was positively correlated with carboxylic acid utilization. The effects of pH and available phosphorus did not reach significant levels.

 4 Discussion

This study showed that no-tillage and straw return significantly enhanced the overall metabolic activity of rhizosphere soil microorganisms in double-cropping paddy fields. This was mainly attributed to two aspects: first, straw return provided abundant carbon sources and nutrients for microorganisms, directly stimulating microbial growth and reproduction; second, no-tillage reduced the destruction of soil aggregates and hyphal networks by mechanical disturbance, which helped maintain a relatively stable microbial habitat. The CTS treatment was more effective than NT, indicating that the synergistic effect of straw input and tillage improvement was more pronounced.

The shift in microbial carbon source utilization preferences reflected adaptive adjustments in community composition and function. Under CTS and NT treatments, microbial metabolism of readily utilizable carbon sources such as carbohydrates and amino acids was enhanced, indicating an increased proportion of copiotrophic microorganisms in the community, which was closely related to the release of large amounts of soluble organic carbon during straw decomposition. At the same time, the increased utilization rate of phenolic acids suggested that some fungi or actinomycetes with lignin-degrading ability were enriched. Under CT treatment, microbial utilization of phenolic acids was relatively higher, possibly related to intensified organic matter mineralization and scarcity of readily utilizable carbon sources caused by long-term plowing.

The improvement in diversity indices further confirmed that conservation tillage is beneficial for maintaining microbial functional diversity. The significant positive correlation between the Shannon index and organic carbon and total nitrogen indicated that soil nutrient status is a key regulator of microbial diversity. The significant effect of available potassium on carbon source utilization in the RDA results may be related to the role of potassium ions in regulating microbial cell osmotic pressure and enzyme activity. In addition, microbial activity in the late rice season was lower than in the early rice season, reflecting the seasonal regulation of microbial metabolism by temperature and hydrothermal conditions.

It should be noted that the Biolog method only reflects the substrate utilization potential of culturable and fast-growing microorganisms and cannot fully represent in situ community function. Future studies should combine high-throughput sequencing and metagenomics approaches to further elucidate the mechanisms by which tillage practices affect microbial community structure and functional genes.

 5 Conclusion

(1) Compared with conventional tillage, no-tillage and conventional tillage + straw return significantly increased the AWCD, Shannon index, and McIntosh index of rice rhizosphere soil microorganisms in double-cropping paddy fields, with conventional tillage + straw return showing the best effect. (2) Microorganisms in all treatments showed higher utilization rates of carbohydrates, amino acids, and carboxylic acids, and lower utilization rates of amines and phenolic acids; straw return and no-tillage enhanced the metabolic capacity of microorganisms for various carbon sources. (3) Microbial carbon source utilization patterns clearly differentiated under different tillage practices, with soil organic carbon, total nitrogen, and available potassium being the main driving factors. (4) In the double-cropping rice region of southern China, promoting tillage measures combining no-tillage with straw return can help enhance rhizosphere soil microbial metabolic activity and functional diversity and improve soil quality.

title: Monetary costs of Alzheimer's disease in China: protocol for a cluster-randomised observational study
text:
Study on the Monetary Costs of Alzheimer's Disease in China: Protocol for a Cluster Randomized Observational Study

Abstract

Objective: Alzheimer's disease (AD) imposes a heavy economic burden on Chinese families and society, but existing cost data are mostly based on small samples or single-center surveys and lack representativeness. This study aims to design a cluster randomized observational study protocol to systematically measure the direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, and indirect costs of AD patients in China, and to analyze their influencing factors. Methods: A cluster random sampling method will be used to select 12 cities across eastern, central, and western China. Two communities will be randomly selected in each city, yielding 24 communities in total. Using the community as the unit, clusters will be randomly divided into two groups: one group will receive standardized cost-recording training, and the other will receive routine recording. Clinically diagnosed AD patients and their primary caregivers will be enrolled and followed for 12 months. Cost data will be collected through medical record review, expense diaries, caregiver interviews, and linkage to medical insurance databases. The primary outcome is annual per capita total cost, and secondary outcomes include cost composition ratios, cost-related factors, and caregiver burden. Expected results: Approximately 1,200 patients are expected to be enrolled, yielding high-quality data on the monetary costs of AD in China and providing evidence for medical insurance policy and the long-term care system. Conclusion: This study protocol is feasible and can provide methodological reference for research on the economic burden of AD.

1 Introduction

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common type of dementia, accounting for 60%-70% of all dementia cases. With the acceleration of population aging in China, the prevalence of AD continues to rise. It is estimated that the prevalence of dementia among people aged 60 years and older in China is about 6%, of which AD accounts for about 3.9%, with more than 9 million patients in total. AD not only causes progressive decline in cognitive function but is also accompanied by psychiatric and behavioral symptoms, ultimately causing patients to lose the ability to perform activities of daily living and requiring long-term care.

The economic burden of AD includes direct medical costs (outpatient, inpatient, medications, examinations), direct non-medical costs (nursing homes, home care, transportation, nutritional supplements), and indirect costs (productivity losses of patients and caregivers). International studies have shown that the annual per capita cost of dementia can reach USD 30,000-50,000 in developed countries and about USD 10,000-20,000 in middle-income countries. Existing studies in China are mostly limited to a single city or hospital, with small sample sizes, inconsistent cost measurement approaches, and a lack of systematic measurement of indirect costs. In addition, AD patients often have multiple comorbid chronic diseases, and their use of medical resources is complex, making traditional retrospective surveys prone to recall bias.

A cluster randomized observational study design can implement interventions at the community level (such as standardized cost-recording training) while observing cost changes under the natural course of disease, balancing representativeness and feasibility. This study aims to develop a protocol for measuring the monetary costs of AD suitable for China's national conditions, providing data support for health economic evaluation and policy making.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Study Design and Sampling Method

This study adopts a cluster randomized observational study design. The community is used as the cluster unit to avoid information contamination among patients within the same community. Sampling is conducted in three stages: In the first stage, China is divided into three strata—eastern, central, and western—according to geographic and economic level, with 4 cities selected from each stratum, for a total of 12 cities. In the second stage, 2 urban districts or counties are randomly selected in each city, and 1 community health service center or township health center is randomly selected in each urban district/county, for a total of 24 communities. In the third stage, AD patients meeting the criteria are consecutively enrolled within the communities.

Cluster randomization: The 24 communities will be randomly divided 1:1 into an intervention group and a control group. The intervention group will receive standardized cost-recording training, including the use of a unified expense diary, monthly telephone reminders, and quarterly face-to-face verification; the control group will receive routine recording and only general health counseling. Randomization will be completed by an independent statistician using a computer-generated random sequence, and allocation concealment will be achieved through sealed envelopes. Due to the nature of the intervention, patients and caregivers cannot be blinded, but personnel collecting and analyzing cost data will be blinded.

Sample size estimation: According to a pilot study, the standard deviation of annual per capita total cost for AD patients is about 20,000 yuan, the allowable error is 10%, the significance level is α=0.05, the design effect considering the cluster effect is 1.5, and the loss to follow-up rate is 20%. It is calculated that about 1,200 patients need to be enrolled, about 50 patients per community.

2.2 Cost Data Collection and Classification

Cost data collection adopts a multi-source mixed model. Direct medical costs: outpatient, inpatient, medication, and examination costs will be obtained through linkage to medical insurance databases; out-of-pocket portions will be verified through expense diaries and receipts. Direct non-medical costs: including nursing home fees, home caregiver wages, transportation, assistive devices, nutritional supplements, etc., which will be recorded monthly by caregivers in expense diaries. Indirect costs: the human capital approach will be used to calculate the productivity lost by patients due to disability (based on local average wages matched by age, sex, and education level) and the work time reduced by caregivers due to caregiving (including leave, reduced working hours, and resignation). Caregiver time will be recorded using caregiver time diaries, 1 day per week, for 12 consecutive months.

Cost classification follows the international consensus on dementia cost research and is divided into: direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, and indirect costs. All costs will be expressed in 2025 RMB prices and adjusted using the consumer price index. For prices that cannot be obtained directly, the market replacement method (such as home care based on local caregiver wages) or the opportunity cost method will be used.

2.3 Outcome Indicators and Measurement Tools

Primary outcome: annual per capita total cost (yuan/year). Secondary outcomes: ① cost composition ratios (proportions of direct medical, direct non-medical, and indirect costs); ② cost-related factors: multiple linear regression will be used to analyze the effects of age, sex, education, dementia severity (CDR score), comorbidity index, caregiver characteristics, etc. on costs; ③ caregiver burden: the Zarit Caregiver Burden Interview (ZBI) and the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) will be used; ④ quality of life: EQ-5D-5L for patients and SF-12 for caregivers.

Measurement tools include: Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), Activities of Daily Living (ADL) scale, Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI), and Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA). All scales will use the Chinese versions, whose reliability and validity have been verified. Data collection time points are baseline, 6 months, and 12 months. The intervention group will additionally record expense diaries monthly, while the control group will record retrospectively every 3 months.

2.4 Quality Control and Ethical Considerations

Quality control measures: ① develop a standardized operations manual and provide unified training for investigators; ② monthly telephone reminders for the intervention group and quarterly on-site verification of expense diaries; ③ randomly select 10% of data for telephone rechecking; ④ use double independent data entry and logical validation. Cluster randomization may lead to baseline imbalance, which will be adjusted using propensity score weighting.

Ethical considerations: The study protocol has been approved by the ethics committee of the lead institution. All patients and caregivers will sign informed consent forms. For patients with cognitive impairment, consent will be signed by their legal representatives. Data will be anonymized and used only for research purposes. The intervention group will receive cost-recording training without changing clinical treatment. If unmet medical needs are identified in patients, they will be referred to community physicians.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

Expected results: Approximately 1,200 AD patients are expected to be enrolled, with an average age of 75 years and women accounting for 60%. Preliminary estimates suggest that the annual per capita total cost of AD patients in China is about 30,000-50,000 yuan, of which direct medical costs account for 30%-40%, direct non-medical costs account for 25%-35%, and indirect costs account for 30%-40%. Costs rise with increasing dementia severity, and the cost for severe patients may be 2-3 times that for mild patients. Caregivers spend an average of about 30-40 hours per week on caregiving, and about 20% of caregivers reduce work or resign because of this. The completeness of cost records in the intervention group is expected to be 20%-30% higher than that in the control group, with reduced recall bias.

Benefit analysis: ① Scientific benefits: provide high-quality, representative data on the monetary costs of AD in China, fill the gap in indirect cost measurement, and provide a methodological template for disease burden research. ② Policy benefits: provide evidence for medical insurance departments to formulate AD-related reimbursement policies and pilot long-term care insurance; provide reference for health departments to plan community care resources. ③ Social benefits: raise public awareness of the economic burden of AD and promote the development of a caregiver support system. ④ Economic benefits: by identifying cost drivers, guide the optimal allocation of resources and potentially save medical expenditures. For example, if home care for severe patients is shifted to community day care, indirect costs could be reduced by about 15%.

4 Conclusion

This study designs a cluster randomized observational study protocol for systematically measuring the monetary costs of Alzheimer's disease in China. This protocol has the following characteristics: using the community as the cluster unit, balancing representativeness and feasibility; adopting multi-source cost data collection to reduce recall bias; using cluster randomization to compare the effects of standardized cost recording and routine recording; and comprehensively measuring direct medical, direct non-medical, and indirect costs. The expected results will provide key data for medical insurance policy, the development of the long-term care system, and caregiver support. This protocol can be extended to economic burden studies of other chronic diseases and has good methodological reference value. Future work needs to further verify the reliability and validity of the cost-recording tools and explore the linkage analysis of cost data with clinical outcomes.

title: Improving Sexual Health Education Programs for Adolescent Students through Game-Based Learning and Gamification
text:
Optimization of Sexuality Health Education Programs for Adolescent Students Based on Game-Based Learning and Game Mechanics

 Abstract

Objective: To explore the application effects of game-based learning and game mechanics in adolescent sexuality health education, and to provide empirical evidence for improving adolescents' sexuality health knowledge, attitudes, and behavioral intentions. Methods: A cluster randomized controlled trial design was adopted. A total of 586 junior high school students from 12 classes in 6 middle schools in a certain region were selected as research subjects and randomly divided into an intervention group (n=293) and a control group (n=293). The intervention group received an 8-week gamified sexuality health education course, while the control group received traditional lecture-based sexuality health education. The Sexuality Health Knowledge Scale, Sexuality Health Attitude Scale, and Sexual Behavior Intention Scale were used for assessments at baseline, post-intervention, and 3-month follow-up. Results: After the intervention, the sexuality health knowledge score of the intervention group (82.36±9.47) was significantly higher than that of the control group (68.52±11.23) (t=15.672, P<0.001); the sexuality health attitude score of the intervention group (76.48±8.92) was significantly better than that of the control group (65.31±10.15) (t=13.845, P<0.001); the safe sexual behavior intention score of the intervention group (79.63±9.18) was significantly higher than that of the control group (67.24±10.86) (t=14.237, P<0.001). At the 3-month follow-up, all indicators of the intervention group remained significantly better than those of the control group (P<0.001). Conclusion: Game-based learning and game mechanics can effectively improve the effectiveness of adolescent sexuality health education. It is recommended to promote and apply them in middle school sexuality health education.

Keywords: game-based learning; sexuality health education; adolescents; game mechanics; randomized controlled trial

 1 Introduction

Adolescence is a critical stage in the development of sexual physiology and sexual psychology. Scientific sexuality health education is of great significance to the healthy physical and mental development of adolescents. However, at present, sexuality health education for adolescents in China still faces many challenges: teaching content emphasizes the transmission of physiological knowledge while neglecting the cultivation of attitudes and skills; teaching methods are mainly traditional lectures, with low student participation; class hours are insufficient and cannot meet students' actual needs. According to relevant surveys, Chinese adolescents generally have a low level of mastery of sexuality health knowledge, with obvious deficiencies in understanding premarital sexual behavior, contraceptive measures, and prevention of sexually transmitted diseases.

In recent years, game-based learning and gamification have been increasingly widely applied in the field of education. Game-based learning refers to integrating game elements into the learning process to improve learners' motivation and participation; gamification refers to applying game design elements (such as points, badges, leaderboards, levels, etc.) in non-game contexts to stimulate target behaviors. Existing studies have shown that game-based learning has achieved good results in fields such as health education and nutrition education, but research on its application in sexuality health education is still insufficient.

This study aims to explore the application effects of game-based learning and game mechanics in adolescent sexuality health education. Through a randomized controlled trial design, it evaluates their impact on adolescents' sexuality health knowledge, attitudes, and behavioral intentions, so as to provide empirical evidence for optimizing middle school sexuality health education programs.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Research Subjects

Using a cluster random sampling method, from September 2024 to January 2025, a total of 586 students from 12 second-year junior high school classes in 6 middle schools in a certain region were selected as research subjects. Inclusion criteria: (1) currently enrolled second-year junior high school students; (2) aged 13-15 years; (3) informed consent and voluntary participation. Exclusion criteria: (1) suffering from severe mental illness or cognitive impairment; (2) having recently participated in similar sexuality health education programs. A total of 586 students were ultimately included, including 298 boys (50.85%) and 288 girls (49.15%), with an average age of (14.12±0.73) years.

 2.2 Research Design

A cluster randomized controlled trial design was adopted. With classes as units, 12 classes were randomly divided into an intervention group (6 classes, 293 students) and a control group (6 classes, 293 students) using the random number table method. The intervention group received a gamified sexuality health education course, while the control group received a traditional lecture-based sexuality health education course. The course content for both groups was designed according to the Guidelines for Health Education in Primary and Secondary Schools and the International Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education, covering topics such as pubertal physiological changes, sexual psychological development, prevention of sexually transmitted diseases, contraception and safe sexual behavior, sexual consent, and prevention of sexual harassment.

 2.3 Intervention Plan

Intervention group: A sexuality health education course designed with game-based learning and game mechanics was adopted, lasting 8 weeks, with 1 class hour per week (45 minutes). The specific design included: (1) Point system: students could earn points by completing classroom tasks, participating in discussions, and answering questions correctly; (2) Badge system: badges such as "Knowledge Expert," "Health Guardian," and "Communication Expert" were set up and could be obtained upon meeting corresponding conditions; (3) Level design: the course content was divided into 8 levels, with tasks of different difficulty set at each level; (4) Leaderboard: the points leaderboard was updated weekly to stimulate competitive awareness; (5) Role-playing: through scenario simulation games, students practiced skills such as refusing unsafe sexual behavior and using condoms; (6) Team cooperation: tasks such as "Sexuality Health Knowledge Competition" and "Scenario Drama Performance" were completed in groups.

Control group: Traditional lecture-based teaching was adopted, with teachers explaining according to textbook content, supplemented by PPT presentations and video playback, and students passively receiving knowledge.

 2.4 Evaluation Tools

Self-developed questionnaires were used for evaluation, including: (1) Sexuality Health Knowledge Scale: 30 items in total, with a full score of 100 points; the higher the score, the higher the level of knowledge; (2) Sexuality Health Attitude Scale: 20 items in total, using a 5-point Likert scale, with a full score of 100 points; the higher the score, the more positive the attitude; (3) Sexual Behavior Intention Scale: 15 items in total, using a 5-point Likert scale, with a full score of 100 points; the higher the score, the stronger the intention to engage in safe sexual behavior. The Cronbach's α coefficients of the scales were 0.87, 0.84, and 0.86, respectively, showing good reliability and validity.

 2.5 Data Collection

Questionnaire surveys were conducted before the intervention (T0), after the intervention (T1, week 8), and at follow-up (T2, month 3). Uniformly trained investigators distributed the questionnaires on site, students filled them out independently, and they were collected on the spot. A total of 586 questionnaires were distributed, and 586 valid questionnaires were recovered, with an effective recovery rate of 100%.

 2.6 Statistical Methods

SPSS 26.0 software was used for statistical analysis. Measurement data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (x̄±s), independent samples t-tests were used for between-group comparisons, and paired t-tests were used for within-group comparisons; count data were expressed as frequencies and percentages, and χ² tests were used for between-group comparisons. P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Comparison of Baseline Data Between the Two Groups

Before the intervention, there were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in terms of gender, age, sexuality health knowledge score, sexuality health attitude score, and sexual behavior intention score (P>0.05), indicating comparability (see Table 1).

Table 1 Comparison of Baseline Data Between the Two Groups (x̄±s)

| Item | Intervention Group (n=293) | Control Group (n=293) | t/χ² Value | P Value |
|------|----------------|----------------|---------|-----|
| Gender (male/female) | 149/144 | 149/144 | 0.000 | 1.000 |
| Age (years) | 14.08±0.71 | 14.16±0.75 | 1.324 | 0.186 |
| Knowledge score | 52.47±12.36 | 53.12±11.89 | 0.651 | 0.515 |
| Attitude score | 58.63±10.24 | 57.89±10.67 | 0.862 | 0.389 |
| Behavioral intention score | 55.74±11.52 | 56.31±11.08 | 0.612 | 0.541 |

 3.2 Comparison of Indicators Between the Two Groups After Intervention

After the intervention, the sexuality health knowledge score, attitude score, and behavioral intention score of the intervention group were all significantly higher than those of the control group, and the differences were statistically significant (P<0.001) (see Table 2).

Table 2 Comparison of Indicators Between the Two Groups After Intervention (x̄±s, points)

| Item | Intervention Group (n=293) | Control Group (n=293) | t Value | P Value |
|------|----------------|----------------|-----|-----|
| Knowledge score | 82.36±9.47 | 68.52±11.23 | 15.672 | <0.001 |
| Attitude score | 76.48±8.92 | 65.31±10.15 | 13.845 | <0.001 |
| Behavioral intention score | 79.63±9.18 | 67.24±10.86 | 14.237 | <0.001 |

 3.3 Comparison of Indicators Between the Two Groups at Follow-Up

At the 3-month follow-up, all indicators of the intervention group remained significantly better than those of the control group, and the differences were statistically significant (P<0.001) (see Table 3).

Table 3 Comparison of Indicators Between the Two Groups at Follow-Up (x̄±s, points)

| Item | Intervention Group (n=293) | Control Group (n=293) | t Value | P Value |
|------|----------------|----------------|-----|-----|
| Knowledge score | 79.85±10.12 | 66.47±11.85 | 14.523 | <0.001 |
| Attitude score | 74.26±9.34 | 63.58±10.72 | 12.876 | <0.001 |
| Behavioral intention score | 77.41±9.86 | 65.73±11.24 | 13.458 | <0.001 |

 3.4 Comparison of Each Time Point Within the Two Groups

In the intervention group, all indicators after the intervention and at follow-up were significantly higher than before the intervention (P<0.001); in the control group, the knowledge score after the intervention was significantly higher than before the intervention (P<0.05), but there were no statistically significant differences in attitude score and behavioral intention score compared with before the intervention (P>0.05), and at follow-up there were no statistically significant differences in any indicators compared with before the intervention (P>0.05).

 4 Discussion

 4.1 Effect of Game-Based Learning on Improving Sexuality Health Knowledge

The results of this study showed that the sexuality health knowledge score of the intervention group after the intervention was significantly higher than that of the control group, and it remained at a relatively high level at the 3-month follow-up, indicating that game-based learning can effectively improve adolescents' level of sexuality health knowledge. This is consistent with the results of existing studies. Through mechanisms such as points, badges, and levels, game-based learning transforms dull sexuality health knowledge into interesting game tasks, stimulating students' learning motivation and enthusiasm for participation. At the same time, gamified activities such as role-playing and scenario simulation help students apply knowledge in simulated situations, deepening understanding and memory.

 4.2 Effect of Game-Based Learning on Improving Sexuality Health Attitudes

The sexuality health attitude score of the intervention group was significantly better than that of the control group, indicating that game-based learning can effectively improve adolescents' attitudes toward sexuality health. Traditional lecture-based teaching often focuses on knowledge transmission and neglects attitude cultivation; in contrast, game-based learning creates an open and inclusive learning atmosphere through mechanisms such as teamwork and competitive ranking, reducing students' sense of shame and avoidance regarding sexual topics. Through role-playing and scenario simulation, students can think about sexual issues from different perspectives and form more positive and rational sexuality health attitudes.

 4.3 Promoting Effect of Game-Based Learning on Sexual Behavior Intention

The safe sexual behavior intention score of the intervention group was significantly higher than that of the control group, indicating that game-based learning can effectively promote adolescents' intention to engage in safe sexual behavior. By simulating real situations, game-based learning allows students to practice skills such as refusing unsafe sexual behavior and negotiating condom use, enhancing self-efficacy. At the same time, incentive mechanisms such as points and badges reinforce students' awareness of safe sexual behavior, making them more inclined to adopt safe sexual behavior.

 4.4 Sustainability Effect of Game-Based Learning

The 3-month follow-up results showed that all indicators of the intervention group remained significantly better than those of the control group, indicating that game-based learning has a relatively good sustainability effect. This may be because game-based learning not only imparts knowledge, but more importantly cultivates students' autonomous learning ability and healthy behavioral habits. Through gamification mechanisms, students can still maintain attention to and interest in learning sexuality health knowledge after class, forming a long-term health education effect.

 4.5 Research Limitations and Prospects

This study has the following limitations: First, the research subjects came only from 6 middle schools in a certain region, so the representativeness of the sample is limited; second, the follow-up time was only 3 months, and the long-term effects need further verification; third, the evaluation indicators were mainly self-reported questionnaires, which may have social desirability bias. Future research can expand the sample range, extend the follow-up time, and combine objective behavioral indicators to further verify the effects of game-based learning in sexuality health education.

 5 Conclusion

This study shows that game-based learning and game mechanics can effectively improve adolescents' level of sexuality health knowledge, improve sexuality health attitudes, and promote safe sexual behavior intentions, and have relatively good sustainability effects. It is recommended to promote and apply game-based learning and game mechanics in middle school sexuality health education. Through gamification elements such as points, badges, levels, leaderboards, and role-playing, students' participation and learning outcomes can be improved, providing new paths and methods for adolescent sexuality health education. At the same time, education departments should strengthen training for sexuality health education teachers, develop gamified sexuality health education resources suitable for Chinese adolescents, and promote the optimization and innovation of sexuality health education programs.

title: Diversification and independent domestication of Asian and European pears
text:
Diversification and Independent Domestication of Asian Pears and European Pears

Abstract: Pear is one of the important temperate fruit trees globally, and its cultivated varieties are mainly divided into two major groups: Asian pears and European pears. This study systematically analyzed the domestication history of Asian pears and European pears through comparative genomics, population genetics, and archaeological evidence. The results indicate that Asian pears and European pears originated from different wild ancestral species and diverged approximately 0.6–1.2 million years ago. The domestication center of Asian pears is located in the Yangtze River Basin and Yellow River Basin of China, represented by Pyrus pyrifolia, Pyrus bretschneideri, Pyrus ussuriensis, and Pyrus sinkiangensis; the domestication center of European pears is located in the Caucasus region and Central Asia, represented by Pyrus communis. The two groups underwent independent selection for traits such as fruit size, sugar-acid content, stone cell number, and disease resistance. Key gene families such as PbWRKY, PyMYB, SOT, and SWEET play differentiated regulatory roles in sugar accumulation and stone cell formation. Genome-wide association analysis identified multiple independent domestication loci associated with fruit quality. This study provides a theoretical basis for the utilization of pear germplasm resources and cross-population hybrid breeding.

Keywords: pear; domestication; population genomics; fruit quality; independent origin

1 Introduction

Pear belongs to the genus Pyrus in the subfamily Maloideae of the family Rosaceae, with approximately 30 species worldwide, widely distributed across Eurasia and North Africa. Based on morphology and geographical distribution, cultivated pears are mainly divided into two major groups: Asian pears and European pears. Asian pears include Pyrus pyrifolia, Pyrus bretschneideri, Pyrus ussuriensis, and Pyrus sinkiangensis, mainly distributed in China, Japan, and South Korea; European pears, namely Pyrus communis, are mainly distributed in Europe, North America, and Oceania. The two groups exhibit significant differences in fruit shape, flavor, texture, and stress resistance, but their domestication origins and divergence relationships have long remained unclear.

Early taxonomic studies based on morphology and cross-compatibility speculated that Asian pears and European pears might share a common ancestor widely distributed across Eurasia. However, with the development of molecular markers and genome sequencing technologies, increasing evidence supports the hypothesis of independent domestication of the two groups. This study integrates recently published pear genome resequencing data, chloroplast genomes, and archaeological literature, aiming to elucidate the diversification process of Asian pears and European pears and the genetic basis of their independent domestication, providing a reference for pear germplasm innovation.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Comparative Genomics Reveals Divergence Time and Chromosomal Structural Variation

Based on whole-genome resequencing data, the research team constructed a high-quality variation map covering four cultivated species of Asian pears and two main cultivars of European pears. Phylogenetic analysis indicated that the divergence time between Asian pears and European pears was approximately 0.6–1.2 million years ago, during the Middle Pleistocene. This period was characterized by drastic climate fluctuations, which led to geographical isolation of populations at the eastern and western ends of Eurasia, resulting in independent evolutionary lineages.

Chromosome-level comparison revealed that Asian pears and European pears harbor multiple large inversions and translocations on chromosomes 3 and 7. These structural variations suppressed gene flow and accelerated population divergence. For example, an approximately 4.2 Mb inversion region on chromosome 3 contains multiple MADS-box genes related to fruit development, which was strongly selected in Asian pears but retained the ancestral haplotype in European pears. Chloroplast genome analysis further supported that the two groups derived from different maternal ancestors: Asian pears mainly belong to the Eastern haplotype group, while European pears belong to the Western haplotype group.

2.2 Population Genetic Structure and Domestication Centers

ADMIXTURE analysis using nuclear genome SNP data showed that when K=2, Asian pears and European pears were completely separated; when K=4, Asian pears further differentiated into four subpopulations: Pyrus pyrifolia/Pyrus bretschneideri, Pyrus ussuriensis, Pyrus sinkiangensis, and Japanese pear. Nucleotide diversity analysis indicated that the diversity of Asian pears was slightly higher than that of European pears, suggesting that Asian pears may have experienced a more complex domestication history.

Based on approximate Bayesian computation, the domestication center of Asian pears was inferred to be located in the Yangtze River Basin and Yellow River Basin of China, approximately 3000–4000 years ago; the domestication center of European pears was located in the Caucasus region and Central Asia, approximately 2500–3500 years ago. Archaeological evidence shows that pear seeds unearthed from Neolithic sites in Hunan and Zhejiang, China, are similar to wild Pyrus ussuriensis, while pear remains unearthed from Bronze Age sites in Switzerland and Italy are closer to wild Pyrus communis. The lack of direct evidence of early gene exchange between the two domestication centers supports the independent domestication model.

2.3 Differentiated Selection of Fruit Quality-Related Traits

Asian pears and European pears differ significantly in fruit size, sugar-acid ratio, stone cell content, and aroma components. Asian pear fruits are generally larger, with more stone cells, and are crisp, sweet, and juicy; European pear fruits are smaller, with fewer stone cells, and are soft, glutinous, and sweet-tart. Genome-wide selection signal analysis identified multiple selected regions.

In terms of sugar accumulation, the SOT (sorbitol transporter) gene family members underwent significant expansion in Asian pears, among which PbSOT2 is highly expressed in the late stage of fruit development, promoting the conversion of sorbitol to fructose; European pears mainly rely on the SWEET gene family to regulate sucrose accumulation, with PySWEET9 expression in mature fruits being 3–5 times that of Asian pears. In terms of stone cell formation, PbWRKY44 and PyMYB10 in Asian pears regulate the lignin biosynthesis pathway, resulting in a large number and large size of stone cells; in European pears, the expression of these two genes is regulated by MYB repressors, significantly reducing stone cell content.

In addition, genes related to malate and citrate metabolism also showed differentiated selection. In Asian pears, the copy number of ALMT (aluminum-activated malate transporter) genes increased, promoting malate accumulation; in European pears, malate degradation was accelerated by upregulating NADP-ME (malic enzyme), forming a low-acid flavor. These independent selection events indicate that the two groups took different paths in fruit quality improvement.

2.4 Independent Evolution of Disease Resistance and Environmental Adaptability

Asian pears and European pears exhibit significant differences in resistance to fire blight, scab, and pear rust. European pears are generally susceptible to fire blight, while Pyrus pyrifolia and Pyrus bretschneideri in Asian pears show strong resistance. Genetic mapping revealed that there is a cluster rich in NBS-LRR disease resistance genes on chromosome 2 of Asian pears, among which PbRGA1 is significantly upregulated after inoculation with fire blight pathogen; this region has a large deletion in European pears, leading to loss of resistance.

In terms of environmental adaptability, Asian pears are tolerant to heat and humidity, suitable for areas with an annual average temperature of 15–18°C and annual precipitation of 800–1200 mm; European pears are tolerant to cold and dry conditions, suitable for areas with an annual average temperature of 9–14°C and annual precipitation of 500–800 mm. Transcriptome analysis showed that HSP70 and CBF gene families in Asian pears were enhanced under high temperature and high humidity conditions, while DREB1 and COR genes in European pears were rapidly induced at low temperatures. These adaptive differences further strengthened the geographical isolation and independent domestication of the two groups.

2.5 Genome-Wide Association Analysis and Identification of Domestication Loci

Genome-wide association analysis was conducted separately for Asian pears and European pears, identifying a total of 42 loci significantly associated with fruit weight, soluble solids, titratable acidity, and stone cell content. Among them, qFW5.1 located on chromosome 5 in Asian pears explained 18.7% of fruit weight variation, and this region contains an auxin response factor PbARF8; qTA10.2 located on chromosome 10 in European pears explained 22.3% of titratable acidity variation, with the candidate gene being the aluminum-activated malate transporter PyALMT9.

Notably, the QTL loci related to fruit size in the two groups hardly overlapped, indicating that fruit enlargement was achieved through different genetic pathways in Asian pears and European pears. Asian pears mainly rely on the upregulation of cell division-related genes (such as PbCYCD3), while European pears rely more on the enhanced expression of cell expansion-related genes (such as PyEXP1). These independent domestication loci provide targets for molecular marker-assisted breeding.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

This study systematically elucidated the independent domestication history and genetic basis of Asian pears and European pears. The main results include: First, the two groups diverged approximately 0.6–1.2 million years ago, with minimal gene exchange after divergence; Second, the domestication center of Asian pears is located in China, and the domestication center of European pears is located in the Caucasus-Central Asia region, with a domestication time difference of approximately 500–1000 years; Third, genes related to fruit quality and disease resistance underwent differentiated selection in the two groups, forming different allele combinations; Fourth, 42 independent domestication loci were identified, among which multiple loci can be used for cross-population hybrid breeding.

From the perspective of breeding benefits, this study provides guidance in three aspects for the utilization of pear germplasm resources. First, the independent domestication of Asian pears and European pears means that their hybrid offspring may exhibit heterosis, especially in the combination of fruit size and flavor. For example, by crossing the crisp, sweet, and large fruits of Asian pears with the low stone cell and soft-glutinous traits of European pears, new varieties such as "Zaosu Mi" and "Jinqiu Li" have been bred, with soluble solids content increased by 2–3 percentage points and stone cells reduced by more than 30%. Second, the identification of disease resistance genes provides Asian pear donors for fire blight resistance breeding in European pears. Introducing the disease resistance gene cluster on chromosome 2 of Asian pears into Pyrus communis showed a 60–75% reduction in disease incidence in field trials. Third, molecular markers of domestication loci can be used for early selection, shortening the breeding cycle by 3–5 years. Based on an increase of 200 kg per mu of pear orchard and a unit price of 4 yuan, promoting 100,000 mu can generate an additional output value of 80 million yuan.

In addition, this study has guiding significance for the conservation of pear germplasm resources. Wild relatives of Asian pears and European pears face risks of habitat loss and genetic erosion, respectively. It is recommended to establish in situ conservation areas in the Yangtze River Basin and the Caucasus region, and to construct core germplasm banks. The establishment of genomic selection models can improve breeding efficiency by more than 30%, especially suitable for early prediction of perennial fruit trees.

4 Conclusion
