First, a rechargeable lithium battery was adopted for power supply, allowing continuous operation for 6–8 hours on a single charge to meet all-day field detection needs. Second, an adjustable-focus lens was added to accommodate detection of tea canopies at different heights. Third, a simple image recording function was developed, using a mobile phone to photograph and save the positions of fluorescent spots, facilitating indoor verification and data management. Fourth, a standardized detection procedure was established: five points are randomly selected in each tea garden plot, 20 tender shoots are detected at each point, the number of fluorescent spots is recorded, and the number of eggs per hundred shoots is calculated. Practice has shown that the method yields the best detection results in spring and autumn; under high temperature and strong light in summer, detection should be conducted in the early morning or evening to avoid background light interference. Compared with conventional dissection methods, the blue-light detection method improves efficiency by approximately threefold, allowing a single person to detect 300–500 tender shoots per day, and enables repeated detection of the same tea shoots to dynamically track the oviposition process.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

Using the blue-light detection method, this study systematically identified the main biological characteristics of the oviposition behavior of the tea green leafhopper: oviposition sites are concentrated beneath the cortex of tender stems, the oviposition peak occurs at night between 20:00 and 24:00, the optimal temperature is 22–28°C, and the pest prefers one-bud-two-leaves to one-bud-three-leaves tender shoots. These characteristics provide clear indicators for tea garden forecasting. In terms of benefits, this method significantly improves detection efficiency, reduces labor intensity, avoids the destruction of tea shoots caused by traditional dissection methods, enables continuous observation of the same batch of samples, and reduces sampling errors. At the same time, detection results can be directly used to determine optimal control timing: when the number of eggs per hundred shoots reaches 5–8, it indicates that nymphs are about to hatch, and this is the optimal window for pesticide application or release of natural enemies. Trials in tea regions such as Anhui and Fujian have shown that precise forecasting based on blue-light detection can reduce the number of pesticide applications by 1–2 times, improve control effectiveness by more than 15%, and save approximately 80–120 yuan per mu, demonstrating favorable economic and ecological benefits. In addition, this method can also be used for screening insect-resistant varieties and investigating parasitism rates of natural enemies, expanding its scope of application.

4 Conclusion

The blue-light detection method is a rapid, non-destructive, and accurate technique for identifying the oviposition behavior of the tea green leafhopper. This method utilizes the pest's taxis toward blue light and the fluorescence reaction of oviposition wounds to directly locate oviposition sites, count egg numbers, and continuously observe oviposition rhythms in the field. Through this method, key biological characteristics of the tea green leafhopper were clarified, including its preference for ovipositing on tender stems, the nighttime oviposition peak, and the optimal temperature of 22–28°C. This technique is simple to operate and relatively low in cost, making it suitable for promotion in grassroots tea garden forecasting. It is recommended to further develop portable integrated equipment combined with automatic image recognition technology to achieve rapid counting and remote monitoring of egg numbers, providing more efficient technical means for green control of the tea green leafhopper.

title: Inclusive growth and environmental sustainability: the role of institutional quality in sub-Saharan Africa
text:
Inclusive Growth and Environmental Sustainability: The Role of Institutional Quality in Sub-Saharan Africa

 Abstract

The coordinated advancement of inclusive growth and environmental sustainability is a core challenge for Sub-Saharan Africa in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Based on panel data from 38 Sub-Saharan African countries from 2000 to 2022, this paper constructs an inclusive growth index and an environmental sustainability index, and employs the system GMM estimation method to empirically examine the moderating effect of institutional quality on the relationship between the two. The findings are as follows: inclusive growth has a significant positive impact on environmental sustainability, and this effect is more pronounced in countries with higher institutional quality; institutional quality exerts a positive moderating effect through three pathways: enhancing the enforcement efficiency of environmental regulations, suppressing rent-seeking behavior, and promoting the diffusion of green technologies. Grouped regressions show that once institutional quality crosses the threshold value, the environmental protection effect of inclusive growth increases by approximately 2.3 times. This paper argues that Sub-Saharan African countries should place institutional capacity building in a policy priority position, and achieve a win-win outcome of growth inclusiveness and environmental sustainability by strengthening governance effectiveness.

Keywords: inclusive growth; environmental sustainability; institutional quality; Sub-Saharan Africa; system GMM

 1 Introduction

Sub-Saharan Africa is undergoing a profound development transformation. Over the past two decades, the region's average annual economic growth rate has remained between 4% and 5%, but the distribution of growth outcomes has been severely uneven, with approximately 40% of the population still living below the extreme poverty line. At the same time, the environmental costs brought about by the resource-intensive growth model are becoming increasingly apparent: forest coverage continues to decline, soil degradation intensifies, and urban air pollution worsens. How to safeguard the environmental bottom line while promoting inclusive growth has become an urgent issue facing policymakers in the region.

Existing research on the relationship between inclusive growth and environmental sustainability presents two opposing views. One view holds that there is a trade-off relationship between the two, and that the inclusive expansion of economic growth inevitably intensifies resource consumption; the other view emphasizes that the two can be synergistic, with the key lying in whether institutional arrangements can effectively correct market failures. However, systematic empirical evidence for Sub-Saharan Africa remains insufficient, especially regarding how institutional quality moderates this relationship, for which cross-country quantitative testing is still lacking.

The marginal contributions of this paper are as follows: First, it constructs an inclusive growth index covering multiple dimensions of income, education, health, and infrastructure, avoiding the limitations of a single income indicator; second, it incorporates institutional quality into the analytical framework to identify its moderating effect on the relationship between inclusive growth and environmental sustainability; third, it adopts the system GMM method to address endogeneity issues and improve estimation reliability. The research conclusions can provide references for policy design in the region and other developing economies.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Sources and Sample

This paper selects panel data from 38 Sub-Saharan African countries from 2000 to 2022. Indicators related to inclusive growth come from the World Bank World Development Indicators database, environmental sustainability data come from Global Forest Watch and the Yale University Environmental Performance Index, and institutional quality data are taken from the World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators. After excluding observations with severe missing values, 836 valid observations were ultimately obtained.

 2.2 Variable Settings

Dependent variable: Environmental Sustainability Index. This index integrates four dimensions: changes in forest coverage, the proportion of renewable energy, carbon emission intensity, and air quality. It is synthesized using the entropy weight method, with values ranging from 0 to 100, where higher values indicate better environmental sustainability.

Core explanatory variable: Inclusive Growth Index. Drawing on the Asian Development Bank's inclusive growth framework, the indicator system is constructed from five dimensions: economic growth, income equity, educational accessibility, health security, and infrastructure, also synthesized using the entropy weight method.

Moderating variable: Institutional Quality. It is measured by the average of four dimensions from the Worldwide Governance Indicators: government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law, and control of corruption, with values ranging from -2.5 to 2.5, standardized and converted to a 0–10 scale.

Control variables: logarithm of GDP per capita, urbanization rate, trade openness, foreign direct investment as a share of GDP, and population growth rate.

 2.3 Model Specification

To test the moderating effect of institutional quality, the following dynamic panel model is specified:

\[
ESI_{it} = \alpha + \beta_1 ESI_{i,t-1} + \beta_2 IG_{it} + \beta_3 IQ_{it} + \beta_4 (IG_{it} \times IQ_{it}) + \gamma X_{it} + \mu_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}
\]

Among them, \(ESI\) is the environmental sustainability index, \(IG\) is the inclusive growth index, \(IQ\) is institutional quality, \(X\) is the vector of control variables, \(\mu_i\) is the country fixed effect, and \(\lambda_t\) is the time fixed effect. The interaction term coefficient \(\beta_4\) is the core focus of this paper. If it is significantly positive, it indicates that institutional quality strengthens the environmental protection effect of inclusive growth.

Considering endogeneity issues, the system GMM method is used for estimation, with lagged terms of the explanatory variables as instrumental variables. The Arellano-Bond test is used for serial correlation testing, and the Hansen test is used for overidentification restriction testing.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Baseline Regression Results

Table 1 reports the system GMM estimation results. Model (1) includes only the inclusive growth index, whose coefficient is 0.284 and significant at the 1% level, indicating that inclusive growth has a positive promoting effect on environmental sustainability. Model (2) adds institutional quality, with a coefficient of 0.317 that is significant, indicating that institutional quality itself is also conducive to environmental improvement. After Model (3) introduces the interaction term, the coefficient of inclusive growth drops to 0.156, and the interaction term coefficient is 0.213 and significant at the 1% level, confirming that institutional quality plays a positive moderating role. This means that in countries with higher institutional quality, for every 1-unit increase in inclusive growth, the environmental sustainability index increases by approximately 0.369 units; while in countries with lower institutional quality, this effect is only 0.156.

The p-values of the AR(2) test are all greater than 0.1, indicating the absence of second-order serial correlation; the p-values of the Hansen test are all greater than 0.1, supporting the validity of the instrumental variables.

 3.2 Threshold Effect Analysis

To further characterize the nonlinear moderating features of institutional quality, a panel threshold model is used for testing. With institutional quality as the threshold variable, Bootstrap sampling was conducted 1,000 times to determine the threshold value. The results show that there is a single threshold for institutional quality, with a threshold value of 5.82 (on a 0–10 scale). When institutional quality is below the threshold value, the impact coefficient of inclusive growth on environmental sustainability is 0.142, significant only at the 10% level; when institutional quality crosses the threshold value, the coefficient jumps to 0.327 and is significant at the 1% level. This finding indicates that there is a "critical mass" effect in institutional quality, and only after reaching a certain level can its moderating function be fully released.

 3.3 Heterogeneity Analysis

The sample is divided into resource-intensive countries and non-resource-intensive countries according to resource endowments. The results show that in non-resource-intensive countries, the interaction term coefficient is 0.268 and significant; in resource-intensive countries, the interaction term coefficient is 0.097 but not significant. This may be because resource rents easily breed rent-seeking behavior, weakening the enforcement effect of institutional quality on environmental regulation. Grouped by income level, the moderating effect in middle-income countries (0.241) is significantly higher than that in low-income countries (0.108), indicating a complementary relationship between the level of economic development and institutional quality.

 3.4 Robustness Tests

Robustness tests were conducted in various ways, including replacing the measurement of core variables (using carbon emission intensity to replace the environmental sustainability index), changing estimation methods (difference GMM and fixed effects instrumental variable method), and excluding extreme values. The core conclusions remain stable. In addition, lagging institutional quality by one period to alleviate reverse causality concerns, the interaction term remains significantly positive.

 4 Discussion

This paper finds that inclusive growth and environmental sustainability are not necessarily in conflict, and institutional quality is the key variable determining whether the two can be synergistic. This conclusion is consistent with the basic logic of institutional economics: sound institutional arrangements can correct externalities, reduce transaction costs, and enhance policy credibility, thereby guiding inclusive growth to evolve in an environmentally friendly direction.

Specifically, the mechanisms through which institutional quality operates can be summarized into three pathways. First, the regulatory enforcement pathway. Improvements in government effectiveness and regulatory quality enhance the enforcement of environmental laws and regulations, enabling the income gains brought by inclusive growth to translate into stricter environmental demands rather than mere expansion of material consumption. Second, the rent-seeking suppression pathway. Improvements in corruption control and the rule of law reduce the space for rent-seeking in resource extraction sectors, curbing short-term growth behavior at the expense of the environment. Third, the technology diffusion pathway. A sound institutional environment facilitates the introduction and promotion of green technologies, enabling educational improvements and infrastructure enhancements within inclusive growth to translate into stronger capacity for adopting environmentally friendly technologies.

The finding of the threshold effect has important policy implications. In countries where institutional quality is below 5.82, the environmental protection effect of inclusive growth is weak, indicating that under a weak institutional environment, merely pursuing growth inclusiveness cannot automatically achieve environmental improvement. This explains why some African countries, despite making progress in poverty reduction, continue to experience worsening environmental degradation. The insignificant moderating effect in resource-intensive countries further warns of the erosive effect of resource rents on institutional quality.

The policy implication of this paper is that Sub-Saharan African countries should place institutional capacity building at the core of their development strategies. Specifically, they should strengthen the independence of environmental regulatory agencies, advance fiscal transparency reform, reinforce anti-corruption mechanisms, and establish cross-sectoral environmental-growth coordination mechanisms. When providing development assistance, the international community should also make institutional capacity building a priority area of support.

The limitations of this study are as follows: the measurement of institutional quality relies on subjective perception data, which may contain measurement error; although the sample time span covers more than two decades, some countries have considerable missing data. Future research can combine micro-survey data to further reveal the micro-level mechanisms through which institutional quality affects the relationship between inclusive growth and environmental sustainability.

 5 Conclusion

Based on panel data from 38 Sub-Saharan African countries from 2000 to 2022, this paper empirically examines the moderating role of institutional quality in the relationship between inclusive growth and environmental sustainability. The main conclusions are as follows: First, inclusive growth has a significant positive impact on environmental sustainability, and the two are not necessarily a trade-off; second, institutional quality positively moderates the environmental protection effect of inclusive growth, and for every 1-unit increase in institutional quality, this effect strengthens by approximately 0.213 units; third, there is a threshold effect in institutional quality, and the moderating effect significantly strengthens after crossing the threshold value; fourth, the moderating effect is more prominent in non-resource-intensive countries and middle-income countries.

The above conclusions indicate that institutional quality is the key hinge for achieving synergy between inclusive growth and environmental sustainability. For Sub-Saharan Africa, growth inclusiveness policies divorced from institutional capacity building can hardly achieve environmental goals, while environmental regulations that ignore the inclusiveness dimension may also be difficult to sustain due to a lack of social support. Future policies should focus on the systematic enhancement of institutional capacity and build a virtuous interaction mechanism among growth, equity, and the environment.

title: Synthesis, self-assembly and drug release behaviors of a bottlebrush polymer-HCPT prodrug for tumor chemotherapy
text:
Abstract: This paper designs and synthesizes a camptothecin (HCPT) prodrug using a bottlebrush polymer as a carrier, aiming to improve the water solubility of HCPT, enhance its tumor targeting capability, and reduce toxic side effects. Through a combination of ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) and click chemistry, a bottlebrush polymer prodrug with HCPT-containing side chains (BBP-HCPT) was constructed. This prodrug can self-assemble into nanomicelles in aqueous solution, with a particle size of approximately 120 nm and a drug loading capacity of up to 28.6%. In vitro release experiments showed that HCPT can be rapidly released under the tumor microenvironment (weakly acidic, high glutathione concentration), while release is slow under normal physiological conditions, demonstrating good environmental responsiveness. Cell experiments and animal experiments showed that BBP-HCPT has a significant inhibitory effect on tumor cells and low toxicity to normal tissues. This bottlebrush polymer prodrug system provides a promising delivery strategy for tumor chemotherapy.

1. Introduction

Camptothecin (HCPT) is a natural alkaloid extracted from Camptotheca acuminata, with strong antitumor activity, and is widely used in the clinical treatment of malignant tumors such as liver cancer, gastric cancer, and colon cancer. However, HCPT suffers from problems such as poor water solubility, unstable lactone ring, susceptibility to metabolic inactivation, and severe toxic side effects, which limit its clinical application. To overcome these deficiencies, researchers have developed various drug delivery systems, such as liposomes, polymeric micelles, and nanoparticles. Among them, the polymeric prodrug strategy, by covalently linking drugs to polymer carriers, can significantly improve drug solubility, stability, and targeting.

Bottlebrush polymers are a class of graft polymers with high-density side chains, whose structure resembles a bottlebrush and which possess unique physicochemical properties, such as high chain rigidity, tunable side-chain density, and good self-assembly ability. In recent years, bottlebrush polymers have received widespread attention in the field of drug delivery. Their dense side chains can effectively encapsulate drugs, increase drug loading, and achieve environmentally responsive release by regulating side-chain structure. Based on this, this study designed and synthesized a bottlebrush polymer-HCPT prodrug (BBP-HCPT), which self-assembles into nanomicelles to achieve controlled release of HCPT in the tumor microenvironment, aiming to improve efficacy and reduce toxic side effects.

2. Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Design and Synthesis of Bottlebrush Polymer Carriers

This study adopts a "grafting-through" strategy to construct bottlebrush polymers. First, a polymer backbone with a polynorbornene main chain was synthesized by ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP), and click-reactive side groups were introduced onto the main chain. Subsequently, copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) was used to graft alkyne-containing polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains and drug linker arms onto the main chain, forming a bottlebrush structure. The introduction of PEG chains can improve the water solubility and biocompatibility of the polymer while prolonging circulation time in vivo. By regulating PEG chain length and grafting density, the self-assembly behavior and drug-loading performance of the polymer can be adjusted.

2.2 Synthesis and Characterization of HCPT Prodrug

HCPT reacts with active ester groups on the linker arm through its 20-position hydroxyl group to form an ester-bond-linked prodrug. The linker arm was designed as a short chain containing a disulfide bond, which can be cleaved in tumor cells with high glutathione (GSH) concentration to achieve drug release. During synthesis, the drug loading was adjusted by controlling the feed ratio of HCPT to the polymer backbone. The prodrug structure was characterized by proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and gel permeation chromatography (GPC), confirming that HCPT was successfully grafted and that the polymer had a relatively narrow molecular weight distribution.

2.3 Self-Assembly Behavior and Preparation of Nanomicelles

BBP-HCPT was dissolved in a small amount of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and slowly added dropwise into deionized water. The organic solvent was removed by dialysis to prepare a nanomicelle solution. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to characterize the particle size, distribution, and morphology of the micelles. The results showed that the micelles were spherical, with an average particle size of about 120 nm and a relatively narrow distribution (PDI < 0.2). The zeta potential was about -15 mV, indicating that the micelle surface was negatively charged, which is favorable for stable existence in blood. The critical micelle concentration (CMC) was measured by fluorescence spectroscopy and found to be 8.6 μg/mL, indicating that the prodrug has good self-assembly ability.

2.4 Study of Drug Release Behavior

The dialysis method was used to study the release behavior of BBP-HCPT micelles under different conditions. Normal physiological conditions (pH 7.4, GSH 10 μM) and the tumor microenvironment (pH 5.0, GSH 10 mM) were simulated. The results showed that under normal conditions, the cumulative release of HCPT within 48 hours was less than 20%; while under the tumor microenvironment, the cumulative release could reach more than 85%. The release mechanism was mainly the synergistic effect of disulfide bond cleavage and ester bond hydrolysis. In addition, the release curve exhibited obvious "burst release-sustained release" characteristics, which is beneficial for rapidly reaching an effective drug concentration and maintaining a therapeutic level.

2.5 Evaluation of Cellular Uptake and Antitumor Activity

Using human hepatoma cells HepG2 as a model, fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry were used to observe the cellular uptake behavior of the micelles. The results showed that BBP-HCPT micelles could be efficiently taken up by tumor cells and distributed in the cytoplasm. MTT assay showed that the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of BBP-HCPT against HepG2 cells was 2.3 μg/mL, significantly lower than that of free HCPT (IC50 8.7 μg/mL), indicating that the prodrug micelles enhanced antitumor activity. At the same time, toxicity experiments on normal liver cells L02 showed that the toxicity of BBP-HCPT was significantly lower than that of free HCPT, indicating that it has good tumor selectivity.

3. Results and Benefit Analysis

3.1 Improvement of Drug Loading and Stability

Through the design of the bottlebrush polymer structure, the drug loading of BBP-HCPT reached 28.6%, significantly higher than that of traditional linear polymer prodrugs (usually <15%). High drug loading reduces the amount of carrier material used, helping to lower systemic toxicity. In addition, the micelles showed good stability in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and serum, with a particle size change of less than 10% within 7 days, indicating good potential for in vivo application.

3.2 Environmentally Responsive Release and Enhanced Targeting

BBP-HCPT micelles can rapidly release HCPT under the tumor microenvironment, while release is slow under normal physiological conditions, achieving "on-demand release." This environmentally responsive release mechanism helps increase drug concentration in tumor tissue and reduce damage to normal tissues. Animal experiment results showed that the drug concentration of BBP-HCPT in tumor tissue was 3.2 times that of free HCPT, indicating good passive targeting ability (EPR effect).

3.3 Evaluation of Antitumor Efficacy and Safety

In a HepG2 nude mouse xenograft tumor model, the tumor inhibition rate of the BBP-HCPT treatment group was 78.5%, significantly higher than that of the free HCPT group (52.3%). At the same time, mice in the BBP-HCPT group showed little change in body weight, and no obvious abnormalities were observed in liver and kidney function indicators, indicating low systemic toxicity. Tissue sections showed obvious necrosis in tumor tissue in the BBP-HCPT group, while normal tissues showed no obvious damage.

3.4 Prospects for Promotion and Application

This bottlebrush polymer-HCPT prodrug system has advantages such as high drug loading, good stability, controllable release, and low toxicity, and is suitable for the delivery of various hydrophobic antitumor drugs. Its synthesis method is mature, raw materials are readily available, and it has a certain foundation for industrialization. In the future, active targeting can be further improved by introducing targeting ligands (such as folic acid and RGD peptides), expanding its application in personalized tumor therapy.

4. Conclusion

This study successfully constructed a bottlebrush polymer-HCPT prodrug (BBP-HCPT), which self-assembles into nanomicelles and achieves controlled release of HCPT in the tumor microenvironment. This prodrug system has high drug loading, good stability, and environmentally responsive release characteristics, and exhibits excellent antitumor activity and low systemic toxicity in both in vitro and in vivo experiments. The bottlebrush polymer structure provides an efficient and safe platform for antitumor drug delivery and has good prospects for clinical translation. In the future, the polymer structure can be further optimized, targeting functions can be introduced, and its development toward clinical application can be promoted.

title: Integrating density and fertilizer management to optimize the accumulation, remobilization, and distribution of biomass and nutrients in summer maize
text:
Optimization Effects of Integrated Density and Fertilization Management on Biomass, Nutrient Accumulation, Redistribution, and Distribution of Summer Maize

 Abstract

【Objective】 To investigate the integrated effects of planting density and fertilization management on biomass, nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) nutrient accumulation, post-silking redistribution, and organ distribution of summer maize, so as to provide a theoretical basis for high-yield and high-efficiency cultivation of summer maize in the Huang-Huai-Hai region. 【Methods】 A field experiment was conducted from 2022 to 2023 at an experimental station in Henan Province, using Zhengdan 958 as the test cultivar. Three planting densities (D1: 60,000 plants/hm², D2: 75,000 plants/hm², D3: 90,000 plants/hm²) and three fertilization levels (F1: conventional fertilization, F2: optimized fertilization, F3: optimized fertilization + 20% organic fertilizer substitution) were arranged in a split-plot design. Dry matter accumulation before and after silking, nutrient accumulation, redistribution, and organ distribution proportions were measured for each treatment. 【Results】 Significant interaction effects of density and fertilization on biomass and nutrient accumulation of summer maize were observed. The D2F3 treatment performed best, with total biomass at maturity reaching 22.6 t/hm², which was 28.4% higher than D1F1; total N, P, and K accumulation amounted to 286.4, 112.7, and 241.5 kg/hm², respectively. Post-silking dry matter accumulation and its contribution rate to grain showed a trend of first increasing and then decreasing with increasing density, with the D2F3 treatment reaching a post-silking contribution rate of 62.3%. In terms of nutrient redistribution, the pre-silking vegetative organ redistribution amounts of N, P, and K under D2F3 were 98.6, 42.3, and 156.8 kg/hm², respectively, with redistribution rates of 48.2%, 46.7%, and 58.4%, respectively. The distribution proportions of N, P, and K in grains reached 61.5%, 68.2%, and 42.3%, respectively, all being highest under D2F3. 【Conclusion】 A density of 75,000 plants/hm² combined with optimized fertilization + 20% organic fertilizer substitution can achieve synergistic optimization of biomass, nutrient accumulation, redistribution, and distribution in summer maize, and is a suitable management strategy for high-yield and high-efficiency summer maize production in this region.

Keywords: summer maize; planting density; fertilization management; biomass accumulation; nutrient redistribution; organ distribution

 1 Introduction

Summer maize is an important food crop in the Huang-Huai-Hai region of China, and its yield formation is closely related to biomass accumulation and nutrient translocation. Biomass is the material basis for yield formation, while nutrient accumulation in pre-silking vegetative organs and post-silking redistribution to grains are key processes determining grain yield and quality. Studies have shown that crop yield depends not only on total nutrient uptake but also on the efficiency of nutrient distribution between source and sink. Therefore, coordinating the relationship between biomass accumulation and nutrient redistribution is an important pathway to achieve high yield and high efficiency in summer maize.

Planting density affects dry matter accumulation by regulating population canopy structure and light interception capacity, while fertilization management directly determines nutrient supply intensity and proportion. Excessive density can lead to canopy closure and restricted nutrient uptake per plant; excessively low density wastes light and heat resources. Insufficient fertilization limits biomass accumulation, while excessive fertilization reduces nutrient use efficiency and increases environmental risks. In recent years, partial substitution of chemical fertilizers with organic fertilizers has been proven to improve soil nutrient supply characteristics, extend the nutrient supply period, and thereby promote post-silking nutrient redistribution. However, systematic studies on the integrated effects of density and fertilization (especially combined organic-inorganic application) on biomass, nutrient accumulation, redistribution, and distribution in summer maize remain relatively lacking.

In this study, different density and fertilization treatments were established to systematically analyze the dynamics of biomass and N, P, K nutrient accumulation, post-silking redistribution characteristics, and organ distribution patterns of summer maize, aiming to identify the optimal integrated model of density and fertilization and provide technical support for green and high-yield cultivation of summer maize in the region.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Experimental Site

The experiment was conducted from 2022 to 2023 at an agricultural experimental station in Henan Province. The soil at the experimental site was fluvo-aquic soil. The basic physicochemical properties of the 0–20 cm plough layer were as follows: organic matter 14.2 g/kg, total nitrogen 0.89 g/kg, available phosphorus 21.5 mg/kg, available potassium 112.6 mg/kg, and pH 7.8. The previous crop was winter wheat with straw return.

 2.2 Experimental Design

The test cultivar was Zhengdan 958. A split-plot design was adopted, with planting density as the main plot and fertilization management as the sub-plot, with three replications. Three planting density levels were set: D1 (60,000 plants/hm²), D2 (75,000 plants/hm²), and D3 (90,000 plants/hm²). Three fertilization management levels were set: F1 (conventional fertilization: pure N 240 kg/hm², P₂O₅ 120 kg/hm², K₂O 150 kg/hm², all chemical fertilizers); F2 (optimized fertilization: pure N 210 kg/hm², P₂O₅ 105 kg/hm², K₂O 135 kg/hm², all chemical fertilizers); F3 (optimized fertilization + 20% organic fertilizer substitution: on the basis of F2, commercial organic fertilizer was used to replace 20% of chemical fertilizer nitrogen). Phosphorus and potassium fertilizers were applied entirely as basal fertilizer, and nitrogen fertilizer was applied in split applications at a ratio of basal fertilizer : large trumpet stage : silking stage = 4:4:2. Row spacing was 60 cm, and plant spacing was adjusted according to density. Sowing was conducted on June 12, 2022, and harvest on October 3, 2022; sowing was conducted on June 14, 2023, and harvest on October 5, 2023. Other management practices were the same as those for conventional high-yield fields.

 2.3 Measurement Items and Methods

Samples were taken at the silking stage and maturity stage. Three representative plants were selected from each treatment and separated into stems, leaves, cobs, grains, and other organs. Samples were killed at 105°C for 30 min, then oven-dried at 80°C to constant weight, and dry matter was weighed. After grinding, samples were digested with H₂SO₄-H₂O₂. Total nitrogen was determined by the Kjeldahl method, total phosphorus by the vanadium-molybdenum yellow colorimetric method, and total potassium by flame photometry.

Pre-silking vegetative organ redistribution amount (kg/hm²) = nutrient accumulation in vegetative organs at silking stage − nutrient accumulation in vegetative organs at maturity stage; redistribution rate (%) = redistribution amount / nutrient accumulation in vegetative organs at silking stage × 100; post-silking accumulation = total accumulation at maturity stage − total accumulation at silking stage; post-silking contribution rate (%) = post-silking accumulation / grain accumulation at maturity stage × 100.

 2.4 Data Processing

Excel 2019 and SPSS 26.0 were used for data organization and analysis of variance, and Duncan's new multiple range test was used for multiple comparisons (α = 0.05).

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Dynamics of Biomass Accumulation

Density and fertilization significantly affected biomass accumulation of summer maize (Table 1). Total biomass at the silking stage and maturity stage showed a trend of first increasing and then decreasing with increasing density, with D2 being the highest; under the same density, the F3 treatment had significantly higher biomass than F1 and F2. The total biomass at maturity under D2F3 reached 22.6 t/hm², which was 28.4% higher than D1F1 (17.6 t/hm²) and 11.9% higher than D3F1. Post-silking dry matter accumulation was highest under D2F3 (9.8 t/hm²), with a post-silking contribution rate of 62.3%, indicating that moderate dense planting combined with combined organic-inorganic application can prolong the photosynthetic functional period of the population and promote post-silking matter production.

Table 1 Biomass accumulation and post-silking contribution rate of summer maize under different treatments (mean of 2022–2023)

| Treatment | Biomass at silking stage (t/hm²) | Biomass at maturity stage (t/hm²) | Post-silking accumulation (t/hm²) | Post-silking contribution rate (%) |
|------|---------------------|---------------------|-------------------|---------------|
| D1F1 | 8.9c | 17.6d | 6.2d | 52.1c |
| D2F2 | 11.2ab | 20.8b | 8.4b | 58.7b |
| D2F3 | 12.8a | 22.6a | 9.8a | 62.3a |
| D3F1 | 10.5b | 19.4c | 7.1c | 54.6c |

Note: Different lowercase letters in the same column indicate significant differences (P < 0.05), the same below.

 3.2 Nutrient Accumulation and Redistribution

Total N, P, and K accumulation were highest under D2F3, reaching 286.4, 112.7, and 241.5 kg/hm², respectively (Table 2). Compared with D1F1, N, P, and K accumulation under D2F3 increased by 41.2%, 35.8%, and 38.6%, respectively. Pre-silking vegetative organ nutrient redistribution was also greatest under D2F3, with N, P, and K redistribution amounts of 98.6, 42.3, and 156.8 kg/hm², respectively, and redistribution rates of 48.2%, 46.7%, and 58.4%, respectively, significantly higher than those of other treatments. This indicates that this treatment not only ensured sufficient pre-silking nutrient reserves but also promoted efficient post-silking nutrient transport to grains. Although D3 had the highest density, its redistribution rate decreased, possibly related to restricted nutrient uptake per plant and early leaf senescence caused by an excessively large population.

Table 2 Nutrient accumulation and redistribution characteristics of summer maize under different treatments

| Treatment | N accumulation (kg/hm²) | N redistribution amount (kg/hm²) | N redistribution rate (%) | K redistribution rate (%) |
|------|------------------|-------------------|---------------|---------------|
| D1F1 | 202.8d | 68.4c | 42.1c | 51.2c |
| D2F2 | 251.6b | 85.2b | 45.6b | 55.8b |
| D2F3 | 286.4a | 98.6a | 48.2a | 58.4a |
| D3F1 | 228.5c | 76.8b | 43.5c | 52.6c |

 3.3 Distribution of Nutrients in Organs

The distribution of nutrients among organs at maturity was regulated by density and fertilization (Table 3). The distribution proportions of N, P, and K in grains under D2F3 were 61.5%, 68.2%, and 42.3%, respectively, all significantly higher than those under other treatments; the distribution proportions in stems and leaves decreased accordingly. This indicates that the integrated optimization of density and fertilization promoted the directional distribution of nutrients to grains and improved the nutrient enrichment capacity of the harvest organ. Under D3F1, the retention proportion of nutrients in stems and leaves was relatively high, while the grain distribution proportion decreased, indicating that excessively high density is not conducive to nutrient transport to grains.

Table 3 Distribution proportions of nutrients in organs at maturity (%)

| Treatment | Grain N | Grain P | Grain K | Stem and leaf N | Stem and leaf K |
|------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| D1F1 | 56.2c | 62.4c | 36.8c | 30.1a | 42.5a |
| D2F2 | 59.4b | 65.8b | 39.6b | 27.5b | 39.2b |
| D2F3 | 61.5a | 68.2a | 42.3a | 25.3c | 36.4c |
| D3F1 | 55.8c | 61.5c | 35.9c | 31.2a | 43.8a |

 4 Discussion

 4.1 Synergistic Regulation of Density and Fertilization on Biomass Accumulation

This study showed that density and fertilization had significant interaction effects on biomass accumulation of summer maize, with D2F3 performing best. Moderate dense planting (75,000 plants/hm²) can construct a reasonable canopy structure and improve light interception rate, while 20% organic fertilizer substitution for chemical fertilizer improved soil nutrient supply performance and extended the nutrient release period. The two together synergistically promoted post-silking dry matter accumulation. This is consistent with previous conclusions that dense planting and combined organic-inorganic application can synergistically improve crop productivity. Excessive density (D3) led to canopy closure and decreased photosynthetic capacity per plant, resulting in reduced biomass accumulation instead.

 4.2 Optimization Mechanism of Nutrient Redistribution and Organ Distribution

Post-silking nutrient redistribution is a key process determining grain yield and quality. In this study, the redistribution rates of N, P, and K under D2F3 reached 48.2%, 46.7%, and 58.4%, respectively, and the grain nutrient distribution proportions were also the highest. The mechanism may lie in the following: after partial substitution of chemical fertilizer with organic fertilizer, soil nitrogen supply was more stable, avoiding leaf early senescence caused by fertilizer deficiency at the late growth stage and maintaining a strong nutrient export capacity of source organs; at the same time, moderate dense planting ensured the nutritional area per plant, which was conducive to root uptake and nutrient transport to grains. The K redistribution rate was higher than those of N and P, possibly related to its existence in ionic form in the plant and its strong mobility.

 4.3 Practical Significance of High-Yield and High-Efficiency Management Strategy

Integrating indicators such as biomass accumulation, nutrient redistribution, and organ distribution, a density of 75,000 plants/hm² combined with optimized fertilization + 20% organic fertilizer substitution (D2F3) is a suitable management strategy for high-yield and high-efficiency summer maize in this region. Under the premise of reducing chemical fertilizer use by 20%, this model still achieved significant improvements in biomass and nutrient accumulation, balancing yield benefits and environmental benefits, and conforming to the direction of green agricultural development. However, it should be noted that the organic fertilizer substitution ratio and density threshold may vary with soil fertility, cultivar, and climatic conditions, and should be adjusted according to local conditions in practical application.

 5 Conclusion

(1) Density and fertilization management had significant interaction effects on biomass, nutrient accumulation, redistribution, and distribution of summer maize, and moderate dense planting combined with combined organic-inorganic application could achieve synergistic optimization.

(2) The treatment of 75,000 plants/hm² combined with optimized fertilization + 20% organic fertilizer substitution (D2F3) reached a total biomass of 22.6 t/hm² at maturity, total N, P, and K accumulation of 286.4, 112.7, and 241.5 kg/hm², respectively, and a post-silking dry matter contribution rate of 62.3%, all significantly superior to other treatments.

(3) Under this treatment, the pre-silking redistribution rates of N, P, and K were 48.2%, 46.7%, and 58.4%, respectively, and the grain distribution proportions of N, P, and K reached 61.5%, 68.2%, and 42.3%, respectively, achieving efficient transport and enrichment of nutrients to grains.

(4) It is recommended to promote the integrated management strategy of 75,000 plants/hm² density and optimized fertilization + 20% organic fertilizer substitution in the Huang-Huai-Hai summer maize region to achieve the unity of high yield and high efficiency.

title: Micro-nano particle formation and transformation mechanisms of broth in meat braised processing
text:
Mechanisms of Formation and Transformation of Micro-Nano Particles in Brine During Meat Braising

Abstract: To reveal the formation and transformation patterns of micro-nano particles in the brine system during meat braising, this study used pork belly as raw material and employed traditional braising techniques, combined with laser particle size analysis, Zeta potential measurement, and microscopic imaging techniques, to systematically investigate the effects of braising time, temperature, and broth composition on the particle size distribution, surface charge, and microscopic morphology of micro-nano particles in brine. The results showed that the formation of micro-nano particles in brine during braising underwent three stages: 0–30 min was the rapid nucleation period, during which the particle size increased from approximately 50 nm initially to 200 nm; 30–90 min was the aggregation and growth period, during which the particle size reached 400–600 nm; after 90 min, the system entered a stable transformation period, in which some large particles dissociated or recombined, and the particle size tended toward 300–500 nm. Elevated temperature (85–95°C) promoted particle formation and aggregation, while the addition of salt and spices inhibited excessive particle aggregation, making the system more stable. Micro-nano particles primarily bound lipids, proteins, and flavor compounds through hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds, and their surface negative charge (Zeta potential of approximately -25 to -40 mV) contributed to system stability. The research results can provide a theoretical basis for quality control and standardized production of brine.

1 Introduction

Braising is an important method in the processing of traditional Chinese meat products. As the core medium for flavor transfer, the physicochemical state of brine directly affects the taste, color, and flavor of the product. In recent years, studies have found that brine is not a true solution but a colloidal dispersion system containing large numbers of micro-nano scale particles. These particles are formed by proteins, lipids, polysaccharides, and active components of spices through self-assembly or aggregation, and play a key role in the adsorption and release of flavor compounds and the stability of brine. However, the formation pathways and transformation mechanisms of micro-nano particles in brine remain unclear, which restricts the development of standardization and recycling technologies for brine. This paper aims to reveal the formation and transformation patterns of particles in brine by systematically analyzing changes in particle size, potential, and morphology during the braising process, thereby providing technical support for quality control of brine.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Particle Size Distribution and Nucleation Mechanism of Micro-Nano Particles in Brine

Dynamic light scattering technology was used for real-time monitoring of particle size in brine during the braising process. The results showed that the initial particle size of fresh brine was approximately 50 nm, mainly consisting of polyphenol-protein complexes dissolved from spices. After heating to 85°C, the particle size rapidly increased to 200 nm within 0–30 min, indicating that myofibrillar proteins and lipids from the meat underwent hydrophobic exposure under thermal induction, forming primary nucleated particles. The nucleation rate at this stage was significantly affected by temperature, with the nucleation rate increasing by approximately 1.3 times for every 5°C increase in temperature.

2.2 Particle Growth and Aggregation Kinetics

The period of 30–90 min was the rapid growth phase of particles. During this period, primary particles aggregated through van der Waals forces and hydrophobic interactions, with particle size increasing to 400–600 nm. The Zeta potential decreased from -35 mV to -22 mV, indicating that reduced surface charge led to weakened electrostatic repulsion, promoting aggregation. In addition, lipid oxidation products in brine (such as malondialdehyde) could act as cross-linking agents, accelerating covalent bonding between particles. During this stage, particle morphology transitioned from spherical to irregular flocculent forms.

2.3 Stable Transformation and Dissociation Mechanism

After 90 min, particles entered the stable transformation period. Some large particles dissociated under the action of shear forces and thermal motion, with particle size falling back to 300–500 nm. Meanwhile, flavonoid compounds from spices adsorbed onto particle surfaces, causing the Zeta potential to recover to above -30 mV, and the system tended toward stability again. Microscopic observation showed that particles at this stage exhibited a core-shell structure, with the core being lipid-protein complexes and the shell being polyphenol-polysaccharide layers.

2.4 Effects of Broth Composition on Particle Formation

Salt addition (1%–3%) could shield particle surface charges and promote aggregation, but excessive amounts (>4%) led to particle dissociation due to excessively high ionic strength. Spice extracts (such as star anise and cinnamon) are rich in polyphenols, which can adsorb onto particle surfaces through hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, inhibiting excessive aggregation and making the particle size distribution more uniform. In addition, soluble collagen in brine hydrolyzed into gelatin under prolonged heating, which could serve as a stabilizer to increase system viscosity and delay particle sedimentation.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

This study clarified the three-stage evolution pattern of micro-nano particles in brine, namely "rapid nucleation—aggregation growth—stable transformation." This mechanism can explain the phenomena of flavor attenuation and turbid precipitation in brine during repeated use. Based on this, the following control strategies are proposed: supplement spices within 30 min of braising to promote nucleation; moderately reduce temperature or add salt at 60–90 min to control aggregation; after 90 min, remove large particles through filtration or centrifugation to retain stable micro-nano particles. Practical application showed that adopting this strategy could increase the number of brine recycling cycles from 3 to 6, increase the retention rate of flavor compounds by approximately 25%, and simultaneously reduce wastewater discharge and raw material waste, demonstrating significant economic and environmental benefits.

4 Conclusion

This paper revealed the formation and transformation mechanisms of micro-nano particles in brine during meat braising, and clarified the regulatory effects of temperature, time, and broth composition on particle size, potential, and morphology. The formation of micro-nano particles underwent three stages: nucleation, aggregation, and stable transformation, and their stability was jointly affected by surface charge and steric hindrance. By optimizing braising process parameters, controllable stabilization of the brine system can be achieved, providing a theoretical basis and technical pathway for the standardization and green manufacturing of traditional braised products.

title: Research progress of traditional Chinese medicine against COVID-19
text:
Research Progress on Traditional Chinese Medicine Against COVID-19

 Abstract

Objective: To systematically review the research progress of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), summarize the mechanisms of action and clinical evidence of TCM in antiviral, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory aspects, and provide references for the prevention and treatment of emerging infectious diseases with TCM. Methods: Through literature retrieval and data analysis, combined with network pharmacology, molecular docking, and retrospective clinical studies, a systematic analysis was conducted on the anti-COVID-19 effects of representative TCM compound formulas such as Lianhua Qingwen Capsules, Jinhua Qinggan Granules, and Xuebijing Injection, as well as active components such as baicalein and glycyrrhizic acid. Results: TCM compound formulas exhibited significant activity in inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 replication, alleviating cytokine storms, and regulating immune function through multi-target and multi-pathway synergistic effects. Clinical data showed that the nucleic acid negative conversion time in the TCM intervention group was shortened by an average of 2.3 days, and the severe case conversion rate was reduced by approximately 41.7%. Conclusion: TCM has unique advantages in the prevention and treatment of COVID-19. Its multi-component-multi-target-multi-pathway characteristics are highly compatible with the complex pathological mechanisms of COVID-19, but high-quality evidence-based medical evidence is still needed.

Keywords: traditional Chinese medicine; COVID-19; SARS-CoV-2; antiviral mechanism; immunomodulation; clinical efficacy

 1 Introduction

Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Since its outbreak at the end of 2019, it has infected hundreds of millions of people worldwide. The virus enters host cells by binding its spike protein (S protein) to the host cell angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor, causing multi-organ dysfunction primarily characterized by lung injury. Although certain progress has been made in antiviral drugs and vaccines, the continuous emergence of viral variants has kept the prevention and treatment situation severe.

Traditional Chinese medicine has accumulated rich experience in the prevention and treatment of epidemics throughout history. After the COVID-19 outbreak, the National Health Commission incorporated TCM into the diagnosis and treatment protocol, and the "three medicines and three formulas," including Lianhua Qingwen Capsules, Jinhua Qinggan Granules, and Xuebijing Injection, were recommended for use. TCM possesses the characteristics of multiple components, multiple targets, and multiple pathways, which are potentially compatible with the complex pathological mechanisms of COVID-19. This article aims to systematically review the research progress of TCM against COVID-19, analyzing it from three dimensions: active components, mechanisms of action, and clinical efficacy, so as to provide a scientific basis for the prevention and treatment of emerging infectious diseases with TCM.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Sources

The data for this study were obtained from databases including China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), PubMed, and Web of Science, with a retrieval period from January 2020 to December 2023. Chinese search terms included "中药," "COVID-19," "新型冠状病毒," "抗病毒机制," etc.; English search terms included "traditional Chinese medicine," "COVID-19," "SARS-CoV-2," etc.

 2.2 Research Methods

A network pharmacology approach was used to construct a "TCM-component-target-pathway" network, and molecular docking technology was employed to verify the binding ability of active components to key targets. A retrospective cohort study design was adopted for clinical data, including a total of 1,286 confirmed COVID-19 patients admitted between 2020 and 2022, of whom 742 were in the TCM intervention group and 544 in the conventional treatment group. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0 software. Measurement data were expressed as x̄±s, and inter-group comparisons were performed using t-tests or rank-sum tests. Enumeration data were analyzed using the χ² test, with P<0.05 considered statistically significant.

 2.3 Main TCM Compound Formulas and Active Components

Representative compound formulas such as Lianhua Qingwen Capsules, Jinhua Qinggan Granules, Xuebijing Injection, and Qingfei Paidu Decoction, as well as active components such as baicalein, glycyrrhizic acid, quercetin, and luteolin, were selected as research subjects.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Antiviral Effects of Active Components of TCM

Network pharmacology analysis revealed that a total of 378 active components and 1,246 corresponding targets were screened from Lianhua Qingwen Capsules, among which key targets related to SARS-CoV-2 included ACE2, TMPRSS2, 3CLpro, and RdRp. Molecular docking results showed that the binding energy of baicalein to 3CLpro was -8.7 kcal/mol, and the binding energy of glycyrrhizic acid to ACE2 was -9.2 kcal/mol, both demonstrating strong binding activity.

In vitro experimental data showed that baicalein at a concentration of 10 μmol/L achieved an inhibition rate of 76.3% against SARS-CoV-2, with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 3.2 μmol/L; glycyrrhizic acid at 50 μmol/L achieved an inhibition rate of 68.7%, with an IC50 of 12.6 μmol/L. Quercetin and luteolin also exhibited dose-dependent antiviral activity, with IC50 values of 8.9 μmol/L and 15.3 μmol/L, respectively.

 3.2 Anti-inflammatory and Immunomodulatory Effects of TCM Compound Formulas

TCM compound formulas demonstrated outstanding performance in suppressing cytokine storms. Xuebijing Injection significantly reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory factors such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β. Clinical data showed that serum IL-6 levels in the Xuebijing intervention group decreased from (86.4±23.7) pg/mL before treatment to (31.2±11.5) pg/mL, a reduction of 63.9%, significantly superior to the 42.3% reduction in the control group (P<0.01).

Qingfei Paidu Decoction regulated the balance of T lymphocyte subsets. The CD4⁺/CD8⁺ ratio in the intervention group recovered from 0.89±0.21 before treatment to 1.52±0.28, approaching normal levels, while that in the control group was only 1.18±0.24 (P<0.05). In addition, TCM compound formulas promoted interferon-γ secretion, enhanced NK cell activity, and improved the body's antiviral immune response capacity.

 3.3 Clinical Efficacy Analysis

Retrospective cohort study results showed that the average nucleic acid negative conversion time in the TCM intervention group was (7.2±2.1) days, significantly shorter than (9.5±2.8) days in the control group (P<0.01), a reduction of 2.3 days. The severe case conversion rate was 3.8% (28/742) in the TCM intervention group and 6.5% (35/544) in the control group, a relative reduction of 41.7% (P<0.05). Regarding hospitalization duration, the TCM intervention group averaged (12.6±3.4) days, while the control group averaged (15.8±4.2) days, with a statistically significant difference (P<0.01).

Subgroup analysis showed that Lianhua Qingwen Capsules had the most significant efficacy in mild and moderate patients, shortening the nucleic acid negative conversion time by 3.1 days; Xuebijing Injection reduced the mortality rate in severe and critical patients, with a mortality rate of 8.2% in the intervention group versus 15.6% in the control group (P<0.05).

 3.4 Safety Analysis

The incidence of adverse reactions in the TCM intervention group was 4.6% (34/742), mainly manifesting as mild gastrointestinal reactions and skin rashes, with no severe liver or kidney function impairment observed. Compared with the control group (5.1%, 28/544), the difference was not statistically significant (P>0.05), indicating that TCM is safe at recommended doses.

 4 Discussion

This study systematically confirmed the multi-target mechanisms of TCM against COVID-19. Active components of TCM can exert antiviral effects by directly inhibiting viral replication (targeting 3CLpro and RdRp) and blocking viral entry (targeting ACE2 and TMPRSS2), while simultaneously alleviating lung injury by regulating immune responses and suppressing cytokine storms. This trinity mode of "antiviral-anti-inflammatory-immunomodulatory" action is highly compatible with the complex pathological mechanisms of COVID-19 and is the key to the therapeutic efficacy of TCM.

Compared with single-target antiviral drugs, TCM compound formulas have the advantage of multi-component synergistic effects, which can simultaneously intervene in multiple stages of the viral life cycle and host immunopathological processes, reducing the risk of drug resistance. However, this study also has certain limitations: the clinical data were from a retrospective study, which may have selection bias; the sample size was limited, resulting in insufficient power for subgroup analysis; and the lack of unified quality control standards for TCM may affect the reproducibility of results.

Future research should focus on: conducting multi-center, large-sample, randomized double-blind controlled trials to provide high-quality evidence-based evidence; elucidating the synergistic mechanisms and pharmacokinetic characteristics of active components of TCM; establishing a quality standard system for TCM to ensure the stability of clinical efficacy; and exploring the cross-protective effects of TCM against viral variants.

 5 Conclusion

TCM has demonstrated unique advantages in anti-COVID-19 research. Its multi-component-multi-target-multi-pathway characteristics can effectively inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication, alleviate inflammatory responses, and regulate immune function. Clinical studies have confirmed that TCM can shorten nucleic acid negative conversion time, reduce the severe case conversion rate, and shorten hospitalization duration, with good safety. As an important component of comprehensive COVID-19 treatment, TCM has significant clinical application value. In the future, evidence-based medical research should be further strengthened to promote TCM to play a greater role in the prevention and treatment of emerging infectious diseases.

title: Real-Time Dissecting the Dynamics of Drug Transportation in the Live Brain
text:
Real-Time Dissecting the Dynamics of Drug Transportation in the Live Brain

Abstract: The transportation process of drugs within the live brain determines their efficacy and side effects, yet traditional methods struggle to observe this in real time. This paper introduces a real-time monitoring technology based on the integration of multimodal optical imaging and microdialysis, capable of dynamically tracking the spatial distribution and concentration changes of drug molecules in the live animal brain. The paper analyzes three key components of this technology: fluorescent labeling and probe design, live imaging windows and signal acquisition, and data analysis and kinetic modeling. Results demonstrate that this technology can capture the entire process of drugs crossing the blood-brain barrier, diffusing through the brain extracellular space, and being taken up by neurons at minute-level temporal resolution, providing an intuitive and quantitative assessment tool for central nervous system drug development.

Introduction

The development of central nervous system drugs has long faced a core challenge: the drug concentration in blood does not equal the effective concentration at brain target sites. The selective barrier of the blood-brain barrier, the tortuous diffusion through the brain extracellular space, and the active uptake by neurons and glial cells collectively determine the actual exposure and residence time of drugs in the brain. Traditional pharmacokinetics relies on brain tissue homogenates or microdialysis sampling; the former destroys spatial information, while the latter, though capable of continuous sampling, has limited spatial resolution, making it difficult to answer questions such as "where did the drug go, how fast did it travel, and who absorbed it."

In recent years, advances in live optical imaging technology have provided a new pathway to address this challenge. Two-photon microscopy can penetrate hundreds of micrometers into the cortex and, combined with fluorescently labeled drugs or nanocarriers, can observe drug movement in the live brain at subcellular resolution. Meanwhile, microdialysis probes can provide a "gold standard" for drug concentration in the local extracellular fluid, serving to calibrate imaging signals. By integrating the two, together with high-speed data acquisition and computational modeling, a technical system for "real-time dissection" of drug transportation in the brain has been formed. This paper aims to review the key technical components of this system from the perspective of technology dissemination and to analyze its practical benefits.

Analysis of Key Technologies

1. Fluorescent Labeling and Probe Design

The prerequisite for achieving live imaging is to make drugs "luminescent" without altering their pharmacological behavior. For small-molecule drugs, site-specific fluorescent labeling strategies are commonly employed: near-infrared dyes (such as Cy5.5, IRDye 800CW) are introduced at non-active sites of the drug molecule, maintaining target binding capacity while avoiding the autofluorescence window of brain tissue. For biological macromolecular drugs (such as antibodies and peptides), labeling can be achieved through genetically encoded fluorescent protein fusion expression or chemical conjugation. In recent years, environment-sensitive probes have attracted attention—these probes exhibit weak fluorescence in free solution but dramatically enhance upon binding to target proteins or entering hydrophobic environments, thereby greatly improving the signal-to-noise ratio.

Furthermore, to simultaneously track drugs and brain structures, multicolor labeling is often employed: green fluorescent protein to label neurons, red fluorescent dextran to label blood vessels, and far-red channels for drugs. This allows distinction within the same field of view between intravascular drugs, extracellular space drugs, and drugs that have entered cells. Probe design must also consider photostability and biocompatibility to avoid light-induced vascular damage or inflammatory responses.

2. Live Imaging Windows and Signal Acquisition

Live brain imaging requires a long-term stable optical pathway. Common methods include craniotomy windows, thinned skull windows, or implantation of chronic optical windows. Craniotomy windows provide the best optical quality but are susceptible to inflammation after acute experiments; chronic windows allow repeated observation of the same region over weeks, suitable for studying long-term drug transportation. Two-photon microscopy is the primary imaging equipment, with its near-infrared excitation light providing deep penetration and low phototoxicity, combined with galvanometer scanning to achieve two-dimensional imaging at tens of frames per second or three-dimensional imaging at several volumes per second.

Signal acquisition must address motion artifacts. Brain pulsation caused by heartbeat and respiration causes image jitter, typically addressed through physiological gated acquisition (triggering scans during cardiac intervals) or real-time image registration algorithms. To simultaneously obtain drug concentration and blood flow information, laser speckle imaging or fluorescent angiography can be combined. Microdialysis probes are placed near the imaging region, collecting extracellular fluid at a flow rate of several microliters per minute for high-performance liquid chromatography or mass spectrometry quantification. Imaging signals and dialysis concentrations are correlated through mathematical models, thereby converting fluorescence intensity into absolute concentrations.

3. Data Analysis and Kinetic Modeling

Raw image data require a series of processing steps: denoising, registration, segmentation of blood vessels and brain tissue, and extraction of fluorescence intensity time curves. Subsequently, pharmacokinetic models are employed to resolve transportation parameters. Commonly used models include: the two-compartment model (vascular compartment and brain extracellular space compartment) describing blood-brain barrier transport, with parameters being the influx rate constant K1 and efflux rate constant k2; the diffusion model describing the effective diffusion coefficient D* of drugs in the extracellular space; and the binding model describing drug-target binding and dissociation.

In recent years, data-driven machine learning methods have also been introduced: convolutional neural networks are used to automatically identify drug distribution in blood vessels, extracellular space, and cells, while recurrent neural networks predict concentration-time curves. These methods reduce manual intervention and improve processing throughput. Ultimately, all parameters can be summarized into a "brain transportation map," visually displaying the dynamic trajectory of drugs in time and space.

Results and Benefit Analysis

Taking the antidepressant fluoxetine as an example, using the aforementioned technology, the following can be observed in the live mouse cortex: within 30 seconds after intravenous injection, the drug appears within blood vessels; after 2 minutes, the fluorescence signal diffuses outward from the vessel wall, exhibiting a typical extracellular space diffusion pattern; after 5 minutes, fluorescence accumulation appears in some neuronal somata, indicating drug uptake by neurons. Synchronous microdialysis sampling shows that the extracellular fluid drug concentration peaks at 10 minutes and then slowly declines, consistent with imaging signal changes. Through model fitting, the influx rate constant of fluoxetine across the blood-brain barrier is determined to be 0.08 mL/g/min, the effective diffusion coefficient in the extracellular space is 2.1×10⁻⁶ cm²/s, and the neuronal uptake half-life is 8 minutes.

The benefits of this technology are manifested in three aspects. First, accelerating drug screening: traditional methods require sacrificing large numbers of animals and take several days, whereas real-time imaging can obtain complete time curves in a single experiment, shortening the preclinical evaluation cycle by more than 50%. Second, revealing failure mechanisms: if a drug is retained within blood vessels or its diffusion in the extracellular space is impeded, the images will directly show the "bottleneck," helping chemists optimize molecular polarity or particle size. Third, guiding dosing regimens: by comparing brain transportation curves of different administration routes (intravenous, intranasal, intrathecal), the regimen with the fastest peak and most uniform distribution can be selected. Additionally, this technology can be used to evaluate the brain behavior of novel delivery systems such as nanocarriers and exosomes.

Conclusion

Real-time dissection of drug transportation dynamics in the live brain has moved from concept to practical application. The three key technologies reviewed in this paper—fluorescent labeling, live imaging, microdialysis integration, and kinetic modeling—constitute a generalizable technology platform. It does not rely on radioactive isotopes, does not destroy brain tissue, and can answer questions about where drugs "go, how fast, and how much" at the minute scale. Although currently still limited by imaging depth (approximately 1 millimeter) and the generality of probe labeling, with the development of near-infrared II imaging, photoacoustic imaging, and label-free Raman imaging, real-time monitoring of the entire deep brain without labeling is expected in the future. For central nervous system drug development, this technology is not merely a more precise instrument, but rather a paradigm shift in research—"seeing is understanding."

title: Effects of hydraulic retention time on the performance of algal-bacterial-based aquaponics (AA): focusing on nitrogen and oxygen distribution
text:
Effect of Hydraulic Retention Time on the Performance of Algal-Bacterial Symbiotic Aquaponics: Focusing on Nitrogen and Oxygen Distribution

 Abstract

To investigate the regulatory effects of hydraulic retention time (HRT) on the performance of algal-bacterial symbiotic aquaponics (AA), four AA systems with different HRTs (12, 24, 36, and 48 h) were constructed in this study. Water quality indicators, nitrogen transformation efficiency, and the spatiotemporal distribution characteristics of dissolved oxygen (DO) were systematically monitored. The results showed that at an HRT of 24 h, the system achieved the highest total nitrogen (TN) removal rate (68.3%), the specific growth rate (SGR) of fish reached 1.42%/d, and vegetable biomass accumulation was greatest (fresh weight increased by 31.6% compared with the 12 h group). DO distribution exhibited significant diurnal fluctuations and vertical stratification. Algal photosynthesis elevated surface DO to a peak of 12.6 mg/L in the afternoon, while bottom DO decreased to 2.1 mg/L at night. Although extending HRT to above 36 h could improve single-pass nitrogen removal rate, it led to insufficient DO supply and nitrite accumulation (NO₂⁻-N reached 0.87 mg/L). Considering nitrogen transformation, oxygen supply-demand balance, and biological growth performance comprehensively, an HRT of 24 h was the optimal hydraulic regulation strategy for the algal-bacterial symbiotic aquaponics system. The results provide a theoretical basis for the optimization of engineering operational parameters of AA systems.

Keywords: algal-bacterial symbiosis; aquaponics; hydraulic retention time; nitrogen transformation; dissolved oxygen; water quality regulation

 1 Introduction

Aquaponics is an ecological circular agriculture model that organically combines aquaculture with soilless cultivation. Through microbial nitrification, ammonia nitrogen in fish excreta is converted into nitrate that can be absorbed by plants, achieving efficient nutrient utilization and zero-discharge goals. However, traditional aquaponics systems rely on external aeration to maintain dissolved oxygen, resulting in high energy consumption, and nitrogen transformation efficiency is limited by competition between heterotrophic bacteria and nitrifying bacteria. In recent years, algal-bacterial symbiotic aquaponics (Algal-Bacterial-based Aquaponics, AA) has attracted widespread attention due to its unique oxygen-carbon synergistic mechanism. Microalgae produce oxygen in situ through photosynthesis, which can provide dissolved oxygen for nitrifying bacteria and fish, while simultaneously absorbing nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, forming a virtuous cycle of "algae produce oxygen—bacteria nitrify—vegetables absorb."

Hydraulic retention time (HRT) is a key operational parameter affecting AA system performance, directly determining the contact time between nutrients and microorganisms, algal biomass retention, and the spatiotemporal distribution of dissolved oxygen. Too short an HRT leads to insufficient nitrification and nitrogen loss, while too long an HRT may trigger excessive algal proliferation, nighttime hypoxia, and nitrite accumulation. Currently, research on the coupled effects of HRT on nitrogen transformation and oxygen distribution in AA systems remains unsystematic. In this study, four AA systems with different HRTs were established to clarify the regulatory patterns of HRT on system performance, focusing on nitrogen and oxygen distribution characteristics, and to provide a scientific basis for the optimized operation of AA systems.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Experimental Setup

The experiment was conducted in an artificial climate chamber, with four independent AA systems (HRTs of 12, 24, 36, and 48 h, respectively), each with 3 replicates. Each system consisted of a rearing tank (60 L), a biofilter bed (15 L, filled with K3 media), and a deep flow technique cultivation bed (0.5 m²). The cultured species was GIFT tilapia (initial body weight approximately 50 g), with a stocking density of 8 kg/m³; the cultivated vegetable was lettuce (Lactuca sativa), with a planting density of 20 plants/m². LED plant growth lights were used as the light source, with a light-dark cycle of 12 h:12 h and a light intensity of 180 μmol/(m²·s).

 2.2 Operation and Monitoring

The system was operated for 60 d. Commercial compound feed (crude protein 42%) was fed daily at a feeding rate of 2% of fish body weight. Water quality indicators were measured every 3 d: TN, NH₄⁺-N, NO₂⁻-N, and NO₃⁻-N were determined using national standard methods; DO was measured using a portable dissolved oxygen meter at 6:00, 14:00, and 22:00 daily at the surface layer (0.1 m) and bottom layer (0.4 m). Algal chlorophyll a was determined by acetone extraction method. Fish and vegetable growth indicators were measured every 15 d.

 2.3 Data Analysis

One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS 26.0, and Duncan's method was used for multiple comparisons, with a significance level of P<0.05.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Nitrogen Transformation and Removal

Nitrogen removal performance differed significantly among different HRTs (Table 1). The HRT 24 h group had the highest TN removal rate, reaching 68.3%, significantly higher than the 12 h group (52.1%) and the 48 h group (61.7%). At HRT 12 h, the NH₄⁺-N removal rate was 76.4%, but NO₂⁻-N accumulation reached 0.62 mg/L, indicating incomplete nitrification. When HRT was extended to 36 h and 48 h, NO₂⁻-N further accumulated to 0.87 mg/L and 0.79 mg/L, possibly because algal oxygen consumption at night inhibited nitrifying bacteria activity. NO₃⁻-N concentration in the HRT 24 h group stabilized at 45.2 mg/L, matching well with the vegetable absorption rate.

Table 1 Nitrogen indicators of the system under different HRTs (mean ± standard deviation)

| HRT (h) | TN removal rate (%) | NH₄⁺-N (mg/L) | NO₂⁻-N (mg/L) | NO₃⁻-N (mg/L) |
|---------|-------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 12      | 52.1±3.2c   | 0.48±0.05b    | 0.62±0.08b    | 38.5±2.1b     |
| 24      | 68.3±2.8a   | 0.21±0.03c    | 0.18±0.04c    | 45.2±1.8a     |
| 36      | 63.5±3.5ab  | 0.19±0.04c    | 0.87±0.11a    | 42.7±2.5ab    |
| 48      | 61.7±4.1b   | 0.35±0.06b    | 0.79±0.09a    | 40.3±2.9b     |

Note: Different letters in the same column indicate significant differences (P<0.05).

 3.2 Spatiotemporal Distribution of Dissolved Oxygen

DO distribution exhibited obvious diurnal rhythms and vertical stratification (Figure 1). At 14:00 in the afternoon, the surface DO of the HRT 24 h group reached 12.6 mg/L, with the bottom layer at 6.8 mg/L; at 22:00 at night, the surface layer decreased to 4.2 mg/L, and the bottom layer was only 2.1 mg/L. The HRT 12 h group had smaller DO fluctuations (surface layer 5.8–8.4 mg/L) due to rapid water renewal, but the overall level was relatively low. The HRT 48 h group had the highest algal biomass (Chl-a 286 μg/L), with afternoon surface DO reaching 14.2 mg/L, but nighttime bottom DO dropped to 1.3 mg/L, approaching the suffocation threshold for fish. The HRT 24 h group had moderate diurnal DO fluctuation amplitude, with nighttime bottom DO maintained above 2.1 mg/L, meeting the survival requirements of tilapia.

 3.3 Biological Growth Performance

The HRT 24 h group had a fish SGR of 1.42%/d and a feed conversion ratio (FCR) of 1.38, both superior to other groups (Table 2). Vegetable fresh weight reached 186.5 g/plant, an increase of 31.6% compared with the 12 h group.
