On PDA plates, the colonies of this strain appeared grayish-green, velvety, with a yellowish-brown reverse. Conidiophores were penicillate, and conidia were spherical to subglobose, arranged in chains.

2.2 In Vitro Antagonistic Activity Assay

The inhibitory effect of *P. griseofulvum* against pathogens was determined using the dual culture method. A pathogen mycelial plug (5 mm diameter) was inoculated at the center of a PDA plate, and *P. griseofulvum* spore suspension (1×10⁶ CFU/mL) was inoculated at three points 25 mm from the center. After dark culture at 25 °C for 5–7 d, the pathogen colony radius was measured, and the inhibition rate was calculated. The results showed that the mycelial growth inhibition rate of *P. griseofulvum* against *S. rolfsii* was 72.3%, and against *Fusarium* spp. was 65.8%. Microscopic observation revealed that pathogen hyphae co-cultured with *P. griseofulvum* exhibited abnormalities such as swelling, distortion, and protoplasm coagulation, indicating that *P. griseofulvum* secreted metabolites with antifungal activity.

2.3 Pot Experiment for Disease Control and Growth Promotion

*P. griseofulvum* spore suspension (1×10⁷ CFU/mL) was mixed into sterilized soil at a ratio of 5% (v/w). *Aconitum carmichaelii* seedlings were planted in pots, with 3 plants per pot. Non-inoculated control and inoculated control were set up. After the plants survived, a mixed pathogen suspension (1×10⁶ CFU/mL each of *S. rolfsii* and *Fusarium* spp.) was inoculated by root irrigation at 20 mL per pot. After 30 d, the disease index and plant growth indicators were investigated. The results showed that the disease index of root rot in *Aconitum carmichaelii* treated with *P. griseofulvum* was 18.5, while that of the inoculated control was 48.1, with a control efficacy of 61.5%. The plant survival rate in the treatment group was 86.7%, an increase of 42.6% compared with the control. Meanwhile, plant height, aboveground fresh weight, and root activity in the treatment group increased by 24.3%, 31.2%, and 35.8%, respectively, compared with the control, demonstrating significant growth-promoting effects.

2.4 Field Plot Efficacy Verification

Field trials were conducted in areas with perennial occurrence of root rot in the main *Aconitum carmichaelii* production area of Jiangyou, Sichuan. Treatments included *P. griseofulvum* formulation (furrow application, 30 kg/hm²), chemical pesticide control (carbendazim, at conventional dosage), and blank control, with 3 replicates per treatment, plot area of 20 m², and randomized complete block arrangement. Disease index was investigated at 60 d and 120 d after sowing, and yield was measured at harvest. The results showed that the disease index of root rot in the *P. griseofulvum* treatment plot was 22.4, that in the chemical pesticide treatment plot was 19.8, and that in the blank control was 54.6. The control efficacy of *P. griseofulvum* was 59.0%, comparable to that of the chemical pesticide. In terms of yield, the fresh *Aconitum carmichaelii* yield in the *P. griseofulvum* treatment plot was 12,450 kg/hm², an increase of 28.7% compared with the blank control, with no significant difference from the chemical pesticide treatment plot (12,780 kg/hm²). In addition, the *Fusarium* population in soil of the *P. griseofulvum* treatment plot decreased by 54.2% compared with the control, indicating that this strain could colonize in soil and continuously suppress pathogens.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

This study demonstrated that *P. griseofulvum* has stable biological control efficacy against *Aconitum carmichaelii* root rot, with efficacy comparable to conventional chemical pesticides, and also promotes plant growth. In terms of mechanism of action, *P. griseofulvum* exerts biocontrol functions through the following pathways: first, competition, as this fungus grows rapidly and can quickly occupy the rhizosphere niche, limiting pathogen infection; second, antibiosis, as its metabolites such as griseofulvin directly inhibit pathogen mycelial growth and spore germination; third, induced resistance, as the activities of phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) and peroxidase (POD) in treated *Aconitum carmichaelii* plants were significantly elevated, indicating activation of the plant's systemic defense response.

From an economic perspective, the cost of using *P. griseofulvum* formulation is approximately 1,200 yuan per hectare, about 20% lower than the cost of chemical pesticide control, while *Aconitum carmichaelii* yield increases by 28.7%, generating an additional income of approximately 15,000 yuan per hectare at market prices. From an ecological perspective, this formulation is a microbial agent with no pesticide residues and does not disrupt soil microbial community structure, meeting the requirements of green production of traditional Chinese medicinal materials. From a social perspective, this technology can reduce chemical pesticide usage, improve the quality and safety of *Aconitum carmichaelii*, and contribute to promoting the sustainable development of the *Aconitum carmichaelii* industry.

4 Conclusion

The *P. griseofulvum* strain isolated in this study has significant antagonistic effects against the main pathogens of *Aconitum carmichaelii* root rot, *S. rolfsii* and *Fusarium* spp., with in vitro inhibition rates of 72.3% and 65.8%, respectively. Pot and field experiments showed that this strain can effectively reduce the disease index of root rot, with control efficacy of 59.0%–61.5%, comparable to chemical pesticides, while promoting *Aconitum carmichaelii* growth and increasing yield by 28.7%. *P. griseofulvum* functions through multiple mechanisms including competition, antibiosis, and induced resistance, making it a biocontrol strain with development potential for *Aconitum carmichaelii* root rot. It is recommended to further optimize the formulation preparation process and field application technology to promote its widespread application in actual production.

title: Will China's fertilizer use continue to decline? Evidence from LMDI analysis based on crops, regions and fertilizer types
text:
Abstract: Reducing fertilizer use and improving its efficiency is key to ensuring food security and advancing the green transition of agriculture. Based on China's provincial panel data from 2010 to 2022, this paper employs the Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) decomposition method to analyze the driving factors of fertilizer application from three dimensions: crop, region, and fertilizer type. The results show that China's fertilizer application peaked in 2015 and has since continued to decline, with a cumulative reduction of approximately 18.7% by 2022. The efficiency effect is the dominant factor in the reduction, contributing -62.3%, followed by the structural effect (-21.5%), while the scale effect remains positive (+16.2%). By crop, vegetables and fruit trees have the greatest reduction potential. By region, the eastern region has achieved significant reductions, while the decline in the central and western regions has slowed. By type, nitrogen fertilizer shows the largest decrease, while the share of compound fertilizer has risen. It is projected that fertilizer application will continue to decline slowly in the future, but vigilance is needed against a rebound in the scale effect. Policies should focus on precision fertilization, cropping structure adjustment, and technology extension in the central and western regions.

Keywords: fertilizer reduction; LMDI decomposition; crop structure; regional differences; fertilizer type

 1 Introduction

Chemical fertilizer is an important guarantee for increasing grain production, but excessive application leads to soil acidification, water eutrophication, and greenhouse gas emissions. Since the Ministry of Agriculture launched the "Action Plan for Zero Growth in Fertilizer Use" in 2015, China's fertilizer application has declined for multiple consecutive years. However, whether this decline can be sustained in the future depends on the interplay between efficiency improvement, structural optimization, and scale expansion. Existing studies mostly analyze from a single dimension and lack a systematic decomposition across crops, regions, and fertilizer types. This paper adopts the LMDI method to construct a multi-dimensional decomposition framework, identify the core driving forces of fertilizer reduction, and provide a basis for differentiated policies.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Sources

This paper uses data on fertilizer application, crop sown area, agricultural output value, and planting structure of various crops for 31 provinces (autonomous regions and municipalities) in China from 2010 to 2022. The data are sourced from the China Statistical Yearbook, the China Rural Statistical Yearbook, and bulletins of the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs. Fertilizer types are classified into nitrogen fertilizer, phosphate fertilizer, potassium fertilizer, and compound fertilizer.

 2.2 LMDI Decomposition Model

Fertilizer application (F) can be decomposed as:

F = ∑ᵢ∑ⱼ∑ₖ Fᵢⱼₖ = ∑ᵢ∑ⱼ∑ₖ (Fᵢⱼₖ / Aᵢⱼₖ) × (Aᵢⱼₖ / Aᵢⱼ) × (Aᵢⱼ / A) × A

where i represents region, j represents crop, and k represents fertilizer type; A is the total sown area. Definitions:
- Efficiency effect: change in fertilizer intensity per unit area;
- Structural effect: change in crop planting structure;
- Regional effect: change in the share of regional sown area;
- Scale effect: change in total sown area.

The additive form of LMDI decomposition is adopted:

ΔF = Fᵗ - F⁰ = ΔF_eff + ΔF_str + ΔF_reg + ΔF_sca

The weight of each effect is determined using the logarithmic mean function.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Evolution of Total Fertilizer Application

From 2010 to 2015, fertilizer application increased from 55.60 million tons to 60.23 million tons, with an average annual growth rate of 1.6%; from 2015 to 2022, it decreased to 48.95 million tons, with an average annual decline rate of 2.9%. The peak occurred in 2015, coinciding with the launch of the "Zero Growth Action."

 3.2 LMDI Decomposition Results

The efficiency effect was consistently negative, contributing a cumulative -62.3% from 2016 to 2022, indicating that the promotion of technologies such as soil testing and formula fertilization and integrated water-fertilizer management significantly reduced fertilizer intensity per unit area. The structural effect was -21.5%, mainly due to the decline in the share of fertilizer-intensive crops (such as vegetables) and the expansion of crop rotation with low-fertilizer crops such as soybean and maize. The scale effect was positive (+16.2%), as the sown area increased steadily, partially offsetting the reduction effect. The regional effect was relatively small (-6.4%), reflecting that the eastern region reduced fertilizer use faster than the central and western regions.

 3.3 Analysis by Crop

Vegetables and fruit trees had the highest fertilizer intensity per unit area, reaching 380 kg/hm² and 420 kg/hm², respectively, but their share of sown area declined, contributing significantly to the structural effect. Among grain crops, fertilizer intensity for maize and wheat decreased notably, while the decline for rice was smaller. Soybean had the lowest fertilizer intensity due to rhizobial nitrogen fixation.

 3.4 Analysis by Region

The eastern region (such as Shandong and Jiangsu) achieved the largest reduction, declining by 24.1% from 2015 to 2022, mainly due to advanced economic development and high technology adoption rates. The central region declined by 15.3%, while the western region declined by only 8.7%, owing to a planting structure skewed toward fertilizer-intensive crops and lagging technology extension.

 3.5 Analysis by Fertilizer Type

Nitrogen fertilizer application decreased from 23.50 million tons in 2010 to 15.80 million tons in 2022, a decline of 32.8%; phosphate fertilizer decreased by 18.5%; potassium fertilizer decreased by 12.3%; compound fertilizer increased by 21.4%, with its share rising from 28% to 39%. This indicates a transition toward higher efficiency and compound-based fertilizer structures.

 4 Discussion

The efficiency effect is the core driver of fertilizer reduction, but the space for further decline is narrowing. Future efforts need to rely on deep technologies such as intelligent fertilization and organic fertilizer substitution. Although the structural effect is significant, fertilizer-intensive crops cannot be excessively compressed due to food security constraints. The scale effect may rebound due to an increase in the multiple cropping index, which requires vigilance. Regional differences indicate that the central and western regions are the focus of the next stage of reduction, and technology training and subsidies should be strengthened. In terms of fertilizer types, although the growth of compound fertilizer improves utilization efficiency, its production involves high energy consumption and requires a full life-cycle assessment. In addition, policies should avoid a "one-size-fits-all" approach and set differentiated targets for different crops, regions, and fertilizer types. The limitation of this paper is that it does not consider organic fertilizer substitution and differences in soil background conditions; future research can deepen the analysis by integrating remote sensing and household survey data.

 5 Conclusions

China's fertilizer application has continued to decline since 2015, dominated by the efficiency effect, assisted by the structural effect, and partially offset by the scale effect. By crop, vegetables and fruit trees have great reduction potential; by region, the central and western regions lag behind; by type, nitrogen fertilizer shows the largest decrease while compound fertilizer rises. It is projected that fertilizer application will continue a slow downward trend in the future, but a rebound in scale and regional imbalance must be guarded against. Policies should strengthen precision fertilization, optimize planting structure, promote technology in the central and western regions, and advance the green upgrading of fertilizer structure.

title: The Quorum Quenching Bacterium Bacillus licheniformis T-1 Protects Zebrafish against Aeromonas hydrophila Infection
text:
Bacillus licheniformis T-1 Protects Zebrafish against Aeromonas hydrophila Infection through Quorum Quenching

Abstract: Aeromonas hydrophila is a common pathogenic bacterium in aquaculture, and its pathogenicity is regulated by the quorum sensing system. Traditional antibiotic-based prevention and control easily lead to drug resistance, and green alternatives are urgently needed. In this study, a strain of Bacillus licheniformis T-1 was isolated from aquaculture water, its quorum quenching activity was verified, and its protective effect was evaluated using a zebrafish infection model. The results showed that strain T-1 could significantly degrade N-acyl homoserine lactone signaling molecules and inhibit the secretion of proteases and hemolysins as well as biofilm formation in Aeromonas hydrophila. In the zebrafish challenge test, the survival rate of the T-1 treatment group was about 50% higher than that of the control group, and the expression of inflammatory factors in fish was reduced. This strain is safe and easy to culture, and can serve as a potential probiotic for preventing and controlling Aeromonas hydrophila infection in aquaculture.

1 Introduction

Aeromonas hydrophila is a Gram-negative opportunistic pathogen widely distributed in freshwater environments. It can cause diseases such as hemorrhagic septicemia and enteritis in fish, resulting in major economic losses to aquaculture. The pathogenic process of this bacterium is tightly regulated by the quorum sensing system. When bacterial density reaches a threshold, the quorum sensing system is activated, leading to massive expression of virulence factors such as proteases, hemolysins, enterotoxins, and biofilms. Therefore, interfering with quorum sensing signals—namely quorum quenching—has become a new approach for preventing and controlling infection by this bacterium.

Quorum quenching refers to the technology of inhibiting bacterial group behavior by degrading or modifying signaling molecules, blocking receptors, and other means. Unlike antibiotics, which directly kill or inhibit bacterial growth, quorum quenching does not impose strong selective pressure, is less likely to induce drug resistance, and targets virulence rather than survival, offering ecological advantages. Some strains of the genus Bacillus have been reported to possess quorum quenching activity, but efficient strains targeting Aeromonas hydrophila still need to be discovered. This study aimed to isolate and screen Bacillus licheniformis with quorum quenching ability and evaluate its protective effect on a zebrafish infection model, so as to provide a practical strain for aquaculture.

2 Analysis of Key Technologies

2.1 Isolation and Screening of Quorum Quenching Strains

Water samples were collected from healthy aquaculture ponds, serially diluted, spread onto LB solid medium, and cultured at 37°C for 24 hours. Single colonies were picked, and Chromobacterium violaceum CV026 was used as the reporter strain for preliminary screening. CV026 produces violacein when exogenous N-acyl homoserine lactone is added. If the test bacterium can degrade or modify the signaling molecules, violacein production decreases. Strains that caused significant fading of violacein were selected, and their 16S rRNA gene sequences were further determined and identified as Bacillus licheniformis, named T-1. This strain grows well in LB medium, with an optimal growth temperature of 30–37°C and an optimal pH of 7.0–8.0, making large-scale culture convenient.

2.2 Signal Molecule Degradation and Virulence Factor Inhibition Tests

The sterile supernatant of T-1 was co-incubated with N-acyl homoserine lactone standards, and the residual amount of signaling molecules was detected by high-performance liquid chromatography. The results showed that the T-1 supernatant could degrade about 80% of C6-HSL and C8-HSL within 4 hours. Furthermore, the T-1 supernatant was co-cultured with Aeromonas hydrophila to detect the expression of its virulence factors. The results showed that the T-1 supernatant significantly inhibited the extracellular protease activity of Aeromonas hydrophila (decreased by about 65%) and hemolysin activity (decreased by about 70%), while biofilm formation was reduced by about 60%. These virulence factors are key to the pathogenicity of Aeromonas hydrophila, and their expression is regulated by quorum sensing, indicating that T-1 effectively weakened bacterial virulence by quenching signals.

2.3 Establishment of the Zebrafish Infection Model and Evaluation of Protective Effect

Healthy adult zebrafish were selected and randomly divided into three groups: the control group (injected with PBS only), the infection group (injected with Aeromonas hydrophila), and the protection group (immersed in T-1 bacterial suspension 24 hours before injection with Aeromonas hydrophila). The infection dose was 10^6 CFU per fish by intraperitoneal injection. Observations were made for 7 days, and mortality was recorded. The results showed that the 7-day survival rate of the infection group was only 30%, while that of the protection group reached 80%, and that of the control group was 100%. Fish in the protection group showed no obvious symptoms such as hemorrhage or ascites, and tissue sections showed a marked reduction in inflammatory cell infiltration in the liver and spleen. At the same time, real-time fluorescence quantitative PCR was used to detect the expression of the fish inflammatory factors TNF-α and IL-1β. Compared with the infection group, the protection group showed decreases of about 55% and 50%, respectively. This indicates that T-1 can not only improve the survival rate but also reduce inflammatory damage.

2.4 Detection of Strain Safety and Colonization Ability

To evaluate the safety of T-1 as a probiotic, zebrafish were immersed in its bacterial suspension at a concentration of 10^8 CFU/mL for 7 days. No death or abnormal behavior was observed, and there was no significant difference in body weight gain compared with the control group. At the same time, when T-1 was intraperitoneally injected into zebrafish, the median lethal dose was greater than 10^9 CFU, indicating extremely low virulence. In addition, T-1 could transiently colonize the intestine of zebrafish and was still detectable 3 days after immersion was stopped, indicating that it has a certain ability to survive in the intestine, which is beneficial for sustaining its quorum quenching effect.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

In this study, a strain of Bacillus licheniformis T-1 was obtained, with clear quorum quenching activity. It can significantly degrade N-acyl homoserine lactone signaling molecules and inhibit the expression of multiple virulence factors in Aeromonas hydrophila. In the zebrafish infection model, T-1 treatment increased the survival rate from 30% to 80% and reduced the inflammatory response. This strain has high safety and simple culture conditions, and is suitable for use as a feed additive or water sprinkling agent.

From the perspective of economic benefits, Aeromonas hydrophila infection in aquaculture often causes 20%–50% mortality. The use of T-1 bacterial agent can reduce antibiotic use, lower the risks of drug residues and resistance, and improve the quality of aquatic products. Calculated per mu of pond, the preparation cost of the bacterial agent is about 60% of that of antibiotics, and it can be produced by continuous fermentation, making it suitable for grassroots promotion. From the perspective of ecological benefits, quorum quenching does not directly kill bacteria, causes little disturbance to the microbial community in water, and helps maintain the microecological balance of the aquaculture environment.

4 Conclusion

Bacillus licheniformis T-1 has clear quorum quenching activity, can effectively inhibit the expression of virulence factors in Aeromonas hydrophila, and significantly protect zebrafish against infection. This strain is safe, low-cost, and convenient to use, and is a probiotic with promotional value for aquaculture. Subsequent research can optimize the fermentation process and dosage forms and carry out field trials to verify its actual protective effects on various cultured fish species.

title: The associations of economic growth and anaemia for school-aged children in China
text:
Abstract: Objective: To investigate the association between China's economic growth and the prevalence of anemia among school-aged children, and to provide evidence for formulating public health policies that balance economic development and child health. Methods: Based on the China Health and Nutrition Survey (CHNS) and provincial macroeconomic data, indicators including anemia among school-aged children aged 7-12 years, per capita GDP, urbanization rate, and Engel coefficient from 2010 to 2020 were selected, and a multilevel logistic regression model was used to analyze the association between economic factors and anemia. Results: A total of 12,845 children were included, and the prevalence of anemia decreased from 14.2% in 2010 to 8.6% in 2020. For every 10,000 yuan increase in per capita GDP, the risk of anemia decreased by 18% (OR=0.82, 95%CI: 0.76-0.89); for every 10 percentage point increase in the urbanization rate, the risk of anemia decreased by 12% (OR=0.88, 95%CI: 0.81-0.95). The Engel coefficient was positively associated with anemia (OR=1.14, 95%CI: 1.05-1.24). Conclusion: Economic growth is significantly associated with a decline in the prevalence of anemia among school-aged children, but regional disparities remain, and nutrition interventions need to be strengthened in less developed areas.

Keywords: economic growth; school-aged children; anemia; per capita GDP; urbanization; nutrition transition

 1 Introduction

Anemia is a common nutritional deficiency disease among school-aged children, affecting their cognitive development, immune function, and academic performance. Since the reform and opening up, China's economy has continued to grow, and residents' dietary patterns have undergone significant changes, but the problem of childhood anemia has not been completely eliminated, showing a complex pattern of "decline in economically developed areas, still high in less developed areas." Existing studies have mostly focused on the relationship between household income or a single economic indicator and childhood anemia, lacking a systematic examination of the comprehensive level of provincial economic growth. Using multi-source data from 2010 to 2020, this paper analyzes the association between economic indicators such as per capita GDP, urbanization rate, and Engel coefficient and anemia among school-aged children aged 7-12 years, aiming to provide empirical reference for nutrition improvement policies in the context of "Healthy China 2030."

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Sources

Childhood anemia data were obtained from three rounds of the China Health and Nutrition Survey (CHNS) in 2010, 2015, and 2020. Children aged 7-12 years were selected, and after excluding those with missing hemoglobin and outliers, a total of 12,845 individuals were included. Economic data were obtained from the China Statistical Yearbook and provincial statistical bulletins, including per capita GDP, urbanization rate, Engel coefficient, and per capita disposable income of rural residents.

 2.2 Determination of Anemia

WHO criteria were adopted: hemoglobin <115 g/L for children aged 6-11 years and <120 g/L for those aged 12-14 years were defined as anemia. Hemoglobin was measured by the cyanmethemoglobin method.

 2.3 Statistical Analysis

Anemia (yes=1, no=0) was used as the dependent variable, economic indicators as the core independent variables, and age, sex, BMI, maternal education level, household income, and region as covariates. A multilevel logistic regression model was used, with province as a random intercept, to control for confounding factors at the individual and provincial levels. R 4.2.0 software was used, and a two-sided P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Changes in Anemia Prevalence

From 2010 to 2020, the prevalence of anemia among school-aged children decreased from 14.2% to 8.6%, with an average annual decline of 0.56 percentage points. The eastern region decreased from 9.8% to 5.1%, the central region from 14.6% to 8.9%, and the western region from 19.3% to 12.4%. The prevalence in the western region was consistently higher than that in the eastern and central regions.

 3.2 Univariate Association Between Economic Indicators and Anemia

Per capita GDP, urbanization rate, and per capita disposable income of rural residents were all negatively correlated with anemia prevalence (r=-0.42, -0.38, -0.35, P<0.01); the Engel coefficient was positively correlated with anemia (r=0.31, P<0.01).

 3.3 Multilevel Logistic Regression Results

After controlling for individual characteristics, for every 10,000 yuan increase in per capita GDP, the risk of anemia decreased by 18% (OR=0.82, 95%CI: 0.76-0.89); for every 10 percentage point increase in the urbanization rate, the risk of anemia decreased by 12% (OR=0.88, 95%CI: 0.81-0.95); for every 1-unit increase in the Engel coefficient, the risk of anemia increased by 14% (OR=1.14, 95%CI: 1.05-1.24). Those whose mothers had a high school education or above had a 22% lower risk of anemia (OR=0.78, 95%CI: 0.70-0.87). The risk of anemia in western provinces was 1.43 times that in the eastern region (OR=1.43, 95%CI: 1.21-1.69).

 3.4 Stratified Analysis

Among low-income households, the association between per capita GDP and anemia was stronger (OR=0.74, 95%CI: 0.66-0.83), while among high-income households the association was weaker (OR=0.91, 95%CI: 0.82-1.01). The effect of urbanization on improving anemia was greater for rural children than for urban children.

 4 Discussion

This study found that China's economic growth is significantly associated with a decline in the prevalence of anemia among school-aged children. Per capita GDP and urbanization rate are important protective factors, while the Engel coefficient, which reflects household economic pressure, increases the risk of anemia. This is consistent with the theory of nutrition transition: economic development promotes a more abundant food supply and increased intake of animal-source foods, fruits, and vegetables, thereby improving iron and vitamin C intake and reducing anemia. At the same time, urbanization brings improved access to health services and the dissemination of nutrition knowledge, which also helps control anemia.

However, the health dividends of economic growth are not evenly distributed. The risk of anemia remains higher among children in the western region, low-income households, and those whose mothers have lower education levels, suggesting that growth in total economic output alone is insufficient to eliminate nutritional inequality. Possible reasons include: the dietary structure in rural western areas is still dominated by grains, with insufficient intake of heme iron; although some households have increased income, they lack nutrition knowledge, leading to the persistence of "hidden hunger." In addition, rapid urbanization may be accompanied by increased consumption of fast food and processed foods, which may adversely affect iron nutrition in some children.

Compared with previous studies, the advantage of this paper lies in simultaneously incorporating per capita GDP, urbanization rate, and Engel coefficient, and controlling for provincial differences from a multilevel perspective. Limitations include: the CHNS data are not from consecutive years, which may miss short-term fluctuations; anemia was not differentiated into iron deficiency and non-iron deficiency; and the economic indicators are at the provincial level, resulting in ecological bias.

Policy implications: First, continue to promote child nutrition improvement programs in western and rural areas, such as free iron supplementation and nutrition packets; second, incorporate nutrition education into primary public health services, especially for households with mothers of lower education levels; third, build a healthy food environment in parallel with urbanization and restrict the marketing of high-sugar, high-fat, low-iron foods; fourth, establish a joint monitoring system for the economy and health to dynamically assess the quality of growth.

 5 Conclusion

From 2010 to 2020, the prevalence of anemia among school-aged children in China declined significantly. Increases in per capita GDP and urbanization rate were associated with a lower risk of anemia, while an increase in the Engel coefficient was associated with a higher risk of anemia. Economic growth has a positive effect on improving childhood anemia, but disparities across regions and households remain. It is recommended that, while maintaining economic development, targeted nutrition interventions be implemented to promote equity in child health.

title: Thymic T-Cell Production Is Associated With Changes in the Gut Microbiota in Young Chicks
text:
Relationship Between Thymic T Cell Generation and Changes in the Gut Microbiota of Chicks

Abstract: This study aimed to investigate the interrelationship between thymic T cell generation and the gut microbiota in chicks. Thymic tissues and cecal contents were collected from chicks at different ages, the proportions of T cell subsets in the thymus were detected by flow cytometry, and the gut microbial composition was analyzed using 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing technology. The results showed that with increasing age of chicks, the proportions of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the thymus increased significantly, while gut microbial diversity gradually increased. The abundance of beneficial bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium was positively correlated with T cell generation, whereas some potentially pathogenic bacteria such as Shigella were negatively correlated with T cell proportions. Further validation through antibiotic treatment and fecal microbiota transplantation experiments confirmed that alterations in the gut microbiota could significantly affect thymic T cell output. This study demonstrates that thymic T cell generation in chicks is closely related to changes in the gut microbiota, and that gut microorganisms can influence early immune capacity of chicks by regulating immune development. The findings provide a theoretical basis for promoting poultry immune health through microecological preparations.

1 Introduction

After hatching, the immune system of chicks is still in a stage of rapid development. In particular, the thymus, as the central immune organ for T cell differentiation and maturation, undergoes significant structural and functional changes within weeks after birth. T cells undergo positive selection and negative selection in the thymus, ultimately forming CD4+ helper T cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells with immune defense functions. This process is not only regulated by genetic factors but is also significantly influenced by external environmental factors.

In recent years, numerous studies have shown that the gut microbiota plays a key role in the development of the host immune system. Gut microorganisms and their metabolites can interact with host immune cells through multiple pathways. For example, short-chain fatty acids can promote regulatory T cell differentiation, and microbial antigens can stimulate the development of gut-associated lymphoid tissues. However, research on whether and how the gut microbiota affects T cell generation in central immune organs (especially the thymus) remains insufficient in poultry. As important economic animals, the early immune capacity of chicks is directly related to survival rate and later production performance. Therefore, exploring the association between thymic T cell generation and the gut microbiota in chicks is of great significance for understanding the mechanisms of poultry immune development and developing microecology-based immune enhancement strategies.

This study used chicks at different ages as subjects, combined flow cytometry with 16S rRNA sequencing technology to systematically analyze the relationship between changes in thymic T cell subsets and gut microbial composition, and verified causality through intervention experiments, aiming to reveal the potential mechanisms by which gut microorganisms regulate thymic T cell generation in chicks.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Experimental Animals and Sample Collection

A total of 120 healthy and active AA broiler chicks from the same hatching batch were selected and randomly divided into 4 groups, with 30 chicks per group, and sampled at 1, 7, 14, and 21 days of age, respectively. Ten chicks were randomly selected from each group, weighed, and sacrificed by jugular vein exsanguination. Thymic tissues were rapidly removed under aseptic conditions and placed in pre-cooled RPMI-1640 medium for later use. Meanwhile, cecal contents were collected, immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and transferred to -80°C for storage for microbial DNA extraction. All procedures followed animal ethics guidelines.

2.2 Flow Cytometry Detection of Thymic T Cell Subsets

Thymic tissues were minced and ground through a 200-mesh sieve to prepare single-cell suspensions. Red blood cells were removed using red blood cell lysis buffer, and the cell concentration was adjusted to 1×10^7/mL. Anti-chicken CD4-FITC and anti-chicken CD8-PE fluorescently labeled antibodies were added separately, followed by incubation at 4°C in the dark for 30 minutes. After washing with PBS, the proportions of CD4+ and CD8+ cells were detected by flow cytometry. At least 1×10^4 cell events were collected per sample, and data were analyzed using FlowJo software. The results showed that the proportions of CD4+ and CD8+ cells in the thymus of 1-day-old chicks were relatively low, at (12.3±1.8)% and (8.7±1.2)%, respectively; by 21 days of age, these increased to (34.6±3.1)% and (26.4±2.7)%, respectively, indicating that thymic T cell output increased significantly with age.

2.3 16S rRNA High-Throughput Sequencing of Gut Microbiota

Total DNA was extracted from cecal contents using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit, and PCR amplification was performed with primers designed for the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene. After purification and quantification, the products were subjected to paired-end sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform. Raw sequences were quality-controlled and chimera-removed through the QIIME2 pipeline, clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs), and compared with the Silva database for species annotation. Alpha diversity indices such as Chao1 and Shannon were calculated, and beta diversity was assessed by principal coordinate analysis (PCoA). The results showed that with increasing age, the Chao1 index of the gut microbiota of chicks increased from (215±32) at 1 day of age to (487±45) at 21 days of age, and the Shannon index also increased significantly (P<0.05). At the genus level, the abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium was significantly positively correlated with the proportions of thymic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (r>0.6, P<0.01), while the abundance of Shigella was negatively correlated with T cell proportions (r=-0.52, P<0.05).

2.4 Antibiotic Treatment and Fecal Microbiota Transplantation Validation

To verify causality, twenty 14-day-old chicks were selected and randomly divided into two groups: the control group received normal drinking water, and the antibiotic group received enrofloxacin (10 mg/kg) in drinking water for 5 consecutive days. The results showed that the proportions of thymic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the antibiotic group decreased to (21.5±2.4)% and (16.8±1.9)%, respectively, significantly lower than those in the control group (P<0.05). Meanwhile, gut microbial diversity was significantly reduced, and Lactobacillus almost disappeared. Subsequently, a fecal microbiota transplantation experiment was conducted on another batch of 14-day-old chicks: a suspension of cecal contents from healthy adult chickens was orally administered to the chicks for 3 consecutive days. The results showed that the proportion of thymic T cells in the transplantation group increased by approximately 18% compared with the non-transplantation group, and the abundance of Lactobacillus in the gut recovered. This further confirmed that changes in the gut microbiota can directly affect thymic T cell generation.

2.5 Preliminary Exploration of Microbial Metabolites and Immune Regulatory Pathways

Cecal contents from chicks at different ages were collected, and short-chain fatty acid content was detected using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. The results showed that the concentrations of acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid increased with age and were positively correlated with thymic T cell proportions. In vitro experiments showed that sodium butyrate could promote chick thymocyte proliferation and upregulate IL-2 and IFN-γ expression. This suggests that gut microorganisms may reach the thymus through the bloodstream via their metabolite short-chain fatty acids, regulating signaling pathways related to T cell development.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

The main results of this study can be summarized in three points: First, thymic T cell generation in chicks increases with age, with CD4+ and CD8+ T cell proportions reaching relatively high levels at 21 days of age; Second, gut microbial diversity and the abundance of specific bacterial genera are significantly correlated with thymic T cell proportions, with Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium as positively associated bacteria and Shigella as a negatively associated bacterium; Third, antibiotic treatment and fecal microbiota transplantation experiments confirmed that changes in the gut microbiota can causally affect thymic T cell output, and short-chain fatty acids may be important mediating factors.

From the perspective of application benefits, this study provides new ideas for immune regulation in poultry farming. Traditionally, early immunity of chicks mainly relies on vaccines and biosecurity measures, but vaccine efficacy is often limited by immature immune system development. This study demonstrates that by regulating the gut microbiota (such as adding probiotics, prebiotics, or fecal microbiota transplantation), thymic T cell generation can be promoted, thereby enhancing the resistance of chicks to pathogens. This helps reduce antibiotic use, lower the risk of drug residues and antimicrobial resistance, and aligns with the trend of green farming development. In addition, the findings can provide targets for the development of microecological preparations, such as screening composite preparations that can promote Lactobacillus colonization and increase short-chain fatty acid production, for use as additives in chick starter feed or drinking water. It is estimated that such measures can reduce early mortality by 5%-10% and improve feed conversion rate by 3%-5%, with favorable economic returns.

4 Conclusion

Through multi-age chick sampling, flow cytometry, 16S rRNA sequencing, and intervention experiments, this study systematically revealed the close association between thymic T cell generation and changes in the gut microbiota. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) The proportions of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the chick thymus increased significantly with age; (2) Gut microbial diversity and the abundance of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium were positively correlated with T cell generation, while Shigella was negatively correlated; (3) Antibiotic treatment reduced microbial diversity and inhibited T cell generation, and fecal microbiota transplantation could partially restore it; (4) Short-chain fatty acids may be important mediators through which microorganisms regulate thymic T cell development. This study provides a theoretical basis and technical reference for enhancing chick immune capacity through microecological approaches, and it is recommended that further large-scale validation and preparation optimization studies be conducted to promote the practical application of the results in poultry production.

title: Co-Amended Synergistic Interactions between Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi and the Organic Substrate-Induced Cucumber Yield and Fruit Quality Associated with the Regulation of the AM-Fungal Community Structure under Anthropogenic Cultivated Soil
text:
Synergistic Effects of Combined Application of Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi and Organic Substrate on Cucumber Yield and Fruit Quality in Anthropogenically Cultivated Soil and Their Relationship with the Regulation of AM Fungal Community Structure

Abstract: To investigate the synergistic mechanisms of combined application of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and organic substrate on cucumber yield and fruit quality in anthropogenically cultivated soil, this study used 'Jinyou 35' cucumber as the experimental material and established four treatments: conventional fertilization (CK), AMF alone (M), organic substrate alone (O), and combined AMF + organic substrate application (MO). Cucumber yield, fruit quality, and AM fungal community structure were analyzed. The results showed that the MO treatment significantly increased per-plant yield by 42.6% compared with CK, and the contents of soluble sugar, vitamin C, and soluble protein in fruits increased by 28.3%, 35.7%, and 22.4%, respectively, while nitrate content decreased by 31.2%. High-throughput sequencing revealed that the Shannon index and Chao1 index of soil AM fungi under the MO treatment increased by 19.4% and 23.7%, respectively, compared with CK, and the relative abundance of the genus Glomus increased significantly. Redundancy analysis indicated that soil organic matter and available phosphorus were the key factors driving the variation in AM fungal communities. In summary, the combined application of AMF and organic substrate achieved synergistic improvement of cucumber yield and quality by optimizing AM fungal community structure and improving the soil microenvironment.

Keywords: arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi; organic substrate; cucumber; yield; fruit quality; community structure

1 Introduction

Cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.) is one of the vegetable crops with the largest protected cultivation area in China, and its yield and quality are directly related to the economic benefits of farmers and consumer health. However, long-term anthropogenic cultivation has led to soil degradation and reduced microbial diversity, with frequent continuous cropping obstacles, severely restricting sustainable cucumber production. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) can form symbioses with the root systems of the vast majority of terrestrial plants, improving crop growth by expanding the root absorption area, promoting the uptake of mineral elements such as phosphorus, and enhancing stress resistance. Organic substrate is rich in humus and beneficial microorganisms and can improve soil structure and increase nutrient availability. In recent years, the synergistic effects of combined application of AMF and organic materials have been reported in crops such as tomato and pepper, but studies on cucumber have mostly focused on single factors, and the regulatory mechanisms by which their combined application affects AM fungal community structure remain unclear. This study hypothesized that the combined application of AMF and organic substrate could synergistically enhance cucumber yield and fruit quality by reshaping AM fungal community structure. To this end, a field microplot experiment was established to investigate the synergistic effects of their combined application and the underlying microbiological mechanisms, providing a theoretical basis for high-quality and high-yield cultivation of cucumber in anthropogenically cultivated soil.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Overview of the Experimental Site

The experiment was conducted from March to July 2023 at a protected vegetable base in Shouguang City, Shandong Province. The test soil was fluvo-aquic soil, with the following basic physicochemical properties: pH 7.82, organic matter 14.3 g·kg⁻¹, alkaline hydrolyzable nitrogen 86.5 mg·kg⁻¹, available phosphorus 32.7 mg·kg⁻¹, and available potassium 118.4 mg·kg⁻¹. The previous crop was cucumber, with four years of continuous cropping.

2.2 Experimental Design

A randomized block design was adopted, with four treatments, three replicates per treatment, and a plot area of 6 m². CK: conventional fertilization (urea 300 kg·hm⁻², superphosphate 150 kg·hm⁻², potassium sulfate 200 kg·hm⁻²); M: conventional fertilization + AMF inoculant (Glomus mosseae, inoculation amount 50 g·plant⁻¹); O: conventional fertilization + organic substrate (decomposed cow manure and straw mixed at 3:1, application rate 15 t·hm⁻²); MO: conventional fertilization + AMF + organic substrate. The cucumber variety was 'Jinyou 35', transplanted on March 10, 2023, at a density of 3.5 plants·m⁻², with conventional field management.

2.3 Measurement Items and Methods

Yield and quality: cumulative per-plant yield at the full fruiting stage; soluble sugar was determined by the anthrone colorimetric method, vitamin C by the 2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol titration method, soluble protein by the Coomassie brilliant blue G-250 method, and nitrate by the salicylic acid nitration method.

Soil AM fungal community: rhizosphere soil was collected at the full fruiting stage, total DNA was extracted by the CTAB method, the 18S rRNA gene was amplified with AMV4.5NF/AMDGR primers, Illumina MiSeq sequencing was performed, and community diversity and composition were analyzed using QIIME2.

2.4 Data Processing

One-way analysis of variance (Duncan's method, P<0.05) was performed using SPSS 26.0, and redundancy analysis (RDA) was conducted using Canoco 5.0.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Effects of Different Treatments on Cucumber Yield

The per-plant yield under the MO treatment reached 2.81 kg, significantly increasing by 42.6% compared with CK (1.97 kg) (P<0.05); the M and O treatments increased by 18.3% and 24.9%, respectively, compared with CK, both reaching significant levels. MO increased by 20.5% and 14.2% compared with M and O, respectively, indicating that the combined application of the two had a synergistic effect.

3.2 Effects of Different Treatments on Cucumber Fruit Quality

The contents of soluble sugar, vitamin C, and soluble protein in fruits under the MO treatment were 3.72%, 18.6 mg·100g⁻¹, and 1.86 mg·g⁻¹, respectively, increasing by 28.3%, 35.7%, and 22.4% compared with CK, with significant differences; the nitrate content was 86.4 mg·kg⁻¹, decreasing by 31.2% compared with CK. The quality indicators of the M and O treatments were also superior to CK, but both were lower than the MO treatment.

3.3 Effects of Different Treatments on AM Fungal Community Diversity and Composition

The Shannon index and Chao1 index of soil AM fungi under the MO treatment were 3.21 and 186.4, respectively, significantly increasing by 19.4% and 23.7% compared with CK (2.69 and 150.7). At the genus level, the relative abundance of the genus Glomus under the MO treatment reached 62.3%, significantly increasing compared with CK (41.5%); while the abundance of the genus Paraglomus decreased. The diversity indices of the M and O treatments were between those of CK and MO.

3.4 Redundancy Analysis of AM Fungal Community and Soil Factors

The RDA results showed that the first two axes cumulatively explained 71.3% of the community variation. Soil organic matter (r²=0.682) and available phosphorus (r²=0.594) were the key environmental factors driving the variation in AM fungal community structure (P<0.05). The soil organic matter and available phosphorus contents under the MO treatment increased by 31.5% and 26.8%, respectively, compared with CK.

4 Discussion

This study showed that the combined application of AMF and organic substrate had significantly better effects on improving cucumber yield and quality than single application, exhibiting an obvious synergistic effect. This may originate from the following mechanisms: First, the organic substrate provides carbon sources and colonization sites for AMF, promoting the expansion of hyphal networks and enhancing the uptake of nutrients such as phosphorus; second, AMF secrete glomalin-related soil protein, improving soil aggregate structure and, in synergy with the organic substrate, enhancing soil water and fertilizer retention capacity. In terms of quality improvement, AMF promote the allocation of photosynthates to fruits, and the medium and trace elements released by the organic substrate participate in sugar metabolism and vitamin synthesis, jointly regulating the formation of fruit quality.

High-throughput sequencing revealed that the combined application treatment significantly increased AM fungal community diversity and the abundance of the genus Glomus. The genus Glomus is a known highly efficient growth-promoting microbial group, and its increased abundance was significantly positively correlated with cucumber yield (r=0.78, P<0.01). RDA analysis further indicated that soil organic matter and available phosphorus were the core factors driving the variation in community structure, indicating that the combined application indirectly regulated the AM fungal community by improving soil physicochemical properties, forming a positive feedback loop of "soil improvement—microbial community optimization—crop yield increase." This study provides a new approach for microbial regulation of anthropogenically cultivated soil, but the optimal ratio and long-term effects of combined application of AMF and organic substrate still require further research.

5 Conclusion

The combined application of AMF and organic substrate significantly improved cucumber yield and fruit quality by synergistically optimizing AM fungal community structure, and its mechanism is closely related to increasing soil organic matter and available phosphorus contents and increasing the abundance of the genus Glomus. This measure can serve as an effective technical approach for high-quality and high-yield cultivation of cucumber in anthropogenically cultivated soil.

title: Effects of rumen cannulation on dissolved gases and methanogen community in dairy cows
text:
Effects of Rumen Fistulation on Dissolved Gases and Methanogen Communities in Dairy Cows

Abstract: To investigate the effects of rumen fistula installation on the rumen internal environment and methanogen communities in dairy cows, six healthy Holstein dairy cows were selected and divided into a control group (without fistula) and an experimental group (with rumen fistula). Gas chromatography was used to determine the concentrations of dissolved gases (hydrogen, methane, carbon dioxide) in rumen fluid, and high-throughput sequencing technology was employed to analyze the methanogen community structure. The results showed that after fistula installation, the concentrations of dissolved hydrogen and methane in rumen fluid were significantly increased (P<0.05), while the carbon dioxide concentration showed no significant change (P>0.05); the methanogen community diversity indices (Shannon, Chao1) were significantly decreased (P<0.05), but the relative abundance of the dominant genus *Methanobrevibacter* was significantly increased (P<0.05). The dry matter intake and milk yield of cows in the experimental group decreased by 4.2% and 3.8%, respectively (P<0.05). The study indicates that rumen fistula installation alters the dissolved gas balance and methanogen community structure in the rumen, and its potential impact on dairy cow production performance must be fully considered in extension and application.

Keywords: rumen fistula; dairy cow; dissolved gases; methanogens; high-throughput sequencing

 1 Introduction

Rumen fistula technology is an indispensable tool in ruminant nutrition research. Through the fistula, rumen contents can be collected dynamically over the long term for studying feed degradation patterns, microbial flora changes, and rumen metabolic regulation. Since its first application in sheep in the 1920s, this technology has been widely used in scientific research and production practices for ruminants such as dairy cows and beef cattle. However, fistula installation is an invasive surgical procedure that inevitably interferes with the rumen internal environment, including disruption of rumen wall integrity, alteration of microbial flora, and disturbance of gas metabolism.

The dissolved gases in the rumen mainly include hydrogen (H₂), methane (CH₄), and carbon dioxide (CO₂). They are important products of rumen fermentation and also the direct substrates and products of methanogen metabolism. Methanogens, as a group of strictly anaerobic archaea in the rumen, utilize H₂ and CO₂ or substrates such as formate to produce CH₄, and play a key role in maintaining low hydrogen partial pressure in the rumen and promoting fiber degradation. Fistula installation may interfere with the dissolved gas balance and methanogen community by altering the rumen physical structure, affecting gas diffusion rates, and changing microbial attachment sites.

Currently, there have been a few reports on the effects of fistulation on rumen fermentation parameters, but most have focused on indicators such as volatile fatty acids and ammonia nitrogen, and systematic studies on dissolved gases and methanogen communities remain insufficient. In particular, in technology extension journals, there is an urgent need to clarify the potential side effects of fistula installation to provide references for research design and production application. This study used Holstein dairy cows as subjects to systematically analyze the effects of fistula installation on rumen dissolved gas concentrations and methanogen community structure, and to evaluate its effects on production performance, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for the scientific application of rumen fistula technology.

 2 Key Technical Analysis

 2.1 Rumen Fistula Installation Surgery and Postoperative Management

Cows in the experimental group underwent permanent rumen fistula installation surgery. They were fasted for 24 h and deprived of water for 12 h before surgery, and atropine (0.02 mg/kg) was injected intramuscularly to reduce saliva secretion. The surgery was performed on the left flank. After local infiltration anesthesia, the skin, external oblique muscle, internal oblique muscle, and transverse abdominal muscle were incised to expose the rumen wall. The fistula base was sutured and fixed to the rumen wall, the abdominal cavity was closed layer by layer, and the outer opening of the fistula was fixed to the skin. Penicillin (8 million IU/d) and streptomycin (5 g/d) were injected continuously for 7 d after surgery to prevent infection. The fistula opening was flushed daily with warm water, and wound healing was observed. Sample collection began 2 weeks after surgery to ensure that the cows had recovered to normal feed intake levels. Cows in the control group did not undergo any surgical procedure and were housed in the same environment.

 2.2 Rumen Fluid Collection and Dissolved Gas Determination

Rumen fluid was collected using the stomach tube method. At 2 h after morning feeding, a stomach tube was inserted through the oral cavity to the middle of the rumen, and approximately 50 mL of rumen fluid was withdrawn and immediately transferred to a pre-evacuated sealed bottle, placed in an ice bath, and brought back to the laboratory. Dissolved gas determination used the headspace equilibrium method: 10 mL of rumen fluid was injected into a 20 mL headspace vial, 0.5 mL of saturated mercuric chloride solution was added to inhibit microbial activity, and after sealing, the vial was shaken at 37 °C for 30 min to equilibrate. The headspace gas was then extracted and injected into a gas chromatograph (GC-2010 Plus, Shimadzu, Japan) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a Porapak Q packed column to determine H₂, CH₄, and CO₂ concentrations. Each sample was measured in triplicate, and the average value was taken.

 2.3 High-Throughput Sequencing Analysis of Methanogen Communities

One mL of rumen fluid sample was taken, and total DNA was extracted using the FastDNA SPIN Kit for Soil. The primer pair Met86F (5′-GCTCAGTAACACGTGG-3′) and Met1340R (5′-CGGTGTGTGCAAGGAG-3′) was used to amplify the V3-V4 region of the methanogen 16S rRNA gene. After purification and quantification, the PCR products were subjected to paired-end sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform. After quality control and chimera removal using QIIME2 software, the raw sequences were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at 97% similarity, and species annotation was performed using the Silva database. The Shannon, Chao1, and Simpson indices were calculated to analyze community diversity and composition.

 2.4 Determination of Production Performance Indicators

The dry matter intake (DMI) of cows in each group was recorded daily for 14 consecutive days. Milk yield was recorded through the automatic metering system in the milking parlor, and milk samples were collected during the same period. Milk fat percentage, milk protein percentage, and lactose content were determined using a milk composition analyzer. The yield of 4% fat-corrected milk (FCM) was calculated. All data were analyzed using SPSS 22.0 software with independent-sample t-tests, and P<0.05 was considered a significant difference.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

 3.1 Changes in Rumen Dissolved Gas Concentrations

As shown in Table 1, the dissolved H₂ concentration in rumen fluid of the experimental group was significantly higher than that of the control group (P<0.05), increasing from 0.42 mmol/L to 0.68 mmol/L, an increase of 61.9%; the dissolved CH₄ concentration increased from 0.87 mmol/L to 1.24 mmol/L, an increase of 42.5% (P<0.05). There was no significant difference in CO₂ concentration between the two groups (P>0.05), which were 12.6 mmol/L and 13.1 mmol/L, respectively. The synchronous increase in H₂ and CH₄ concentrations indicates that fistula installation may reduce the efficiency of gas expulsion from the rumen, leading to the accumulation of reducing gases in the liquid phase. The fistula base occupies part of the rumen wall area, which may affect the transmission of rumen contraction waves and weaken gas transport to the cardia region; at the same time, the fibrotic tissue formed around the fistula may alter the local gas diffusion gradient.

Table 1 Comparison of rumen dissolved gas concentrations between the two groups of dairy cows (mmol/L)

| Indicator | Control group | Experimental group | P value |
|------|--------|--------|-----|
| H₂   | 0.42±0.06 | 0.68±0.09 | 0.021 |
| CH₄  | 0.87±0.11 | 1.24±0.15 | 0.013 |
| CO₂  | 12.6±1.4 | 13.1±1.6 | 0.472 |

 3.2 Methanogen Community Diversity and Composition

A total of 1,286,432 valid sequences were obtained by high-throughput sequencing, with an average of 107,203 sequences per sample. Clustering at 97% similarity yielded a total of 342 OTUs. The Shannon index of the control group was 3.86±0.21, and that of the experimental group decreased to 3.12±0.18 (P<0.05); the Chao1 index decreased from 287±24 in the control group to 213±19 in the experimental group (P<0.05), indicating that fistula installation significantly reduced methanogen community diversity. There was no significant difference in the Simpson index between the two groups (P>0.05), indicating that the concentration of dominant flora did not undergo a fundamental change.

At the genus level, both groups had *Methanobrevibacter* as the absolute dominant genus, but its relative abundance in the experimental group increased from 68.3% in the control group to 79.6% (P<0.05). The relative abundances of *Methanosphaera* and *Methanomassiliicoccus* decreased by 42.1% and 35.7%, respectively (P<0.05). *Methanobrevibacter* is mostly hydrogenotrophic methanogens, and the increase in its abundance was consistent with the elevated H₂ concentration, indicating that this genus is more sensitive to changes in rumen H₂ partial pressure and rapidly occupies the ecological niche under fistula interference. In contrast, *Methanosphaera* and *Methanomassiliicoccus* mostly utilize methyl compounds or formate, and the decrease in their abundance may be related to fistula-induced changes in rumen methyl substrate supply.

 3.3 Changes in Production Performance

The dry matter intake of cows in the experimental group was 18.6 kg/d, a decrease of 4.2% compared with the control group (19.4 kg/d) (P<0.05); milk yield decreased from 28.4 kg/d to 27.3 kg/d, a decrease of 3.8% (P<0.05); 4% FCM yield decreased from 26.8 kg/d to 25.5 kg/d (P<0.05). There were no significant differences in milk fat percentage, milk protein percentage, or lactose content between the two groups (P>0.05). The decrease in feed intake may be related to chronic stress caused by fistula installation, weakened rumen motility, and mild digestive dysfunction. Although the fistula itself does not directly interfere with feeding behavior, postoperative pain and changes in the rumen internal environment may inhibit the appetite center through neuro-endocrine pathways.

 3.4 Technical Benefits and Risk Analysis

From the perspective of research benefits, rumen fistula provides an irreplaceable window for long-term dynamic monitoring of rumen fermentation. This study shows that after fistula installation, dissolved H₂ and CH₄ concentrations increased and methanogen diversity decreased, suggesting that caution and correction are needed when extrapolating fistula data to normal herds. For example, when evaluating methane mitigation strategies, fistulated cows may overestimate the response magnitude of methanogens to inhibitors. From the perspective of production benefits, fistula installation led to a small decrease in DMI and milk yield. Based on a daily milk loss of 1.1 kg per cow and a milk price of 3.5 yuan/kg, the annual economic loss is approximately 1,400 yuan per cow. Therefore, it is recommended to use fistulated cows only in necessary research scenarios, and postoperative nutritional regulation should be strengthened, such as adding rumen buffers or yeast culture, to alleviate gas metabolism disorders.

 4 Conclusion

This study systematically revealed the significant effects of rumen fistula installation on rumen dissolved gases and methanogen communities in dairy cows. Fistula installation resulted in increases of 61.9% and 42.5% in dissolved H₂ and CH₄ concentrations, respectively, significantly reduced methanogen Shannon and Chao1 indices, increased the abundance of the dominant genus *Methanobrevibacter*, and was accompanied by small decreases in dry matter intake and milk yield. These changes suggest that fistula installation is not merely an "observation window" but an active intervention in the rumen ecosystem. In research design, non-fistulated control groups should be set up to correct systematic errors; in production extension, the research value and economic cost need to be weighed, and nutritional regulation measures should be adopted to mitigate negative effects. Future studies may explore minimally invasive fistula techniques or non-invasive gas monitoring methods to reduce interference with dairy cow welfare and production performance.

title: Natural variation at OsCERK1 regulates arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis in rice
text:
Natural variation at OsCERK1 regulates arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis in rice

Abstract: Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) symbiosis is an important pathway for rice to acquire mineral nutrients such as phosphorus. However, the natural variation in AM symbiosis efficiency among rice germplasm and its genetic basis remain unclear. In this study, 312 rice mini-core germplasm accessions were used to evaluate AM colonization rate and mycorrhizal dependency under low-phosphorus field conditions, and a key regulatory locus was identified through genome-wide association study (GWAS). The results showed that a 12-bp insertion/deletion (InDel) in the OsCERK1 promoter region was significantly associated with AM colonization rate (P = 3.17 × 10⁻⁸). This InDel affects the expression level of OsCERK1 in roots, thereby regulating the transcription of downstream symbiotic signaling pathway genes OsMYC2, OsRAM1, and OsPT11. Rice materials carrying the short-fragment allele (OsCERK1^S) showed an 18.6%–27.3% increase in AM colonization rate, a 14.2%–22.8% increase in plant phosphorus accumulation, and an 8.4%–12.1% increase in yield under low-phosphorus conditions. Haplotype analysis revealed that OsCERK1^S is mainly distributed in the indica subspecies and has been under mild selection in modern breeding. This study reveals the molecular mechanism by which natural variation at OsCERK1 regulates AM symbiosis in rice, providing a new target for breeding green and high-efficiency rice varieties.

Keywords: rice; arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis; OsCERK1; natural variation; genome-wide association study; phosphorus efficiency

 1 Introduction

Arbuscular mycorrhiza (AM) is a mutualistic symbiosis formed between terrestrial plants and fungi of the phylum Glomeromycota. AM fungi expand the host plant's nutrient uptake range for phosphorus, zinc, nitrogen, and other nutrients through extraradical hyphal networks, while obtaining carbon sources from the host. Rice (Oryza sativa L.), as one of the most important food crops worldwide, can still form symbiosis with AM fungi under flooded conditions, and especially in dry direct-seeded and low-phosphorus soils, the contribution of AM symbiosis to rice nutrient acquisition and yield formation can reach 10%–30%. Therefore, mining the natural variation in AM symbiosis efficiency in rice and dissecting its genetic basis is of great significance for reducing phosphorus fertilizer input and achieving green agricultural development.

Plant recognition of AM fungal signals depends on a conserved symbiotic signaling pathway. In legumes, the LysM receptor kinase CERK1 together with NFR1/NFR5 participates in chitin oligosaccharide signal perception. The rice genome contains only one CERK1 homolog, OsCERK1, which encodes a LysM receptor kinase that has been demonstrated to be a common key factor for both AM symbiosis and blast disease resistance. Loss-of-function mutants of OsCERK1 (oscerk1) completely lose AM colonization ability, while blast disease resistance is significantly reduced. However, allelic variation of OsCERK1 in natural germplasm and its regulatory role in AM symbiosis efficiency have not been systematically reported.

This study hypothesizes that natural variation at the rice OsCERK1 locus regulates AM symbiosis efficiency. To test this hypothesis, we used 312 rice mini-core germplasm accessions to evaluate AM colonization rate and mycorrhizal dependency under low-phosphorus field conditions, conducted a genome-wide association study, and performed functional validation of candidate loci. The results will provide a theoretical basis and genetic resources for mycorrhiza-efficient rice breeding.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Plant materials and field experiments

The materials used were 312 rice mini-core germplasm accessions from China, Southeast Asia, and South Asia, including 156 indica, 118 japonica, and 38 aus/other subgroup accessions. Experiments were conducted at the experimental base of the Guangdong Academy of Agricultural Sciences during 2021–2022. The soil was lateritic red soil with available phosphorus content of 6.8 mg·kg⁻¹ (low phosphorus). A randomized complete block design was used, with 3 rows per material, row spacing of 25 cm, plant spacing of 20 cm, and 3 replications. No phosphorus fertilizer was applied throughout the growth period, and nitrogen and potassium fertilizers were managed conventionally. Dry direct-seeded cultivation was used to promote AM colonization.

 2.2 Determination of AM colonization rate and mycorrhizal dependency

Root samples were collected at the peak tillering stage, and AM colonization rate was determined using the trypan blue staining method. Thirty root segments per sample were examined microscopically, and colonization rate was calculated using the gridline intersect method. Mycorrhizal dependency (MD) was defined as: MD = (biomass_AM − biomass_NM) / biomass_NM × 100%, where AM represents the inoculated treatment and NM represents the non-inoculated control. Pot experiments used sterilized soil, with 200 Glomus intraradices spores added per pot for the inoculated treatment.

 2.3 Genome-wide association study

Leaf DNA was extracted using the CTAB method, and genotyping was performed using the rice 55K SNP chip. After filtering, 42,318 high-quality SNPs were retained. Population structure was analyzed using ADMIXTURE, and the kinship matrix was calculated using SPAGeDi. GWAS was performed using a mixed linear model (MLM) with the first principal component and kinship matrix as covariates. The significance threshold was set at P < 1 × 10⁻⁶.

 2.4 Gene expression and haplotype analysis

Root samples were collected at 7 d, 14 d, and 21 d after inoculation, total RNA was extracted, and after reverse transcription, qRT-PCR was used to detect the expression levels of OsCERK1, OsMYC2, OsRAM1, and OsPT11, with OsUBQ5 as the internal reference. The OsCERK1 promoter region was amplified and sequenced to identify InDel variation. Haplotype networks were constructed using NETWORK 10.0.

 2.5 Transgenic validation

A vector with the OsCERK1 promoter driving the GUS reporter gene was constructed and transformed into calli carrying the long-fragment (OsCERK1^L) and short-fragment (OsCERK1^S) alleles, respectively. Meanwhile, CRISPR/Cas9 was used to knock out OsCERK1, and AM colonization phenotypes were observed.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Natural variation in AM symbiosis efficiency in rice

The AM colonization rate among the 312 accessions ranged from 12.4% to 68.7%, with a mean of 38.2%, and broad-sense heritability of 0.72. The average colonization rate of the indica subgroup (42.6%) was significantly higher than that of japonica (31.8%) (P < 0.01). Mycorrhizal dependency ranged from 5.2% to 34.8% and was significantly positively correlated with colonization rate (r = 0.68, P < 0.001). Under low-phosphorus conditions, the phosphorus accumulation of high-colonization materials was 21.4% higher than that of low-colonization materials.

 3.2 GWAS identified the OsCERK1 locus

GWAS detected a signal significantly associated with AM colonization rate at 27.3 Mb on chromosome 3 (P = 3.17 × 10⁻⁸), explaining 14.6% of the phenotypic variation. This region contains the OsCERK1 gene. Further analysis revealed a 12-bp InDel (5′-CGTACGATCGAT-3′) at −1,248 bp in the OsCERK1 promoter region. The short-fragment allele (OsCERK1^S) was significantly associated with high colonization rate (P = 1.24 × 10⁻⁷).

 3.3 OsCERK1 allelic variation regulates gene expression

qRT-PCR results showed that after AM fungal inoculation, OsCERK1 expression in roots of materials carrying OsCERK1^S was 2.1-fold, 1.8-fold, and 1.6-fold higher than that in OsCERK1^L materials at 7 d, 14 d, and 21 d, respectively. The expression levels of downstream symbiotic signaling genes OsMYC2, OsRAM1, and the phosphorus transporter gene OsPT11 were also significantly upregulated (P < 0.05). GUS staining showed that GUS activity driven by the OsCERK1^S promoter was markedly stronger in root cortical cells than that driven by OsCERK1^L.

 3.4 Functional validation of OsCERK1

CRISPR/Cas9 knockout lines (oscerk1) had an AM colonization rate of 0%, and plants were dwarfed with yellowed leaves. In complementation experiments, when the OsCERK1 coding region driven by the OsCERK1^S promoter was introduced into the oscerk1 mutant, the colonization rate recovered to 92.4% of wild type; while the complementation line with the OsCERK1^L promoter recovered to only 68.7%. This indicates that the OsCERK1^S allele has a stronger symbiosis-promoting effect.

 3.5 Haplotype distribution and breeding selection

Among the 312 accessions, the allele frequency of OsCERK1^S was 47.8%, including 62.3% in indica and 28.1% in japonica. The haplotype network showed that OsCERK1^S is an ancient haplotype. Analysis of 86 major cultivars bred from 1970 to 2020 revealed that the frequency of OsCERK1^S increased from 31.4% to 52.3%, indicating that this allele has been under positive selection in modern breeding.

 3.6 Field yield performance

Under low-phosphorus conditions, cultivars carrying OsCERK1^S had an average yield of 6.84 t·hm⁻², which was 11.8% higher than that of OsCERK1^L cultivars (6.12 t·hm⁻²). Under normal phosphorus conditions, the yield difference between the two was not significant (P > 0.05). This indicates that the yield-increasing effect of OsCERK1^S depends on a low-phosphorus environment.

 4 Discussion

This study systematically reveals for the first time the regulatory role of natural variation in the rice OsCERK1 promoter region on AM symbiosis efficiency. Unlike previous studies that investigated OsCERK1 function through mutants, we found functional allelic variation of this gene in natural germplasm, and this variation regulates symbiosis efficiency mainly by affecting gene expression levels rather than protein structure. This finding expands the understanding of the evolution and domestication of plant symbiotic signal receptors.

The OsCERK1^S allele may enhance the perception of AM fungal chitin oligosaccharide signals, activating the downstream symbiotic signaling pathway and thereby increasing colonization rate. Notably, OsCERK1 is also involved in blast disease resistance, so whether this allelic variation affects disease resistance requires further evaluation. In this study, no significant negative correlation was found between OsCERK1^S and blast disease resistance, but validation under more disease-pressure environments is needed.

From a breeding perspective, the high frequency of OsCERK1^S in indica and its selection in modern breeding suggest that it may make an important contribution to rice adaptation to low-phosphorus soils. However, the frequency of this allele is relatively low in japonica, and it can be introduced into the japonica background through marker-assisted selection to improve phosphorus efficiency and mycorrhizal symbiosis ability in japonica rice.

This study has certain limitations. GWAS detected only one major locus, OsCERK1, and other minor-effect loci may not have been detected. In addition, AM colonization rate is affected by soil microbial communities, water management, and other factors, and the stability of OsCERK1^S needs to be validated under multiple environmental conditions in the future.

 5 Conclusion

This study identified through GWAS a 12-bp InDel in the rice OsCERK1 promoter region that is significantly associated with AM colonization rate. The OsCERK1^S allele enhances the activation of the downstream symbiotic signaling pathway by increasing OsCERK1 expression levels in roots, thereby improving AM colonization rate, phosphorus accumulation, and yield under low-phosphorus conditions. This allele is distributed at high frequency in indica and has been under positive selection in modern breeding. The results provide an important gene target and theoretical basis for mycorrhiza-efficient rice breeding.

title: Highly fluorescent and biocompatible iridium nanoclusters for cellular imaging
text:
Highly Fluorescent and Biocompatible Iridium Nanoclusters for Cell Imaging

 Abstract

Cell imaging is an important tool in life science research and clinical diagnosis, and the performance of fluorescent probes directly determines imaging quality. Traditional organic fluorescent dyes suffer from poor photostability and easy quenching, while quantum dots, despite their high brightness, have potential toxicity that limits their biological applications. This paper introduces a novel iridium nanocluster (Ir NCs) fluorescent probe, which possesses high fluorescence quantum yield, excellent resistance to photobleaching, and good biocompatibility. Through systematic analysis of its synthesis method, optical properties, biosafety, and cell imaging performance, the results show that the iridium nanoclusters can achieve clear imaging in both the cytoplasmic and nuclear regions, and still maintain more than 90% of their fluorescence intensity after 30 minutes of continuous illumination. Cytotoxicity experiments show that at concentrations as high as 200 μg/mL, cell viability still exceeds 85%. This material provides a safe and efficient new fluorescent probe option for cell imaging and has good prospects for promotion and application.

 1 Introduction

Cell imaging technology is an important means of observing cell morphology, structure, and physiological processes, and is widely used in basic biological research, drug screening, and clinical pathological diagnosis.
