Fluorescence imaging has become one of the most commonly used techniques in the field of cell imaging due to its high sensitivity, high resolution, and real-time dynamic monitoring capability.

Fluorescent probes are the core element of fluorescence imaging. Currently commonly used fluorescent probes mainly include organic fluorescent dyes (such as FITC and rhodamine), fluorescent proteins (such as GFP), and quantum dots. Although organic dyes are convenient to use, they generally suffer from insufficient photostability and are prone to photobleaching under continuous illumination, leading to rapid signal decay. Fluorescent proteins need to be introduced into cells through genetic engineering, which is relatively complex to operate and may interfere with normal cellular physiological functions. Quantum dots have excellent brightness and photostability, but they usually contain heavy metal elements such as cadmium and selenium, posing potential cytotoxicity risks and limiting their long-term application in live-cell imaging.

Therefore, developing novel fluorescent probes that combine high fluorescence performance and high biocompatibility has always been a research hotspot in the field of cell imaging. In recent years, metal nanoclusters, as an emerging class of fluorescent nanomaterials, have attracted extensive attention from researchers. Metal nanoclusters are composed of several to dozens of metal atoms, with sizes usually below 2 nanometers, approaching the Fermi wavelength of electrons, and thus exhibiting unique molecule-like fluorescence properties. Compared with traditional gold and silver nanoclusters, research on iridium nanoclusters is relatively limited, but iridium complexes themselves possess excellent photophysical properties, such as high intersystem crossing efficiency and long fluorescence lifetime, which provides new ideas for developing high-performance fluorescent probes.

This paper focuses on the preparation, characterization, and application in cell imaging of a novel iridium nanocluster, with emphasis on discussing its fluorescence performance, biocompatibility, and imaging effects, aiming to provide a relatively comprehensive reference for readers interested in technology promotion.

 2 Key Technology Analysis

 2.1 Synthesis and Surface Modification of Iridium Nanoclusters

The synthesis of iridium nanoclusters adopts a mild one-step reduction method. Specifically, chloroiridic acid is used as the precursor, polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) as the stabilizer, and the reaction is carried out in an aqueous phase in the presence of a reducing agent. The carbonyl groups and pyrrolidone rings in PVP molecules can form coordination interactions with the surface of iridium atoms, effectively inhibiting agglomeration of the nanoclusters while endowing them with good water dispersibility.

During the synthesis process, reaction temperature, reducing agent dosage, and pH value are key parameters affecting the size and fluorescence performance of the nanoclusters. Studies show that reacting at 70°C under weakly alkaline conditions for 2 hours can yield iridium nanoclusters with an average particle size of about 1.5 nanometers and a relatively narrow size distribution. Excessively high reaction temperatures lead to increased nanocluster size and decreased fluorescence quantum yield, while excessively low temperatures result in incomplete reduction reactions and low yield.

To further enhance the biocompatibility and targeting capability of the nanoclusters, researchers have also introduced functionalized modifications on their surfaces. For example, by connecting molecules containing carboxyl or amino groups to the nanocluster surface through ligand exchange reactions, not only is water solubility enhanced, but active sites are also provided for subsequent conjugation of targeting molecules such as antibodies and peptides. This surface modification strategy significantly expands the biological application scope of the nanoclusters while maintaining the fluorescence performance of the nanocluster core.

 2.2 Optical Performance Analysis

The optical performance of iridium nanoclusters is the core factor determining their imaging quality. Experimental results show that under 365 nm ultraviolet excitation, the nanoclusters emit strong blue fluorescence at around 470 nm. Their fluorescence quantum yield was measured at approximately 28%, which is relatively high among metal nanoclusters. Although this value is lower than some quantum dots, it is significantly better than the performance of most organic dyes under the same conditions.

Fluorescence lifetime testing shows that the fluorescence decay of iridium nanoclusters exhibits biexponential characteristics, with an average fluorescence lifetime of approximately 1.2 microseconds. The longer fluorescence lifetime is beneficial for time-resolved imaging, which can effectively avoid interference from cellular autofluorescence and improve the imaging signal-to-noise ratio.

Resistance to photobleaching is an important indicator for evaluating the practicality of fluorescent probes. After 30 minutes of continuous ultraviolet illumination, the fluorescence intensity of iridium nanoclusters still maintained more than 90% of the initial value, while FITC dye under the same conditions decayed to less than 50% of the initial value within 10 minutes. This indicates that iridium nanoclusters have excellent photostability and are suitable for long-term dynamic cell imaging observation.

In addition, the fluorescence emission peak position of iridium nanoclusters is insensitive to changes in pH value and ionic strength, with fluorescence intensity fluctuations of less than 5% within the physiological condition range (pH 6.5–8.0), which provides a guarantee for their stable imaging in complex biological environments.

 2.3 Biocompatibility Evaluation

Biocompatibility is a prerequisite for whether a fluorescent probe can be used for live-cell imaging. The study used the MTT method to evaluate the toxicity of iridium nanoclusters to HeLa cells and NIH-3T3 cells. The results show that when the nanocluster concentration is in the range of 10–200 μg/mL, the viability of both cell types remains above 85%. Even at the highest tested concentration of 200 μg/mL with continuous incubation for 24 hours, cell morphology showed no obvious abnormalities, and the adherent growth state was good.

To further verify its biosafety, hemolysis experiments and reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection were also conducted. The hemolysis rate was below 2%, indicating that the nanoclusters do not disrupt the integrity of red blood cell membranes. ROS levels showed no significant difference compared with the control group, indicating that they do not trigger oxidative stress responses. These results collectively demonstrate that iridium nanoclusters have good biocompatibility within the tested concentration range and are suitable for live-cell imaging research.

 2.4 Cell Imaging Applications

In cell imaging experiments, iridium nanoclusters were co-incubated with HeLa cells for 4 hours, then washed with phosphate buffer to remove nanoclusters that had not entered the cells, followed by observation under a fluorescence microscope. The results show that the nanoclusters can efficiently enter cells, mainly distributed in the cytoplasmic region, with some entering the nucleus. Cell contours are clear, fluorescence signals are bright and uniform, and the signal-to-noise ratio is high.

It is worth noting that the cellular uptake efficiency of nanoclusters is positively correlated with incubation concentration and time. At a concentration of 50 μg/mL with 4 hours of incubation, satisfactory imaging results can be obtained. Extending the incubation time to 8 hours further enhanced the fluorescence signal, but cell morphology remained normal, with no obvious cell damage observed.

In addition, co-localization experiments of nanoclusters with lysosomal markers were also attempted. The results show that some nanocluster signals overlapped with the lysosomal probe, suggesting that they may enter cells through endocytic pathways and partially accumulate in lysosomes. This finding provides a basis for subsequent targeted imaging of subcellular structures.

 2.5 Comparison with Other Fluorescent Probes

To objectively evaluate the imaging performance of iridium nanoclusters, they were compared with several commonly used fluorescent probes. In terms of brightness, the single-particle brightness of iridium nanoclusters is approximately 3 times that of FITC, comparable to some quantum dots. In terms of photostability, their resistance to photobleaching is significantly superior to FITC and rhodamine B, approaching that of quantum dots. In terms of biocompatibility, iridium nanoclusters are clearly superior to cadmium-containing quantum dots and comparable to organic dyes.

Overall, iridium nanoclusters achieve a good balance among brightness, stability, and safety, making them particularly suitable for live-cell imaging experiments requiring long-term observation. Their shortcomings lie in that the fluorescence quantum yield still has room for improvement, and they currently mainly emit blue light, which is inferior to near-infrared probes in terms of tissue penetration depth. These issues can be improved through subsequent composition regulation and surface engineering.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

From the experimental results, the iridium nanoclusters exhibit comprehensive advantages in multiple aspects in cell imaging. First, their high fluorescence quantum yield and excellent resistance to photobleaching ensure the intensity and durability of imaging signals, reducing the need for repeated excitation and long exposure times, which is beneficial for reducing phototoxicity. Second, good biocompatibility enables their use in live-cell and potentially in vivo imaging research, expanding application scenarios. Third, the mild aqueous-phase synthesis method and convenient surface modification strategy give them potential for scaled-up preparation and functional customization.

From the perspective of application benefits, iridium nanoclusters, as a novel fluorescent probe, are expected to generate practical value in the following areas. In basic research, they can be used for organelle dynamic tracking, protein interaction observation, and drug delivery monitoring. In clinical diagnosis, they can be used for fluorescence labeling of pathological sections and detection of circulating tumor cells. In drug screening, they can be used for high-throughput imaging analysis, improving screening efficiency and accuracy.

Compared with existing commercial fluorescent probes, iridium nanoclusters have relatively low preparation costs, readily available raw materials, and do not rely on expensive quantum dot synthesis equipment. Their aqueous-phase synthesis process also avoids environmental problems caused by organic solvents, aligning with the development direction of green chemistry. These factors are all conducive to the promotion and industrialization of this technology.

Of course, this material is still at the laboratory research stage, and there is still some distance from large-scale clinical application. Future work needs to further optimize the synthesis process to improve batch-to-batch consistency; conduct more systematic in vivo safety evaluations; and explore targeting modification strategies to achieve precise imaging of specific cell types or subcellular structures.

 4 Conclusion

This paper systematically introduces a highly fluorescent and biocompatible iridium nanocluster and its application in cell imaging. The nanoclusters are prepared through a mild aqueous-phase reduction method, with a particle size of approximately 1.5 nanometers, a fluorescence quantum yield of 28%, and excellent resistance to photobleaching. Biocompatibility experiments show that at a concentration of 200 μg/mL, they have no significant effect on cell viability, and both hemolysis rate and ROS levels are within safe ranges. Cell imaging results show that the nanoclusters can efficiently enter cells, achieving clear imaging of the cytoplasm and nucleus, with bright and stable signals.

Overall, iridium nanoclusters achieve a good balance among fluorescence performance, biosafety, and imaging effects, providing a competitive new probe option for cell imaging. With further development of synthesis processes and surface modification technologies, iridium nanoclusters are expected to play a greater role in the field of biomedical imaging and deserve continued attention and in-depth research.

title: Identification of a 3-miRNA Signature Associated With the Prediction of Prognosis in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
text:
Identification of a 3-miRNA Signature Associated With the Prediction of Prognosis in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

Abstract: Objective: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a highly aggressive malignant tumor of the head and neck, and its prognosis assessment lacks reliable molecular markers. This study aimed to screen microRNAs (miRNAs) associated with the prognosis of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, construct a multi-miRNA prognostic prediction model, and validate its clinical value. Methods: The nasopharyngeal carcinoma miRNA expression profile dataset (GSE32960) was obtained from the public Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, including 312 nasopharyngeal carcinoma tissue samples and 18 normal nasopharyngeal tissue samples. Differential expression analysis, univariate Cox regression, LASSO regression, and multivariate Cox regression were used to progressively screen prognosis-related miRNAs, construct a risk score model, and validate it in an independent dataset. Results: A total of 47 differentially expressed miRNAs were identified, and 3 miRNAs significantly associated with overall survival (OS) (miR-142-3p, miR-93-5p, miR-451a) were further screened to construct a 3-miRNA prognostic risk score model. The overall survival of patients in the high-risk group was significantly lower than that in the low-risk group (HR=2.87, 95%CI: 1.94–4.25, P<0.001). Multivariate Cox regression showed that the risk score was an independent prognostic factor for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (HR=2.31, 95%CI: 1.52–3.51, P<0.001). Conclusion: The 3-miRNA prognostic model constructed in this study can effectively predict the survival risk of patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma and has potential clinical application value.

Keywords: nasopharyngeal carcinoma; microRNA; prognostic model; risk score; biomarker

1 Introduction

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) originates from the nasopharyngeal epithelium and has a relatively high incidence in southern China and Southeast Asia, with obvious regional clustering. Although intensity-modulated radiotherapy and concurrent chemoradiotherapy have significantly improved the efficacy for early-stage patients, the five-year survival rate of locally advanced and metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma remains unsatisfactory, and recurrence and distant metastasis are the main reasons for treatment failure. Therefore, identifying reliable molecular prognostic markers is of great significance for achieving individualized treatment and improving patient survival.

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of non-coding RNAs approximately 22 nucleotides in length that regulate gene expression by targeting the 3' untranslated region of mRNA, and are widely involved in tumor proliferation, apoptosis, invasion, and metastasis. Recent studies have shown that abnormal miRNA expression is closely related to the occurrence, development, and prognosis of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. The prognostic value of a single miRNA is limited, whereas a combined multi-miRNA model may have higher predictive efficacy. However, there are still few studies on multi-miRNA prognostic models for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and systematic validation is lacking. Based on public databases, this study screened miRNAs associated with the prognosis of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, constructed a 3-miRNA risk score model, and evaluated its independent prognostic value, aiming to provide a new molecular tool for the clinical prognosis assessment of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Data Sources

The nasopharyngeal carcinoma miRNA expression profile dataset GSE32960 was downloaded from the GEO database, including 312 nasopharyngeal carcinoma tissues and 18 normal nasopharyngeal tissues, and all samples had complete clinical follow-up information. The data were obtained in Series Matrix File format and processed by log2 transformation and quantile normalization. GSE70970 was additionally selected as an independent validation set, including 246 nasopharyngeal carcinoma samples.

2.2 Differential Expression Analysis

The limma package in R language was used for differential expression analysis, and differentially expressed miRNAs (DEMs) were screened with |log2FC|>1 and adjusted P value<0.05 as the threshold.

2.3 Screening of Prognosis-Related miRNAs and Model Construction

In the training set (GSE32960), univariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was used to screen miRNAs associated with overall survival (OS) (P<0.05). Subsequently, LASSO regression was used for dimensionality reduction and feature selection, and the optimal penalty parameter was determined by ten-fold cross-validation. Finally, multivariate Cox regression was included to construct a risk score model: risk score = Σ(βi × expressioni), where βi is the multivariate Cox regression coefficient. Patients were divided into a high-risk group and a low-risk group according to the median risk score.

2.4 Model Validation and Statistical Analysis

Risk scores were calculated and grouped in the validation set GSE70970, Kaplan-Meier method was used to plot survival curves, and the log-rank test was used to compare differences between groups. Time-dependent ROC curves were used to evaluate the efficacy of the model in predicting 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year survival rates. Multivariate Cox regression was used to analyze whether the risk score was an independent prognostic factor. All statistical analyses were completed using R 4.2.1 software, and two-sided P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Identification of Differentially Expressed miRNAs

A total of 47 differentially expressed miRNAs were identified between 312 nasopharyngeal carcinoma samples and 18 normal tissues, of which 28 were upregulated and 19 were downregulated in tumors. The clustering heatmap showed that tumor and normal tissues could be clearly distinguished.

3.2 Screening of Prognosis-Related miRNAs and Model Construction

Univariate Cox regression analysis showed that 11 of the 47 DEMs were significantly associated with OS (P<0.05). LASSO regression further screened 5 candidate miRNAs, and multivariate Cox regression ultimately identified 3 independent prognostic miRNAs: miR-142-3p (HR=0.62, P=0.008), miR-93-5p (HR=1.74, P=0.002), and miR-451a (HR=0.71, P=0.013). The risk score formula was: risk score = (-0.478 × miR-142-3p expression) + (0.554 × miR-93-5p expression) + (-0.342 × miR-451a expression).

3.3 Prognostic Value of the Risk Score Model

Patients in the training set were divided into high- and low-risk groups according to the median risk score. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that OS in the high-risk group was significantly lower than that in the low-risk group (median OS: 38.5 months vs 62.7 months, HR=2.87, 95%CI: 1.94–4.25, P<0.001). Time-dependent ROC curves showed that the AUCs of the model for predicting 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year OS were 0.78, 0.74, and 0.71, respectively.

3.4 Independent Validation

In the validation set GSE70970, OS in the high-risk group was also significantly lower than that in the low-risk group (HR=2.13, 95%CI: 1.46–3.10, P<0.001), and the AUCs of the ROC curves were 0.72, 0.70, and 0.68, respectively, suggesting that the model has good generalization ability.

3.5 Independent Prognostic Factor Analysis

Multivariate Cox regression analysis included age, sex, TNM stage, and risk score, and the results showed that both the risk score (HR=2.31, 95%CI: 1.52–3.51, P<0.001) and TNM stage (HR=1.89, 95%CI: 1.28–2.79, P=0.001) were independent prognostic factors.

4 Discussion

Through systematic bioinformatics analysis, this study constructed a 3-miRNA prognostic model composed of miR-142-3p, miR-93-5p, and miR-451a, and validated its predictive efficacy in an independent dataset. The risk score of this model is an independent prognostic factor for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, suggesting that it can serve as a useful supplement to traditional TNM staging.

miR-142-3p plays a tumor-suppressive role in a variety of tumors, and its low expression is associated with poor prognosis; miR-93-5p has been reported to promote tumor cell proliferation and invasion and to exert oncogene functions; miR-451a is involved in regulating the cell cycle and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The prognostic directions of the three miRNAs in this study are basically consistent with previous reports, further supporting their biological plausibility.

The advantages of this study lie in the relatively large sample size, rigorous modeling method, and independent validation. However, the study still has limitations: first, the data were derived from public databases and lack validation in prospective clinical cohorts; second, the specific target genes and regulatory mechanisms of the miRNAs have not been experimentally verified; finally, the model is based only on miRNA expression and does not integrate clinicopathological features and gene mutation information. Future studies will combine multi-omics data and in vitro experiments to further optimize the model and clarify its molecular mechanism.

5 Conclusion

This study identified and validated a prognostic risk score model for nasopharyngeal carcinoma composed of 3 miRNAs. This model can effectively distinguish high- and low-risk patients and predict overall survival as an independent prognostic factor. This 3-miRNA signature has potential clinical application value and is expected to provide a reference for individualized prognosis assessment and treatment decision-making for patients with nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

title: Immune and gut bacterial successions of large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea) during Pseudomonas plecoglossicida infection
text:
Succession Patterns of Immunity and Gut Microbiota in Large Yellow Croaker (*Larimichthys crocea*) During *Pseudomonas plecoglossicida* Infection

Abstract: *Pseudomonas plecoglossicida* is the primary pathogen causing visceral white spot disease in large yellow croaker (*Larimichthys crocea*), resulting in severe economic losses to the aquaculture industry. To elucidate the immune response and dynamic changes in gut microbiota of large yellow croaker following infection with this bacterium, this study employed an artificial immersion infection method and collected samples of spleen, head kidney, and intestinal contents at different time points post-infection (0 h, 12 h, 24 h, 48 h, 72 h, 96 h). Immune-related gene expression was measured by real-time quantitative PCR, and gut microbiota structure was analyzed using 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing. The results showed that from 12 h post-infection, pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 were significantly upregulated in the spleen and head kidney, peaking at 48 h. TLR5 and MyD88 genes were activated early in infection, indicating that the bacterium may trigger innate immunity through the flagellin-TLR5 pathway. Regarding gut microbiota, the relative abundance of Proteobacteria significantly increased at the phylum level post-infection, while the proportions of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes decreased. At the genus level, the abundance of potential pathogens such as *Vibrio* and *Pseudomonas* increased, while beneficial bacteria such as *Lactococcus* decreased. The α-diversity index reached its lowest point at 48 h post-infection, and β-diversity analysis showed significant separation of microbiota structure between the infected group and the control group. This study revealed the temporal characteristics of immune activation and gut microbiota dysbiosis in large yellow croaker after infection with *P. plecoglossicida*, providing a theoretical basis for disease early warning and microecological regulation.

Keywords: Large yellow croaker; *Pseudomonas plecoglossicida*; Immune response; Gut microbiota; 16S rRNA sequencing

 1 Introduction

Large yellow croaker (*Larimichthys crocea*) is an important marine aquaculture fish species along the southeastern coast of China, with an annual production exceeding 250,000 tons and an output value of over 10 billion yuan. However, with increasing stocking density and environmental pressure, bacterial diseases have become frequent, among which visceral white spot disease caused by *Pseudomonas plecoglossicida* is particularly severe. The typical symptom of this disease is the appearance of white nodules in visceral organs such as the spleen and kidney, with mortality rates reaching over 60%, causing enormous losses to farmers.

*Pseudomonas plecoglossicida* is a Gram-negative short rod bacterium with a single polar flagellum and strong motility. Studies have shown that this bacterium can invade fish through water, feed, and other routes, proliferating extensively in the spleen and head kidney and causing systemic infection. As lower vertebrates, fish rely primarily on innate immunity, and the Toll-like receptor (TLR) family plays a key role in recognizing pathogen-associated molecular patterns. Among these, TLR5 can specifically recognize bacterial flagellin, activating the MyD88-dependent signaling pathway and inducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression.

The gut microbiota, as the host's "forgotten organ," plays important functions in nutritional metabolism, immune regulation, and pathogen defense. Recent studies have found that bacterial infection can lead to disruption of fish gut microbiota structure, and dysbiosis in turn exacerbates the disease. However, systematic research on the temporal succession patterns of immune response and gut microbiota during *P. plecoglossicida* infection in large yellow croaker is still lacking. This study aims to simultaneously monitor immune gene expression and gut microbiota dynamics through artificial infection experiments, revealing their coordinated change characteristics and providing scientific support for disease prevention and control.

 2 Key Technical Analysis

 2.1 Infection Model Construction and Sample Collection

Experimental large yellow croaker (body weight 80±10 g) were purchased from a farm in Ningde, Fujian, and acclimated in a recirculating water system at 22±1°C, salinity 25±1, with daily feeding of commercial feed. After 7 days of adaptive acclimation, fish were randomly divided into an infection group and a control group, with 3 parallel tanks per group and 30 fish per tank. The infection group was immersed in seawater containing *P. plecoglossicida* (strain number: XSD-01, concentration 2×10⁷ CFU/mL) for 1 h using the immersion method; the control group was immersed in sterile physiological saline. Samples were collected at 0, 12, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-infection, with 3 fish taken from each group at each time point. After anesthesia, spleen, head kidney, and intestinal contents were collected aseptically. Spleen and head kidney were immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80°C for RNA extraction; intestinal contents were placed in sterile EP tubes and stored at -80°C for DNA extraction.

 2.2 Detection of Immune-Related Gene Expression

Total RNA was extracted from spleen and head kidney using the Trizol method, treated with DNase I, and reverse-transcribed into cDNA. Specific primers were designed based on the large yellow croaker genome sequence, with β-actin as the internal reference gene. Relative expression levels of immune-related genes including IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, TLR5, MyD88, and NF-κB were detected by real-time quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR). The reaction system was 20 μL, containing 10 μL SYBR Green Master Mix, 0.4 μL each of forward and reverse primers, 1 μL cDNA template, and 8.2 μL ddH₂O. Amplification program: 95°C pre-denaturation for 30 s; 95°C for 5 s, 60°C for 30 s, 40 cycles. The 2^(-ΔΔCt) method was used to calculate relative gene expression, with 3 biological replicates per group.

 2.3 16S rRNA High-Throughput Sequencing of Gut Microbiota

Total DNA was extracted from intestinal content samples using the QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit. DNA integrity was detected by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis, and concentration and purity were measured using NanoDrop 2000. Using diluted DNA as template, the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified by PCR with primers 341F (5'-CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG-3') and 805R (5'-GACTACHVGGGTATCTAATCC-3'). PCR products were purified, quantified, and subjected to paired-end sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform. Raw sequences were quality-controlled, denoised, and assembled using QIIME2 software, then clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at 97% similarity, with taxonomic annotation based on the Silva database. α-diversity indices including Chao1, Shannon, and Simpson were calculated, and β-diversity was assessed through principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) and analysis of similarities (ANOSIM).

 2.4 Data Statistics and Correlation Analysis

Immune gene expression data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. One-way ANOVA was performed using SPSS 22.0, with Duncan's multiple comparison test for inter-group differences, and P<0.05 considered significant. Gut microbiota data were statistically analyzed using the vegan package in R. Spearman correlation analysis was used to explore the association between immune gene expression and dominant genus abundance. Additionally, PICRUSt2 was used to predict functional pathway changes in the microbiota, focusing on KEGG pathways related to inflammation and metabolism.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

 3.1 Temporal Changes in Immune Gene Expression

After infection with *P. plecoglossicida*, immune-related genes in the spleen and head kidney of large yellow croaker showed significant upregulation trends. In the spleen, TLR5 and MyD88 genes were significantly elevated at 12 h post-infection (P<0.05), reaching 3.2-fold and 2.8-fold of the control group, respectively, indicating rapid activation of the flagellin recognition pathway. NF-κB peaked at 24 h (4.1-fold), followed by expression peaks of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 at 48 h, reaching 6.5-fold, 5.2-fold, and 4.8-fold of the control group, respectively. Gene expression trends in the head kidney were similar to those in the spleen, but peak times were slightly earlier, with IL-1β reaching its highest level at 36 h. In the late infection period (72–96 h), gene expression gradually declined but remained higher than the control group. This indicates that the innate immune response of large yellow croaker to *P. plecoglossicida* is characterized by "rapid initiation, strong burst, and slow resolution."

 3.2 Dynamic Succession of Gut Microbiota Structure

Through 16S rRNA sequencing, a total of 2,356,842 valid sequences were obtained, averaging 78,561 per sample, and 1,842 OTUs were clustered. At the phylum level, the control group was dominated by Firmicutes (38.2%), Proteobacteria (31.5%), and Bacteroidetes (22.7%). At 12 h post-infection, the relative abundance of Proteobacteria rose to 45.3%, while Firmicutes decreased to 28.6%; by 48 h, Proteobacteria further increased to 62.8%, while Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes decreased to 18.4% and 12.1%, respectively. At the genus level, the abundance of *Vibrio* and *Pseudomonas* significantly increased post-infection, reaching 12.7% and 18.3% at 48 h, respectively, while the abundance of beneficial bacteria such as *Lactococcus* and *Bacillus* decreased. α-diversity analysis showed that Chao1 and Shannon indices reached their lowest at 48 h post-infection (P<0.01), while Simpson index increased, indicating significant reductions in both community richness and evenness. PCoA analysis showed that infected group and control group samples were clearly separated on the coordinate axes (ANOSIM R=0.72, P=0.001), and samples at 48 h and 96 h post-infection formed independent clusters, indicating significant succession of microbiota structure over time.

 3.3 Correlation Analysis Between Immunity and Microbiota

Spearman correlation analysis showed that spleen IL-1β expression was significantly positively correlated with intestinal *Vibrio* abundance (r=0.68, P<0.01) and negatively correlated with *Lactococcus* abundance (r=-0.54, P<0.05). TLR5 expression was positively correlated with *Pseudomonas* abundance (r=0.61, P<0.05). This suggests that immune activation and gut microbiota dysbiosis exhibit coordinated changes: pathogen invasion triggers a strong inflammatory response, disrupting intestinal microecological balance, leading to proliferation of opportunistic pathogens, while the reduction of beneficial bacteria further weakens intestinal barrier function, forming a vicious cycle. PICRUSt2 functional prediction showed that pathways related to lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis and bacterial secretion systems were significantly enriched in the infected group microbiota, while pathways related to short-chain fatty acid metabolism and secondary bile acid synthesis showed decreased expression, which may be a potential mechanism by which dysbiosis exacerbates inflammation.

 3.4 Analysis of Technology Extension Benefits

The infection model and immune-microbiota synchronized monitoring technology established in this study can provide three aspects of benefits for aquaculture production. First, genes such as TLR5 and IL-1β can serve as molecular markers for early disease warning, with significant changes detectable at 12–24 h post-infection, 2–3 days earlier than traditional symptom observation, facilitating early intervention. Second, the *Vibrio*/*Lactococcus* ratio in gut microbiota can serve as a microecological health indicator; when the ratio exceeds 0.5, it indicates risk of dysbiosis, guiding farmers to adjust feeding strategies or add probiotics. Third, based on microbiota function prediction results, composite microecological preparations containing *Bacillus* and *Lactococcus* can be developed to reduce disease incidence through competitive exclusion and immune enhancement. Preliminary trials showed that adding 0.2% composite probiotics to feed could reduce mortality of infected large yellow croaker by more than 35% and increase intestinal Shannon index by 18.6%. This technology is simple to operate and low in cost, suitable for promotion and application in cage and factory farming.

 4 Conclusion

This study systematically revealed the temporal succession patterns of immune response and gut microbiota in large yellow croaker after infection with *P. plecoglossicida*. In the early infection stage (12–24 h), the TLR5/MyD88/NF-κB pathway was rapidly activated, inducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression; in the mid-infection stage (48 h), the inflammatory response peaked, while gut microbiota diversity dropped to its lowest, with significant enrichment of potential pathogens such as Proteobacteria and *Vibrio* and reduction of beneficial bacteria; in the late infection stage (72–96 h), the immune response gradually subsided, but the microbiota structure still deviated from normal. Immune gene expression was significantly correlated with specific genus abundance, indicating close interaction between immunity and microbiota. Based on these findings, it is recommended for large yellow croaker aquaculture: ① Use TLR5 and IL-1β as early warning indicators; ② Monitor the intestinal *Vibrio*/*Lactococcus* ratio to assess microecological risk; ③ Add composite probiotics (*Bacillus* + *Lactococcus*) to feed to enhance anti-infection capability. This study provides theoretical basis and technical support for ecological prevention and control of visceral white spot disease in large yellow croaker, and is of great significance for promoting green and healthy development of marine aquaculture. Future research can further explore the specific molecular mechanisms by which probiotics regulate immune-microbiota interactions and optimize field application protocols.

title: Optimizing hyper-parameters of neural networks with swarm intelligence: A novel framework for credit scoring
text:
Neural Network Hyperparameter Optimization Based on Swarm Intelligence Optimization: A Novel Framework for Credit Scoring

 Abstract
Objective: Credit scoring is a core component of risk control in financial institutions. Neural networks are widely used due to their strong nonlinear fitting capability, but hyperparameter selection relies heavily on experience, which constrains model performance and generalization ability. This paper aims to construct a neural network hyperparameter optimization framework based on swarm intelligence optimization to improve the prediction accuracy and stability of credit scoring models. Methods: Using small-scale farmer credit data from a rural commercial bank from 2020 to 2023 as samples (effective sample size 12,860, with default samples accounting for 8.7%), a neural network hyperparameter optimization framework based on a hybrid strategy of particle swarm optimization (PSO) and artificial bee colony (ABC) (PSO-ABC-BPNN) was constructed to jointly optimize the number of hidden layer nodes, learning rate, momentum factor, and L2 regularization coefficient, and to compare it with grid search, genetic algorithm, and default-parameter BPNN. Results: The AUC of PSO-ABC-BPNN on the test set was 0.892, and the KS value was 0.641, both significantly better than the comparison models (P<0.05); its training time was shortened by approximately 62.4% compared with grid search. Conclusion: This framework can effectively alleviate the problem of hyperparameter sensitivity and provides a generalizable technical path for credit risk assessment in rural finance.

Keywords: credit scoring; neural network; hyperparameter optimization; swarm intelligence; particle swarm optimization; artificial bee colony algorithm

 1 Introduction
Credit scoring provides a basis for credit decisions by quantifying the probability of borrower default. With the advancement of inclusive rural finance, farmer credit exhibits the characteristics of "small amount, dispersed, and weak guarantee." Traditional logistic regression is insufficient in depicting nonlinear interaction relationships, while BPNN, although advantageous, is highly sensitive to hyperparameters. If parameters such as the number of hidden layer nodes and learning rate are improperly set, overfitting or training stagnation can easily occur.

Existing studies mostly use grid search or genetic algorithms to optimize hyperparameters, but the computational cost of grid search grows exponentially with dimensionality, and genetic algorithms are prone to premature convergence. Swarm intelligence algorithms, by simulating collective behaviors such as bird flocks and bee colonies, show strong global search capability in continuous-space optimization. However, a single algorithm still suffers from an imbalance between exploration and exploitation. This paper proposes a PSO-ABC hybrid optimization framework, embeds it into the BPNN hyperparameter optimization process, and validates its effectiveness using farmer credit data, with the aim of providing methodological support for rural financial risk management.

 2 Materials and Methods
 2.1 Data Sources and Preprocessing
The data came from small-scale farmer credit records of a rural commercial bank from January 2020 to June 2023. The original sample contained 13,542 records. After removing missing values and outliers, 12,860 records were retained, including 1,119 default samples (8.7%). The features covered borrowers' basic attributes (age, years of education, number of household laborers), economic attributes (annual income, cultivated land area, debt-to-income ratio), credit attributes (number of historical delinquencies, loan amount, term), and external environment (regional per capita GDP, agricultural insurance coverage), totaling 18 variables. Continuous variables were standardized by Z-score, and categorical variables were one-hot encoded. The training set and test set were divided by 7:3 stratified sampling, and SMOTE was used to address class imbalance.

 2.2 PSO-ABC-BPNN Framework
The BPNN structure was "input layer-single hidden layer-output layer," with the output being the default probability. The hyperparameter vector to be optimized was: number of hidden layer nodes \(n_h\in[5,50]\), learning rate \(\eta\in[0.001,0.1]\), momentum factor \(\alpha\in[0.1,0.9]\), and L2 regularization coefficient \(\lambda\in[10^{-5},10^{-2}]\).

The hybrid optimization process was as follows:
(1) Initialization: population size \(N=40\), with 20 in each of the PSO and ABC subpopulations, and maximum iterations \(T=100\);
(2) PSO stage: global exploration was carried out through velocity-position updates, with the inertia weight decreasing linearly;
(3) ABC stage: neighborhood search was performed on the better solutions output by PSO; employed bees and onlooker bees selected nectar sources according to probability, and scout bees randomly reset solutions trapped in local optima;
(4) Fitness function: constructed as the mean AUC of 5-fold cross-validation minus a complexity penalty term, balancing accuracy and generalization;
(5) Termination condition: when the maximum number of iterations was reached or fitness showed no improvement for 10 consecutive generations, the optimal hyperparameters were output and the final model was trained.

 2.3 Comparison Models and Evaluation Metrics
The comparison models included default-parameter BPNN, grid search BPNN, genetic algorithm BPNN (GA-BPNN), and logistic regression. The evaluation metrics were AUC, KS value, accuracy, F1 value, and training time. Statistical significance was tested using the DeLong test and paired t-test.

 3 Results and Analysis
 3.1 Hyperparameter Optimization Results
PSO-ABC-BPNN converged at the 47th generation. The optimal hyperparameters were: number of hidden layer nodes 31, learning rate 0.023, momentum factor 0.68, and L2 coefficient 0.0047. GA-BPNN converged at the 73rd generation, while grid search needed to traverse 1,440 combinations. The convergence speed of the hybrid algorithm was about 35.6% higher than that of GA.

 3.2 Model Performance Comparison
The test set results are shown in Table 1. PSO-ABC-BPNN achieved an AUC of 0.892, KS of 0.641, and F1 of 0.734, all superior to the other models; its training time was 187 seconds, 62.4% shorter than grid search (497 seconds). The DeLong test showed that the AUC difference between PSO-ABC-BPNN and GA-BPNN was statistically significant (Z=2.31, P=0.021).

Table 1 Performance Comparison of Models
| Model | AUC | KS | Accuracy | F1 | Time/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic | 0.812 | 0.523 | 0.801 | 0.612 | 12 |
| Default BPNN | 0.834 | 0.551 | 0.816 | 0.638 | 96 |
| Grid Search BPNN | 0.871 | 0.612 | 0.847 | 0.701 | 497 |
| GA-BPNN | 0.879 | 0.623 | 0.853 | 0.712 | 312 |
| PSO-ABC-BPNN | 0.892 | 0.641 | 0.864 | 0.734 | 187 |

 3.3 Robustness Analysis
Using 5 repeated stratified sampling validations, the AUC standard deviation of PSO-ABC-BPNN was 0.008, lower than the 0.015 of GA-BPNN, indicating stronger resistance to random fluctuations. In a sensitivity test in which the proportion of default samples was reduced to 5%, the AUC of this framework decreased by only 0.013, outperforming the comparison models.

 4 Discussion
The results of this paper support the effectiveness of a swarm intelligence hybrid strategy in credit scoring hyperparameter optimization. The global exploration of PSO and the neighborhood exploitation of ABC complement each other, avoiding premature convergence or stagnation of a single algorithm. Compared with grid search, the hybrid framework significantly reduces computational cost in a four-dimensional hyperparameter space; compared with GA, it requires fewer convergence generations and has smaller variance.

From the perspective of rural finance, this framework has good adaptability to farmer data characterized by weak guarantees and high noise. The combination of 31 hidden layer nodes and a relatively low learning rate of 0.023 indicates that the model tends toward smooth fitting, which helps suppress overfitting caused by the scarcity of default samples. The L2 regularization coefficient of 0.0047 further constrains the weights and improves generalization ability.

The limitations are as follows: the samples come from a single region, and external validity remains to be verified; deep network architecture search was not considered; and the parameters of the swarm intelligence algorithm itself (population size, number of iterations) also need to be set. In the future, Bayesian optimization and multi-objective optimization can be introduced to balance accuracy, fairness, and interpretability.

 5 Conclusion
This paper constructed a PSO-ABC-BPNN credit scoring hyperparameter optimization framework, achieving prediction performance of AUC 0.892 and KS 0.641 on farmer credit data, while significantly reducing parameter tuning time. The study shows that a swarm intelligence hybrid strategy can effectively alleviate the problem of neural network hyperparameter sensitivity and provides an efficient and robust technical solution for credit risk assessment in rural financial institutions. Subsequent research should expand sample coverage and explore multi-objective optimization and interpretability enhancement mechanisms.

title: The FLUXNET2015 dataset and the ONEFlux processing pipeline for eddy covariance data
text:
Abstract: The eddy covariance technique is a core method for global carbon, water, and energy flux observations. However, for a long time, the data processing procedures, quality control, and format specifications of observation sites have lacked unified standards, severely constraining cross-site data comparison and synthesis. This paper systematically introduces the FLUXNET2015 dataset and its accompanying ONEFlux processing pipeline. This dataset integrates eddy covariance observations from 212 sites worldwide, covering the period from 1991 to 2014, and adopts a unified data format, quality control system, and post-processing algorithms. As an open-source automated processing tool, ONEFlux enables full-pipeline processing from raw data to standardized flux products, including key steps such as data screening, friction velocity correction, energy closure correction, nighttime flux partitioning, and data gap-filling. This paper provides a detailed analysis of the key technical aspects of the dataset and processing pipeline, and evaluates their application benefits. The results show that FLUXNET2015 and ONEFlux significantly lower the barrier to using flux data, enhance data comparability and reusability, and provide important infrastructure for global change ecology, climate model validation, and carbon cycle research.

Keywords: eddy covariance; FLUXNET2015; ONEFlux; flux data; data processing pipeline; quality control

 1 Introduction

The eddy covariance (EC) technique directly calculates CO₂, H₂O, and energy fluxes between ecosystems and the atmosphere by measuring the covariance of high-frequency fluctuations in wind velocity and gas concentrations. It is currently one of the most direct and reliable methods for quantifying the carbon budget of terrestrial ecosystems. Since the 1990s, numerous flux observation sites have been established worldwide, forming multiple regional networks such as AmeriFlux, EuroFlux, and AsiaFlux. In the late 1990s, these networks were further integrated into the global flux observation network FLUXNET, marking the entry of flux observations into a phase of global coordination.

However, early FLUXNET data products had obvious limitations: data processing methods varied across sites, quality control standards differed, and data formats were diverse, making cross-site synthesis studies extremely difficult. In addition, raw flux data are affected by issues such as atmospheric stability, friction velocity, and energy closure, requiring a series of complex post-processing steps before they can be used for scientific analysis. These technical barriers made it difficult for non-specialist users to effectively utilize flux data.

To address these issues, the FLUXNET community released the FLUXNET2015 dataset in 2015, along with the open-source automated processing tool ONEFlux (Open Network-Enabled Flux processing pipeline). The combination of this dataset and tool achieved, for the first time at the global scale, standardized processing and open sharing of flux data. This paper systematically introduces the key technologies of the FLUXNET2015 dataset and the ONEFlux pipeline, analyzes their application benefits, and discusses future development directions.

 2 Key Technical Analysis

 2.1 Dataset Architecture and Site Coverage

The FLUXNET2015 dataset integrates observations from 212 sites worldwide, spanning the period from 1991 to 2014. The sites cover multiple ecosystem types including boreal coniferous forests, temperate deciduous forests, tropical rainforests, grasslands, croplands, wetlands, and urban areas, with spatial coverage across North America, Europe, Asia, South America, Africa, and Australia. The dataset uses a unified NetCDF format and includes two temporal resolutions: half-hourly and daily. Variables include CO₂ flux, latent heat flux, sensible heat flux, momentum flux, and key meteorological elements. Each site's data is accompanied by detailed metadata, including site description, instrument information, vegetation type, and climatic background, facilitating rapid screening and understanding by users.

 2.2 Data Quality Control and Screening

The ONEFlux pipeline employs a multi-level quality control strategy. First, fluxes are calculated from raw high-frequency data, and each half-hourly flux is quality-flagged (levels 0, 1, 2) using the steady-state test and the turbulence development test. Second, nighttime data are screened based on friction velocity thresholds, removing fluxes under conditions of insufficient turbulence. Third, data during rainfall events and from anomalous sensors are removed. Finally, data are classified into three categories: high-quality data (QC=0), acceptable-quality data (QC=1), and low-quality data (QC=2). Users can select different quality levels according to their research needs, balancing data quantity and reliability.

 2.3 Friction Velocity Correction and Energy Closure Correction

Under low-turbulence conditions at night, eddy covariance systems often underestimate CO₂ flux, leading to underestimation of ecosystem respiration. ONEFlux applies the friction velocity (u*) threshold method for correction: by analyzing the relationship between nighttime flux and u*, a critical u* value is determined, and data below this threshold are screened or replaced. In addition, the energy closure problem is ubiquitous in flux observations, i.e., turbulent fluxes (sensible + latent heat) are typically smaller than available energy (net radiation − soil heat flux). ONEFlux provides an energy closure correction option, adjusting fluxes via the Bowen ratio method or the residual method to improve data consistency.

 2.4 Nighttime Flux Partitioning and Data Gap-Filling

To obtain a complete ecosystem carbon budget, net ecosystem exchange (NEE) must be partitioned into gross primary production (GPP) and ecosystem respiration (Reco). ONEFlux adopts the nighttime data method: a respiration model is established based on the relationship between nighttime NEE and temperature, extrapolated to daytime to obtain Reco, and then GPP is calculated as GPP = Reco − NEE. For missing data, the marginal distribution sampling (MDS) method or the look-up table method is used for gap-filling to ensure continuity of the time series. Uncertainty estimates are also provided during the gap-filling process to facilitate subsequent analysis.

 2.5 Automated Pipeline and Open-Source Ecosystem

ONEFlux is written in Python and R, supports command-line and graphical user interface operation, and can run on Linux, Windows, and macOS platforms. Users only need to provide raw data and configuration files, and the full pipeline from data reading, quality control, correction, and partitioning to gap-filling is completed automatically. The pipeline outputs standardized NetCDF files with detailed logs and quality reports. ONEFlux follows an open-source license, with code hosted on GitHub, supporting community contributions and secondary development, forming an active technical ecosystem.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

The release of the FLUXNET2015 dataset and the ONEFlux pipeline has significantly improved the usability of flux data and research efficiency. First, the unified data format and quality control system make cross-site comparison possible. For example, researchers can conveniently analyze differences in carbon use efficiency among ecosystems across different climate zones, or validate the simulation capability of terrestrial ecosystem models at the global scale. Second, automated processing has greatly lowered the technical barrier to data processing. Previously, processing data from a single site required months of manual operation; now, with ONEFlux, it can be completed within hours, greatly accelerating the research process.

In addition, this dataset has become important infrastructure for global change research. As of 2023, the FLUXNET2015 data has been cited by thousands of academic papers, supporting research in a wide range of fields including the carbon cycle, water cycle, energy balance, and climate change responses. ONEFlux has also been adopted as a standard processing tool by multiple regional networks, advancing the standardization of global flux observations. Its open-source nature has also promoted methodological innovation, such as the application of machine learning in flux gap-filling and improvements in uncertainty quantification methods.

 4 Conclusion

The FLUXNET2015 dataset and the ONEFlux processing pipeline are important milestones in the field of eddy covariance. Through standardized data formats, unified quality control, and automated post-processing, they have resolved the technical bottlenecks that have long constrained the synthesis of flux data. This achievement not only enhances data comparability and reusability but also lowers the barrier to use, promoting deep integration of global change ecology, climate modeling, and carbon cycle research. In the future, as observation sites continue to expand and data processing methods continue to evolve, FLUXNET and ONEFlux are expected to further integrate remote sensing data, machine learning algorithms, and real-time quality control, building a more intelligent, open, and collaborative global flux observation data system, providing more solid scientific support for addressing climate change.

title: A Deep-Learning-Based Approach for Wheat Yellow Rust Disease Recognition from Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Images
text:
Deep Learning-Based UAV Image Recognition Method for Wheat Stripe Rust

Abstract: Wheat stripe rust is one of the major diseases threatening the safe production of wheat in China, and achieving rapid, accurate, and non-destructive identification of this disease is of great significance for disease prevention and control. To address the problems of low efficiency and strong subjectivity in traditional manual field surveys, this study proposes a deep learning-based UAV image recognition method for wheat stripe rust. The research was conducted from 2022 to 2023 at the experimental base of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences in Xinxiang City, Henan Province. A multi-rotor UAV equipped with an RGB camera was used to acquire wheat canopy images, and a dataset containing 8,640 images across four grades—healthy, mild, moderate, and severe—was constructed. Based on the ResNet-50 backbone network, an attention mechanism and a multi-scale feature fusion module were introduced to construct an improved recognition model, WYR-Net. The results showed that WYR-Net achieved an overall recognition accuracy of 94.7% on the test set, with a Kappa coefficient of 0.928, outperforming comparison models such as ResNet-50, VGG-16, and MobileNet-V2. Ablation experiments confirmed that the attention module and the multi-scale fusion module improved accuracy by 2.1 and 1.8 percentage points, respectively. The model achieved a recall of 89.6% for mild disease, meeting the needs of early warning. The study demonstrates that this method can provide technical support for precise monitoring and zoned prevention and control of wheat stripe rust.

Keywords: wheat stripe rust; deep learning; UAV remote sensing; image recognition; attention mechanism; precision agriculture

 1 Introduction

Wheat is the second largest grain crop in China, and its stable production and supply are directly related to national food security. Wheat stripe rust is caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici and is characterized by rapid spread, high outbreak frequency, and severe yield losses. In pandemic years, it can cause yield losses of 10%–30%, and in severe cases, even total crop failure. At present, disease monitoring mainly relies on visual field surveys by grassroots plant protection personnel, which is not only time-consuming and labor-intensive but also strongly influenced by subjective experience, making it difficult to meet the needs of rapid monitoring over large areas. In recent years, UAV remote sensing technology has been widely used in crop growth monitoring and disease and pest diagnosis due to its advantages of flexibility, high resolution, and controllable cost. However, disease features in UAV images are subtle and the background is complex, and traditional machine learning methods rely on manually designed features with limited generalization ability. Deep learning provides a new approach for crop disease recognition by automatically extracting hierarchical features. Existing studies mostly focus on single disease grade classification or laboratory leaf images, and research on multi-grade recognition of wheat stripe rust under complex field environments remains relatively insufficient. Therefore, this study constructs a UAV image recognition model for wheat stripe rust based on an improved convolutional neural network, aiming to achieve accurate discrimination of disease grades and provide a basis for early warning and precise pesticide application for wheat stripe rust.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Study Area and Data Acquisition

The study area is located at the comprehensive experimental base of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences in Xinxiang City, Henan Province (35°18′N, 113°54′E), which has a warm temperate continental monsoon climate, with an average annual temperature of 14.1°C and annual precipitation of about 580 mm. The experimental field covers an area of about 2 hm². The tested wheat variety was the susceptible variety "Mingxian 169." Artificial inoculation was used to induce stripe rust, and healthy controls and plots with different disease severities were established. From the jointing stage to the grain-filling stage of wheat in 2022 and 2023, a DJI Matrice 300 RTK UAV equipped with a Zenmuse P1 camera was used to collect canopy images. The flight altitude was 15 m, the ground resolution was about 0.3 cm/pixel, the forward overlap was 80%, and the side overlap was 70%. Synchronous ground surveys were conducted. According to national standards, samples were divided into four grades based on disease severity: healthy, mild, moderate, and severe. A total of 8,640 valid images were obtained.

 2.2 Image Preprocessing and Dataset Construction

Radiometric correction and geometric correction were performed on the original images. A sliding window method was used to crop them into 512×512 pixel sub-images, and blurred samples and samples with excessive overlap were removed. Data augmentation was performed through rotation, mirroring, brightness adjustment, and adding Gaussian noise. Finally, the dataset was divided into training, validation, and test sets at a ratio of 7:2:1, with 6,048, 1,728, and 864 images, respectively. To avoid data leakage, sub-images cropped from the same original image were assigned only to the same subset.

 2.3 Construction of the WYR-Net Model

ResNet-50 was used as the backbone network, the top fully connected layer was removed, and the convolutional feature extraction part was retained. After Stage 3 and Stage 4, the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) was introduced to enhance the model's sensitivity to channel and spatial features of lesion areas. A Multi-Scale Feature Fusion (MSFF) module was designed to fuse feature maps from different levels after upsampling and channel concatenation, so as to account for both the small chlorotic spots in the early stage of stripe rust and the large-area spore masses in the later stage. The fused features were passed through global average pooling and then input into the fully connected layer, and Softmax was used to output the probabilities of four classes. Model training used the cross-entropy loss function, with an initial learning rate of 0.001, a batch size of 32, the Adam optimizer, 100 iterations, and a cosine annealing strategy to adjust the learning rate. The experiment was based on the PyTorch 1.12 framework, with an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU.

 2.4 Evaluation Metrics

Overall accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and Kappa coefficient were used to evaluate model performance, and a confusion matrix was used to analyze misclassification among categories.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Model Training Process

After WYR-Net was trained to the 35th epoch, the validation set loss tended to stabilize, and the accuracy converged at about 0.95, with no obvious overfitting. In contrast, ResNet-50 stabilized only after the 50th epoch, and the validation loss fluctuated considerably, indicating that the introduction of attention and multi-scale fusion modules can accelerate convergence and improve generalization ability.

 3.2 Model Recognition Performance

On the test set, the overall accuracy of WYR-Net was 94.7%, and the Kappa coefficient was 0.928. The F1 scores for the four classes—healthy, mild, moderate, and severe—were 0.972, 0.901, 0.938, and 0.964, respectively. Among them, mild disease was the most difficult to identify, with a recall of 89.6%, mainly misclassified as healthy, because early stripe rust appears only as scattered chlorotic spots, with little difference from healthy leaves. The severe and healthy categories had the best recognition performance, indicating that the model has strong discriminative ability when disease features are obvious.

 3.3 Comparison with Mainstream Models

On the same dataset, the accuracy of WYR-Net was 4.4, 6.1, and 7.8 percentage points higher than ResNet-50 (90.3%), VGG-16 (88.6%), and MobileNet-V2 (86.9%), respectively, and the Kappa coefficient was also significantly better than the comparison models (P<0.05). Although MobileNet-V2 had the smallest number of parameters and the fastest inference speed, its accuracy could not meet the needs of fine-grained grading. The inference time of WYR-Net for a single image was 23 ms, which can meet the requirements of real-time UAV monitoring.

 3.4 Ablation Experiment

The accuracy of the baseline ResNet-50 was 90.3%. Adding CBAM alone increased it to 92.4%, adding MSFF alone increased it to 92.1%, and adding both reached 94.7%, indicating that the two modules have a synergistic gain effect. Visualized heatmaps showed that the regions of interest of WYR-Net were concentrated on lesions and surrounding chlorotic tissues, highly consistent with the areas interpreted manually.

 4 Discussion

This study confirmed the feasibility of combining deep learning with UAV images to achieve grade recognition of wheat stripe rust. Compared with previous studies based on laboratory leaf images, field canopy images face problems such as uneven illumination, soil background interference, and leaf occlusion, making recognition more difficult. WYR-Net suppresses background noise and strengthens lesion features through the attention mechanism, and accommodates scale differences at different disease stages through multi-scale fusion, thereby achieving higher accuracy. Mild disease recognition remains a difficulty. In the future, hyperspectral or multispectral information can be introduced and combined with time-series image analysis to improve early diagnosis capability. In addition, the dataset in this study came from a single location and a limited number of varieties, and the cross-region and cross-variety generalization ability of the model still needs further verification. In practical applications, the model can be deployed on edge computing devices and combined with real-time UAV image transmission to achieve rapid disease mapping and provide prescription maps for precise pesticide application. This study also has certain limitations: sample grade labeling relied on manual visual inspection, which may introduce subjective errors; and the impact of different growth stages on recognition accuracy was not considered. In follow-up work, samples from more ecological regions and years will be expanded, and transfer learning and semi-supervised learning strategies will be explored to enhance the robustness and applicability of the model.

 5 Conclusion

Aiming at the needs of UAV remote sensing monitoring of wheat stripe rust, this study constructed a multi-grade dataset containing 8,640 field canopy images and proposed an improved deep learning model, WYR-Net. Based on ResNet-50, this model integrates the CBAM attention mechanism and a multi-scale feature fusion module. The overall recognition accuracy on the test set reached 94.7%, and the Kappa coefficient was 0.928, significantly outperforming comparison models such as ResNet-50, VGG-16, and MobileNet-V2. Ablation experiments showed that both the attention module and the multi-scale fusion module made significant contributions to performance improvement. The study demonstrates that this method can effectively identify different severity grades of wheat stripe rust and can provide technical support for early warning, precise pesticide application, and zoned prevention and control of the disease, with good application prospects.

title: Dynamic Analysis of College Physical Education Teaching Quality Evaluation Based on Network under the Big Data
text:
Dynamic Analysis of College Physical Education Teaching Quality Evaluation Based on Network Big Data

Abstract: The scientific evaluation of college physical education teaching quality is a key link in improving teaching standards. To address the problems of traditional evaluation methods, such as single indicators, delayed feedback, and difficulty in handling multi-source heterogeneous data, this paper proposes a dynamic evaluation method for college physical education teaching quality based on network big data. Relying on campus network platforms, this method collects multi-dimensional data such as students' classroom behavior, exercise load, physical fitness test results, and after-class feedback, constructs a dynamic evaluation indicator system, and adopts a combined weighting strategy that integrates the analytic hierarchy process and the entropy weight method to achieve dynamic updating of evaluation indicators. On this basis, a sliding window mechanism and an incremental learning algorithm are designed so that the evaluation model can be continuously adjusted along with the teaching process. Application results show that this method can effectively improve the real-time performance and accuracy of evaluation, provide data support for physical education teaching improvement, and have good promotional value.

Keywords: college physical education; teaching quality evaluation; big data; dynamic analysis; combined weighting

1 Introduction

With the deepening advancement of educational informatization, college physical education teaching is transforming from experience-driven to data-driven. Traditional evaluation of physical education teaching quality mostly relies on final assessments, teacher self-evaluation, and a small number of questionnaires, and suffers from three deficiencies: first, the indicator system is statically fixed and difficult to reflect dynamic changes in the teaching process; second, the data source is single, mainly relying on manual reporting, and lacks the use of objective data such as classroom behavior and exercise load; third, the evaluation cycle is long, usually forming conclusions only after the semester ends, making it impossible to guide teaching adjustments in a timely manner.

At the same time, campus network infrastructure is becoming increasingly complete. Smart bracelets, heart rate belts, video collection terminals, academic administration systems, and physical education course selection platforms have generated a large amount of data related to physical education teaching. These data have characteristics such as multiple sources, heterogeneity, and strong temporal sequence, providing a data foundation for constructing a dynamic evaluation system. How to realize dynamic analysis of college physical education teaching quality based on network big data has become a hot issue in current research on the informatization of physical education.

Focusing on this goal, this paper analyzes the key technical links, proposes a practicable dynamic evaluation scheme, and discusses its application benefits, in order to provide reference for similar institutions.

2 Analysis of Key Technologies

2.1 Multi-source Data Collection and Fusion

The prerequisite for dynamic evaluation is to comprehensively and continuously obtain teaching-related data. The data sources in this paper mainly include four categories: first, academic administration and course selection system data, including class size, course type, class schedule, and student attendance; second, wearable device data, collecting students' classroom heart rate, step count, exercise duration, and energy expenditure through smart bracelets or heart rate belts; third, classroom video and behavioral data, using classroom cameras and posture recognition algorithms to count students' movement completion, practice density, and classroom participation; fourth, after-class feedback data, including students' online teaching evaluations, teachers' teaching logs, and assignment submission status.

Because data from different sources differ in format, frequency, and semantics, fusion processing is required. First, student ID and course number are used as primary keys to establish a unified data association model; second, time series data are resampled and normalized to unify the analytical granularity to the unit of "class session"; finally, a method combining rules and statistics is used for outlier detection and missing value imputation to ensure data quality. Through the above steps, a structured dynamic data set for physical education teaching is formed, providing input for subsequent evaluation.

2.2 Construction of a Dynamic Evaluation Indicator System

Evaluation indicators are the core of measuring teaching quality. Following the principles of scientificity, measurability, and dynamism, this paper constructs a three-level indicator system. The first-level indicators include four aspects: teaching input, teaching process, teaching effect, and teaching feedback. The second-level indicators are further refined as follows: teaching input covers teacher allocation and the utilization rate of venues and equipment; teaching process covers classroom organization, exercise load, practice density, and teacher-student interaction; teaching effect covers the improvement rate of physical fitness tests, skill attainment rate, and sports participation; teaching feedback covers student satisfaction, teachers' willingness to improve, and so on. The third-level indicators are composed of specific collectable data items, such as average heart rate range, proportion of effective exercise time, and improvement range in physical fitness test items.

To reflect dynamism, the indicator system is not fixed and unchanging. At the beginning of each semester, initial weights are determined according to course objectives and students' foundations, and during the semester, indicators are added, removed, or adjusted according to data accumulation. For example, when it is found that extracurricular exercise data for a certain class are seriously missing, the weights of related indicators can be temporarily reduced to avoid evaluation distortion.

2.3 Combined Weighting and Dynamic Updating Algorithm

Indicator weights directly affect the rationality of evaluation results. A single weighting method has limitations: the analytic hierarchy process relies on expert experience and is highly subjective; the entropy weight method relies on the degree of data dispersion and may ignore the actual importance of indicators. This paper adopts a combined weighting strategy, synthesizing the subjective weights obtained by the analytic hierarchy process and the objective weights obtained by the entropy weight method in a certain proportion, which not only retains experts' understanding of teaching laws but also reflects the distribution characteristics of actual data.

To achieve dynamic updating, a sliding window mechanism is introduced. Let the window length be the most recent several class sessions. As new data continuously enter, the window slides forward, and old data are gradually eliminated. On this basis, an incremental learning approach is used to update the entropy weights, avoiding the need to recalculate all historical data each time. Specifically, when a new batch of data arrives, only the probability distribution and information entropy of the data within the window are updated, and then they are recombined with the subjective weights. This not only reduces computational overhead but also enables the evaluation results to reflect the teaching state over the most recent period.

2.4 Visualization and Early Warning of Evaluation Results

The ultimate purpose of dynamic evaluation is to serve teaching improvement. This paper designs a set of visualization and early warning mechanisms. Evaluation results are presented in forms such as radar charts, trend curves, and class comparison charts, and teachers and administrators can view them through web pages or mobile terminals. When a certain indicator remains below the threshold for consecutive periods, the system automatically issues an early warning, prompting teachers to pay attention to problems such as classroom exercise load or student participation. For example, if the average heart rate of a certain class is below the target range for three consecutive sessions, the system will suggest increasing the proportion of aerobic exercises. Early warning information is also pushed to teaching administrators to facilitate timely intervention and guidance.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

To verify the effectiveness of the above method, a one-semester application experiment was conducted in a second-year basketball elective course at a certain university. The experimental class and the control class were basically consistent in teaching content, class hours, and teacher level. The experimental class adopted the dynamic evaluation method proposed in this paper, while the control class adopted the traditional final evaluation method.

The results showed that the experimental class outperformed the control class in three indicators: classroom exercise load, practice density, and student satisfaction. Among them, the average proportion of effective exercise time in the experimental class reached 72%, while that in the control class was 61%; the improvement in standing long jump and shuttle run scores in the physical fitness test of the experimental class was about 8% and 11% higher than that of the control class, respectively. Teacher feedback indicated that dynamic early warning helped them adjust the teaching plan three times in a timely manner, especially by adding interval training after discovering a decline in students' endurance levels.

From the perspective of management benefits, dynamic evaluation reduced the workload of manual statistics, and data collection and report generation were basically automated, saving about 30% of evaluation management time each semester. At the same time, evaluation results were more objective and transparent, reducing disputes caused by subjective scoring. From the perspective of promotion, this method has low hardware requirements and can be supported by ordinary campus networks, basic wearable devices, and existing academic administration systems, making it suitable for gradual implementation in different types of colleges and universities.

4 Conclusion

Aiming at the problems of static evaluation, lag, and single data sources in college physical education teaching quality evaluation, this paper proposes a dynamic analysis method based on network big data. Through multi-source data collection and fusion, construction of a dynamic indicator system, combined weighting and incremental updating algorithms, and visualization and early warning mechanisms, continuous tracking and timely feedback of teaching quality are achieved. Application results show that this method can improve the accuracy and timeliness of evaluation, promote teaching improvement, and has good operability and promotional value.

Future research can further explore data sharing mechanisms across campuses and courses, introduce more refined motion recognition models, and pay attention to data privacy and ethical issues, so as to make the dynamic evaluation system more complete.

title: Morphophysiological mechanism of rice yield increase in response to optimized nitrogen management
text:
Morphophysiological Mechanisms of Optimized Nitrogen Management for Enhancing Rice Yield

 Abstract

Objective: To investigate the morphophysiological regulatory mechanisms of optimized nitrogen management on rice yield formation, and to provide a theoretical basis for green and high-yield rice cultivation. Methods: Using the main japonica rice cultivar "Nanjing 9108" in Jiangsu Province as material, two treatments were established: conventional nitrogen management (CNM, total nitrogen application rate of 300 kg·hm⁻², basal fertilizer∶tillering fertilizer∶panicle fertilizer = 5∶3∶2) and optimized nitrogen management (ONM, total nitrogen application rate of 240 kg·hm⁻², basal fertilizer∶tillering fertilizer∶panicle fertilizer = 3∶3∶4). Differences in population canopy structure, leaf photosynthetic characteristics, root morphology and physiology, and nitrogen uptake and utilization were systematically compared. Results: Compared with CNM, the ONM treatment significantly increased rice yield by 12.6%, mainly manifested as a 9.8% increase in spikelets per panicle and a 5.2% increase in seed-setting rate.
