This temporal expression pattern of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory factors reflects the fine regulatory capacity of the immune system of A. sinensis.

It is noteworthy that the expression magnitude of immune genes varied significantly among different tissues, with head kidney > spleen > liver, which may be related to differences in immune cell composition and TLR expression abundance among organs. In addition, as an ancient fish species, the immune regulatory mechanisms of A. sinensis may possess both primitive and specialized characteristics, warranting further in-depth investigation.

 5 Conclusion

(1) C. freundii exhibits significant pathogenicity to juvenile A. sinensis, with an LD₅₀ of 3.2×10⁶ CFU/mL, and infection can cause septicemia and multi-organ damage.

(2) Infection can significantly induce the expression of IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-10, MyD88, and NF-κB genes in the head kidney, spleen, and liver of A. sinensis, showing明显的 temporal changes.

(3) The head kidney is the primary immune responsive organ of A. sinensis against C. freundii infection, and the TLR/MyD88/NF-κB signaling pathway plays a key role in its innate immunity.

(4) The results of this study provide a theoretical reference for the immune prevention and control of bacterial diseases in A. sinensis, and further research on vaccine development and disease-resistant breeding can be carried out in the future.

title: 3-Dimensional simulations and student learning in orthodontic education
text:
Application of Three-Dimensional Simulation Technology in Orthodontic Teaching and Its Impact on Student Academic Outcomes

Abstract: Objective: To investigate the impact of applying three-dimensional simulation technology in orthodontic teaching on students' understanding of orthodontic biomechanics and improvement of clinical thinking ability. Methods: Sixty fourth-year undergraduate students majoring in stomatology at a certain university were selected and randomly divided into an experimental group and a control group, with 30 students in each group. The experimental group received instruction assisted by three-dimensional simulation software, while the control group received instruction using traditional two-dimensional images and plaster models. After the teaching was completed, the teaching effectiveness was evaluated through theoretical examinations, case analysis tests, and questionnaire surveys. Results: The theoretical examination score of the experimental group was (85.3±6.2) points, and the case analysis score was (82.7±5.9) points, both significantly higher than those of the control group (P<0.05). The questionnaire survey showed that students in the experimental group outperformed those in the control group in terms of spatial understanding, learning interest, and clinical confidence. Conclusion: Three-dimensional simulation technology can effectively improve the effectiveness of orthodontic teaching and is worthy of further application in technology promotion-oriented teaching.

1 Introduction

Orthodontics is a highly practice-oriented branch of stomatology, the core of which lies in understanding the positional relationships and movement patterns of teeth, jaws, and soft tissues in three-dimensional space. Traditional teaching mainly relies on two-dimensional X-ray films, plaster models, and schematic diagrams, making it difficult for students to intuitively grasp the spatial process of alveolar bone remodeling and tooth movement under orthodontic forces. In recent years, with the development of computer graphics and image reconstruction technology, three-dimensional simulation technology has gradually entered the field of stomatological education. This technology can transform cone-beam CT data into interactive three-dimensional models, simulate tooth movement, anchorage control, and mechanical effects of orthodontic appliances, providing students with visual and operational experiences close to clinical reality. However, the promotion of this technology in orthodontic teaching still faces issues such as cost, faculty, and curriculum integration. This paper aims to analyze the actual impact of three-dimensional simulation technology on students' learning outcomes through a controlled teaching study, providing a reference for technology promotion.

2 Analysis of Key Technologies

2.1 Three-Dimensional Data Acquisition and Model Reconstruction

The foundation of three-dimensional simulation teaching is high-quality data acquisition. Currently, cone-beam CT scanning is commonly used to obtain raw data of the patient's craniomaxillofacial region and dentition, with slice thickness controllable at 0.2–0.4 mm. Subsequently, threshold segmentation and region growing algorithms are used to separate structures such as teeth, alveolar bone, maxillary sinus, and mandibular nerve canal, generating independent three-dimensional mesh models. The reconstructed models can accurately reflect root morphology, cortical bone thickness, and alveolar process undercuts, providing an anatomical basis for subsequent simulation. In teaching practice, instructors can select typical malocclusion cases, such as Angle Class II Division 1 or Class III skeletal crossbite, for students to repeatedly observe and measure.

2.2 Mechanical Simulation of Orthodontic Tooth Movement

The essence of orthodontic treatment is periodontal tissue remodeling guided by mechanics. Three-dimensional simulation software can set the magnitude, direction, and point of application of orthodontic forces, and based on finite element analysis or spring-damper models, calculate the initial displacement of teeth in three-dimensional space and the stress distribution of the periodontal ligament. Students can observe differences in tooth tipping, translation, or rotational movement by adjusting bracket positions, archwire materials, and traction force directions. For example, when closing extraction spaces, students can simulate the degree of labial inclination of anterior teeth under different torque control conditions, understanding the mechanical mechanism of anchorage loss. This interactive simulation transforms abstract mechanical concepts into visual displacement contour maps, helping to overcome teaching difficulties.

2.3 Dynamic Visualization of the Treatment Process

Traditional teaching finds it difficult to present the continuous process of orthodontic treatment. Three-dimensional simulation technology can divide treatment into several stages, each corresponding to a set of tooth positions and occlusal relationships, displayed in the form of animations or sequential models. Students can drag the timeline to observe the gradual movement of teeth from the initial position to the target position, as well as the effects of intermaxillary traction, arch expansion, and other auxiliary devices. Dynamic visualization can also simulate jaw changes during growth modification treatment, such as the effect of functional appliances on mandibular advancement. The introduction of this temporal dimension helps students establish a logical chain between "treatment plan–biomechanics–clinical outcome."

2.4 Virtual Tooth Setup and Appliance Design

Virtual tooth setup is the connecting link between orthodontic teaching and clinical practice. In a three-dimensional environment, students move malpositioned teeth to ideal arch positions and check overbite, overjet, midline, and occlusal contacts. The software can automatically generate the post-setup dentition model and output bracket positioning guides for indirect bonding or clear aligner models. Through this process, students not only practice tooth setup standards but also understand the relationship between appliance design and tooth movement efficiency. Some software supports force feedback devices, allowing students to feel operational differences under different archwire stiffness, enhancing immersion.

2.5 Teaching Platform Integration and Assessment Evaluation

Three-dimensional simulation teaching needs to rely on a stable software platform and course management system. The platform should support case library management, operation record playback, and automatic scoring. For example, the system can record the error values of students' simulated tooth setup, tooth movement paths, and deviations from preset plans, and generate quantitative reports. Teachers can use these for formative assessment and timely correction of students' mechanical misjudgments. The platform can also set up typical error cases, such as excessive anchorage tooth movement or root resorption risk, for student discussion and reflection. In technology promotion, attention should be paid to balancing software interface friendliness and hardware configuration to avoid increasing cognitive load due to operational complexity.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

A total of 60 students were included in this study, with no significant difference in baseline scores between the two groups. After 8 weeks of teaching intervention, the average theoretical examination score of the experimental group was (85.3±6.2) points, while that of the control group was (76.8±7.1) points; the case analysis test score of the experimental group was (82.7±5.9) points, while that of the control group was (71.4±6.8) points, with statistically significant differences (P<0.05). In the questionnaire survey, 92% of students in the experimental group believed that three-dimensional simulation helped them understand the three-dimensional direction of tooth movement, 88% of students indicated that it increased their learning interest, and 85% of students believed that it enhanced their clinical operational confidence. The corresponding proportions in the control group were 63%, 67%, and 58%, respectively.

From the perspective of teaching benefits, three-dimensional simulation technology has the following advantages: First, it reduces the consumption of extracted teeth and plaster models, lowering material costs; Second, it allows repeated operations, enabling students to repeatedly trial and error without affecting patients; Third, the standardized case library facilitates unified assessment standards and reduces evaluation differences among teachers. At the same time, this technology also has limitations: the initial equipment investment is relatively high, the software learning curve is relatively steep, and the simulation results still require clinical validation. Therefore, it is recommended to adopt a "virtual-real combination" strategy in promotion, that is, three-dimensional simulation, plaster models, and clinical clerkship complement each other rather than completely replace one another.

4 Conclusion

Through data reconstruction, mechanical simulation, dynamic visualization, and virtual tooth setup, three-dimensional simulation technology provides an intuitive, interactive, and quantifiable learning environment for orthodontic teaching. This study demonstrates that this technology can significantly improve students' theoretical scores and case analysis abilities, and has a positive impact on learning interest and clinical confidence. Despite the challenges of cost and integration, with the decline in software and hardware costs and the improvement of teaching resource libraries, three-dimensional simulation is expected to become an important auxiliary means of orthodontic education. Future research can expand the sample size, extend the follow-up time, and explore the optimal combination of different teaching models.

title: Nutritional quality, mineral and antioxidant content in lettuce affected by interaction of light intensity and nutrient solution concentration
text:
Abstract: To investigate the interactive effects of light intensity and nutrient solution concentration on the nutritional quality, mineral elements, and antioxidant capacity of lettuce, this study used 'Italian Bolting-Resistant' lettuce as the material, setting two light intensities (200 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹, L1; 400 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹, L2) and two nutrient solution concentrations (1.5 dS·m⁻¹, C1; 3.0 dS·m⁻¹, C2), and conducted a two-factor experiment using hydroponic cultivation. The results showed that under the L2C2 treatment, the contents of soluble sugar, soluble protein, vitamin C, and total antioxidant capacity in lettuce leaves were significantly higher than those under other treatments (P<0.05); under the L2C1 treatment, the aboveground biomass of plants was the largest, but the quality indicators were lower than those under L2C2. In terms of mineral elements, high light intensity significantly promoted the accumulation of Ca, Mg, Fe, and Zn, and the interaction effect with high-concentration nutrient solution was significant. Comprehensive membership function evaluation showed that the L2C2 treatment had the highest comprehensive score. The study indicates that appropriately increasing light intensity combined with a relatively high concentration of nutrient solution can synergistically improve the nutritional and antioxidant quality of lettuce, providing a theoretical basis for high-quality lettuce cultivation in plant factories.

Keywords: lettuce; light intensity; nutrient solution concentration; nutritional quality; mineral elements; antioxidant

1 Introduction

Lettuce (*Lactuca sativa* L.) is a leafy vegetable widely cultivated worldwide, rich in vitamins, dietary fiber, and various mineral elements, and occupies an important position in facility hydroponics and plant factories. Light and nutrient solution are the two core environmental factors for hydroponic lettuce growth. Light intensity directly affects photosynthetic carbon assimilation and the accumulation of secondary metabolites, while nutrient solution concentration determines the level of mineral nutrient supply. Previous studies have shown that singly increasing light intensity or nutrient solution concentration can improve lettuce quality, but systematic reports on the comprehensive effects of their interaction on nutritional quality, mineral elements, and the antioxidant system are still lacking. This study analyzed the effects of the interaction between light intensity and nutrient solution concentration on the nutritional quality, mineral element content, and antioxidant capacity of lettuce, aiming to provide theoretical support for high-quality and efficient lettuce production in plant factories.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Experimental Materials and Design
The experiment was conducted from March to May 2024 in an artificial climate chamber, and the tested lettuce variety was 'Italian Bolting-Resistant'. After disinfection, seeds were sown in sponge seedling blocks, and when they reached the two-leaf-one-heart stage, they were transferred to hydroponic devices. A two-factor completely randomized design was adopted: light intensity was set at 200 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ (L1) and 400 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ (L2); nutrient solution concentration was set at 1.5 dS·m⁻¹ (C1) and 3.0 dS·m⁻¹ (C2), for a total of 4 treatments (L1C1, L1C2, L2C1, L2C2), with 3 replicates per treatment. The photoperiod was 12 h/12 h, temperature was (22±1)°C, and relative humidity was 65%±5%. The nutrient solution used the Hoagland formula and was replaced every 3 d. Samples were taken for determination after 28 d of treatment.

2.2 Determination Indicators and Methods
Soluble sugar was determined by the anthrone colorimetric method; soluble protein was determined by the Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 method; vitamin C was determined by the 2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol titration method; total antioxidant capacity was determined by the FRAP method. Mineral elements (Ca, Mg, Fe, Zn) were determined by atomic absorption spectrophotometry. Biomass was expressed as aboveground fresh weight.

2.3 Data Processing
SPSS 26.0 was used for two-way analysis of variance, Duncan's method for multiple comparisons (P<0.05), and the membership function method for comprehensive evaluation.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Effects of Light Intensity and Nutrient Solution Concentration on Lettuce Biomass
The aboveground fresh weight under the L2C1 treatment was the highest (128.6 g/plant), significantly higher than that under L1C1 (86.4 g/plant) and L1C2 (92.1 g/plant), but not significantly different from that under L2C2 (121.3 g/plant). This indicates that high light intensity promotes biomass accumulation, while excessively high nutrient solution concentration showed no beneficial effect under low light.

3.2 Effects on Nutritional Quality
Under the L2C2 treatment, the contents of soluble sugar (18.7 mg·g⁻¹ FW), soluble protein (2.94 mg·g⁻¹ FW), and vitamin C (42.6 mg·100g⁻¹ FW) were all the highest, significantly higher than those under L1C1 and L1C2 (P<0.05). Under the L2C1 treatment, soluble sugar and vitamin C contents increased by 36.2% and 28.4%, respectively, compared with L1C1, but the increase in soluble protein was limited. Two-way analysis showed that light intensity had an extremely significant effect on vitamin C (P<0.01), nutrient solution concentration had a significant effect on soluble sugar (P<0.05), and their interaction had a significant effect on soluble protein (P<0.05).

3.3 Effects on Mineral Element Content
High light intensity significantly increased the contents of Ca, Mg, Fe, and Zn. Under the L2C2 treatment, the contents of Ca (1.42 mg·g⁻¹ DW), Mg (0.86 mg·g⁻¹ DW), Fe (98.6 μg·g⁻¹ DW), and Zn (54.2 μg·g⁻¹ DW) all reached the highest levels, increasing by 41.3%, 33.7%, 52.1%, and 46.8%, respectively, compared with L1C1. Interaction effect analysis showed that light intensity × nutrient solution concentration had significant effects on Fe and Zn contents (P<0.05), but no significant effects on Ca and Mg.

3.4 Effects on Antioxidant Capacity
The FRAP value under the L2C2 treatment was the highest (1.86 mmol·g⁻¹ FW), significantly higher than that under other treatments. L2C1 was next (1.52 mmol·g⁻¹ FW), and L1C1 was the lowest (0.94 mmol·g⁻¹ FW). This indicates that high light intensity combined with an appropriate nutrient solution concentration can effectively enhance the antioxidant capacity of lettuce.

3.5 Comprehensive Evaluation
Membership function analysis showed that the average membership function value under the L2C2 treatment was the highest (0.82), followed by L2C1 (0.61), L1C2 was 0.43, and L1C1 was the lowest (0.28). This indicates that L2C2 is the optimal combination.

4 Discussion

This study shows that light intensity and nutrient solution concentration have significant interactive effects on lettuce quality. High light intensity promotes photosynthetic electron transport and carbon assimilation, providing more substrates and precursors for the synthesis of soluble sugar and vitamin C; while a relatively high nutrient solution concentration ensures the supply of nitrogen and mineral elements, promoting protein synthesis and ion accumulation. Their synergy can maximize quality improvement. It is worth noting that although the biomass under L2C1 was high, the quality indicators were lower than those under L2C2, indicating that biomass accumulation and quality formation are not completely consistent in their resource requirements. Under high light intensity, if the nutrient solution concentration is insufficient, it may limit secondary metabolism and the synthesis of antioxidant substances. Among mineral elements, Fe and Zn are more sensitive to the interaction between light intensity and nutrient solution concentration, possibly related to their participation in photosynthetic electron transport and the enzymatic antioxidant system. Considering both quality and biomass, L2C2 is a suitable combination for high-quality lettuce cultivation in plant factories.

5 Conclusion

The combination of light intensity at 400 μmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ and nutrient solution concentration at 3.0 dS·m⁻¹ can significantly increase the contents of soluble sugar, soluble protein, and vitamin C, as well as the accumulation of Ca, Mg, Fe, and Zn in lettuce, and enhance total antioxidant capacity, with the best comprehensive quality. It is recommended to adopt a management strategy of high light intensity combined with moderately increased nutrient solution concentration in lettuce production in plant factories.

title: Nurses' Experiences in Safe Handling of Chemotherapeutic Agents: The Taiwan Case
text:
Nurses' Experiences of Safely Handling Chemotherapy Drugs: A Case Study in Taiwan

 Abstract

Chemotherapy drugs are widely used in cancer treatment, but occupational exposure to them poses a potential threat to the health of nursing staff. This study aims to explore the actual experiences of nurses in Taiwan in safely handling chemotherapy drugs, and to analyze the barriers they face and their coping strategies. Through semi-structured interviews and on-site observations, data were collected from 32 oncology nurses at 6 hospitals in northern, central, and southern Taiwan. The study found that nurses mainly face problems in the safe handling of chemotherapy drugs, including insufficient accessibility of protective equipment, excessive workload, inconsistent implementation of operating standards, and lack of continuous training. By introducing standardized operating procedures, improving the allocation of protective equipment, and establishing peer support mechanisms, nurses' risk of occupational exposure was significantly reduced. This study can provide a reference for other regions to improve occupational safety management for chemotherapy drugs.

Keywords: chemotherapy drugs; occupational safety; nurses' experiences; Taiwan; protective behaviors

 1 Introduction

Chemotherapy drugs are cytotoxic, mutagenic, and carcinogenic. Nursing staff may be occupationally exposed during preparation, administration, and waste disposal through skin contact, inhalation, or ingestion. The International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified multiple chemotherapy drugs as carcinogens. Taiwan has more than 120,000 new cancer cases each year, and oncology nurses frequently handle chemotherapy drugs in their daily work, making their occupational safety an issue worthy of attention.

Since the 1990s, Taiwan has gradually implemented guidelines for the safe handling of chemotherapy drugs, requiring the use of biological safety cabinets, the wearing of personal protective equipment, and the implementation of classified waste management. However, in clinical practice, problems remain, such as low compliance with protective behaviors and uneven equipment allocation. Previous studies have mostly focused on European and American countries, while localized research on the experiences of nurses in Taiwan is relatively limited. Through qualitative research methods, this study aims to gain an in-depth understanding of the real experiences of nurses in Taiwan in the process of safely handling chemotherapy drugs, identify key barriers and facilitating factors, and provide a basis for formulating safety management strategies that fit local realities.

 2 Analysis of Key Technologies

 2.1 Main Routes of Chemotherapy Drug Exposure and Risk Perception

Nurses mainly face three types of exposure routes during chemotherapy drug handling: first, aerosols and splashes generated when opening drug vials and withdrawing liquid during the preparation stage; second, drug leakage when connecting and disconnecting infusion tubes during the administration stage; and third, secondary exposure caused by needle recapping and squeezing infusion bags during the waste disposal stage. Interviews showed that most nurses could identify the above risks, but had insufficient understanding of the cumulative effects of long-term low-dose exposure. Some nurses believed that "as long as it does not splash directly onto the skin, it does not matter," reflecting blind spots in risk perception. Hospitals in Taiwan generally require annual occupational safety training, but the training content emphasizes theory and lacks scenario simulation and practical assessment, resulting in uneven sensitivity to exposure risks among nurses.

 2.2 Current Status of Protective Equipment Allocation and Use

Biological safety cabinets are the core protective equipment for chemotherapy drug preparation. This study found that 4 of the 6 hospitals had dedicated chemotherapy preparation centers equipped with Class II Type B2 biological safety cabinets; the other 2 had ward nurses operating in treatment rooms, equipped only with Class I biological safety cabinets or clean benches, with insufficient protection levels. In terms of personal protective equipment, most hospitals provided double gloves, isolation gowns, goggles, and N95 masks, but in actual use, problems often occurred, such as inappropriate glove sizes and poor breathability of isolation gowns, affecting operational flexibility and comfort. Some nurses reported that during busy periods they simplified protective steps to save time, such as not wearing goggles or reusing the same pair of gloves. In addition, problems such as unclear labeling of waste collection containers and unreasonable placement of sharps boxes also increased the risk of exposure.

 2.3 Implementation of Operating Standards and Work Organization Factors

With reference to the guidelines of the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration and the Oncology Nursing Society, Taiwan has formulated safe operating standards for chemotherapy drugs, covering drug receipt, storage, preparation, administration, waste disposal, and post-exposure management. However, there are obvious differences at the implementation level. The study found that workload is the primary factor affecting the implementation of standards. In outpatient chemotherapy units, nurses need to handle 20 to 30 patients per day on average, and during peak periods prepare drugs for multiple patients at the same time, leading to rushed operations and simplified protective steps. When staffing is insufficient, nurses often need to balance chemotherapy administration with general nursing work, making it difficult to focus on implementing safety procedures. In addition, team atmosphere and peer supervision have a significant impact on protective behaviors. When senior nurses take the lead in complying with standards, new staff are more likely to develop good habits; conversely, if the team generally neglects protection, individuals also tend to follow suit.

 2.4 Training Models and Knowledge Translation

Continuing education is key to maintaining nurses' safety protection capabilities. This study found that chemotherapy drug safety training in Taiwan mostly adopts the form of centralized lectures, once or twice a year, with content mainly focused on regulatory updates and theoretical explanations. Nurses generally reported that the training content was disconnected from clinical reality and lacked differentiated protection guidance for different administration routes (such as intravenous push, continuous infusion, and oral administration). Some hospitals introduced scenario simulation teaching, conducting drills by simulating scenarios such as drug spills and needlestick injuries, and nurses reported that such training was more practical. However, scenario simulation requires more time and manpower and is difficult to carry out routinely in hospitals with tight staffing. In terms of knowledge translation, nurses' mastery of post-exposure management procedures varied, and some personnel were unclear about the specific steps of immediately rinsing, reporting, and receiving follow-up examinations after exposure.

 2.5 Post-Exposure Management and Support Systems

Post-exposure management for occupational exposure to chemotherapy drugs includes local treatment, reporting and registration, risk assessment, and subsequent health monitoring. The study found that hospitals in Taiwan generally have occupational exposure reporting systems, but nurses' willingness to report is affected by multiple factors. Fear of being blamed, believing the exposure was not serious, and cumbersome reporting procedures are the main barriers. After a small amount of drug liquid splashed onto the skin, some nurses only rinsed it themselves without reporting, resulting in underreporting of exposure incidents. In terms of support systems, most hospitals provide post-exposure consultation and follow-up examinations, but psychological support is relatively weak. After exposure, nurses often experience anxiety, self-blame, and other emotions, lacking timely psychological counseling. Establishing a non-punitive reporting culture, simplifying reporting procedures, and providing peer support can help improve the reporting rate and quality of management of exposure incidents.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

Through the implementation of the above improvement measures, the hospitals participating in the study achieved positive results in occupational safety management for chemotherapy drugs. First, the implementation of standardized operating procedures increased nurses' compliance with protective behaviors from 62% before the intervention to 89% after the intervention, among which goggle use increased from 45% to 82%, and double glove use increased from 70% to 95%. Second, centralized management of chemotherapy drug preparation centers reduced the risk of drug exposure in wards, and aerosol concentrations during the preparation stage decreased by about 70%. Third, nurses covered by scenario simulation training improved their average score on the post-exposure management knowledge test by 23 points, and their willingness to report was significantly enhanced. Fourth, the establishment of a non-punitive reporting system increased the reporting rate of exposure incidents from 35% to 78%, providing a more complete data basis for risk assessment and improvement.

In terms of benefits, reducing nurses' occupational exposure risk directly reduced sick leave and manpower losses caused by health damage. Taking the participating hospitals as an example, within one year after the intervention, chemotherapy drug-related occupational exposure incidents decreased from an annual average of 14 cases to 5 cases, a decrease of 64%. At the same time, nurses' satisfaction with occupational safety increased from 58% before the intervention to 81%, and turnover intention decreased. From a cost-benefit perspective, although the initial investment included costs such as equipment updates, training organization, and process reform, in the long run, the medical expenses, compensation expenditures, and manpower replacement costs saved by reducing exposure incidents are more considerable. In addition, a safe working environment helps improve nursing quality and patient safety, forming a virtuous cycle.

 4 Conclusion

Nurses in Taiwan have accumulated rich experience in safely handling chemotherapy drugs, but still face challenges such as uneven allocation of protective equipment, excessive workload, a single training model, and insufficient post-exposure support. Through standardized operating procedures, centralized preparation management, scenario simulation training, and the establishment of a non-punitive reporting system, nurses' compliance with protective behaviors can be effectively improved and the risk of occupational exposure reduced. The results of this study can provide practical reference for Taiwan and other regions with similar resources to optimize occupational safety management for chemotherapy drugs. In the future, further attention should be paid to improving protective conditions in primary hospitals and outpatient chemotherapy units, promoting the transformation of safety culture from institutional constraints to conscious behavior, and effectively safeguarding the occupational health of nursing staff.

title: Workplace violence against nurses in the Gambia: mixed methods design
text:
Workplace Violence Against Nurses in The Gambia: A Mixed-Methods Design

Abstract

Objective: To investigate the prevalence, types, influencing factors, and coping strategies of workplace violence against nurses in The Gambia, and to provide evidence for developing targeted interventions. Methods: A mixed-methods design was employed. From January to June 2023, a cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted among 312 registered nurses in 6 public hospitals and 4 private hospitals across three major administrative regions of The Gambia (Banjul, Kanifing, and Brikama), and semi-structured in-depth interviews were conducted with 20 of these nurses. Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0 for descriptive statistics and logistic regression analysis, while qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Results: The overall prevalence of workplace violence among nurses was 68.3% (213/312), with verbal abuse accounting for 52.6%, physical assault 14.7%, sexual harassment 9.9%, and bullying 23.1%. Emergency department (OR=2.84, 95%CI: 1.52-5.31), night shift work (OR=2.17, 95%CI: 1.24-3.79), and years of service ≤5 years (OR=1.96, 95%CI: 1.08-3.55) were independent risk factors for violence. Qualitative analysis identified four themes: normalization of violence, institutional silence, psychological trauma and burnout, and lack of coping resources. Conclusion: Workplace violence against nurses in The Gambia is a serious problem that requires a comprehensive intervention system built from three aspects: hospital management, legal protection, and occupational support.

Keywords: workplace violence; nurses; The Gambia; mixed methods; occupational health

1 Introduction

Workplace violence (WPV) has become a prominent issue in the field of global public health. The World Health Organization defines WPV as direct or indirect acts of abuse, threats, or attacks against workers in work-related environments. The healthcare sector, due to its unique characteristics, has become a high-incidence area for WPV. An International Council of Nurses survey showed that approximately 60% of nurses worldwide have experienced violence to varying degrees.

The Gambia is a developing country in West Africa, with scarce healthcare resources and a severe nursing shortage. According to 2022 statistics from the Ministry of Health of The Gambia, there are only approximately 1,800 registered nurses nationwide, with a nurse-to-patient ratio of approximately 1:1500, far below the WHO recommended standard. A high-burden work environment may exacerbate the risk of violence. However, research on WPV among nurses in The Gambia is extremely limited, lacking systematic data. This study employed a mixed-methods design to comprehensively reveal the characteristics, influencing factors, and coping experiences of nurses regarding WPV in The Gambia, providing empirical evidence for developing localized intervention strategies.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Design

An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed, conducted in two phases: the first phase was a quantitative cross-sectional survey, and the second phase was qualitative in-depth interviews, with in-depth interpretation based on the quantitative results.

2.2 Study Participants and Sampling

Quantitative phase: Stratified random sampling was used. From January to March 2023, 312 registered nurses were selected from 10 hospitals (6 public and 4 private) across three administrative regions of The Gambia: Banjul, Kanifing, and Brikama. Inclusion criteria: holding a Gambian nursing practice certificate, currently employed and on duty, and having worked for at least 6 months. Exclusion criteria: student nurses, nurses in administrative positions, and those who refused to participate. A total of 340 questionnaires were distributed, and 312 valid questionnaires were returned, with a valid response rate of 91.8%.

Qualitative phase: Purposive sampling was used. Based on the characteristics of high-violence departments and low reporting rates identified in the quantitative results, 20 nurses were selected for in-depth interviews until information saturation was reached.

2.3 Research Instruments

Quantitative instrument: A self-developed "Nurse Workplace Violence Survey Questionnaire" was used, including sociodemographic characteristics, violence experiences (type, frequency, perpetrator, reporting status), influencing factors, and coping strategies. The questionnaire was reviewed by 5 experts, with a Cronbach's α coefficient of 0.87.

Qualitative instrument: A semi-structured interview guide was developed, focusing on violence experiences, feelings, coping strategies, and support needs.

2.4 Data Collection

Quantitative data were collected by trained research assistants who distributed questionnaires face-to-face, with anonymous completion. Qualitative interviews were audio-recorded with consent, each lasting 40-60 minutes, and transcribed verbatim.

2.5 Statistical Analysis

Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0, including descriptive statistics, χ² tests, and multivariate logistic regression. Qualitative data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis method, with two researchers independently coding and reaching consensus through discussion.

2.6 Ethical Review

This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Gambia Medical Research Council (No.: GMRC/2022/089). All participants signed informed consent forms.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Sociodemographic Characteristics

Among the 312 nurses, 78.2% were female and 21.8% were male; ages ranged from 21 to 54 years, with a mean of (31.4±7.2) years; 41.3% had ≤5 years of service, 32.1% had 6-10 years, and 26.6% had >10 years; 18.9% were emergency department nurses, 27.6% internal medicine, 22.4% surgery, 15.7% pediatrics, and 15.4% other departments.

3.2 Prevalence and Types of Workplace Violence

In the past 12 months, 68.3% (213/312) of nurses experienced at least one incident of WPV. Verbal abuse was the most common (52.6%), followed by bullying (23.1%), physical assault (14.7%), and sexual harassment (9.9%). Perpetrators were mainly patients' family members (46.5%), followed by patients themselves (31.2%), colleagues (12.7%), and administrators (9.6%).

3.3 Violence Reporting Status

Only 27.2% of victims formally reported violence incidents. Reasons for non-reporting were, in order: believing "reporting is useless" (38.5%), "fear of retaliation" (26.4%), "not knowing the reporting channels" (18.3%), "self-blame" (11.7%), and others (5.1%).

3.4 Analysis of Influencing Factors

Univariate analysis showed that department, years of service, night shift frequency, and nurse-to-patient ratio were significantly associated with the occurrence of WPV (P<0.05). Multivariate logistic regression indicated that emergency department (OR=2.84, 95%CI: 1.52-5.31), night shift work (OR=2.17, 95%CI: 1.24-3.79), and years of service ≤5 years (OR=1.96, 95%CI: 1.08-3.55) were independent risk factors.

3.5 Qualitative Interview Results

Four themes were identified:

Theme 1: Normalization of violence. Most nurses regarded violence as an "inevitable part" of their work. Interviewee N7: "You might get yelled at every day at work; we've gotten used to it."

Theme 2: Institutional silence. Hospitals lacked effective reporting and protection mechanisms. N12: "After reporting, no one handles it; instead, they say 'it's because you didn't communicate well.'"

Theme 3: Psychological trauma and burnout. Violence led to anxiety, insomnia, and increased turnover intention. N15: "After being pushed by a family member once, I was afraid to go to work for a whole week."

Theme 4: Lack of coping resources. There was a lack of psychological support and training. N19: "No one taught us how to deal with violence; we just have to endure it ourselves."

4 Discussion

This study is the first to systematically reveal the high prevalence of WPV among nurses in The Gambia (68.3%), which is higher than the global average and similar to reports from some sub-Saharan African countries. The high risk in emergency departments and during night shifts is consistent with domestic and international studies, reflecting the compounding effects of complex work environments and insufficient staffing. The low reporting rate (27.2%) highlights institutional barriers, with nurses lacking trust in reporting mechanisms and insufficient attention from management.

Qualitative results further revealed that violence is not merely an individual experience but a manifestation of systemic problems. Scarce healthcare resources, imbalanced nurse-to-patient ratios, and the absence of legal protection collectively constitute the breeding ground for violence. Nurses' "normalization" cognition reflects a distortion of professional culture, and long-term exposure leads to psychological trauma and burnout, exacerbating the instability of the nursing workforce.

Compared with high-income countries, The Gambia lacks specific anti-violence legislation and hospital-level zero-tolerance policies. Recommendations: ① Formulate national-level regulations for the prevention and control of healthcare violence; ② Establish anonymous reporting systems and rapid response mechanisms in hospitals; ③ Conduct violence prevention and communication skills training; ④ Provide psychological support services; ⑤ Optimize nurse-to-patient ratios and improve working conditions.

Limitations of this study: The cross-sectional design cannot establish causality; self-reporting may have recall bias; the sample only covered three administrative regions, limiting generalizability.

5 Conclusion

The prevalence of workplace violence against nurses in The Gambia is as high as 68.3%, with verbal abuse being the most common. Emergency department nurses, night shift workers, and junior nurses are high-risk groups. The violence reporting rate is low, and institutional silence and psychological trauma are prominent issues. It is recommended to build a comprehensive intervention system from four aspects: legal protection, hospital management, occupational support, and staffing allocation, to safeguard nurses' occupational safety and physical and mental health.

title: The Impact of Abusive Supervision on Job Insecurity: A Moderated Mediation Model
text:
Abusive Supervision and Its Impact on Job Insecurity: A Moderated Mediation Model

 Abstract

As a negative leadership behavior, abusive supervision has a significant impact on employees' psychological states and work attitudes. This paper aims to explore the mechanism through which abusive supervision affects job insecurity, and to examine the mediating role of psychological distress and the moderating effect of perceived organizational support. Based on two-wave questionnaire survey data from 328 corporate employees, hierarchical regression analysis and the Bootstrap method were employed to test the hypotheses. The results indicate that: abusive supervision positively affects employees' job insecurity; psychological distress partially mediates the relationship between abusive supervision and job insecurity; perceived organizational support negatively moderates the indirect effect of abusive supervision on job insecurity through psychological distress, such that the higher the perceived organizational support, the weaker the indirect effect. These findings reveal the psychological mechanism and boundary conditions through which abusive supervision affects job insecurity, providing theoretical foundations and intervention suggestions for corporate management practice.

Keywords: abusive supervision; job insecurity; psychological distress; perceived organizational support; moderated mediation

 1 Introduction

In recent years, with the rapid changes in the organizational environment and intensifying market competition, job insecurity has become an important factor affecting employees' physical and mental health and work performance. Job insecurity refers to employees' concerns and anxiety about the continuity of their jobs and the stability of their career development. It not only affects employees' work engagement and organizational commitment but may also lead to negative consequences such as increased turnover intention and reduced innovative behavior. Therefore, exploring the formation mechanism of job insecurity has important theoretical value and practical significance.

Among the many factors influencing job insecurity, leadership behavior is considered one of the key situational variables. Abusive supervision, as a typical negative leadership behavior, refers to subordinates' perception of the sustained hostile verbal and nonverbal behaviors exhibited by their supervisors (excluding physical contact). Existing studies have shown that abusive supervision leads to a series of negative outcomes such as emotional exhaustion, increased psychological stress, and decreased job satisfaction. However, whether and how abusive supervision affects employees' job insecurity remains insufficiently explored in terms of its underlying mechanism.

Based on conservation of resources theory, this paper constructs a moderated mediation model. Conservation of resources theory posits that individuals strive to acquire and protect resources they value, and when resources are threatened or actually lost, they experience tension and stress responses. Abusive supervision, as a negative leadership behavior, not only directly depletes employees' psychological resources but also further exacerbates employees' concerns about job stability by triggering psychological distress. Meanwhile, perceived organizational support, as an important external resource, may buffer the negative effects of abusive supervision.

The research objectives of this paper include: first, to examine the direct effect of abusive supervision on job insecurity; second, to explore the mediating role of psychological distress between the two; third, to investigate the moderating effect of perceived organizational support on the mediating path. The findings will provide theoretical guidance and practical implications for organizational interventions targeting the negative effects of abusive supervision.

 2 Key Technology Analysis

 2.1 Direct Effect of Abusive Supervision on Job Insecurity

Abusive supervision is employees' subjective perception of sustained hostile behaviors exhibited by their supervisors, including public criticism, ridicule, ignoring, and shifting blame. Such behaviors send signals to employees of "not being valued" and "being replaceable at any time," thereby directly triggering employees' concerns about the stability of their positions.

From the perspective of conservation of resources theory, abusive supervision constitutes a significant threat to employees' psychological resources. When employees are chronically exposed to a work environment characterized by belittlement and negation, their personal resources such as self-esteem and self-efficacy continuously deplete, and their ability to cope with work stress declines accordingly. In this resource-depleted state, employees are more likely to interpret ambiguous organizational signals as threats, thereby generating stronger job insecurity. Accordingly, this paper proposes the following hypothesis:

H1: Abusive supervision positively affects employees' job insecurity.

 2.2 Mediating Role of Psychological Distress

Psychological distress refers to negative emotional states such as anxiety, depression, and tension that individuals experience when facing stressful situations. Abusive supervision, as a sustained interpersonal stressor, significantly elevates employees' levels of psychological distress. According to affective events theory, inappropriate supervisory behaviors trigger employees' negative affective reactions, which in turn influence employees' attitudes and behaviors.

The exacerbation of psychological distress further affects employees' cognitive appraisal of their work situation. When employees are in a state of high psychological distress, their cognitive resources are heavily occupied, information processing is biased toward threatening cues, and they are prone to making more pessimistic judgments about the organizational environment and their own circumstances. This cognitive bias amplifies employees' perception of job instability factors, thereby enhancing job insecurity. Therefore, abusive supervision indirectly increases employees' job insecurity by triggering psychological distress. Accordingly, this paper proposes the following hypothesis:

H2: Psychological distress mediates the relationship between abusive supervision and job insecurity.

 2.3 Moderating Role of Perceived Organizational Support

Perceived organizational support refers to employees' overall perception of whether the organization values their contributions and cares about their well-being. As an important organizational resource, perceived organizational support can provide employees with emotional support and instrumental assistance, alleviating the negative effects of stressful events.

In contexts of high perceived organizational support, employees perceive the organization as a reliable backing, and even when facing abusive behaviors from supervisors, they believe that the organization as a whole still values them. This belief can buffer the activating effect of abusive supervision on psychological distress and reduce the likelihood of employees interpreting abusive supervision as "organizational disapproval." Conversely, in contexts of low perceived organizational support, employees lack supplementary external resources, and abusive supervision is more likely to translate into intense psychological distress, thereby exacerbating job insecurity.

Accordingly, this paper proposes a moderated mediation model hypothesis:

H3: Perceived organizational support negatively moderates the indirect effect of abusive supervision on job insecurity through psychological distress. Specifically, the higher the perceived organizational support, the weaker the indirect effect.

 2.4 Research Methods

This paper adopts the questionnaire survey method to collect data, with corporate employees as the research subjects, and reduces common method bias through a two-wave, multi-source design. In the first wave, data on employees' perceived abusive supervision and perceived organizational support were collected; in the second wave (two weeks later), data on psychological distress and job insecurity were collected. A total of 328 valid questionnaires were obtained.

Established domestic and international scales were used to measure each variable: abusive supervision was measured using the 15-item scale developed by Aryee et al. (2007); psychological distress was measured using the 6-item short-form scale developed by Kessler et al. (2003); job insecurity was measured using the 4-item scale developed by De Witte (2000); perceived organizational support was measured using the 8-item short-form scale developed by Eisenberger et al. (1986). All scales used a 5-point Likert scoring format. Reliability and validity test results indicated that all scales had good internal consistency and construct validity.

Data analysis was conducted using SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.3, including confirmatory factor analysis, descriptive statistics, hierarchical regression analysis, and Bootstrap mediation effect testing.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

 3.1 Descriptive Statistics and Correlation Analysis

Correlation analysis results showed that abusive supervision was significantly positively correlated with psychological distress (r=0.42, p<0.01) and job insecurity (r=0.38, p<0.01); psychological distress was significantly positively correlated with job insecurity (r=0.45, p<0.01); perceived organizational support was significantly negatively correlated with psychological distress (r=-0.31, p<0.01) and job insecurity (r=-0.28, p<0.01). These results provided preliminary support for subsequent hypothesis testing.

 3.2 Mediation Effect Test

The Baron and Kenny stepwise regression method was used to test the mediation effect. In the first step, the positive effect of abusive supervision on job insecurity was significant (β=0.36, p<0.001), supporting H1. In the second step, the positive effect of abusive supervision on psychological distress was significant (β=0.40, p<0.001). In the third step, after simultaneously incorporating abusive supervision and psychological distress into the regression equation, the positive effect of psychological distress on job insecurity was significant (β=0.35, p<0.001), and the effect of abusive supervision decreased from 0.36 to 0.22 (p<0.01), indicating that psychological distress played a partial mediating role.

The Bootstrap method (5,000 resamples) was further employed to test the indirect effect. Results showed that the indirect effect value was 0.14, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.08, 0.21], not containing zero, supporting H2.

 3.3 Moderated Mediation Effect Test

Hierarchical regression analysis was used to test the moderating effect of perceived organizational support. After incorporating the interaction term of abusive supervision and perceived organizational support into the regression equation, the negative effect of the interaction term on psychological distress was significant (β=-0.15, p<0.01), indicating that perceived organizational support negatively moderated the effect of abusive supervision on psychological distress.

Simple slope analysis showed that under low perceived organizational support conditions (mean minus one standard deviation), the effect of abusive supervision on psychological distress was 0.52 (p<0.001); under high perceived organizational support conditions (mean plus one standard deviation), this effect decreased to 0.28 (p<0.001). This indicates that perceived organizational support effectively buffered the negative effects of abusive supervision.

The moderated mediation effect test results showed that under low perceived organizational support conditions, the indirect effect of abusive supervision on job insecurity through psychological distress was 0.18, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.10, 0.28]; under high perceived organizational support conditions, the indirect effect was 0.09, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.03, 0.17]. The between-group difference was significant (Δβ=-0.09, 95% confidence interval of [-0.17, -0.02]), supporting H3.

 3.4 Benefit Analysis

The research findings of this paper have practical benefits in multiple aspects. First, the study reveals the psychological mechanism through which abusive supervision affects job insecurity, providing a clear target for organizational intervention. Managers can reduce employees' job insecurity by reducing abusive behaviors and attending to employees' psychological states. Second, the study identifies the buffering role of perceived organizational support, suggesting that organizations can counteract the negative effects of abusive supervision by enhancing perceived support. Specifically, organizations can establish employee assistance programs, improve grievance channels, and strengthen team building to enhance employees' perceived organizational support.

From an economic benefit perspective, reducing employees' job insecurity helps decrease turnover rates, improve work performance, and reduce recruitment and training costs. From a social benefit perspective, reducing abusive supervision and job insecurity helps improve employees' physical and mental health and promotes the construction of harmonious labor relations.

 4 Conclusion

This paper empirically investigates the mechanism through which abusive supervision affects job insecurity and draws the following main conclusions:

First, abusive supervision significantly positively affects employees' job insecurity. Hostile behaviors from supervisors directly trigger employees' concerns about the stability of their positions, a finding consistent with the predictions of conservation of resources theory.

Second, psychological distress partially mediates the relationship between abusive supervision and job insecurity. Abusive supervision indirectly enhances employees' job insecurity by triggering negative emotional states such as anxiety and depression. This indicates that the emotional mechanism is an important pathway for explaining the negative effects of abusive supervision.

Third, perceived organizational support negatively moderates the indirect effect of abusive supervision on job insecurity through psychological distress. High perceived organizational support can buffer the activating effect of abusive supervision on psychological distress, thereby weakening its indirect effect on job insecurity. This finding reveals the important protective role of perceived organizational support as an external resource.

The theoretical contributions of this paper are as follows: on the one hand, it extends research on abusive supervision to the field of job insecurity, enriching the literature on the outcomes of negative leadership behavior; on the other hand, it constructs a moderated mediation model based on conservation of resources theory, revealing the internal mechanism and boundary conditions through which abusive supervision affects job insecurity.

The practical implications of this paper are as follows: organizations should pay attention to the harms of abusive supervision and reduce its occurrence through leadership training and behavioral norms; meanwhile, they should strive to enhance employees' perceived organizational support and establish a comprehensive support system to help employees cope with work stress; in addition, they should attend to employees' mental health status and promptly identify and intervene in psychological distress issues.

The limitations of this paper are as follows: the use of the questionnaire method makes it difficult to completely rule out limitations in causal inference; the sample is drawn from a specific industry, and the generalizability of the conclusions needs further verification; future research could employ experimental methods or longitudinal tracking designs to further verify causal relationships and explore other potential mediating and moderating variables.

title: Deceleration of China's human water use and its key drivers
text:
Deceleration Trend of China's Human Water Use and Its Key Driving Factors

 Abstract

Objective: To analyze the evolutionary characteristics of China's total human water use from 2000 to 2022, identify the key driving factors behind the deceleration of water use, and provide a scientific basis for water resource management and sustainable development. Methods: Based on provincial water resource bulletins and socioeconomic statistical data, an improved IPAT-LMDI decomposition model was constructed to decompose changes in water use into four effects: population scale, economic development, industrial structure, and water use intensity, with scenario simulations used to assess the contribution of each factor. Results: China's total human water use peaked in 2013 (approximately 623.0 billion m³), after which it entered a deceleration phase with an average annual rate of -0.42%; the share of agricultural water use declined from 68.5% to 61.2%, industrial water use peaked first in 2011, and domestic water use continued to grow at an average annual rate of 1.8% but with a slowing trend. Decomposition results indicate that the decline in water use intensity (contribution rate -58.3%) and industrial structure upgrading (-24.7%) were the dominant factors in the deceleration, while economic development (+52.1%) and population growth (+8.6%) played water-increasing roles. Conclusion: China's water use has achieved preliminary decoupling from economic growth; agricultural water conservation, industrial recycling, and industrial structure adjustment are the core mechanisms of deceleration; in the future, vigilance is needed regarding the rigid growth of domestic water use and the risk of regional water use rebound.

Keywords: human water use; deceleration; LMDI decomposition; driving factors; water resource management; decoupling

 1 Introduction

Water is a fundamental resource for sustaining socioeconomic development and ecosystem health. Over the past two decades, China has supported approximately 18% of the world's population and more than 17% of global economic output with about 6% of the world's freshwater resources, achieving significant improvements in water use efficiency. From 2000 to 2013, China's total water use increased from 549.7 billion m³ to 623.0 billion m³, with an average annual growth rate of 0.96%; however, from 2013 to 2022, it shifted to a negative growth rate of -0.42% per year, exhibiting a typical "water use peaking—deceleration" pattern. Whether this turning point is stable, what factors drive it, and whether it can be sustained are directly related to the implementation effectiveness of the national water security strategy and the "Four Waters and Four Determinations" policy.

Existing studies have mostly focused on water use efficiency or water use changes in a single sector, with few systematically identifying the driving mechanisms of deceleration from a total volume perspective. Based on provincial panel data from 2000 to 2022, this paper adopts an improved IPAT-LMDI model to quantify four types of effects—population, economy, structure, and intensity—and combines scenario simulations to reveal the key driving factors of water use deceleration, aiming to provide empirical support for the rigid constraint system of water resources.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Sources

Water use data were obtained from the 2000–2022 China Water Resources Bulletin and water resources bulletins of each province (autonomous region, municipality), covering four categories: agricultural, industrial, domestic, and ecological water use. Socioeconomic data were taken from the China Statistical Yearbook and provincial statistical yearbooks, including permanent resident population, GDP (converted at constant 2000 prices), value added of the three industries, and industrial value added. For individual missing data, linear interpolation and the mean method of adjacent years were used for completion.

 2.2 Research Methods

An improved IPAT identity and LMDI additive decomposition method were adopted. Let total water use W be expressed as:

W = P × (G/P) × (W/G) = P × g × i

where P is population scale, g is per capita GDP, and i is water use intensity per unit of GDP. Further, i is decomposed into industrial structure effect and sectoral water use intensity effect:

i = Σ_j (G_j/G) × (W_j/G_j)

where j represents the agricultural, industrial, domestic, and ecological sectors. LMDI additive decomposition decomposes the change in water use ΔW into:

ΔW = ΔW_P + ΔW_g + ΔW_s + ΔW_i

Each effect is calculated using logarithmic mean weights to eliminate the residual term. Scenario simulations set a baseline scenario, a water conservation enhancement scenario, and a structural optimization scenario to project water use evolution trends from 2025 to 2035.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Phased Evolution of Total Water Use

From 2000 to 2022, China's total human water use followed an inverted U-shaped trajectory of "first increasing, then decreasing." The period 2000–2013 was a growth phase, with water use increasing from 549.7 billion m³ to 623.0 billion m³, at an average annual growth rate of 0.96%; after peaking in 2013, it entered a deceleration phase, declining to 598.4 billion m³ by 2022, at an average annual rate of -0.42%. By sector, agricultural water use peaked in 2013 (426.8 billion m³), industrial water use peaked first in 2011 (146.2 billion m³), and domestic water use increased from 57.4 billion m³ in 2000 to 86.3 billion m³ in 2022, with an average annual growth rate of 1.8%, though the growth rate dropped to 1.1% after 2018. The share of ecological water use rose from 1.2% to 3.5%, becoming the only functional water use category that continued to grow.

 3.2 Decomposition of Driving Factors of Water Use Change

LMDI decomposition results show that from 2000 to 2013, the economic growth effect (+52.1%) was the dominant force increasing water use, while the water use intensity effect (-38.6%) and industrial structure effect (-12.4%) partially offset the water-increasing pressure, with the population effect contributing +6.8%. From 2013 to 2022, the contribution rate of the water use intensity effect rose to -58.3%, and the industrial structure effect rose to -24.7%; together they offset the water-increasing effects of economic growth (+52.1%) and population growth (+8.6%), turning total water use into negative growth. This indicates that the core mechanism of water use deceleration has shifted from "end-of-pipe water conservation" to "structural optimization and efficiency improvement combined."

 3.3 Regional Differences and Scenario Simulation

Water use in the eastern region peaked first around 2010, with the largest deceleration magnitude (average annual -1.2%); the central region peaked in 2014, with an average annual rate of -0.5%; the western region is still in a plateau period, with water use in some provinces still growing. Scenario simulations indicate that under the baseline scenario, total water use in 2035 will decline to 572.0 billion m³; under the water conservation enhancement scenario, it will decline to 548.0 billion m³; and under the structural optimization scenario, it will decline to 535.0 billion m³. Agricultural water conservation and industrial recycling are the main sources of differences among the scenarios.

 4 Discussion

The essence of China's water use deceleration is the substitution of "efficiency dividends" and "structural dividends" for "scale dividends." In agriculture, the area of high-efficiency water-saving irrigation increased from 130 million mu in 2000 to 580 million mu in 2022, and the irrigation water use coefficient rose from 0.43 to 0.57, directly reducing agricultural water use by approximately 42.0 billion m³. In industry, water use per 10,000 yuan of industrial value added decreased from 285 m³ in 2000 to 42 m³ in 2022, and the recycling rate increased to over 93%. In terms of industrial structure, the share of the tertiary industry rose from 39.0% to 52.8%, while water use per unit of value added in the tertiary industry is only about one-fifth that of the secondary industry; structural upgrading significantly reduced total water use intensity.

However, the deceleration trend faces three challenges: first, the rigid growth of domestic water use—for every 1 percentage point increase in the urbanization rate, domestic water use increases by approximately 0.8–1.2 billion m³; second, regional imbalance—water use in western energy and heavy chemical industrial bases still faces rebound pressure; third, climate change has reduced surface water recharge in the north, potentially forcing groundwater overexploitation. Therefore, under the framework of "Four Waters and Four Determinations," it is necessary to strengthen dual control of total water use and intensity, and promote water rights trading and water-saving technology innovation.

Compared with existing studies, the contributions of this paper are: first, it identifies 2013 as the national water use peak year, earlier than the 2015–2020 estimates in some literature; second, it quantifies the leap in the contribution rate of the industrial structure effect during the deceleration period (from 12.4% to 24.7%); third, it reveals the sectoral heterogeneity in which agricultural water use peaked about 2 years later than industrial water use. The limitation is that virtual water trade and climate change feedback were not included, and future research can further deepen the analysis by incorporating CGE models.

 5 Conclusions

(1) China's total human water use peaked in 2013 (623.0 billion m³), after which it entered a deceleration phase with an average annual rate of -0.42%; agricultural and industrial water use peaked successively, and the growth rate of domestic water use slowed but remained rigid.

(2) The decline in water use intensity and industrial structure upgrading were the dominant factors in the deceleration, with contribution rates of -58.3% and -24.7%, respectively, from 2013 to 2022, offsetting the water-increasing effects of economic growth and population growth.

(3) Regional water use peaking shows a pattern of "earlier in the east and later in the west," with the eastern region experiencing the largest deceleration magnitude, while the western region remains in a plateau period, requiring vigilance against localized rebound.

(4) In the future, it is necessary to strengthen the synergy of agricultural water conservation, industrial recycling, and structural optimization, promote deep decoupling of water use from economic growth, and safeguard national water security.

title: Estimation of municipal solid waste amount based on one-dimension convolutional neural network and long short-term memory with attention mechanism model: A case study of Shanghai
text:
Prediction of Municipal Solid Waste Generation in Shanghai Based on a One-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network and an Attention-Enhanced Long Short-Term Memory Network

Abstract: Accurate prediction of municipal solid waste (MSW) generation is an important basis for urban sanitation planning and the construction of resource recovery and disposal facilities. To address the difficulty that traditional prediction methods face in simultaneously capturing local fluctuation characteristics and long-range dependencies in waste generation data, this paper proposes a hybrid prediction model that integrates a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN), a long short-term memory (LSTM) network, and an attention mechanism. The model takes the MSW collection and transport volume of Shanghai from 2010 to 2023 and related socioeconomic indicators as inputs, uses 1D-CNN to extract local temporal features, LSTM to learn long-term evolution patterns, and the attention mechanism to weight key time steps. The results show that the mean absolute percentage error of the model on the test set is 3.82%, and the coefficient of determination is 0.94, outperforming a single LSTM, support vector regression, and a grey prediction model. This study can provide technical support for the dynamic adjustment of Shanghai's MSW collection, transport, and disposal system.

1 Introduction

With the acceleration of urbanization and the improvement of residents' consumption levels, urban MSW generation has continued to grow, and the contradiction between waste siege and insufficient disposal capacity has become increasingly prominent. As a megacity, Shanghai's MSW collection and transport volume exceeded 9 million tons in 2023. Accurately predicting future generation is of great significance for the planning and layout of classified collection and transport, transfer and compaction, and terminal disposal facilities. MSW generation is affected by multiple factors such as population size, economic level, consumption habits, seasonal variation, and policy intervention, and the series exhibits obvious non-stationarity and nonlinear characteristics. Traditional methods such as multiple linear regression, grey GM(1,1), and support vector regression find it difficult to balance local abrupt changes and long-term trends when dealing with such complex series. In recent years, deep learning methods have performed excellently in time series forecasting. One-dimensional convolutional neural networks are good at extracting local temporal patterns, long short-term memory networks can alleviate gradient vanishing and remember long-term information, and attention mechanisms can adaptively assign weights to different time steps. Taking Shanghai as an example, this paper constructs a 1D-CNN-LSTM-Attention hybrid model, aiming to improve the accuracy of MSW generation prediction and provide decision-making reference for sanitation management.

2 Analysis of Key Technologies

2.1 Data Sources and Preprocessing

The data mainly include the monthly MSW collection and transport volume of Shanghai from 2010 to 2023, as well as annual or monthly indicators such as the permanent resident population, gross regional product, total retail sales of consumer goods, and per capita disposable income of residents. Missing values were filled by linear interpolation, and outliers were identified and corrected using box plots. To eliminate the influence of dimensions, Min-Max normalization was used to map the data to the [0,1] interval. The first 80% of samples were used as the training set and the last 20% as the test set, and a sliding window was used to construct supervised learning samples.

2.2 Feature Extraction by One-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network

By sliding convolution kernels along the temporal direction, 1D-CNN can automatically extract local fluctuation features in the waste generation series, such as monthly peaks, holiday effects, and seasonal cycles. Two convolutional layers were set, with kernel sizes of 3 and 5, respectively, the activation function was ReLU, and max pooling was used to reduce the sequence length. The convolution operation can be expressed as:

$$C_i = f(W_i * X_{t:t+k-1} + b_i)$$

where $W_i$ is the convolution kernel weight, $b_i$ is the bias, and $f$ is the ReLU function. This module effectively enhances the model's sensitivity to short-term abrupt information.

2.3 Temporal Modeling by Long Short-Term Memory Network

LSTM controls the update of the cell state through the forget gate, input gate, and output gate, and is suitable for learning long-term dependencies in the waste generation series. The forget gate determines which historical information to discard, the input gate controls the writing of new information, and the output gate generates the current hidden state. Its core formulas are:

$$f_t = \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1},x_t]+b_f)$$
$$i_t = \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1},x_t]+b_i)$$
$$\tilde{C}_t = \tanh(W_C[h_{t-1},x_t]+b_C)$$
$$C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t$$

This module can effectively memorize the impact of long-term driving factors such as population growth and consumption upgrading on waste generation.

2.4 Weighting by Attention Mechanism

The attention mechanism calculates weights for the hidden states at each time step output by LSTM, highlighting the influence of key periods. Let $h_t$ be the output of LSTM at time $t$; then the attention score is $e_t = u^T \tanh(W_h h_t + b_h)$, the normalized weight is $\alpha_t = \exp(e_t)/\sum_{j=1}^T \exp(e_j)$, and the final context vector is $c = \sum_{t=1}^T \alpha_t h_t$. This mechanism enables the model to pay more attention to periods with sharp increases in waste generation, such as the Spring Festival and National Day, when making predictions, thereby improving the pertinence of prediction.

2.5 Model Training and Parameter Settings

The model was implemented using the PyTorch framework, the loss function was mean squared error, the optimizer was Adam, the initial learning rate was 0.001, the batch size was 32, and the number of training epochs was 200. An early stopping strategy was adopted to prevent overfitting. The number of convolution kernels was set to 64 and 128, the number of LSTM hidden units was 128, and the attention dimension was 64. The optimal hyperparameter combination was determined by grid search.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

On the test set, the mean absolute percentage error of the model in this paper for predicting Shanghai's MSW generation was 3.82%, the root mean square error was 186,000 tons, and the coefficient of determination was 0.94. Compared with a single LSTM (MAPE=5.67%), support vector regression (MAPE=7.21%), and grey GM(1,1) (MAPE=9.34%), the accuracy of the hybrid model improved by about 1.85, 3.39, and 5.52 percentage points, respectively. From the perspective of monthly prediction, the model had smaller errors from March to May and from September to November, and slightly higher errors around the Spring Festival, but the overall fluctuation was controllable. In terms of benefits, the model can predict waste generation 12 months in advance, helping the sanitation department optimize the scheduling of collection and transport vehicles, the capacity allocation of transfer stations, and the operation plans of incineration and landfill facilities. Based on an estimated average annual MSW collection and transport volume of 9 million tons in Shanghai, if precise prediction reduces emergency scheduling costs by 5%, tens of millions of yuan in operating expenses can be saved each year, while also reducing temporary stockpiling and environmental risks caused by insufficient disposal capacity.

4 Conclusion

This paper constructs a 1D-CNN-LSTM-Attention hybrid model and applies it to the prediction of MSW generation in Shanghai. The model fully leverages the advantages of convolutional networks in local feature extraction, LSTM in long-term memory, and attention mechanisms in weighting key information, and its prediction accuracy is significantly better than that of traditional methods. The research results show that this technical route is suitable for waste generation prediction in megacities and has strong value for promotion. In the future, meteorological data, waste classification policy variables, and holiday factors can be further introduced, and transfer learning can be attempted to adapt to different urban scenarios, providing a more reliable technical tool for the refined management of municipal solid waste.

title: Effects of processing adjuvants on traditional Chinese herbs
text:
Effects of processing adjuvants on traditional Chinese herbs

Abstract: Processing adjuvants for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) are an indispensable component of the TCM processing procedure, exerting significant effects on the efficacy, toxicity, and physicochemical properties of TCM. In this study, three commonly used Chinese medicinal materials—Scutellaria baicalensis, Coptis chinensis, and Glycyrrhiza uralensis—were selected as research subjects and processed with different adjuvants, including wine, ginger juice, and honey, respectively. The effects of processing adjuvants on the quality of TCM were systematically evaluated by determining the content of active ingredients, antioxidant activity, and cytotoxicity. The results showed that the baicalin content in wine-processed Scutellaria baicalensis increased by 18.6% compared with the raw product, the berberine content in ginger-processed Coptis chinensis increased by 12.4%, and the glycyrrhizic acid content in honey-processed Glycyrrhiza uralensis increased by 15.2%. Antioxidant experiments showed that the DPPH free radical scavenging capacity of all processed products was superior to that of the raw products, among which the IC₅₀ value of honey-processed Glycyrrhiza uralensis was 0.42 mg/mL, 31.1% lower than that of the raw product. Cytotoxicity experiments indicated that the inhibitory effects of all three processed TCMs on HepG2 cells were enhanced. This study provides a theoretical basis for the scientific selection of processing adjuvants and the optimization of processing technology for TCM.

Keywords: traditional Chinese medicine processing; adjuvants; Scutellaria baicalensis; Coptis chinensis; Glycyrrhiza uralensis; active ingredients; antioxidant activity

1 Introduction

Traditional Chinese medicine processing is an important component of traditional Chinese medicine and pharmacy, with a history dating back to the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods.
