The validation results of 120 samples showed that the coefficient of determination between the predicted values and the values determined by the potassium dichromate oxidation method was 0.89, the average relative error was 7.6%, a single detection took about 3 min, no chemical reagents were required, and the operation was simple. Although this method cannot completely replace standard methods in terms of accuracy, it is suitable as an auxiliary means for rapid field screening and grassroots agricultural technology extension. Subsequent research should focus on solving problems such as sensor drift correction, regional model transfer, and adaptability to multiple soil types, so as to promote the transition of this technology from the laboratory to practical application.

title: Treatments for Iron Deficiency (ID): Prospective Organic Iron Fortification
text:
Abstract: Iron deficiency (ID) is one of the most common nutritional deficiencies worldwide. Traditional inorganic iron fortifiers suffer from problems such as low absorption rates and significant gastrointestinal irritation. In this study, porcine blood hemoglobin was used as a raw material to prepare an organic iron fortifier through enzymatic hydrolysis and chelation processes, and its physicochemical properties, bioavailability, and economic feasibility were evaluated. The results showed that the prepared organic iron fortifier had an iron content of 12.3 mg/g, an iron release rate exceeding 85% in simulated gastrointestinal fluid, and a hemoglobin regeneration efficiency in rats approximately 23% higher than that of ferrous sulfate. When the fortifier was added to biscuits, no significant decrease in sensory scores was observed. Cost estimation showed an additional cost of approximately 42 yuan per ton of biscuits, indicating market promotion potential. This study provides a theoretical basis and data support for the development of organic iron-fortified foods.

Keywords: iron deficiency; organic iron fortification; hemoglobin; bioavailability; food fortification

 1 Introduction

Iron deficiency (ID) is one of the most prevalent nutrient deficiency problems in the world today. According to World Health Organization estimates, approximately 2 billion people worldwide suffer from varying degrees of iron deficiency, with pregnant women, infants, and adolescents being high-risk populations. Iron deficiency can lead to iron deficiency anemia, affecting cognitive development, immune function, and labor capacity, and imposing a heavy burden on society and the economy.

Currently, iron fortification is one of the main strategies for preventing and controlling iron deficiency. Commonly used iron fortifiers include inorganic iron salts such as ferrous sulfate and ferrous fumarate. Although these are low in cost, they have disadvantages such as low absorption rates, tendency to cause gastrointestinal discomfort, and potential to promote lipid oxidation. In contrast, organic iron (such as heme iron, amino acid-chelated iron, and polysaccharide-iron complexes) offers advantages including high absorption rates, good biocompatibility, and fewer side effects, making it a research hotspot in recent years.

China is a major pig farming country, producing large quantities of porcine blood by-products annually, among which hemoglobin is abundant and serves as an excellent raw material for preparing organic iron. However, the current utilization rate of porcine blood resources is relatively low, with few deep-processed products. Therefore, this study used porcine blood hemoglobin as a raw material to prepare an organic iron fortifier through enzymatic hydrolysis and chelation processes, and systematically evaluated its physicochemical properties, bioavailability, and economic feasibility, aiming to provide a scientific basis for developing efficient, safe, and economical organic iron-fortified foods.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Materials and Reagents

Fresh porcine blood was collected from a local slaughterhouse and stored at 4°C for later use. Papain and neutral protease were purchased from a biological reagent company. Ferrous sulfate, ascorbic acid, and phenanthroline were all of analytical grade. SD rats (male, body weight 180±10 g) used in the experiment were purchased from an experimental animal center.

 2.2 Preparation of Organic Iron Fortifier

Porcine blood was centrifuged to separate plasma and red blood cells. The red blood cells were washed with physiological saline, then hemolyzed by adding deionized water. The pH was adjusted to 6.5, papain was added (enzyme-to-substrate ratio 1:100), and enzymatic hydrolysis was carried out at 55°C for 4 h. After enzyme inactivation, the mixture was centrifuged and the supernatant was collected. Subsequently, ferrous sulfate and ascorbic acid were added, and the chelation reaction was carried out at pH 5.0 and 60°C for 2 h. After alcohol precipitation and drying, the organic iron fortifier was obtained.

 2.3 Determination of Physicochemical Properties

Iron content was determined by the phenanthroline colorimetric method; iron release rate was determined by the simulated gastrointestinal fluid method in vitro; protein degradation was analyzed by SDS-PAGE.

 2.4 Bioavailability Evaluation

Forty SD rats were randomly divided into 4 groups: control group (basal diet), ferrous sulfate group, organic iron group, and organic iron + vitamin C group. After 4 weeks of feeding, hemoglobin (Hb), serum ferritin (SF), and liver iron content were measured.

 2.5 Food Fortification and Sensory Evaluation

The organic iron fortifier was added to biscuits at a ratio of 0.5 mg Fe/g, with unfortified biscuits as the control. Ten trained panelists were invited to score color, flavor, mouthfeel, and overall acceptability (9-point scale).

 2.6 Data Analysis

Data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. One-way analysis of variance was performed using SPSS 22.0, with P<0.05 considered a significant difference.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Physicochemical Properties of Organic Iron Fortifier

The prepared organic iron fortifier appeared as a dark brown powder with an iron content of 12.3±0.6 mg/g and a protein content of 48.5±2.1%. SDS-PAGE showed that most of the hemoglobin was degraded into small molecular peptides (<10 kDa) after enzymatic hydrolysis, which is favorable for iron absorption. In vitro simulated gastrointestinal fluid digestion tests showed that the release rate of the fortifier in gastric fluid was 52.4%, and the cumulative release rate in intestinal fluid reached 85.7%, significantly higher than that of the ferrous sulfate group (P<0.05).

 3.2 Bioavailability Evaluation

After 4 weeks of feeding, the hemoglobin concentration of rats in the organic iron group was 142.3±6.8 g/L, significantly higher than that in the ferrous sulfate group (128.5±7.2 g/L) and the control group (105.6±5.4 g/L) (P<0.05). Serum ferritin and liver iron content showed the same trend. The hemoglobin level in the organic iron + vitamin C group was slightly higher than that in the organic iron group, but the difference was not significant (P>0.05). Using ferrous sulfate as a reference, the relative bioavailability (RBV) of organic iron was 123%.

 3.3 Food Fortification and Sensory Evaluation

The iron content of biscuits fortified with the organic iron fortifier was 0.52 mg/g. The sensory evaluation scores were as follows: color 7.8±0.6, flavor 7.5±0.7, mouthfeel 8.1±0.5, overall acceptability 7.9±0.6, with no significant difference from the control group (8.0±0.5, 7.8±0.6, 8.2±0.4, 8.1±0.5) (P>0.05), indicating that the fortifier had little effect on the sensory quality of biscuits.

 3.4 Economic Feasibility Analysis

Based on current raw material and process cost estimates, the cost of preparing 1 kg of organic iron fortifier (iron content 12.3 g) is approximately 320 yuan. At an addition level of 0.5 mg Fe/g, approximately 40.7 g of fortifier is needed per ton of biscuits, with an additional cost of approximately 13 yuan; considering packaging, mixing, and losses, the total additional cost is approximately 42 yuan per ton. At a market price of 20 yuan/kg, the cost increase is approximately 0.21%, demonstrating good economic feasibility.

 4 Discussion

In this study, porcine blood hemoglobin was used as a raw material to prepare an organic iron fortifier through enzymatic hydrolysis and chelation processes, significantly improving iron bioavailability. The mechanism may lie in the following: small molecular peptides produced by enzymatic hydrolysis can form soluble chelates with iron, reducing interference from inhibitory factors such as phytic acid and polyphenols, and promoting iron absorption in the intestine. In addition, the organic iron fortifier has little effect on food sensory quality, making it suitable for fortifying staple foods such as biscuits and flour.

Compared with inorganic iron, the organic iron fortifier has a higher cost, but this study shows that at a reasonable addition level, the cost increase of the final product is limited, and consumer acceptance is relatively high. China has abundant porcine blood resources at low prices, providing a raw material guarantee for the industrial production of organic iron fortifiers. However, this study still has certain limitations: first, no human feeding trials were conducted, and bioavailability data were mainly based on animal models; second, the safety of long-term intake was not evaluated; third, the effects of different food matrices on iron absorption were not considered. Future research can further optimize process parameters, conduct human intervention trials, and explore synergistic effects with other nutrients (such as vitamin C and zinc).

 5 Conclusion

This study successfully prepared an organic iron fortifier based on porcine blood hemoglobin, with an iron content of 12.3 mg/g, an in vitro release rate exceeding 85%, and a relative bioavailability in rats of 123%, significantly superior to ferrous sulfate. The fortifier had no significant effect on the sensory quality of biscuits, with an additional cost of approximately 42 yuan per ton of biscuits, demonstrating good economic feasibility. The results provide a theoretical basis and technical support for developing efficient, safe, and economical organic iron-fortified foods, and also offer a new approach for the high-value utilization of porcine blood by-products.

title: Jejunal tube feeding and pancreatoduodenectomy
text:
Jejunal Tube Feeding and Pancreatoduodenectomy

Abstract: Pancreatoduodenectomy is the primary surgical approach for treating benign and malignant diseases of the pancreatic head and periampullary region, but postoperative nutritional support has always been a challenge in clinical management. Because the surgery alters the anatomical structure of the digestive tract, complications such as delayed gastric emptying, anastomotic edema, and pancreatic fistula often lead to difficulty with oral intake. Jejunal tube feeding, as an enteral nutrition route, can provide nutritional support in the early postoperative period through an intraoperatively placed jejunostomy tube or nasojejunal tube, bypassing the stomach and anastomotic region and reducing stimulation to the gastrointestinal anastomosis. Combining clinical practice, this article analyzes the application points, key technical aspects, and clinical benefits of jejunal tube feeding after pancreatoduodenectomy. Practice has shown that rational application of jejunal tube feeding can shorten hospital stay, reduce nutrition-related complications, and improve the quality of postoperative recovery, making it a postoperative nutritional support method worthy of promotion.

Keywords: jejunal tube feeding; pancreatoduodenectomy; enteral nutrition; postoperative management; nutritional support

1 Introduction

Pancreatoduodenectomy (PD) is one of the most technically demanding operations in general surgery, mainly used to treat pancreatic head cancer, periampullary carcinoma, duodenal tumors, and some cases of chronic pancreatitis. This surgery requires resection of the pancreatic head, duodenum, gallbladder, lower common bile duct, and part of the stomach, followed by reconstruction of the digestive tract, including pancreaticojejunostomy, choledochojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy. The surgical trauma is significant and the operative time is long, with a relatively high incidence of postoperative complications, among which delayed gastric emptying, pancreatic fistula, and infection are the most common postoperative problems.

Nutritional support occupies a central position in postoperative management after PD. Postoperative patients are in a hypercatabolic state, and if nutritional supply is insufficient, they are prone to weight loss, immunocompromise, delayed wound healing, and increased risk of infection. Traditionally, total parenteral nutrition or fasting plus fluid supplementation has often been used after PD, but long-term parenteral nutrition has disadvantages such as catheter-related infection, liver function impairment, and intestinal mucosal atrophy. In recent years, enteral nutrition has gradually become the preferred method of postoperative nutritional support, and jejunal tube feeding is one practical and effective route among them.

Jejunal tube feeding refers to the direct infusion of nutrient solution into the jejunum through an intraoperatively placed jejunostomy tube or a postoperatively placed nasojejunal tube. Because edema and emptying disorders often exist in the stomach and anastomotic region after PD, jejunal tube feeding can bypass these areas and achieve early enteral nutrition. This article aims to analyze the key technical aspects and clinical benefits of jejunal tube feeding after PD, providing a reference for primary hospitals and promotable medical institutions.

2 Analysis of Key Techniques

2.1 Selection of Jejunal Tube Placement Methods

The implementation of jejunal tube feeding first depends on the method of feeding tube placement. At present, there are mainly three commonly used clinical methods: intraoperative jejunostomy tube, nasojejunal tube, and percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy tube.

The intraoperative jejunostomy tube is the most commonly used method. After completing digestive tract reconstruction during PD, the surgeon can select a segment of jejunum approximately 20 to 40 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz, place a silicone tube or polyurethane tube into the intestinal lumen using the Witzel method or Stamm method, and bring it out through the abdominal wall for fixation. This method is simple to perform, has a definite tube position, can be used immediately after surgery, and is not prone to displacement. The disadvantage is that an additional abdominal wall puncture is required, with risks of leakage and infection at the stoma, although the incidence is relatively low.

The nasojejunal tube is placed postoperatively through the nasal cavity, with the tube tip guided to the jejunum under X-ray or endoscopic guidance. This method requires no additional surgical procedure, but the tube is prone to displacement or dislodgement, causes greater patient discomfort, and long-term placement may cause nasopharyngeal irritation and sinusitis. For patients requiring prolonged nutritional support after PD, the nasojejunal tube is not an ideal choice.

The percutaneous endoscopic jejunostomy tube is suitable for patients who require long-term feeding after surgery but cannot tolerate a nasojejunal tube. However, in the early postoperative period after PD, due to altered anatomical structures, endoscopic operation is relatively difficult, so it is usually not the first choice.

Overall, the intraoperative jejunostomy tube has clear advantages in early postoperative nutritional support after PD and is the recommended first choice.

2.2 Timing of Feeding and Selection of Nutrient Solution

The timing of initiating jejunal tube feeding after PD directly affects patient recovery. The traditional view holds that patients should fast for several days after surgery and begin feeding only after gastrointestinal function recovers. However, in recent years, the concept of enhanced recovery after surgery advocates early postoperative enteral nutrition, usually starting within 24 to 48 hours after surgery.

The physiological basis for early feeding lies in the fact that jejunal peristalsis and absorptive function can recover within several hours after surgery and do not require waiting for gastric emptying or colonic function recovery. Direct infusion of nutrient solution through the jejunal tube can stimulate intestinal mucosal cell proliferation, maintain intestinal barrier function, and reduce bacterial translocation and endotoxemia. In addition, early enteral nutrition can promote anastomotic healing and reduce infectious complications.

The choice of nutrient solution should be determined according to patient tolerance and clinical conditions. In the early postoperative period, isotonic short-peptide or amino acid-based nutrient solutions are usually selected. These preparations are easy to absorb, have little dependence on digestive enzymes, and are suitable for early postoperative use. As patient tolerance improves, a gradual transition to whole-protein nutrient solutions can be made. The infusion rate should start low, such as 20 to 30 mL/hour, and gradually increase according to patient tolerance, eventually reaching 80 to 100 mL/hour. The infusion method can be continuous pump infusion or intermittent drip; continuous pump infusion is more easily tolerated, but intermittent drip is closer to the physiological state.

It should be noted that the temperature of the nutrient solution should be maintained at around 37 degrees Celsius; if too cold, it easily causes intestinal spasm and diarrhea. The tube should be flushed with warm water before and after infusion to prevent blockage.

2.3 Prevention and Management of Complications

Although jejunal tube feeding is enteral nutrition, it is not without complications. Common problems include tube-related complications, gastrointestinal intolerance, and metabolic disturbances.

Tube-related complications mainly include tube blockage, displacement, and stoma infection. Tube blockage is the most common problem, mostly caused by residual nutrient solution or inadequately dissolved drugs. Preventive measures include flushing the tube with 20 to 30 mL of warm water before and after each infusion, and drugs should be crushed and injected separately followed by flushing. If blockage occurs, sodium bicarbonate solution or pancreatin solution can be used to attempt to clear it, but forceful injection must be avoided. The stoma should be cleaned and dressed daily, observing for redness, swelling, or exudation, and antibiotics should be used when necessary.

Gastrointestinal intolerance manifests as abdominal distension, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. Diarrhea is the most common symptom and may be related to excessively rapid infusion, excessively low nutrient solution temperature, or excessively high concentration. The management principles are to slow the infusion rate, adjust the concentration and temperature of the nutrient solution, and add antidiarrheal drugs when necessary. When abdominal distension is obvious, feeding should be suspended, and intestinal obstruction or anastomotic leakage should be evaluated.

Metabolic disturbances include hyperglycemia, electrolyte imbalance, and refeeding syndrome. Patients after PD often have concurrent diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance, and blood glucose fluctuates greatly after nutrient solution infusion, requiring close monitoring of blood glucose and adjustment of insulin dosage. Refeeding syndrome is mostly seen in patients with long-term malnutrition and manifests as hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia. Calories should be increased slowly in the initial feeding period, and electrolytes should be supplemented.

2.4 Monitoring and Nursing During Feeding

The smooth implementation of jejunal tube feeding cannot be separated from systematic monitoring and nursing. Postoperatively, the feeding volume, patient tolerance, and stool characteristics should be recorded daily. Body weight, albumin, prealbumin, and electrolyte levels should be monitored regularly to evaluate the effectiveness of nutritional support. If the patient develops persistent diarrhea or weight loss, the nutritional regimen should be adjusted promptly.

In terms of nursing, the tube should be kept patent and properly secured to prevent traction and dislodgement. The patient's position should preferably be semi-recumbent to reduce the risk of reflux and aspiration. For patients with impaired consciousness or weakened cough reflex, special attention should be paid to the possibility of aspiration, and feeding should be suspended when necessary to assess airway protective capacity.

In addition, patients should be encouraged to resume oral intake as early as possible. Jejunal tube feeding is a transitional measure. When gastric emptying function recovers and oral intake reaches more than 60% of the required amount, consideration can be given to gradually reducing tube feeding volume and eventually removing the jejunal tube.

2.5 Implementation Model of Multidisciplinary Collaboration

Jejunal tube feeding is not a single technical procedure but a systematic project involving multidisciplinary collaboration among surgery, nutrition, nursing, and rehabilitation. Surgeons are responsible for intraoperative tube placement and management of complications, the nutrition department is responsible for formulating and adjusting nutritional plans, the nursing team is responsible for daily management and monitoring, and the rehabilitation department participates in the patient's functional exercise and feeding training.

During implementation, it is recommended to establish standardized operating procedures and record forms, clarifying the responsible persons and time nodes for each step. For example, on the first postoperative day, assess whether to initiate feeding; on the second day, begin low-speed infusion; on the third day, evaluate tolerance and adjust the plan. Through multidisciplinary rounds and regular discussions, problems arising during feeding can be resolved promptly, improving the success rate of nutritional support.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

From the perspective of clinical practice, the application of jejunal tube feeding after PD has achieved benefits in multiple aspects.

First, in terms of nutritional indicators, patients receiving early jejunal tube feeding show smaller postoperative decreases in albumin and prealbumin, reduced weight loss, and improved nitrogen balance. Compared with total parenteral nutrition, enteral nutrition is more physiological and can better maintain intestinal mucosal structure and function.

Second, in terms of complications, early enteral nutrition can reduce the incidence of infectious complications. Studies have shown that the incidence of postoperative pulmonary infection, abdominal infection, and incisional infection in the enteral nutrition group is lower than that in the parenteral nutrition group. This is related to the ability of enteral nutrition to maintain intestinal barrier function and reduce bacterial translocation. In addition, jejunal tube feeding does not pass through the stomach and anastomosis, reducing mechanical and chemical stimulation to the anastomosis, which may help reduce the risk of anastomotic leakage.

Third, in terms of health economics, the cost of jejunal tube feeding is significantly lower than that of total parenteral nutrition. Enteral nutrition preparations are lower in price, do not require central venous catheters or complex compounding procedures, and the nursing workload is relatively less. For primary hospitals with limited medical resources, this advantage is particularly evident.

Fourth, in terms of quality of patient recovery, early enteral nutrition helps shorten postoperative hospital stay, promote recovery of gastrointestinal function, reduce intravenous fluid volume, and improve patient comfort. Patients can ambulate earlier, reducing the risk of deep vein thrombosis and muscle atrophy.

Of course, jejunal tube feeding also has certain limitations. Some patients cannot tolerate full-volume feeding due to diarrhea or abdominal distension and require supplemental parenteral nutrition. A small number of patients develop tube blockage or stoma infection and require additional management. Overall, however, its benefits far outweigh its risks.

4 Conclusion

Nutritional support after pancreatoduodenectomy is a key link affecting patient recovery. As a safe, effective, and economical enteral nutrition route, jejunal tube feeding can bypass the stomach and anastomotic region and achieve early postoperative nutritional supply through intraoperative tube placement, early initiation, rational selection of nutrient solution, and systematic monitoring. Clinical practice has shown that jejunal tube feeding can improve nutritional indicators, reduce infectious complications, shorten hospital stay, and lessen the medical burden.

To promote jejunal tube feeding technology, attention should be paid to the following points: first, standardize tube placement procedures, with intraoperative jejunostomy as the first choice; second, initiate feeding within 24 to 48 hours after surgery, starting with low speed and low concentration; third, strengthen tube care and complication monitoring; fourth, establish a multidisciplinary collaboration mechanism to ensure individualized adjustment of nutritional plans.

For primary hospitals and promotable medical institutions, jejunal tube feeding technology has a low operational threshold and simple equipment requirements, making it suitable for widespread implementation. In the future, nutrient solution formulas and infusion protocols can be further optimized, and more precise feeding strategies can be explored to provide better postoperative management for patients undergoing pancreatoduodenectomy.

title: Scientific computation of big data in real-world clinical research
text:
Scientific Computing of Big Data in Real-World Clinical Research

 Abstract

Objective: To explore the application value of big data scientific computing methods in real-world clinical research and to construct an analytical framework suitable for multi-source heterogeneous clinical data. Methods: Based on electronic medical record data collected from a regional medical data center from 2019 to 2023, structured laboratory indicators and unstructured text records were integrated, and a distributed computing framework and machine learning algorithms were used for data cleaning, feature extraction, and predictive modeling. A total of 12,847 valid cases were included, covering three major disease categories: cardiovascular diseases, metabolic diseases, and respiratory system diseases. Results: After data governance, the completeness rate of key fields increased from 61.3% to 94.7%; the AUC of disease risk prediction models based on random forest and XGBoost reached 0.862 and 0.891, respectively, significantly outperforming the traditional Logistic regression model (AUC=0.784). The model maintained stable performance on the external validation set (AUC=0.873). Conclusion: The scientific computing framework can effectively improve the utilization efficiency and prediction accuracy of real-world clinical data, providing methodological reference for clinical decision support and public health management.

Keywords: real-world research; big data; scientific computing; machine learning; clinical prediction model

 1 Introduction

Real-World Clinical Research, based on data generated in routine diagnosis and treatment processes, evaluates the actual effects and safety of interventions and has become an important supplement to evidence-based medicine. With the widespread adoption of hospital information systems, wearable devices, and regional health platforms, clinical data exhibit characteristics of large scale, multiple sources, and heterogeneous structures. Traditional statistical methods face dual challenges of efficiency and accuracy when processing high-dimensional, sparse, and imbalanced data.

Scientific computing, using numerical algorithms and high-performance computing as its means, provides underlying support for large-scale data analysis. In recent years, the development of distributed storage, parallel computing, and deep learning has made real-time processing and deep mining of clinical big data possible. However, data silos, inconsistent coding, and privacy constraints in Chinese medical scenarios still constrain the implementation of methods. This study aims to construct a big data scientific computing framework for real-world clinical research and to verify its effectiveness in disease risk identification through data governance, feature engineering, and predictive modeling.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Data Sources

The data were obtained from a provincial regional medical data center, covering the electronic medical record systems of 8 tertiary hospitals from January 2019 to December 2023. There were 31,562 original records in total. After deduplication, exclusion of cases with missing key fields, and loss to follow-up, 12,847 valid cases were included. Among them, there were 6,712 males and 6,135 females, with a mean age of (58.4±13.7) years. The disease distribution was as follows: 5,216 cases of cardiovascular diseases (40.6%), 4,387 cases of metabolic diseases (34.1%), and 3,244 cases of respiratory system diseases (25.3%).

 2.2 Data Governance and Feature Extraction

A five-stage data governance process was adopted: ① field standardization, unifying diagnoses and laboratory items according to ICD-10 and LOINC codes; ② missing value handling, using multiple imputation for continuous variables and mode imputation for categorical variables; ③ outlier detection, identified based on the interquartile range and the isolation forest algorithm; ④ text structuring, using a BiLSTM-CRF model to extract entities of symptoms, medications, and complications from course records; ⑤ privacy de-identification, applying hash encryption to identity identifiers. Finally, a clinical dataset containing 187 features was constructed.

 2.3 Scientific Computing Framework

The framework was divided into three layers: the data layer used Hadoop HDFS and Parquet columnar storage to support PB-level data reading and writing; the computing layer was based on Spark and GPU acceleration to realize parallel feature computation and distributed model training; the application layer provided interfaces for risk prediction, cluster subtyping, and trend analysis. In terms of algorithms, Logistic regression was selected as the baseline, random forest and XGBoost as the main models, and 5-fold cross-validation was used to optimize hyperparameters.

 2.4 Evaluation Metrics

The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score were used to evaluate model performance. Data from 2019 to 2022 were used as the training set, and data from 2023 were used as the external validation set.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Data Governance Effects

After governance, the completeness rate of key fields increased from 61.3% to 94.7%, and the consistency rate of diagnostic coding increased from 72.5% to 96.2%. The F1 score of text entity extraction was 0.887, among which symptom entity recognition performed best (F1=0.912), followed by medication entities (F1=0.876). Data governance increased the available sample size by approximately 34.8%, laying the foundation for subsequent modeling.

 3.2 Comparison of Model Performance

On the training set, the AUCs of Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were 0.784, 0.862, and 0.891, respectively. XGBoost performed best in sensitivity (0.843) and F1 score (0.829), while random forest had the highest specificity (0.881). On the external validation set, the AUC of XGBoost was 0.873, a decrease of 1.8 percentage points compared with the training set, indicating good generalization ability of the model. Although Logistic regression has strong interpretability, it is clearly insufficient in handling nonlinear interaction features.

 3.3 Feature Importance Analysis

The ranking of XGBoost feature importance showed that the top 10 predictors were, in order: age, systolic blood pressure, fasting blood glucose, low-density lipoprotein, smoking history, BMI, glycated hemoglobin, disease duration, number of complications, and types of medications. Among them, the gain contribution rates of age and systolic blood pressure were 14.2% and 11.7%, respectively. Among text features, symptom entities such as "chest tightness," "shortness of breath," and "fatigue" contributed significantly to the prediction of respiratory system diseases.

 3.4 Subgroup Analysis

Stratified by disease type, the prediction AUC was 0.897 for cardiovascular diseases, 0.881 for metabolic diseases, and 0.846 for respiratory system diseases. Stratified by age, the AUC of the group aged over 60 years was 0.889, higher than 0.854 in the group aged under 60 years. Stratified by hospital level, the model performance based on data from tertiary hospitals (AUC=0.883) was slightly better than that from secondary hospitals (AUC=0.861), which may be related to differences in data completeness.

 4 Discussion

This study verified the feasibility of the scientific computing framework in real-world clinical research. Compared with previous studies, the advantages of this framework are reflected in three aspects: first, through standardized governance and text structuring, the usability of multi-source data is significantly improved; second, distributed computing and GPU acceleration shorten model training time by approximately 62%, meeting the needs of near-real-time clinical analysis; third, XGBoost performs prominently in nonlinear feature modeling, with AUC improved by approximately 10.7 percentage points compared with traditional models.

However, the study still has limitations. First, the data sources are concentrated in a single province, resulting in limited regional representativeness; second, the recognition accuracy of the text extraction model for traditional Chinese medicine terminology and dialect expressions needs to be improved; third, the balance between privacy protection and data sharing needs further exploration. In the future, a federated learning mechanism can be introduced to achieve multi-center collaborative modeling without data leaving the domain.

From an application perspective, this framework can be embedded in hospital information systems to assist physicians in screening high-risk patients and providing personalized interventions. At the public health level, regional disease spectrum analysis and resource allocation can also benefit from this method. It is worth noting that model outputs should serve as decision-making references rather than replacements for clinical judgment and should be comprehensively considered in combination with physicians' experience and patients' preferences.

 5 Conclusion

This study constructed a big data scientific computing framework for real-world clinical research, covering the entire process of data governance, feature extraction, and predictive modeling. Empirical analysis based on 12,847 multi-disease clinical cases showed that the framework can effectively improve data quality and model prediction accuracy. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.873 on the external validation set, demonstrating good generalization ability. The results provide methodological reference for the efficient utilization of clinical big data and have positive significance for promoting the standardized application of real-world evidence in Chinese medical scenarios. Subsequent research will focus on multi-center federated modeling and dynamic risk prediction to further enhance the applicability and robustness of the framework.

title: Chinese Medicine Protein and Peptide in Gene and Cell Therapy
text:
Application of Traditional Chinese Medicine Proteins and Peptides in Gene and Cell Therapy

 Abstract

Gene therapy and cell therapy are among the most transformative therapeutic strategies in the current biomedical field; however, their clinical application remains limited by low delivery efficiency, insufficient targeting, high immunogenicity, and high production costs. Proteins and peptides derived from traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) have recently been gradually explored as gene delivery vectors, cell function regulatory factors, and combination therapeutic components due to their characteristics of wide sources, structural diversity, good biocompatibility, and low immunogenicity. This paper systematically reviews the key technological pathways of TCM proteins and peptides in gene therapy and cell therapy, with a focus on research progress in four aspects: their use as non-viral delivery vectors, cell surface engineering modification molecules, immune cell function modulators, and gene editing auxiliary factors, and evaluates their application benefits in combination with existing experimental data. The analysis indicates that TCM proteins and peptides have clear potential in improving delivery efficiency, reducing toxicity, enhancing targeting, and improving the accessibility of cell therapy products, but their standardization, large-scale preparation, and in vivo stability remain key bottlenecks constraining translation. This paper aims to provide technical references for the development of TCM active proteins and peptides in advanced therapeutic products.

 1 Introduction

Gene therapy corrects or compensates for abnormal gene function by introducing exogenous genetic material, while cell therapy achieves therapeutic purposes by modifying autologous or allogeneic cells in vitro and then reinfusing them. Both have demonstrated definitive efficacy in genetic diseases, malignant tumors, and refractory immune diseases. As of 2024, dozens of gene and cell therapy products have been approved for marketing worldwide. However, the promotion of these therapies still faces multiple obstacles: viral vectors carry risks of insertional mutagenesis and immune reactions; non-viral vectors such as lipid nanoparticles and polyethyleneimine struggle to balance transfection efficiency and cytotoxicity; cell therapy products have complex and costly manufacturing processes; and the solid tumor microenvironment exerts significant inhibitory effects on immune cells.

TCM proteins and peptides are one of the important material bases for the pharmacological effects of traditional Chinese medicine, such as trichosanthin, bitter melon antiviral protein, Pinellia ternata lectin, melittin, and antimicrobial peptides from various sources, which have been confirmed to possess anti-tumor, antiviral, and immunomodulatory activities. Compared with synthetic polymers and recombinant viral vectors, these natural biomolecules have advantages such as degradability, low accumulation, and ease of chemical modification. In recent years, researchers have begun to introduce TCM proteins and peptides into the fields of gene delivery and cell engineering, attempting to leverage their membrane activity, nuclear localization signals, and receptor recognition properties to address the aforementioned bottlenecks. This paper focuses on this interdisciplinary direction, analyzing key technological advances and evaluating their application benefits.

 2 Key Technology Analysis

 2.1 TCM Proteins and Peptides as Non-Viral Gene Delivery Vectors

The core contradiction in non-viral gene delivery lies in how to enable negatively charged nucleic acids to cross the cell membrane and enter the nucleus while avoiding high cytotoxicity. Cationic peptides and membrane-active proteins derived from TCM provide new molecular templates for this purpose. For example, melittin is a 26-amino-acid amphipathic α-helical peptide that can insert into lipid bilayers and form pores, and has been used to modify liposomes and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) nanoparticles, significantly improving the cellular uptake of plasmid DNA and siRNA. Studies have shown that a reduction-responsive vector formed by linking melittin to protamine via disulfide bonds can rapidly release nucleic acids under high glutathione concentrations in tumor cells, with transfection efficiency approximately 5 to 8 times higher than protamine alone, while hemolytic activity is significantly reduced after conjugation.

Another noteworthy example is trichosanthin. This protein possesses ribosome-inactivating activity and also contains a nuclear localization signal sequence, enabling it to carry plasmid DNA across the nuclear membrane. Researchers covalently conjugated it with polyethyleneimine, and the resulting complex increased reporter gene expression by approximately 3-fold in HeLa cells, with cell viability maintained above 80%. In addition, Pinellia ternata lectin and bitter melon-derived peptides have also been used to modify chitosan nanoparticles, enhancing targeted delivery to intestinal epithelial cells and tumor cells through lectin-glycan recognition. Overall, the functions of TCM proteins and peptides in non-viral vectors are mainly manifested in three aspects: membrane penetration promotion, nuclear localization assistance, and reduction-responsive release.

 2.2 Cell Surface Engineering and Targeted Modification Based on TCM Peptides

Whether cell therapy products can effectively home to lesion sites after reinfusion is one of the key factors determining therapeutic efficacy. TCM peptides can modify the cell membrane surface through hydrophobic insertion or covalent conjugation, endowing cells with new recognition and adhesion properties. For example, chlorotoxin derived from scorpion venom has high affinity for matrix metalloproteinase-2 and chloride channels on the surface of glioma cells. After conjugating it to the membrane surface of mesenchymal stem cells, the tumor accumulation of cells in a glioma mouse model increased approximately 4-fold compared with the unmodified group, with no significant cytotoxicity observed.

Furthermore, RGD sequence-containing TCM-derived peptides (such as RGD-containing cyclic peptides isolated from Agkistrodon acutus venom) can be used to modify T cells or natural killer cells, enhancing their adhesion to tumor vascular endothelium and extracellular matrix. Studies have shown that chimeric antigen receptor T cells modified with RGD peptides exhibit improved infiltration depth and persistence in solid tumor models. The advantage of such surface engineering strategies lies in their mild operation, no alteration of the cell genome, and the degradability of peptides by proteases, avoiding long-term retention risks. The key challenges of this technology currently lie in the batch consistency of modification efficiency and the stability of peptides in serum.

 2.3 Regulation of Immune Cell Function by TCM Proteins and Peptides

In cell therapy, the functional status of immune cells directly determines therapeutic efficacy. Various TCM proteins and peptides have been confirmed to regulate the activation, proliferation, and exhaustion of T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. For example, although Astragalus polysaccharides are not proteins, their associated protein components can promote dendritic cell maturation; more directly, small molecule peptides derived from Astragalus can upregulate CD69 and CD25 expression on T cell surfaces and enhance interleukin-2 secretion. During the preparation of chimeric antigen receptor T cells, adding such peptides to the culture medium can shorten the in vitro expansion period by approximately 20% and increase the proportion of central memory T cells.

Another typical example is the Ganoderma immunomodulatory protein LZ-8. This protein can bind to Toll-like receptor 4 on T cell surfaces, activate the nuclear factor κB signaling pathway, and enhance interferon-γ release. Introducing LZ-8 into tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte expansion protocols can significantly enhance cytotoxic activity. It should be noted that such regulatory effects are concentration-dependent, and excessive doses may induce excessive inflammatory responses; therefore, the safety window needs to be determined in preclinical studies.

 2.4 TCM Proteins and Peptides Assisting Gene Editing

The CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system is increasingly widely used in cell therapy, but its delivery efficiency and off-target effects remain limiting factors. Nuclear localization proteins and peptides derived from TCM can be used to assist the intracellular delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein complexes. For example, fusion expression of the nuclear localization signal peptide of trichosanthin with Cas9 can improve its nuclear entry efficiency by approximately 2-fold, thereby achieving equivalent editing efficiency at lower doses and indirectly reducing off-target risk. In addition, melittin-modified lipid nanoparticles have been used to deliver Cas9 mRNA and single guide RNA, achieving approximately 40% target gene knockout in mouse liver, with inflammatory cytokine levels lower than the control lipid nanoparticle group.

In base editing and prime editing, TCM peptides mainly serve as auxiliary components to improve the endosomal escape capability of delivery vectors. For example, a histamine-like peptide derived from leech can transiently increase endosomal membrane permeability, promoting the release of editing complexes into the cytoplasm. Such strategies are still in the early exploratory stage, but their low immunogenicity and degradability provide safer candidate approaches for in vivo gene editing.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

From existing research data, the application benefits of TCM proteins and peptides in gene and cell therapy are mainly reflected in four aspects. First, improved delivery efficiency. Multiple in vitro experiments have shown that the transfection efficiency of vectors modified with TCM peptides is 2 to 8 times higher than unmodified controls, with particularly notable effects in hard-to-transfect primary T cells and stem cells. Second, reduced toxicity. Compared with polyethyleneimine and cationic liposomes, the median lethal concentration of the melittin-protamine complex is approximately 3 to 5 times higher, with hemolysis rates below 10% at effective concentrations. Third, enhanced targeting. Modification with chlorotoxin and RGD peptides increases the enrichment of cells or vectors at lesion sites by 3 to 5 times, reducing exposure to non-target tissues. Fourth, improved production cost and accessibility. TCM proteins and peptides can be produced at scale through prokaryotic expression or plant expression systems, with costs lower than viral vectors and some synthetic polymers, and without the need for complex cold chains, facilitating promotion in resource-limited areas.

However, the benefit analysis must also acknowledge limitations. The in vivo half-life of TCM proteins and peptides is generally short, and they are susceptible to degradation by serum proteases; differences in protein composition among different batches of TCM raw materials may lead to activity fluctuations; some peptides still exhibit hemolytic or cell membrane damage at high concentrations. Therefore, the stable realization of their benefits depends on standardized preparation, structural optimization, and delivery system design.

 4 Conclusion

TCM proteins and peptides provide a class of functional molecules with natural advantages for gene therapy and cell therapy. As non-viral delivery vectors, they can promote membrane penetration, nuclear localization, and reduction-responsive release; as cell surface modification molecules, they enhance targeted homing and lesion retention; as immune regulatory factors, they improve the expansion quality and cytotoxic activity of cell therapy products; as gene editing auxiliary components, they enhance editing efficiency and reduce toxicity. Although bottlenecks remain in stability, standardization, and in vivo safety, these issues are expected to be gradually resolved through protein engineering modification, nanocarrier encapsulation, and strict quality control. Future research should focus on clarifying structure-activity relationships, conducting systematic preclinical pharmacokinetic and toxicological evaluations, and promoting the establishment of good manufacturing practice-compliant production systems for TCM protein and peptide raw materials. Overall, TCM proteins and peptides have clear technological translation value in the field of advanced therapeutic products and merit further investment and development.

title: Lipidomics insight into chronic exposure to ambient air pollution in mice
text:
Effects of Chronic Exposure to Atmospheric Fine Particulate Matter on the Lipidome of Mice: A Lipidomics-Based Mechanistic Study

Abstract: To investigate the effects of chronic exposure to atmospheric fine particulate matter (PM2.5) on lipid metabolism, 24 six-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were randomly divided into a control group (exposed to filtered air) and an exposure group (exposed to concentrated ambient PM2.5) for 12 consecutive weeks. Untargeted lipidomic analysis of mouse serum and liver tissues was performed using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-quadrupole-electrostatic field orbitrap mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-Exactive Orbitrap MS). The results showed that chronic PM2.5 exposure significantly elevated serum total cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels (*P*<0.05), and significantly reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels (*P*<0.05). Lipidomic analysis identified a total of 326 lipid molecules, of which 58 were significantly altered in the exposure group, mainly including glycerophospholipids (PC, PE), sphingolipids (SM, Cer), and triglycerides (TG). Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that the differential lipids were mainly involved in glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphingolipid metabolism, and fatty acid biosynthesis pathways. In liver tissue, the proportions of saturated fatty acids and monounsaturated fatty acids increased, while the proportion of polyunsaturated fatty acids decreased. This study reveals that chronic exposure to ambient PM2.5 can lead to lipid metabolism disorders in mice, providing lipidomic evidence for elucidating the pathogenesis of air pollution-related cardiovascular diseases.

Keywords: PM2.5; chronic exposure; lipidomics; lipid metabolism disorders; mouse; cardiovascular disease

 1 Introduction

Air pollution has become a major public health issue worldwide. Data from the World Health Organization show that approximately 99% of the global population lives in environments where air quality fails to meet standards, and the number of premature deaths caused by air pollution-related diseases exceeds 6.7 million annually. Fine particulate matter (PM2.5, aerodynamic equivalent diameter ≤2.5 μm) is one of the most harmful components of atmospheric pollutants. Due to its large specific surface area and strong adsorption capacity, it can carry toxic and harmful substances such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, heavy metals, and biological aerosols into the deep respiratory tract and even the bloodstream.

Epidemiological studies have confirmed that long-term exposure to PM2.5 is significantly associated with the risk of cardiovascular diseases, metabolic syndrome, and type 2 diabetes. Lipid metabolism disorders are the core pathological basis of cardiovascular diseases, and lipidomics, as an important branch of systems biology, can comprehensively analyze the composition and changes of lipid molecules in organisms, providing a powerful tool for revealing the effects of environmental pollutants on body metabolism. However, research on the overall impact of chronic PM2.5 exposure on the body's lipidome remains relatively limited, and systematic understanding of the coordinated changes in lipid metabolism in serum and liver tissues is still lacking.

In this study, by establishing a mouse model of chronic PM2.5 exposure and employing untargeted lipidomic technology, we systematically analyzed the effects of PM2.5 exposure on the lipid profiles of mouse serum and liver, aiming to elucidate the potential hazards of air pollution to body health and their possible mechanisms from the perspective of lipid metabolism.

 2 Materials and Methods

 2.1 Experimental Animals and Grouping

Twenty-four six-week-old SPF-grade male C57BL/6 mice (body weight 18–22 g) were purchased from an experimental animal center. After one week of adaptive feeding, they were randomly divided into a control group (n=12) and an exposure group (n=12). The control group was exposed to air purified by high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters, while the exposure group was exposed to concentrated ambient PM2.5 (average concentration of (85.6±12.3) μg/m³). The exposure system used a certain type of animal exposure chamber, with daily exposure of 6 h, 5 d per week, for 12 consecutive weeks. During the exposure period, mice had free access to food and water, with a housing environment temperature of (22±2)°C, relative humidity of (55±10)%, and a 12 h/12 h light-dark cycle. The experimental protocol was approved by the Animal Ethics Committee (approval number: IACUC-2023-0416).

 2.2 Sample Collection and Biochemical Indicator Detection

After the exposure period, mice were fasted for 12 h, anesthetized with isoflurane, and orbital venous blood was collected. After standing at room temperature for 30 min, the blood was centrifuged at 3000 r/min for 15 min to separate serum. Subsequently, mice were sacrificed by cervical dislocation, and liver tissues were rapidly removed, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80°C. Serum TC, TG, HDL-C, and LDL-C levels were measured using an automatic biochemical analyzer.

 2.3 Lipidomic Analysis

Fifty μL of serum or 50 mg of liver tissue was mixed with internal standard mixture (PC(17:0/17:0), PE(17:0/17:0), TG(17:0/17:0/17:0)), and lipids were extracted using a methyl tert-butyl ether-methanol-water (10:3:2.5, v/v/v) system. The extract was dried under nitrogen and reconstituted with isopropanol-acetonitrile (1:1, v/v), filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane, and then loaded for analysis.

Untargeted lipidomic analysis was performed using a UHPLC-Q-Exactive Orbitrap MS system. The chromatographic column was a C30 column (2.1 mm×150 mm, 2.6 μm), mobile phase A was acetonitrile-water (60:40, containing 10 mmol/L ammonium formate), mobile phase B was isopropanol-acetonitrile (90:10, containing 10 mmol/L ammonium formate), with gradient elution for 60 min. Mass spectrometry was performed in positive and negative ion full-scan mode, with a scan range of m/z 200–2000 and a resolution of 70,000.

 2.4 Data Processing and Statistical Analysis

Raw data were processed using Compound Discoverer 3.3 software for peak extraction, alignment, and identification, and compared with the LipidSearch database. MetaboAnalyst 5.0 was used for multivariate statistical analysis and pathway enrichment analysis. Data are expressed as mean±standard deviation, and comparisons between two groups were performed using independent sample t-tests, with *P*<0.05 considered statistically significant.

 3 Results and Analysis

 3.1 Effects of PM2.5 Exposure on Body Weight and Serum Biochemical Indicators in Mice

During the exposure period, there was no significant difference in body weight growth trend between the two groups (*P*>0.05), but the body weight growth of mice in the exposure group was slightly slower than that in the control group. After 12 weeks of exposure, serum TC, TG, and LDL-C levels in the exposure group were increased by 28.6%, 35.2%, and 42.1%, respectively, compared with the control group (*P*<0.05), while HDL-C levels were decreased by 21.4% (*P*<0.05) (Table 1). These results indicate that chronic PM2.5 exposure can cause a shift in the mouse blood lipid profile toward an atherogenic direction.

Table 1 Comparison of serum lipid biochemical indicators between the two groups of mice (mmol/L, x±s, n=12)

| Indicator | Control Group | Exposure Group |
|------|--------|--------|
| TC | 3.42±0.31 | 4.40±0.38* |
| TG | 1.05±0.14 | 1.42±0.18* |
| HDL-C | 2.38±0.22 | 1.87±0.19* |
| LDL-C | 0.57±0.08 | 0.81±0.11* |

Note: Compared with the control group, *P*<0.05.

 3.2 Serum Lipidomic Analysis

Untargeted lipidomic analysis identified a total of 326 lipid molecules, covering categories such as glycerophospholipids (PC, PE, PI, PS), sphingolipids (SM, Cer, S1P), triglycerides (TG), and cholesteryl esters (CE). Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that the serum lipid profiles of the control group and exposure group were clearly separated, with the first two principal components cumulatively explaining 62.3% of the variance. The orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) model parameters were R²Y=0.926 and Q²=0.847, indicating that the model had good discriminative ability.

Using VIP>1.0 and *P*<0.05 as screening criteria, a total of 58 differential lipid molecules were identified. Compared with the control group, serum levels of PC(16:0/18:1), PC(18:0/18:2), PE(16:0/18:1), and SM(d18:1/16:0) were significantly elevated in the exposure group (*P*<0.05), while levels of lipid molecules containing polyunsaturated fatty acid chains such as PC(18:0/20:4), PE(18:0/22:6), and PC(16:0/22:6) were significantly reduced (*P*<0.05). Among TG lipids, molecules containing saturated and monounsaturated fatty acid chains such as TG(16:0/16:0/18:1) and TG(16:0/18:1/18:1) were significantly elevated.

 3.3 Liver Lipidomic Analysis

A total of 412 lipid molecules were identified in liver tissue, of which 67 were significantly altered in the exposure group. Consistent with the serum results, levels of saturated and monounsaturated glycerophospholipids and triglycerides were elevated in the liver, while levels of phospholipids containing polyunsaturated fatty acids (such as ARA, DHA, EPA) were reduced. Liver TG(16:0/18:1/18:2) and TG(18:1/18:1/18:2) were increased by 1.8-fold and 2.1-fold, respectively (*P*<0.01). In addition, liver ceramide Cer(d18:1/16:0) and Cer(d18:1/18:0) levels were increased by 36.5% and 42.8%, respectively (*P*<0.05).

 3.4 Lipid Metabolism Pathway Enrichment Analysis

Pathway enrichment analysis showed that the differential lipids were mainly enriched in glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphingolipid metabolism, fatty acid biosynthesis, and unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis pathways (*P*<0.05). Among these, the glycerophospholipid metabolism pathway had the highest enrichment degree (Impact value=0.42), involving an imbalance in the synthesis and degradation of PC and PE. In the sphingolipid metabolism pathway, ceramide synthesis increased while sphingomyelin hydrolysis was enhanced, suggesting that sphingolipid metabolic homeostasis was disrupted.

 4 Discussion

In this study, through a 12-week chronic PM2.5 exposure mouse model combined with untargeted lipidomic technology, we systematically revealed the profound effects of atmospheric fine particulate matter exposure on body lipid metabolism. The main findings include: (1) PM2.5 exposure led to changes in the serum atherogenic lipid profile; (2) significant remodeling of the serum and liver lipidome occurred, manifested as an increase in saturated and monounsaturated lipids and a decrease in polyunsaturated lipids; (3) glycerophospholipid metabolism and sphingolipid metabolism pathways were the main targeted pathways of PM2.5 exposure.

Dyslipidemia is an important risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. In this study, serum TC, TG, and LDL-C were elevated and HDL-C was reduced in PM2.5-exposed mice, consistent with the results of multiple epidemiological studies. The underlying mechanisms may involve PM2.5-induced oxidative stress and inflammatory responses. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and heavy metals in PM2.5 can activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) and nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) pathways, promoting the expression of hepatic lipid synthesis-related genes (such as SREBP-1c, FAS, and ACC), while inhibiting the expression of fatty acid β-oxidation-related genes (such as PPARα and CPT-1), leading to hepatic lipid accumulation and release into the blood.

The lipidomic results further revealed the fine-scale effects of PM2.5 exposure on lipid molecular composition. Phospholipids containing polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) (such as PC(18:0/20:4) and PE(18:0/22:6)) were significantly reduced, suggesting that PM2.5 exposure may promote peroxidative consumption of PUFA. PUFA are important components of cell membranes, and their reduction can affect membrane fluidity and signal transduction functions. Meanwhile, the increase in saturated and monounsaturated lipids may reflect enhanced stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD-1) activity, which is closely related to the occurrence of insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome.

Sphingolipid metabolism disorder is one of the important findings of this study. Ceramide, as a core molecule of sphingolipid metabolism, plays a key role in apoptosis, inflammation, and insulin resistance. PM2.5 exposure led to elevated liver ceramide levels, which may inhibit insulin signal transduction by activating protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) and protein kinase Cζ (PKCζ) pathways, thereby exacerbating metabolic disorders. In addition, ceramide can also promote the formation and instability of atherosclerotic plaques.

It is noteworthy that the changes in serum and liver lipidomes in this study showed both consistency and tissue specificity. The elevation of PC and SM in serum may reflect increased hepatic lipid secretion, while the accumulation of TG and Cer in the liver suggests an increased hepatic lipid metabolic burden. This cross-tissue coordinated change in lipid metabolism may be an important mechanism by which PM2.5 exposure leads to systemic metabolic disorders.

This study has certain limitations. First, no different dose exposure groups were set, so the dose-response relationship could not be evaluated; second, transcriptomic or proteomic data were not combined, and the mechanistic interpretation still needs further verification; finally, there are species differences between mouse models and humans in lipid metabolism, and extrapolation of results should be done with caution. Future studies can combine multi-omics approaches and population cohorts to further explore the long-term effects of PM2.5 exposure on lipid metabolism and its health effects.

 5 Conclusion

Based on untargeted lipidomic technology, this study systematically revealed the effects of chronic PM2.5 exposure on lipid metabolism in mouse serum and liver. The results showed that PM2.5 exposure led to changes in the atherogenic lipid profile, with significant remodeling of the serum and liver lipidomes, mainly manifested as elevated lipids containing saturated and monounsaturated fatty acid chains, reduced lipids containing polyunsaturated fatty acid chains, and ceramide accumulation. Glycerophospholipid metabolism and sphingolipid metabolism are the main targeted pathways of PM2.5 exposure. This study provides new lipidomic evidence for understanding the pathogenesis of air pollution-related cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, and also provides a scientific basis for developing potential intervention targets.

title: Crucial enzymes in the hydroxylated triacylglycerol-ricinoleate biosynthesis pathway of castor bean
text:
Key Enzymes in the Biosynthesis Pathway of Hydroxylated Triacylglycerol—Ricinoleic Acid in Castor

 Abstract

The seed oil of castor (*Ricinus communis* L.) contains up to 85%–90% ricinoleic acid, making it one of the few plants in nature capable of synthesizing hydroxylated fatty acids in large quantities. Ricinoleic acid has irreplaceable industrial value, and its biosynthesis depends on a unique enzyme catalytic system. This paper focuses on the biosynthesis pathway of hydroxylated triacylglycerol—ricinoleic acid in castor, with emphasis on analyzing the functions and regulatory mechanisms of key enzymes such as fatty acid desaturase, hydroxylase, diacylglycerol acyltransferase, and phospholipid:diacylglycerol acyltransferase, and provides a benefit analysis of the application prospects of this pathway in oil quality improvement and industrial production. The analysis indicates that clarifying the types of rate-limiting enzymes and their expression regulatory patterns is an important prerequisite for achieving efficient heterologous production of ricinoleic acid.

Keywords: castor; ricinoleic acid; hydroxylase; triacylglycerol; biosynthesis; key enzymes

 1 Introduction

Castor is an annual or perennial herbaceous plant of the genus *Ricinus* in the family Euphorbiaceae. Its seeds contain approximately 45%–55% oil, of which ricinoleic acid (12-hydroxy-cis-9-octadecenoic acid) accounts for more than 85% of the total fatty acids. The ricinoleic acid molecule contains both a hydroxyl group and a double bond, and this special structure endows it with excellent properties such as high viscosity, high-temperature resistance, low-temperature resistance, and biodegradability, making it widely used in industries including lubricants, coatings, nylon-11 engineering plastics, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetics. According to statistics, global annual castor oil production is approximately 600,000–800,000 tons, and with the growing demand for bio-based materials, the market demand for ricinoleic acid continues to rise.

However, castor itself suffers from problems such as limited yield, concentrated cultivation regions, and the presence of the toxic protein ricin, making it difficult to meet industrial demand solely by expanding cultivation area. Therefore, elucidating the biosynthetic pathway of ricinoleic acid in seeds and subsequently reconstructing this pathway heterologously in yeast, *Arabidopsis*, or oilseed crops through genetic engineering has become a research hotspot in recent years. The synthesis of ricinoleic acid is not accomplished by a single enzyme but involves multiple steps including de novo fatty acid synthesis, desaturation, hydroxylation, and triacylglycerol assembly, among which multiple enzymes act synergistically to determine the final accumulation level of hydroxy fatty acids in the oil. This paper aims to systematically review the key enzymes in this pathway, analyze their catalytic properties and regulatory patterns, and evaluate their application benefits, with the hope of providing references for the promotion of related technologies.

 2 Key Technology Analysis

 2.1 Synergistic Action of Fatty Acid Desaturase and Hydroxylase

The first key modification in ricinoleic acid biosynthesis is the conversion of oleic acid (18:1Δ9) to linoleic acid (18:2Δ9,12), followed by the introduction of a hydroxyl group at the C12 position by a hydroxylase. The enzyme catalyzing the former step is fatty acid desaturase, namely Δ12 desaturase (FAD2). In castor, the FAD2 gene has multiple copies, among which RcFAD2-1 is highly expressed during the mid-stage of seed development and is responsible for desaturating oleic acid on the acyl carrier to linoleic acid. This enzyme is a membrane-bound desaturase that uses cytochrome b5 as an electron donor, and its activity directly affects the supply of substrate for subsequent hydroxylation.

The enzyme that truly determines ricinoleic acid production is fatty acid hydroxylase (FAH), which belongs to the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase family (CYP450) and has been identified in castor as a member of the CYP94 family, commonly referred to as RcFAH12 or CYP94B1. RcFAH12 uses linoleic acid as substrate and, with the participation of NADPH and cytochrome P450 reductase, introduces one oxygen atom from molecular oxygen into the C12 position to produce 12-hydroxyoleic acid, i.e., ricinoleic acid. Studies have shown that RcFAH12 has high substrate specificity, preferentially binding linoleic acid in the form of acyl-ACP or acyl-CoA, and its expression level is significantly positively correlated with ricinoleic acid content in seeds.

Notably, there is substrate competition between FAD2 and FAH12. If FAD2 activity is too strong, oleic acid may be largely converted to linoleic acid and enter the membrane lipid synthesis pathway rather than the hydroxylation pathway; if FAH12 expression is insufficient, linoleic acid accumulates while hydroxylated products decrease. Therefore, the expression ratio and spatiotemporal coordination of the two enzymes are important factors determining the efficiency of ricinoleic acid accumulation. In heterologous expression studies, introducing RcFAH12 alone often yields only a low proportion of hydroxy fatty acids, whereas co-expression of FAD2 and FAH12 can significantly increase ricinoleic acid production, indicating that their synergy is a prerequisite for pathway flux.

 2.2 Role of Diacylglycerol Acyltransferase (DGAT) in the Assembly of Hydroxylated Triacylglycerol

After hydroxylated fatty acids are synthesized, they need to be esterified onto the glycerol backbone to form triacylglycerol (TAG) and stored in seed oil bodies. This process relies on the stepwise catalysis of acyltransferases. Among them, diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) catalyzes the final step of TAG synthesis, transferring the fatty acid from acyl-CoA to the sn-3 position of diacylglycerol (DAG) to generate TAG. Two families, DGAT1 and DGAT2, exist in castor, among which RcDGAT2 is highly expressed in seeds and has high affinity for hydroxyl-containing acyl-CoA.

Studies have shown that RcDGAT2 can effectively utilize ricinoleoyl-CoA as an acyl donor, whereas DGAT2 from other plants has weak acceptance of hydroxylated acyl-CoA. This explains why, when RcFAH12 is heterologously expressed in *Arabidopsis*, hydroxy fatty acids mainly accumulate in phospholipids rather than TAG—because endogenous DGAT lacks the ability to recognize hydroxy acyl groups. When RcFAH12 and RcDGAT2 are co-expressed, the incorporation ratio of hydroxy fatty acids into TAG is significantly increased. In addition, RcDGAT2 shows preference for DAG with hydroxylated acyl groups already at the sn-2 position, which favors the formation of trihydroxylated or dihydroxylated TAG, further increasing the degree of hydroxylation of the oil.

Therefore, DGAT2 is not only a key enzyme for TAG assembly but also a critical "gate" determining whether hydroxy fatty acids can efficiently enter storage lipids. In metabolic engineering, selecting DGAT with hydroxy acyl recognition capability is a necessary strategy for increasing target oil production.

 2.3 Alternative Pathway of Phospholipid:Diacylglycerol Acyltransferase (PDAT)

In addition to the acyl-CoA-dependent pathway catalyzed by DGAT, castor also possesses an acyl-CoA-independent TAG synthesis pathway, namely the reaction catalyzed by phospholipid:diacylglycerol acyltransferase (PDAT). PDAT directly transfers the acyl group at the sn-2 position of phospholipids (such as phosphatidylcholine, PC) to DAG, generating TAG and lysophospholipid. In castor seeds, RcPDAT1 is highly expressed during the mid-development stage and shows good substrate adaptability for PC containing hydroxylated acyl groups.

Since the hydroxylation reaction catalyzed by FAH12 mainly occurs on PC-bound linoleic acid, hydroxylated products first appear in the PC pool. The PDAT pathway can directly transfer these hydroxylated acyl groups from PC to DAG, thereby bypassing the acyl-CoA pool and forming TAG containing ricinoleic acid. This pathway makes a non-negligible contribution to ricinoleic acid accumulation. Studies have found that inhibiting PDAT1 expression leads to decreased TAG content in seeds while the proportion of hydroxy fatty acids in PC increases, indicating that PDAT plays an important role in channeling hydroxy fatty acids from membrane lipids into storage lipids.

The DGAT and PDAT pathways coexist in castor and may have functional redundancy. Together, they ensure efficient synthesis of hydroxylated TAG. In heterologous expression systems, simultaneously introducing FAH12, DGAT2, and PDAT1 often yields a higher ricinoleic acid proportion than introducing FAH12 alone, further confirming the necessity of multi-enzyme synergy.

 2.4 Auxiliary Functions of Lysophosphatidic Acid Acyltransferase (LPAT) and Phosphatidic Acid Phosphatase (PAP)

In the Kennedy pathway of TAG synthesis, lysophosphatidic acid acyltransferase (LPAT) and phosphatidic acid phosphatase (PAP) catalyze the formation of phosphatidic acid (PA) and the dephosphorylation of PA to DAG, respectively. In castor, RcLPAT2 shows certain acceptance of hydroxyl-containing acyl-CoA and can incorporate ricinoleoyl-CoA into the sn-2 position of PA, thereby introducing hydroxy fatty acids at an early stage of TAG synthesis. RcPAP is responsible for converting PA to DAG, providing substrate for DGAT. Although these two enzymes do not directly determine the hydroxylation reaction, their substrate selectivity affects the distribution position of hydroxy fatty acids on the glycerol backbone.

Studies have shown that hydroxy fatty acids in castor seeds are mainly distributed at the sn-1 and sn-3 positions of TAG, with relatively fewer at the sn-2 position, which is related to the substrate preferences of LPAT and DGAT. Through targeted modification of the substrate recognition domains of LPAT or PAP, it may be possible to regulate the distribution of hydroxy fatty acids, thereby improving the physicochemical properties of the oil. Therefore, these auxiliary enzymes are also links that cannot be overlooked in pathway optimization.

 3 Results and Benefit Analysis

From the perspective of basic research, significant progress has been made in the identification and functional characterization of the aforementioned key enzymes. It is currently known that RcFAD2, RcFAH12, RcDGAT2, RcPDAT1, and other enzymes together constitute the core module for ricinoleic acid synthesis and assembly. Heterologous expression experiments in yeast and *Arabidopsis* have shown that expressing RcFAH12 alone can make hydroxy fatty acids account for 5%–15% of total fatty acids, while co-expression of RcFAH12 with RcDGAT2 or RcPDAT1 can increase the proportion to 20%–35%. If FAD2 expression levels are further optimized and endogenous competing pathways are knocked out, some studies report that the hydroxy fatty acid proportion can reach over 40%. These results provide clear targets for metabolic engineering.

From an economic benefit perspective, the market price of ricinoleic acid and its derivatives is far higher than that of common vegetable oils. Taking nylon-11 as an example, its monomer undecenoic acid is obtained by cleavage of ricinoleic acid, with a selling price of up to several thousand US dollars per ton. If efficient heterologous production of ricinoleic acid can be achieved in yeast or oilseed crops, it would be expected to eliminate dependence on castor cultivation, shorten production cycles, and reduce transportation and processing costs. In addition, improving castor varieties through gene editing technology to increase seed oil content and ricinoleic acid proportion can also directly enhance cultivation benefits.

From the perspective of technology promotion, the current main bottlenecks are: first, insufficient expression levels of hydroxylase in heterologous hosts, resulting in low substrate conversion efficiency; second, hydroxy fatty acids entering membrane lipids may affect cell membrane fluidity and inhibit host growth; third, the regulatory network for multi-enzyme coordinated expression is not yet well established. Future efforts should focus on promoter optimization, directed enzyme evolution, subcellular localization modification, and construction of multi-gene co-expression systems to achieve high-throughput adaptation of the pathway.

 4 Conclusion

The biosynthesis of ricinoleic acid is a complex metabolic pathway catalyzed by multiple enzymes, in which FAD2, FAH12, DGAT2, PDAT1, as well as LPAT and PAP, each play key roles in substrate supply, hydroxylation modification, and TAG assembly. The synergy between FAD2 and FAH12 determines hydroxylation efficiency, DGAT2 and PDAT1 determine the capacity for importing hydroxy fatty acids into storage lipids, while LPAT and PAP affect the distribution of hydroxy fatty acids on the glycerol backbone. Clarifying the functions and regulatory patterns of these enzymes not only helps reveal the molecular mechanism of castor oil synthesis but also provides clear modification targets for heterologous production of ricinoleic acid. With the continuous development of synthetic biology and gene editing technologies, metabolic engineering based on key enzyme modules is expected to achieve efficient and sustainable production of ricinoleic acid, possessing important scientific significance and application prospects.

title: Genetic and epigenetic changes in somatic hybrid introgression lines between wheat and tall wheatgrass
text:
Genetic and Epigenetic Variation in Somatic Hybrid Introgression Lines of Wheat and Thinopyrum ponticum

 Abstract

Objective: To dissect the variation characteristics of somatic hybrid introgression lines between wheat and Thinopyrum ponticum at the genomic and epigenetic levels, and to provide a theoretical basis for broadening the genetic foundation of wheat through distant hybridization. Methods: Twelve introgression lines (IL1–IL12) obtained through somatic hybridization between common wheat (*Triticum aestivum* L.) and Thinopyrum ponticum, along with their wheat parent, were used as materials. SSR molecular markers, genomic in situ hybridization (GISH), methylation-sensitive amplified polymorphism (MSAP), and transcriptome sequencing were employed to analyze their genetic structure, chromosome composition, DNA methylation levels, and gene expression changes. Results: Among the 12 introgression lines, 8 were whole-chromosome addition lines and 4 were small-fragment translocation lines. SSR analysis showed that the average proportion of polymorphic loci in the introgression lines was 18.7%, with genetic similarity coefficients ranging from 0.73 to 0.89. MSAP analysis revealed that the genomic DNA methylation level of the introgression lines was on average 6.4 percentage points higher than that of the wheat parent, with the most significant increase observed at CG sites. Transcriptome analysis identified 2,347 differentially expressed genes, mainly enriched in stress response, metabolism, and developmental regulation pathways. Conclusion: Somatic hybrid introgression lines of wheat and Thinopyrum ponticum exhibit extensive variation at both genetic and epigenetic levels. DNA methylation changes may be involved in the regulation of gene expression following the introduction of alien chromosomes, providing abundant variation resources for wheat genetic improvement.

Keywords: wheat; Thinopyrum ponticum; somatic hybridization; introgression lines; genetic variation; DNA methylation; epigenetics

 1 Introduction
