title: Examining the effects of education level inequality on energy consumption: Evidence from Guangdong Province
text:
Abstract: To investigate the impact of educational attainment disparities on energy consumption, this paper takes Guangdong Province as the research object. Based on panel data of prefecture-level cities from 2010 to 2020, it employs a fixed effects model and mediation effect testing methods to analyze the mechanism through which educational inequality affects residential and industrial energy consumption. The findings reveal that for every 0.1 increase in the education Gini coefficient, per capita energy consumption rises by approximately 3.8%, and this effect is more pronounced in industrial-dominated cities. The education gap primarily drives up energy consumption through two pathways: widening income disparities and reducing energy utilization efficiency. Accordingly, countermeasures are proposed, including promoting balanced allocation of educational resources, strengthening vocational skills training and energy-saving publicity, with the aim of providing references for regional energy consumption regulation.

Keywords: educational inequality; energy consumption; Guangdong Province; Gini coefficient; mediation effect

1 Introduction

Energy consumption growth and unequal distribution of educational resources are dual challenges facing China's regional sustainable development. As the largest provincial economy, Guangdong Province had a total energy consumption of 340 million tons of standard coal in 2020, while educational attainment disparities within the province remain significant: the gross enrollment rate of higher education in the Pearl River Delta region exceeds 60%, whereas some cities in eastern and western Guangdong fall below 40%. Existing studies have mostly focused on the impact of income disparities on energy consumption, but as education is a decisive factor of income, the independent effect of educational inequality on energy consumption remains unclear. This paper aims to quantify the impact of educational inequality on energy consumption in Guangdong Province, identify its transmission pathways, and provide a basis for formulating differentiated energy-saving policies.

2 Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Measurement of Educational Inequality

The education Gini coefficient (EduGini) is adopted to measure differences in educational distribution across cities. Based on the years of schooling of the population aged 6 and above, educational levels are divided into five categories: below primary school, primary school, junior high school, senior high school/technical secondary school, and college and above. The calculation follows the formula \( G = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - X_{i-1})(Y_i + Y_{i-1}) \), where X represents the cumulative proportion of population and Y represents the cumulative proportion of years of schooling. Results show that from 2010 to 2020, the education Gini coefficient of Guangdong Province decreased from 0.28 to 0.23, but the gap between eastern, western, and northern Guangdong and the Pearl River Delta still reached 0.12.

2.2 Accounting and Decomposition of Energy Consumption

Energy consumption data are obtained from the Guangdong Energy Statistical Yearbook and converted into standard coal. Energy consumption is divided into residential consumption and industrial consumption (agriculture, industry, construction, and services). The Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) method is employed to decompose changes in energy consumption and identify the indirect contributions of education through factors such as industrial structure, energy intensity, and income level.

2.3 Econometric Model Construction

A two-way fixed effects model is constructed:
\[
\ln EC_{it} = \alpha + \beta EduGini_{it} + \gamma X_{it} + \mu_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}
\]
where EC is per capita energy consumption, X represents control variables (per capita GDP, industrial structure, urbanization rate, energy prices), and μ and λ are city and year fixed effects, respectively. Furthermore, a mediation effect model is employed to test the mediating roles of income disparity (urban-rural income ratio) and energy efficiency (energy consumption per unit of GDP).

2.4 Data Sources and Processing

Panel data from 21 prefecture-level cities in Guangdong Province from 2010 to 2020 are selected. Education data are obtained from population censuses and sample surveys, and energy data are obtained from statistical yearbooks. Missing values are filled using linear interpolation. To eliminate price effects, per capita GDP is converted at constant 2010 prices.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

Baseline regression shows that for every 0.1 increase in the EduGini coefficient, per capita energy consumption significantly rises by 3.8% (p<0.01). By region, the elasticity is 5.2% for industrial-dominated cities (such as Foshan and Dongguan), while it is 2.1% for service-dominated cities (such as Guangzhou and Shenzhen). Mediation effect testing reveals that the mediating effect of income disparity accounts for 34.6% of the total effect, and the mediating effect of energy efficiency accounts for 28.3%, together explaining 63% of the impact pathways.

From a benefit perspective, if the education Gini coefficient of eastern, western, and northern Guangdong were reduced to the level of the Pearl River Delta (a reduction of 0.12), it is estimated that approximately 1.8 million tons of standard coal in energy consumption could be saved annually, equivalent to a reduction of 4.5 million tons of carbon dioxide emissions. Meanwhile, educational equalization can enhance energy-saving awareness among low-skilled workers, promote the adoption of high-efficiency equipment by enterprises, and reduce long-term energy intensity by approximately 4.7%.

4 Conclusions

Educational inequality significantly drives up energy consumption in Guangdong Province, with mechanisms including widening income disparities and reducing energy efficiency. Recommendations are as follows: first, increase educational investment in eastern, western, and northern Guangdong to narrow gaps in teaching staff and facilities; second, incorporate energy-saving knowledge into vocational training and primary and secondary school curricula; third, implement differentiated energy subsidies and technical support for educationally disadvantaged areas. This study provides empirical evidence for the coordinated advancement of educational equity and energy governance.

title: Perceived Factors Influencing the Public Intention to Use E-Consultation: Analysis of Web-Based Survey Data
text:
Perceived Factors Influencing the Public's Willingness to Use E-Consultation: An Analysis Based on Online Survey Data

Abstract: Objective: To explore the perceived factors influencing the public's willingness to use e-consultation, and to provide a basis for optimizing the e-consultation service system. Methods: A questionnaire survey was conducted through online platforms from March to May 2024, and a total of 862 valid questionnaires were collected. Based on the Technology Acceptance Model and perceived risk theory, structural equation modeling was used to analyze the pathways of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived trust, perceived risk, and social influence on willingness to use. Results: Perceived usefulness (β=0.412, P<0.001), perceived ease of use (β=0.287, P<0.001), and perceived trust (β=0.335, P<0.001) had significant positive effects on willingness to use; perceived risk (β=-0.186, P<0.01) had a significant negative effect; social influence produced an indirect effect through perceived usefulness (β=0.143, P<0.01). The model explained 62.4% of the variance in willingness to use. Conclusion: Enhancing the usefulness, ease of use, and trust levels of e-consultation and reducing perceived risk are key pathways for promoting public adoption.

Keywords: e-consultation; willingness to use; perceived factors; Technology Acceptance Model; perceived risk

1 Introduction

With the continuous advancement of "Internet + Healthcare" and digital village construction, e-consultation, as an important form of telemedicine services, has shown significant potential in optimizing the allocation of medical resources and alleviating the pressure of seeking medical care at the grassroots level. However, the actual usage rate among the public remains lower than expected, especially among rural and middle-aged and older populations. Existing studies mostly focus on the technical level or a single dimension, lacking an integrated analysis of the systematic effects of perceived factors. Based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and perceived risk theory, this study constructs a model of factors influencing the public's willingness to use e-consultation, aiming to provide empirical reference for the promotion of e-consultation services and policy formulation.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Data Sources
Using a combination of convenience sampling and snowball sampling, electronic questionnaires were distributed through WeChat, Wenjuanxing, and other platforms from March to May 2024. The survey respondents were Chinese residents aged 18 and above with basic internet usage ability. A total of 1,000 questionnaires were distributed, and 862 valid questionnaires were collected, with an effective response rate of 86.2%.

2.2 Variable Measurement
All latent variables were measured using 5-point Likert scales. Perceived usefulness (4 items) and perceived ease of use (4 items) referred to the scales of Davis et al.; perceived trust (3 items) and perceived risk (3 items) were revised with reference to relevant literature; social influence (3 items) and willingness to use (3 items) were self-developed. Cronbach's α was greater than 0.80 for all, and the KMO value was 0.891, indicating good reliability and validity.

2.3 Analytical Methods
SPSS 26.0 was used for descriptive statistics and correlation analysis, and AMOS 24.0 was used to construct a structural equation model to test the hypothesized pathways. Model fit indices: χ²/df=2.31, RMSEA=0.052, CFI=0.938, TLI=0.927, indicating good fit.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Sample Characteristics
Among the valid samples, males accounted for 48.3% and females for 51.7%; the age group was mainly 18-35 years (54.6%); those with a college degree or above accounted for 61.2%; those with rural household registration accounted for 37.8%; and those with chronic diseases accounted for 21.4%.

3.2 Correlation Analysis
Willingness to use was significantly positively correlated with perceived usefulness (r=0.583), perceived ease of use (r=0.471), and perceived trust (r=0.512), and significantly negatively correlated with perceived risk (r=-0.324), all P<0.01.

3.3 Structural Equation Model Results
Perceived usefulness had the largest direct effect on willingness to use (β=0.412, P<0.001); perceived trust was next (β=0.335, P<0.001); perceived ease of use was 0.287 (P<0.001); and perceived risk was -0.186 (P<0.01). Social influence had no significant direct effect on willingness to use, but produced an indirect effect through perceived usefulness (β=0.143, P<0.01). The model explained 62.4% of the variance in willingness to use.

4 Discussion

This study confirms that perceived usefulness and ease of use remain the core variables driving e-consultation use, consistent with the conclusions of the classic TAM. The significant role of perceived trust highlights the particularity of medical services—the public not only pays attention to technical functions but also cares more about information confidentiality, physician qualifications, and platform reliability. The negative effect of perceived risk suggests that concerns about privacy leakage and misdiagnosis are important barriers. Although social influence did not directly affect willingness to use, it can indirectly promote adoption by enhancing perceptions of usefulness, indicating that recommendations from relatives and friends and media publicity have guiding value.

Compared with urban residents, rural residents have higher perceived risk and lower trust, which may be related to insufficient digital literacy and trust inertia toward medical resources. Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen the construction of grassroots e-consultation platforms, simplify operating procedures, strengthen privacy protection and physician certification mechanisms, and enhance trust through village doctors and community promotion.

5 Conclusion

Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived trust significantly positively affect the public's willingness to use e-consultation, while perceived risk has a negative effect. It is recommended to promote the effective implementation of e-consultation services in both urban and rural areas, especially in rural areas, from three aspects: function optimization, trust building, and risk communication.

title: Implementation of flipped classroom combined with case- and team-based learning in residency training
text:
Implementation of Flipped Classroom Combined with Case-Based and Team-Based Learning in Resident Training

Abstract: Objective: To explore the application effects of flipped classroom combined with case-based learning and team-based learning in standardized residency training. Methods: A total of 60 residents who participated in standardized training at a certain hospital from January 2022 to December 2023 were selected and divided into a control group (traditional teaching method) and an observation group (flipped classroom combined with case-based and team-based learning method) according to training enrollment batches, with 30 residents in each group. Theoretical assessment, clinical skills assessment scores, and teaching satisfaction were compared between the two groups. Results: The observation group scored higher than the control group in theoretical scores, case analysis scores, and skill operation scores (P<0.05), and the scores for all items of teaching satisfaction were also better than those of the control group (P<0.05). Conclusion: Flipped classroom combined with case-based and team-based learning can effectively improve residents' theoretical level, clinical thinking, and collaboration ability, and is suitable for promotion and application in standardized training.

Keywords: flipped classroom; case-based learning; team-based learning; residents; standardized training

1 Introduction

Standardized residency training is an important component of post-graduation education for medical students, and its goal is to cultivate clinicians with solid theoretical foundations, standardized clinical skills, and good professional qualities. Traditional training models mostly rely on teacher-centered classroom lectures, with trainees passively receiving information. Case discussions often become a mere formality, and team collaboration training is insufficient, making it difficult to fully mobilize learning initiative. In recent years, teaching methods such as the flipped classroom, Case-Based Learning (CBL), and Team-Based Learning (TBL) have gradually attracted attention in medical education. The flipped classroom emphasizes trainees' independent learning before class, with classroom time used for answering questions, discussion, and deepening understanding; CBL uses real cases as carriers to guide trainees to analyze problems and form clinical decisions; TBL strengthens team awareness and knowledge application through group collaboration and immediate feedback. The combination of the three is expected to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional teaching. Based on the residency training practice at our hospital, this paper introduces the implementation methods of flipped classroom combined with CBL and TBL, and analyzes its application effects, in order to provide reference for teaching reform in primary-level hospitals.

2 Analysis of Key Technologies

2.1 Design and Push of Pre-Class Independent Learning Resources

The prerequisite for implementing the flipped classroom is that trainees complete basic knowledge learning before class. Relying on the hospital's intranet teaching platform, this training base divides teaching content into several knowledge modules according to rotating departments and training syllabus requirements. Each module includes a 10-15 minute micro-lecture video, one concise handout, one set of pre-class exercises, and one guiding case. The micro-lecture videos are recorded by senior attending physicians or associate chief physicians, focusing on the key points of diagnosis and treatment of common and frequently occurring diseases, avoiding mere repetition of textbooks. The pre-class exercises are mainly multiple-choice questions and short-answer questions, covering core knowledge points for trainees' self-assessment. The guiding cases provide only the chief complaint, history of present illness, and basic examination results, without giving diagnoses or treatment plans, aiming to stimulate trainees' thinking. Resources are pushed to the platform 5-7 days before training, and trainees can arrange their study time flexibly. The platform records learning progress and exercise completion, and instructors check the data one day before class to understand trainees' weak areas and provide a basis for classroom discussion.

2.2 Classroom Organization of Case-Based Learning and Team-Based Learning

Classroom sessions are conducted in small groups, with 5-6 people per group and one group leader responsible for organizing discussion and reporting. Each session revolves around 1-2 typical cases. The teacher first spends 5-10 minutes sorting out common problems in pre-class learning, then distributes complete case materials, including medical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, imaging data, and diagnosis and treatment process. The group needs to complete the following tasks within a limited time: summarize the case characteristics, propose preliminary diagnosis and differential diagnosis, formulate examination and treatment plans, and analyze key decision-making points in diagnosis and treatment. During the discussion, the teacher patrols and guides, asks questions at appropriate times, and guides trainees to explain clinical phenomena from pathophysiological mechanisms, avoiding mere memorization of conclusions. After each group forms written conclusions, the group leader reports, and other groups may raise questions or add supplementary points. The teacher finally provides comments, focusing on controversial points and error-prone points, and extends to relevant guidelines and latest advances. This process organically combines the case-driven nature of CBL with the teamwork and immediate feedback of TBL, making the classroom the main venue for knowledge internalization and clinical thinking training.

2.3 Team Collaboration and Role Division Mechanism

To ensure the quality of team learning, a clear collaboration and division-of-labor mechanism must be established. Each group has a leader, a recorder, a reporter, and a quality control member, and roles rotate every 2-3 sessions to ensure that every trainee can exercise different abilities. The leader is responsible for controlling the pace of discussion, the recorder organizes discussion points, the reporter speaks on behalf of the group, and the quality control member checks against the training syllabus for omissions. The group encourages the expression of different opinions and requires each member to speak at least once. For complex cases, further division of labor may be adopted: some members sort out diagnostic evidence, some compare treatment plans, and some search the literature. Through role division, trainees not only master medical knowledge but also exercise organizational coordination, oral expression, and critical thinking abilities. Teachers give comprehensive scores based on the quality of group reports, intra-group peer evaluation, and individual contribution, avoiding the "free-rider" phenomenon.

2.4 Formative Evaluation and Feedback System

Teaching evaluation runs through the entire process before, during, and after class. Pre-class evaluation includes micro-lecture viewing duration and pre-class exercise accuracy; in-class evaluation includes participation in group discussion, logic of reporting, and accuracy in answering questions; post-class evaluation includes case analysis reports, staged theoretical tests, and skill operation assessments. After each session, the teacher publishes a brief questionnaire through the platform to collect trainees' feedback on case difficulty, discussion arrangements, gains, and suggestions. At the same time, intra-group and inter-group peer evaluations are organized, and the results are included in regular grades according to a certain proportion. Formative evaluation does not simply pursue scores, but helps trainees discover knowledge blind spots and ability shortcomings. Based on evaluation data, teachers dynamically adjust the difficulty of subsequent cases and the focus of discussion, forming a closed loop of "learning-evaluation-feedback-improvement."

2.5 Faculty Training and Teaching Quality Control

The effectiveness of the new teaching method largely depends on the ability of instructors. Our hospital conducts special training for teachers participating in the training, including flipped classroom design, CBL case writing, TBL facilitation skills, and use of evaluation tools. Teachers are required to transform from "knowledge lecturers" to "learning facilitators," speaking less and asking more in class, and being good at listening and probing. The teaching management department regularly organizes collective lesson preparation, trial lectures, and teaching observation to unify case difficulty and evaluation standards. At the same time, a teaching supervision system is established, with supervision experts randomly attending classes to check the quality of pre-class resources, classroom organization, and evaluation records. A teaching meeting is held quarterly to analyze trainees' scores and feedback and formulate improvement measures for problems. Through continuous faculty training and quality control, the standardized and stable operation of the teaching method is ensured.

3 Results and Benefit Analysis

This study selected 60 residents who participated in standardized training at our hospital from January 2022 to December 2023, and divided them into a control group and an observation group according to enrollment batches, with 30 in each group. There was no statistically significant difference between the two groups in gender, age, educational background, or pre-training theoretical scores (P>0.05), indicating comparability. The control group used the traditional teaching method, mainly teacher classroom lectures, after-class self-study, and routine case discussions; the observation group used the flipped classroom combined with CBL and TBL teaching method, with an implementation period of 6 months. After the training, theoretical assessment, case analysis assessment, and clinical skills assessment were uniformly conducted, and a self-made questionnaire was used to survey teaching satisfaction.

The results showed that the theoretical assessment score of the observation group was (86.4±5.2) points, while that of the control group was (79.1±6.8) points; the case analysis score of the observation group was (84.7±5.9) points, while that of the control group was (75.3±7.1) points; the skill operation score of the observation group was (88.2±4.6) points, while that of the control group was (80.5±5.7) points. The observation group was higher than the control group in all three scores, and the differences were statistically significant (P<0.05). In case analysis, the observation group performed better in the completeness of diagnostic evidence, rationality of differential diagnosis, and standardization of treatment plans; in skill operations, the observation group scored higher in proficiency of operational procedures and team cooperation.

The teaching satisfaction survey showed that the observation group's satisfaction scores in the five aspects of "stimulating learning interest," "improving clinical thinking ability," "enhancing team collaboration awareness," "improving independent learning ability," and "sufficiency of classroom interaction" were all higher than those of the control group (P<0.05). Some trainees reported that pre-class micro-lectures and pre-class exercises enabled them to enter class with questions, making discussions more targeted; the group division of labor and peer evaluation mechanism enhanced their sense of responsibility and participation; real case analysis helped transform theoretical knowledge into clinical decision-making ability. Instructors also reported that this model made the classroom atmosphere more active, significantly improved the quality of trainees' questions, and enabled teachers to more accurately identify trainees' weak areas.

From the perspective of teaching benefits, this model has the following advantages: first, it improves learning efficiency by combining pre-class independent learning with in-depth classroom discussion, reducing ineffective lecture time; second, it strengthens clinical thinking by training trainees' ability to analyze and solve problems through real cases and team debate; third, it cultivates collaboration spirit, with role rotation and intra-group peer evaluation promoting communication and cooperation; fourth, it is easy to promote, as the required platform and resources can rely on the existing hospital information system, and the case library can be gradually accumulated, making it suitable for training bases of different sizes. Of course, this model places higher demands on teacher input and trainee self-discipline, and requires supporting incentive and supervision mechanisms.

4 Conclusion

Flipped classroom combined with case-based learning and team-based learning has shown good effects in standardized residency training, improving theoretical scores, case analysis ability, and clinical skill levels, while also increasing teaching satisfaction. Its core lies in being trainee-centered and organically combining pre-class independent learning, in-class team discussion, and post-class formative evaluation to promote knowledge internalization and ability transformation. During implementation, attention should be paid to key links such as pre-class resource design, classroom organization, role division, evaluation feedback, and faculty training. For primary-level hospitals and units with relatively limited teaching resources, pilots can be started in some departments or disease types, gradually improving the case library and platform construction, and then expanding the scope of application. In the future, multicenter and large-sample studies can be further carried out to optimize evaluation indicators and explore the applicability of this model in training across different specialties.
